I swear though, I’d much sooner be in flats and dressed casual, than feelin’ sad in heels the whole night.      Oh definitely. I mean, I love lookin’ nice, but I’m not a fan of bein’ in hides, you know? I go out in boots most times, or just a pair of jeans and a top. Keeps it easy.      You’re all sane. I only wear heels when I’m goin' to a fancier bar, or when it’s one of them nights – Mate’s been askin’ me out, so I thought I’d spruce up somethin’.      Oh, well done! When’s that been, then?      Like Thursday. Just a simple dinner, innit? I dunno why I made it all awkward.      Don’t be like that! Lookin’ good is all in about how yer feel. Just don’t let the boots beat yer to it.      Yeah, it’s better to be comfortable and have a proper night out. I remember bein’ over dressed once and ended up sitnin’ on a park bench just to take me shoes off!      Hah! That’s a classic. I did that too, only I had to hide in the loos for twenty mins with my trainers on and them shoes tucked in me bag. Wasn’t a proper bash after that.      That goin’ on a night out is always a gamble, innit? First off yer dressed up, wanna make a good impression, then yer just tryin’ to keep up with the lads and gerts and manage yer drinkin’ hours!      Oh right, talk about the drinkin’ – anyone had a faight like that? Me and my missus got so done once we ended up in Cowcaddens, singin’ Right Said Fred in a taxi.      Aah, you’re no slouch! I’ve had some nights in them bars in Holbeck, night bazaars where we didn’t know each other, but now we're still great mates!

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses my name. I know it's nothing personal, but it feels like I've been forgotten. Otherwise, my day has been pretty standard.      It probably is quite aggravating, I mean, you go there almost every morning. Has it improved? I went to the dry cleaners today, and they completely mixed up my shirt with someone else's. Rather damaging to my professionalism.      They gave me a free latte, which is better than nothing. It was the same for me last week when they called me 'Emma' again. Not the end of the world.      What I found fascinating was thinking about attending an imaginary party, like during the Renaissance or something eccentric like that. I suppose you'd get dressed up and pretend for a bit. I think it could be a rather intriguing experience, breaking free from the mundane for a night.      That actually sounds like fun. Imagine, you and I in hides, debating the merits of the qwen. One could pretend to be a scholar and engage oneself in deep discussions. I rather enjoy the occasional bit of role-playing.      Haha, as long as we're not banished for heresy. Speaking of intriguing thoughts, have you ever considered whether you've found your soulmate, or if it's something we imagine and project onto others?      I've considered it, yes. I mean, is it even a real thing? Some people believe in it deeply, while others rush into partnerships looking for a quick fix. I’d rather weigh my options and take the time to find someone I genuinely get along with, rather than assume I’ve found 'the one' the first round.      I understand precisely what you mean. Going into relationships with too many ideals can lead to unmet expectations. I do think, however, that the emotional bond that certain people can create is something exceptional and worth recognizing.      Do you think there’s a way you can scientifically study or calculate who the perfect partner for you could be? With all our data and algorithms now, I feel like one could do such a thing.      Perhaps with enough data! But would the algorithm go so far as to predict if you'd cook dinner or at least pretend to? I think not. Some things remain beyond the reach of even the mightiest of computers.      There's something reassuring about that, oddly enough.

Rather annoying the new tax rules, isn't it? Small business is getting more squeezed by the week. Mind you, I've been focusing on knitting this week more than work! Got a new pattern for a scarf that is rather complicated. You wouldn’t believe the kind of things people expect now when it comes to product descriptions—mind if I mention it?      Oh, tax rules— ugh ! I’ve only had to deal with that side from my job, so I can't really speak from experience. But as a civil servant, I occasionally handle small business queries when they come in. You know what I find ironic is that even knitting patterns now have to be labeled in the EU supply chain guidlines? It’s like the craziest bit of red tape I’ve heard in years. And I’m not the only one upset, I assure you.      Honestly, it’s a mess for everyone. I've been trying to sort this out for my staff for the HR team. It’s not just tax but also the cultural differences we have to consider. One of my employees from Northern Ireland was shocked when I told her we can’t just take occasional attendance shortfalls quite as casually as some might in the South. Small businesses might not have the same kind of regulatory cushion as a larger employer like us. And don’t even get me started on trying to explain air conditioning to some of the older clients.      It’s all very trying. I understand the need for consistency, though, even if it feels someone somewhere in Whitehall must be making a joke about a knitting shop needing customs declarations. You’d think something as simple as a scarf shouldn’t require being split into 12 different product codes. Still, at least I’m not seeing any violence in society round here—except when I drop a fifth stitch in what should be a simple row. Not that I’d know much about guns, but I imagine those things are  very  hard to drop!      Well, I have no idea about guns either, but I do know about tombstones. My sister just had a baby, so while visiting the graveyard over the weekend to lay a rose, I noticed people leave a little teddy sometimes. It’s quite touching. Reminds you that even around death, there’s room for humanity.

Rather annoying this new tax thing eh? You know, me an’ the flatmates 'ave ‘ad to up our rent cos the landlord’s passed on more costs. I can barely cover my bills as it is.      No, I mean—get in, like—it’s mental. Got eenough to sort out with rent in Londinium as it is. My flat's in Walthamstow but I wouldn't call it central. Proper far, honestly. And since I started at uni, ain't got a clue how to stretch the cash. Didn’t even want to go out last weekend—we just like, sat in.      Oh no! I'm still in my home in Norfolk and My parents are paying for my halls-place though. I’m not sure how I’d do it otherwise, honestly, cos I’ve not worked for ages. Living with uni friends is brilliant, but it costs breakfast, no doubt.      I used to live with me cousins and it was rough, you know? Cos they was working and I was nae, so I was like, the spareperson, taking their place up I mean. Felt a bit like a parasite early days. But since uni started, I got a little part-time job at a little café. It's okay, just cheeky ones, but it adds up, y'know?      It's brilliant you've got that. I've been trying to find a job, but they all want this work experience people already have and I don’t. I tried this shop near campus, but they said I had to be 21 and have a qualification—feeble if you ask me.      Yeah, I know what you mean. Employers always want this “practical experience” or whatever and you can't get that without a job. It's a classic loop. I do do a bit for cash—delivery stuff—but it’s like 50p a mile, to be accurate.      At least you're getting some pennies. My mate Casey’s got a bit of a player of a boyfriend now. He’s like a complete legend with the lassies and he’s got money from delivering something around town. But he's proper busy now goin' on pond life about football or whatever.      Oh, I see. He sounds like a bloke who’s already one step ahead. So are you planning to go to his match this weekend, then?      Nah, I’ve got a bit of a project this weekend anyway—ain't gonna bore you.

Rather annoying the queue at the supermarket, innit? Eh, least the food here in Istria is pally. That squid ink pasta was bobbins, eh?      Aye, it was right up there with the best I've tasted! Mind you, the queue was a fair een, but at least the weather's good for a bus ride if we need to get back.      I don’t knoaaaw, uncle Tim. The bus was a pain, like it broke down halfway. And me an’ my mates had a right laugh with the mopeds—we saw one crash near the prom!      That's not reassuring, Rob. On the other hand, you're still young enough to skive off sums and survive.      Oliver, leave the lad alone. A bit of moped adventure is all part of growing up. Just doesn’t bear thinking of when I used to push a pram around hospitals!      Oh, don’t bore us with that, grandma!      Naa, I mean, I listen—mom, I’m doing A-levels now and trying to keep off the internet as much as possible…      Well, don’t get too addicted to the books. I got a tattoo last semester, and no one said a word. You lot better not tell Gran.      Bless you, Aura! A tat? Are you in your right mind? That’s a lifetime thing.      Relax, it’s just a little serpent on my ankle. You can’t even see it under jeans. Besides, it looked good when we were about to fall off the boat the other day.      Ah yes, what chaos that was! The dogs got off-leash and nearly chased a student into the sea. My, my! Life’s certainly no less eventful than the office.      I’d say eventful is an understatement. Oliver, you miss your hospital days, but I’m just as grateful I’m not doing night shifts now!      More importantly, have we got a plan for tomorra? I heard there are some good hiking points nearby. I bet it’s better than another day of house-bound work.      Hmmm, maybe. But only if gran agrees to stop worrying about virtual facials and join us.      Oh pooh, I can manage a bit of walking—and I’ll talk to your aunt over Facetime when we get back! It’s a modern world; I need to keep up.      That's the spirit, Karen! Listen, we haven’t even discussed the main event—Aura, how's university?

Rather a grand trip we've had, innit? Brought back a stack of photos, they’re piling up on the table by the fire now.      Oh, do tell! Where did you fancy off to then? Was it that Cornish YHA like you two talked about? I saw the holidays on the telly one night and thought 'oh, that's dashing of you'!      That's exactly where we went! Oh, and what a trip! We did the 'Yorkshire in a Day' drive the previous week, but the Cornwall jaunt was... well, it had its ups and downs. Found a lovely little lighthouse, only got to see it from a distance, though. The weather played up!      I didn’t like the sea on that last day, not one bit! But then, I was far more interested in the wildlife. Fancied taking up volunteering again, so I asked in the YHA’s office about getting involved with local birdwatching or crab surveys. They said I could help out—set up tides, maybe tag some crabs—oh I don’t rightly know the details yet!      Blimey, that does sound fun! But I thought you didn’t like being near the water?      Well, mind you, it’s not exactly the deep sea! It’s more like wading at high tide, or picking up litter at low tide, they said. They wanted volunteers with an eye for detail. That rings my bell, mind you.      Just the sort of adventure I’d imagine you being suited for! I was more taken in by the cycle race we about missed. Someone told us it was a mammoth 200 miles from Exeter to Plymouth—that kind of thing appeals to you younger ones, no doubt.      Well, for me, it’s less about cycling and more about the people and experiences. I remember my children told me stories about their school field trips to Cornwall. I always thought I’d stick to my own backyard and never leave!      And what of your new role with the childminding? Still no grand plans beyond delivering the odd cake or helping feed the strays in the street?      Well, I did think about getting active in the community, but I’ve been a bit busy learning to manage your holiday photographs! So many red skies, so many crabs and one very tired-looking tea shop cat.      Tell me about the ‘cycle race’ again—was it a charity one?

Rather skip the chips an’ go for the jacket potato, innit? That’d fill us up mair than proper, an’ we’d save the cash for the cake!      Nah, I’m tellin’ you, the chips are what it’s all about. Ain’t proper without een! I went there last week an’ they’re thick an’ crispy—still hot even when you get them. A lot better than me tupper from last night, I tell ya.      Honestly, you two are like kids. We could do a compromise. Let’s go for meatballs, share a couple of sides, and then grab a slice each. I’ve only got a few hours before my MySpace update, an’ I’m not left hungry.      That sounds reasonable. But I’m sayin’ the jacket potato—nutritious an’ all that!      Look, I’d say a bit o’ emotional support’s more important than what we eat, to be truthful. I mean, why did she end it like that? Just tellin’ me we’d listen to the occasional r&b song was rude innit? I dunno, maybe I should’ve known…      Oh, Josh, you really shouldn’t have told her you fancied Rihanna, least not because you thought she wanted to imagine a new dance move! You know what? Maybe trying to win her back with a proper mexican meal and some smooth talkin’ might work. Let’s talk about it after dinner.      Yeah, something’d better have gone right with my date last weekend. Can’t believe I hadn’t prepared for the most obvious question—‘so what do you do?’ I ended up blinking at this fella for a good minute—he thought I was drunk!      You sound like my stepdad. Had ‘em all stumped once at the pub. Said he was a ‘cook’—it took forever for any ‘nother to get it was a ‘cookery demonstrator’ in the market!      Websites and waitin’ lunches—both new spots? Well, I say grab our food, set the table, and shoot it like a proper dinner party. Let's really get deep into matters of the heart. And so, the friends settled in for a hearty meal and a further exploration of love, life, and the occasional funny mishaps that made it all memorable and ultimately quite delicious. As hours passed, laughter and bellyfuls sufficed, and plans for further adventurers—both emotional and culinary—began to take form, all over the course of a simple, shared dinner.

I can't believe you've just got back from Barcelona and didn't text me one photo! What were you thinking?! Oh, I’m so sorry, I had no signal most of the time and I was trying to keep my battery alive for the Barcelona-BLACKPINK reunion night we had on Saturday. Oh, really?! I missed it. I wanted to come with you! I know! Next time, promise me you'll tag along. It’s supposed to be one of the best clubs in the city. We literally saw the full lineup. Okay, I won’t forget that. Now, tell me everything, right from the start. Did you try the tapas? I’m still dreaming about the one you brought home last time – the one with the pastry and oregano? Yes, definitely the tapas! And breakfast, and whatever that late-night jamón with a twist in this basque bar. Honestly, I thought I ate the whole city. Also, the escalivada was divine—charred vegetables, you know? I can never get the seasoning right at home. Do tell me, what else did you do? Well, first of all, we hiked up Montjuïc Hill at sunrise and saw the Magic Fountain show. Then the rest of the weekend was just wanderlust through the Gothic Quarter and some shopping in El Born. And, of course, a spontaneous visit to one of those little sidestreet bars where they just handed out sourdough with nutella—surreal. Okay, I need more details on the sourdough and about how you afforded any of this! I know your mental health nursing job isn't exactly a holiday fund giveaway! I shared everything with Roomie! She handled the bills and, honestly, she’s the reason I even went. Said it was 'soul-saving expenditure'. I'm still recovering from all the happiness, I swear. Impressive. As for me, I just binge-watched every space-themed documentary on Netflix and made five batches of mismatched pasta sauce. My parents called asking if I’ve ‘given up on the notion of plans altogether.’ Don’t give up so soon! You’re coming to Paris with me next weekend. I’ve got an early morning ferry from Dover and you’ll be pestering me for pastries and champagne by 10 am. True to your word? I have a cab booked at 9 o’clock. I’m not entirely sure if I'm going for the pastries or to finally meet my Parisian crush, though.

I must say, the sea here is absolutely magical at this hour. A bit chilly for a dip, but the coffee’s hot and the view is dreamy. How often do you take these Sunday mornings where you are? Honestly, not as often as I should. Between the two startups I’m running, and my passive investments, weekends are usually either meetings or ticking off tasks. But today? This is a treat. What about you? Pretty much the same, really. I teach English to a mix of adults and older teens. Funny you called it passive investments—it's a bit like my weekend plans. Passive. mostly just reading and enjoying a quiet cuppa. Though I have to admit, I’m jealous of your schedule. I love my job, but school holidays and evenings spent planning lessons for the week can feel a bit all-consuming. I get that. Starting something from scratch doesn’t come without its late nights and coffee-stained spreadsheets. But the upside is the autonomy. No one telling me when I can’t have the day off, or that I need to do ten minutes of reading comprehension practice with teenagers. I mean, don’t get me wrong, your job sounds incredibly rewarding. Have you always worked in education? Yes, actually. I studied literature at uni, then got a postgrad in teaching because I thought if I was going to work with words, I might as well help people get the most out of them. Though if I’m being honest, someone once asked me to teach summer school in a different country and I thought I’d do one year and never come back. But then I fell in love with the structure and the feedback loops in teaching. You know, about how you see your students grow. That’s an inspiring thought. I think that kind of daily growth is why I enjoy building things. There's a certain kind of joy in seeing someone else use something you created. Though I’ll be the first to say, I don’t always get it right. I once tried to start an app for waiting times at coffee shops. It didn’t take off. Let’s just say, people were either not interested in waiting better or just happened to be very loyal to their usual barista. That’s classic go-to-market myopia! I see it a lot in my classes—students think their topics are fascinating, but if the audience isn’t interested, what your idea is might matter less than how you reach them.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? Our new housemate. I mean, it's not like 'e's got to be 'ere all the time, but it's like 'e's always where we are. I don’t mind sharing t'house, but sometimes it's a bit much.      Yeah, I 'ave noticed it as well. I mean, not all the time, but you’ve only just started to get t'hang o’ it. Still, I suppose we’ll get used to it. 'E was me mate from uni, so when 'e said 'e needed somewhere... I thought it'd be fine.      I know, and I do like 'im well 'nough, I suppose. It's just... 'e's a bit messy, innit? It's like one day after another and 'e's still in 'is uni mess mode. And breakfast, oh yeah, 'e loves t'make toast in his socks. It’s ever so bloody messy, Ken.      Oh, I 'eard that one. My mate told me, and I was thinking I should sort 'im out as well. But I dunno, maybe give 'im time? I reckon 'e'll get it out of 'is system.      I 'ope so, because if 'e doesn't sort hisself out soon, I'll be the one who ends up cleaning up after 'im. And I dunno 'bout you, but I'm also paying rent. I don’t want to be looking after a grown man like 'e's a toddler.      That’s fair 'nough, love. We could do with a bit of a talk, just the two of us, maybe have a chat with 'im and make it clear that we all need a bit of space. No one's to treat the house like their 'enity.      Yeah, that's probably for t'te best. But bloody give me time to grow a liver for it. I'm still not too sure about 'aving that conversation. Doesn't mean to ignore 'im, I s'pose, but I do need boundaries.      Course, course. I 'ave no go at you on that. I'll talk to 'im first, maybe get 'im in on that. See if he's bloomin’ aware what your feelings are. If I have to, I’ll let 'im 'ave it.      That's a relief, love. Thank you. I mean, I trust 'e's a good bloke and all that, but if 'e doesn't get it together, I'm always 'ere, and you're working.

Rather a lot to carry, eh, love? That supermarket do be a bit of a trek when yer gettin’ on a bit. Hope you didn’t run into too many stairs on the way in.      Not at all, dear. I managed fine. Just had a quick lie down when I got in. You’d think shopping with an older body would be exhausting, wouldn’t you? But I reckon I cope all right. Got the best trolley, didn’t I? The one with the squeaky wheel. Knows how to draw the eye when you chase it halfway round.      Ha, well, if you can still charm a trolley round the shop, you can charm the lot of 'em round the town. Still, best get these put away before the weather takes a turn for the worse. Looks like rain comin’ in off the east, if you ask me. Got a bit of a damp bone in me this mornin’, and I always listen to me leg when it goes all arthritic on me.      You worry too much about the weather, you know that? I say, let it rain if it wants to. We still got the kettle on, didn’t we? Make a nice little pot of tea while we unpack all this. I picked up some of those custard creams you like and, lucky for us, the baker had a fresh batch of fruit loaf.      Aye, that’s the way. Tea and cake in this damp old house. Sounds like the recipe for a man a bit past his best to doze out in an armchair with a cat on his lap and tea gone cold.      Don’t talk like that, old man. You’re not quite the touchpaper yet. I had a chat with old Mrs. Peabody at the store. She’s still cruel about the snow in January. Says, ‘It put the lot of us out for six months, did that lot.’ Still, she brought round a few fresh currants last week.      Aye, I hope you didn’t overstep on me account. Her bark’s worse 'an a Grimsby fog in winter, but she’s got a heart in there somewhere.      Don’t go wasting your sympathy on her if she don’t want none. Let’s just line the fruit loaf with some of these currants and make something worth eating.      Aye, and let’s see if we can’t start with the custard creams first.

Rather chilly this mornin', innit? Thought me ‘n the missus’d pop ‘round first thing wi’ a spot o’ tea an’ a few scones, sure we’d best get this flat sorted before the rest o’ the mob drift in wi’ their muddy boots an’ muddy ideas een!      Thanks, Nan. I reckon me mam's gone afta clean a clean one ‘gain, but I'll best go see. She was bletherin’ earlier about dumpin’ the old fridge or sommat. Slightly odd for a woman wi’ a PhD in domestic order, but hey, even examiners made mistakes.      That fridge was me and Arthur’s best friend when we were first settled ‘ere. I remember when we moved in wi’ the kids, Arthur nearly pickled the whole house when he tried to plug in the toaster an’ forget the lead. Funnily enough, I found it still plugged into the wall at the end o’ the 80s. Still working.      Aye, I was there, Florence—personally I think it takes skill to short-circuit a kitchen to the sound of Duran Duran. Reminds me… I reckon the missus is been stashin’ her cuppa spoons in the sock draw again. Always blames me because I once put a pair of knickers in the fruit bowl by accident. Silly old fool.      Oh, don’t give someone a complex. But anyway, while you two are reminiscing, let’s not forget the main reason we’re all here: the renovation. I’ve got plans for the garden wall, William, and it involves a about forty square feet of concrete. You’re the reliable one, right? Gonna help Nancy lift things and not fall over?      Aye, I can help. My granddad taught me how to lay bricks. Though I might not be quite up to 1982 standards. ‘Course I’ll help, Nan. I just hope Arty’s not about to resurrect that mysterious recipe for "nuclear" stew.      Oh, that was a classic. Me knees still remember that one. Said it was a secret wartime recipe or goenvironmental sabotage. Turns out it was just a carrot cake recipe wi’ a spoon of baking soda mixed in wi’ a spoon of something else.      That was  me  on the stairs, mindin’ me own business. Just like your granddad to come back in from ‘the plot’ with a green face an’ a mutter o’ “second world war tastes better!”      Listen, laughs and memories are fine, but we’ve got to keep the ball rollin’.

I can't believe we've got to wait四十分钟for this appointment. I was just looking at that new health supplement advert on my phone—some of them make yer think yer gonna need an ambulance after takin’ 'em. Nah, I'd rather just stick to good old protein powder. Got eeny fitness plan, yeah? Or are you all just sitting on yer arses all day like most a' us? Cheers for the support, mate. Oh, and I   have   got a fitness tracker now. My step count for yesterday hit 10K. Still don't know why I bothered. I've been into technology lately. Just got myself a new smartwatch like that one you're talking about, Speaker_3. The one that tracks yer heartrate an' whatnot. Aye? Is it worth it, then? Mee ma says I'm wastin’ me money on all this fancy stuff in me early twenties, an' I tell 'er, "Mum, this is the future." I'd rather spend the money on some sturdy trainers—nothing fancy, just puts your feet in it and you're good to go. Speaking of trainers, I got this limited edition pair from London last week. My nan nearly had a heart attack, she was so proud. Yeah, an' I reckon yer nan's phone’s probably runnin’ on a Windows 98 and proud of it. Haha, my gran's still got one o' them Nokia bricks in the house, just in case the world ends and she needs to make a call. Not a bad idea, really. I mean, all the touchscreens crash, this thing vibes and a picture of your fails. I've got it on my student budget to go to uni, but for trainers and tech, it’s like trying to live on a bird’s meagre. Any chance any of you can lend me tenner? I could lend you my good side and that’ll get you out of trouble. Grapes of wrath. Now, whilst we're stuck here, does anyone fancy watching telly on the tablet? There's that new series everybody's talking about. Nah, I just started reading this book I got from the boxset—educational, your lot. It's all aboot the history of fitness and how humans went from walking hours to sitting on social media. Sounds like a metaphor for our lives right now, innit? You lot are joking. Books? My brain needs more CowBell, less CBeebies.

Right, I’m just scribbling down what we need for tomorrow’s shop. We need bread, pints of milk, some apples—oh, and more anti-itch cream, probably. That mosquito or whatever it was finally left Tom alone last night, but now it looks like it’s back for a second bite!      Aye, I know what you mean. Tom’s been scratching like a rabbit with a sore paw! I tried putting calendula cream on it last night, but it’s still red. We might need sommat stronger than what we’ve got, or maybe even a local antihistamine.      Can I get some anti-itch sweets? My teacher gave me a sweet once when I got stung by a bee. It helped me calm down and the itching went away.      Oh, you had an allergic reaction to a bee sting once, didn’t you Tom? I remember Mum taking you to the A&E at the old hospital. Proper white as a ghost you were for a few hours.      Don’t forget, you were the one who ran into the ant hill in the garden a week before and got like twenty stings!      That was  you , not me! I only had the one – Mate, I got the sting, and I had to go to the nurse. You lot nearly died of laughing when I was sitting there with the ant one!      Now, now. Let’s focus. If the anti-itch stuff doesn’t work, we can always buy some calamine or see about a specialist cream. It’s not uncommon for bites to flare up in the evenings when it’s about forty degrees in the house.      Oh, mind you don’t say sommat like that in front of the kids or they'll start unzipping all their coats and sticking ‘em on the fire!      Hah! Come on, the only thing I was thinking about was the windows. Proper breeding ground for little blighters out there, with all the light on.      I told you the wasps are back again! We should get sommat proper, like a fly trap or a buzzing light to kill the bad ones. They’ve already taken our tomatoes again – I think one even tried to fly into my face when I was eating breakfast earlier!      We could try citronella candles again, like last year. Put those by the window and the wasps stayed away.      That’s not a bad idea.

I can't believe today's PE class. Mr. Sparks made us do laps around the entire field like it was a competition or something! And no one was even warmed up properly! Honestly, I think he just watched too much of those physics YouTubers and got carried away thinking he can apply it to humans too! Ugh, I was so done within the first five minutes! And don’t even get me started on how he yelled at Liam because he tripped over a puddle. It wasn’t like it was dry! Honestly, I don’t get how people even want to be teachers. You'd think he’d remember what it's like to be a teenager. Ugh, I know right? My science teacher, Miss Farrell, is so much better. She’s more laid back and actually tries to make the lessons cool. She even lets us talk to each other for group work and sometimes shows us videos about famous scientists or random experiments. Yeah, she sounds cool. I haven’t had her yet, though. All the teachers we've had since we moved to Linton are just, like, copying from some outdated system. I swear, even the way they teach math is so dry, it could put anyone to sleep—except maybe for our geography teacher, Mr. Norris. He’s actually funny. I often watch his Instagram stories, because they’re like mini lectures with memes. Oh my gosh, I've seen one of his videos! He shows those random facts about countries and people and dress-up photos with his students. Like the one where he dressed as an ancient Egyptian pharaoh and wore a cartoon headscarf. Anyway, at least someone’s trying to make school fun! I know! And you can just tell the teachers who are “mainstream” versus ones who are part of that new school influencer culture. The problem is, I don’t think all of them do it well. Some are just trying too hard to be relatable without actually caring. It's exhausting being the audience. I miss when school was just school. Before Instagram and YouTube. Now every teacher has to be this persona online, and the whole experience feels like being in the simulation. Even our school trips are now shootable adventures! I mean, can go-karting in Cambridge be more cringey than our preps posters on the walls?

I can't believe I've got a cold again. I swear I've caught one every other week since moving to Cambridge. You'd think I'd be used to the weather by now. Aw, that's not fair. You’ve been working nonstop at the uni. And it was freezing when I saw you at the store last week with that coat open. Take it easy for a day or two. Yeah, I tried! I went to that new café on the High Street, you know the one with the photographer guy—Lloyd Grossman—and his cameras? He made me feel like a part of a reality TV show when I ordered a sandwich. Oh, yeah, that one’s popular. I’ve heard his system uses body language recognition to customise the menu for customers. A bit invasive for my taste, but he’s got an interesting background in AI and psychology. Honestly? I just felt awkward after I accidentally nodded at his camera. I looked like I was agreeing to something I didn’t even know about. I know what you mean. I’d rather just be written off as a nervous customer than to be experimented on by tech startups with fancy algorithms. You'd think in a town like Cambridge we'd at least be warned when newfangled stuff like that is being trialled. Anyway, enough about him. I got food poisoning after that café trip too. Twice in two days? What's up with that? Maybe the system not only recognises body language but oddly arranges the menu? Just saying. I've heard the admin team at the hospital is using body language recognition in waiting rooms now to prioritise people who seem worse off. Oh, is that part of a new vaccination campaign? I know there are some new immunisation guidelines out. Not quite. That hospital stuff is for triage. They’re saying it saves time and helps sort the most urgent cases. But as scientists, we both know accurate triage relies on more than just superficial cues. True. But if people with lunches and a new AI watching them aren't enough, let’s at least remember to sanitise our hands. I swear, the more goings-on with tech and health, the more I feel like I should just line my home with hand sanitisers. Speak for yourself. I still believe in the flu jab, but kudos to you for making those doctors and PhDs like me think twice about how we approach health and surveillance in one breath.

Rather annoying this gridlock at the shopping centre. I couldn't get the sausages for the evening meal.      Oh, I’m so sorry to hear that. I think I might have been in the queue at the butcher’s shop during the same time. It was a madhouse in there.      I do hope you didn’t miss out on anything important. It seems most shops are extremely busy these days. I saw that too at the post office; it was a terribly long queue.      Yes, the modern demand for convenience services can be rather overwhelming. I remember my youth, when one could mostly just plan and go without such considerations.      On the other hand, our time here together has proven to be quite valuable. I just posted a picture from the game on Facebook, and it already has comments from relatives.      That’s very nice of you, dear. You always know how to keep our family in touch across the generations. I looked at that new music magazine the other day and was thinking of adding it to the family discussion over the weekend, maybe we can choose a theme for next week’s family dinner.      It sounds like an engaging idea. It might be a fun way to keep our little family discussions going. I remember my days as a school master, curriculum and discussions were the core of learning.      Indeed, as a headmistress myself, I found that a good discussion can teach and unite in equal measure. Oh, and also, I found a rather interesting word to use in our Scrabble game: ‘quizzed’.      What a great addition! We can continue learning and playing in about forty minutes. That gives us time to cook the sausages I had meant to buy. Maybe we could also talk about that cooking class I read about online.      That does sound like a good plan. To play while we are preparing the meal and have open discussions as it is a time when all can contribute and relish the fruits of our labour. After all, it is as much about being together as it is about playing the game. I think it is a small price to pay for the delays we sometimes face.      I couldn’t agree more. The conversations we share are sometimes more precious than the items we go out to purchase, no matter how essential.      A fine sentiment from a woman with such rich experience in education and family life.

Rather a lot of memories floating about today, isn’t it? I was just watching the lads string up those banners and I thought to myself—how times have changed since we used to schlep over to Hanover for the trade fair.      Aye, things were a mite different back then. Still, I’ll say one thing—I’ll never forget the first time I helped demo a printing press that I had a hand in designing. Proper show-stopper. Oh, and the way some of the German salesmen would dance around me when I called the booth “straightforward,” well, it was a language lesson every day.      That’s the very word they use the wrong way around, isn’t it? When I was running the gallery, I had an awful time with some of these types in the printing trade. They’d say,  “Oh yes, very straightforward, no problems,”  just before creating enough complications for a dozen manuals.      You’re not wrong. And the exhibitions themselves? Ah, now that was something. The noise, the smells, the constant clatter of prototypes and presses going flat as if they were supplying the whole of Germany with posters in an hour. But I suppose we did it then. Tell me, what was the most important thing you learned along the way?      Let me think… It wasn’t just the machinery, it was the people. You don’t get anywhere in this business unless you can talk to someone for ten minutes and not mention business a single time. I remember a salesman—looked like he hadn’t slept in weeks and still poured his heart out about  Speer’s latest builds . I about cried I laughed.      Ha! We were all looking for a purpose, weren’t we? I suppose you and I are proof it does pay off in the end. Running a business like that, facing down clients who thought they knew more than you? Well, the blood, sweat, and all that.      You said it. We had to be as clever as our machines. And if you couldn’t outwit a client or a sales rep, well, you were stuck for good. Mind you, it was a man’s game back in the day. But I had my breaks, thank you. Gave me a head start when I opened up the gallery, I can tell you.      That you did. And I suppose we’re both proof that those breaks are never just handed over.

Rather annoying when the satnav goin’ mental, ain't it?      Oh aye, an' sometimes them local roads owtta be mucked about with. A proper muddle it were.      D’ya think we'll ever get t’university een time if we keep losin'ourselves?      Proper important t’learn how t’navigate by self, love. Proper world-wise, that is. Philosophy, innit?      Nah, I mean like the English subj, the language coursework. You gotta compare like, say, Shakespeare t' modern texts. Bit heavy sometimes.      Ah right, My grammar still proper dodgy, but I got good sense. Ten o'clock, proper junction, D’you see it?      It's alright, uni doesn't bother me. I wanna do English lit proper. Maybe like... study word origins and stuff, you know, like etymology, or history of the language?      Aye, clever lass. Bet you’d listen t’changing words in different counties. Here in Manchester, we say “bairn” fer child, but down South it’s “baby” all the way.      Anyroad, down in Cornwall, they'll say “tide” somethin’ different again. Proper interesting, innit?      Yeah, I reckon Cornish English must be like its own thing. Ever been?      Oh yeah, had a cousin near St. Ives. Bit hillier than I expected!      I about daft question—why does "Cornwall" spell different to “Cornish”? I thought they’d be same.      Good question. Probably Norman French influence. My grandma ‘ud say the language always borrowin’ bits here an’ there. Words come an’ go like a storm ‘at times.      You ever see a lightning crackle clear as day? Strikes me how a word like "lightning" can survive centuries whippin’ through the air.      Pretty wild. I sometimes get spooked by thunder, but it's more of a buzz for me now—like watching how language works in between.      By the way, da you like quinoa? I bought a bag, and it smells weirder than pig slop.      Aw lass, quinoa pronounces “keen-wah,” and the taste? Nah, I prefer a buttery saveloy. Right, we passing a service station, so you want a cuppa?      Aye, before it goes, I'm pickin’ up some apples an' last-minute supplies for university.      And while you're at it, think ’bout nex’ time ya can go, love.      Like a farmer’s market visit? If you like, we can sketch out a route. Maybe do a bike ride down their lanes?      Fine with me. A bit of fresh air, a quieter road, more of a blinkin' day than this.

Rather than chuck a bar of chocolate in the bin, I thought we could have it for dessert.      Never mind me, I’m more than happy! I haven’t had a proper meal since I moved out. Chances are the telly would've picked up on the dinner was on. I saw the place, I don’t think they got handed over yet.      I reckon that Aneurin would love that too. His top man, but don’t get me started on it. We’ve been through that before and he never shuts up about the days he was a meat fetcher.      Aneurin is the real deal, always up for something like that.      So, what’s the deal with the dinner? I reckon you're stealing it from the sad bloke upstairs?      Nah, forget it. I just thought we could do this together. Maybe a bit of rep at his place.      We could always bring the goods. I'm not too precious about it. Just tell him we're going in.      Right, as long as you don't mind, I fancy a go on something else. I've got rhythm in me from the way I bounce at the table.      Let's just get this sorted. Let me know if you're bringing any mortal sin with you. I'll probably try to cook it.      As long as we get the recipe book from the shelves, I'll try to do the cooking.      What exactly is it you cook? I mean, your grandmother, or is it a family secret passed down?      She passed it on to me. I’ve only boiled anything once. I’m more of a plate handle.      My grandma had that little book. She always said if passed it down mulher. I reckon me granddad would've told any mate about it.      You mustn't stick too much salt in it. My Auntie once mentioned it nearly flipped the switch on the whole whack.      Still, I'll try not to kill it. That's the go. Unless I get it from your mum or wherever you got it.      I don’t think she’d let you near the kitchen after what you did with the toast.      That was a crime! I never had that much fun unless I had it in the oven overcooked.      I tell you, my cousin tried to make a custard cream and it looked like he accidentally mixed plaster in it.

Rather annoying driving instructor I've got. You know what they do—drill it in, drill it out... got to go round roundabouts the same way every time. Not like real life, where you’ve got to keep your eyes open and make the best call as you go.      Oh, I know exactly what you mean. I was helping a colleague out with some translations recently, and she mentioned that in Spain, when they teach driving, they focus a lot on defensive driving and adaptability, not just repetition. Interesting how different countries approach the same thing.      Still, I'd rather not crash into a lamppost because I forgot to check my mirrors, you know? You can't be too careful. Speaking of being careful, how's the teaching going? Still working with the same group?      I am, and to be honest, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. We’ve got this new student who’s taken up sports at the centre, and it's amazing how much energy that’s brought to the class. It’s inspiring, really. I do tell the others they need to get out more sometimes.      That is good grief. I’d love to get into some sport—it would probably help me stop getting out of breath after climbing the stairs at work. But with the long hours and the weekend shifts, there’s barely time to eat, let alone exercise.      I understand completely. When I first started, I worked in a school forty hours a week and collapsed every Sunday. Now I try to keep it to a reasonable pace and make the most of my weekends. I even manage to squeeze in a yoga class sometimes.      I daaaaaare you to try that round the area here. We’ve had so much rain recently, and the sports fields are all like muddy bogs. The only sport left in action is the squirrel that lives in the trellis out back. Jumps all over the place, man. I’d love to know where it goes.      You mustn’t knock the squirrel. Those little creatures are full of secrets and skills. And honestly, I think it takes more determination to survive the British weather than it does to get around with cars or play football.      You might well be right. If squirrels can manage, I reckon I can too. I might give the boxercise class a go at your leisure centre.

Rather annoying when the clock’s gone walkabout, isn’t it? I was just about ready with the first cup of the day, and now it’s gone past break time! Mind, I’ve got a proper pot made up. Not the instant stuff, I mean—proper Ceylon blend, slow brewed. Hasn’t got a drop of milk in it, but I reckon it’ll do as well as most. You’ve got a liking for that, haven’t you, Doris?      Oh, it’s just me and Bernard coming along for this one. Harold, don’t you think you’ve had enough to keep you going already? Last time I popped in, the floor was still wet where you managed to spill the turkey on Christmas Day! I swear, left to yourself you’d drink the lot and then try to ring the church bell!      Blimey, Doris, you’re not breakfast, you’re a bit of a scold! I only ever spill what’s properly spilled, and that’s on purpose, for the sake of the cats. Or at least I used to do, before I sold the place. Though I might take up bell ringing myself as a hobby. I’ve got a spare hand, what with the firm not needing me any more. Speaking of which—I’ve been thinking of doing something with that old box, turning it into a donation box for the local church. Now don’t laugh, Doris, but I rather fancy myself as a banner-maker too, and I might just chuck in a few plants on the side. Ever fancied having your own garden, Doris?      Don’t you start pulling her leg, Bernard—I’ve had enough of that nonsense when she nearly about blocked the main road with all those bunting and banners she had on the first day of business. At least he’s been to school and knows the difference between a proper letter and that lot he found in the dumpster. Still, it’s all passed me by. I just sit here with the kettle forever on and the newspaper folded three times.      Harold, don’t be such a grumpy old sprite. If he’s got a grand idea to keep the church from collapsing with his bell ringing, who are you to scoff? I’ve heard of people going all the way go Munchausen for a bit of recognition, but at least he’s just trying to do something decent.

Rather annoying when a new app takes up so much space, isn't it? I deleted it only to realize it got all my photos copied somehow. I’m so over tech these days.      You’re lucky. I can barely even read the terms and conditions for them. Honestly, I don’t care—I use my phone more for games than anything else. But if it starts crashing all the time, I hit delete instantly.      Honestly, I’m terrified of watching any horror films by myself. I had one last week where the sounds were so realistic, it genuinely gave me the shivers. I had to sleep with the TV on.      Oh, I only watch them with someone else. My friend and I have this annual marathon—it’s so much fun pretending to be brave while screaming at the screen! Always end up in a pile of blankets laughing afterward.      Do you ever see old friends these days? I’ve been a bit in my own world, thanks to work. I miss going to the pub and just chatting. Good old friends never let you down.      Yeah, we should really meet up soon. Like a week from now, maybe? We can take the kids to the park—it would be nice to get out of the house.      I’d love that! I still think it's important to support each other despite being busy. We did grow up through everything together, after all.      True! Now, food. Let’s talk about that. I made my mom's lasagna recipe last night. It was hotter than the oven it came out of! I still ate it all, though.      Sounds delicious. I’ve been trying to impress my girlfriend the past week by watching this cooking show and cooking what I see. Let’s just say… I burnt the chicken. She wasn’t impressed.      Oh no! What did you do? I did something similar and had to trash the whole meal. But she insisted we had a picnic in the garden anyway.      That sounds sweet. I’m always up for a picnic. Do you plan a lot of dates?      Not really—most of the time it's just spontaneous stuff. I think go with the flow usually works best.      True, but planning is also important, especially for holidays. We might need to finalize what we are doing for Christmas soon. I’m seriously thinking of heading to the coast—we could use some fresh air and not worry about anything for a week.

Rather annoying this, having to rely on public transport when you're used to driving. Mind you, it's not got the seats like they used to, has it?      Oh, I know what you mean. Not only that, the bus fairs have gone up yet again. I don’t een know if it’s wirth the bother some days. Still, better than not gettin’ anywhere at all.      That’s a bit much, Tim. If you’ve not worked a day in your life, how are you supposed to keep up with the costs of everything? I swear, these days, even a baked bean is made of money!      That’s the lot of us, I suppose. You rely too long on the state, you start takin' it for granted, and suddenly, there you are—faced with all the bills and no idea how to cover 'em.      Fair point, Hilda. Though at my age, the only place I really need to get to is the doctor and the shop, and that’s only when it doesn’t rain! Speaking of, I’ve got that check-up next week. The clinic's a bit off, so I might have to get a lift with neighbour Derek if I can’t get one of the taxi grants sorted.      Derek, that lovely lad? He’s the one who drives like a banshee, ain’t he? I’d sooner try catchin’ the 8:47 than ride with 'im!      Laughter, Alan, that's the worst you can do is have a good laugh. Mind you, I still miss the car. My pride and joy was a Ford Fiesta—tiny little thing but reliable as the day is long. I used to wheel it all around for the kids. Properly zipped up and down the High Street for years.      Aye, those were the days. I used to drive up to Norwich every weekend. Used to pass your house, Hilda, didn’t I?      Oh, you did. I remember being out with the grandkids and seeing you flying past in your banger like it was going out of fashion. I swear, you made a Jag feel slow!      Well, if you lot had your cars now, you wouldn’t be whingeing so much about the bloody buses!      Can you see me trying to get hold of a car these days? I'm down to broken toast and bellyfuls of tea, and I’ve got more chance of flying to Mars than fitting a deposit for a secondhand motor.

Rather annoying this new traffic system on the M6, isn't it? I was trying to get up to Manchester last weekend and it took ages. I’m more used to navigating Dublin's clogged streets than this!      Yes, the motorways are such a maze now. I was trying to get to an airport meeting last month and got completely turned around. Makes me miss the old days of working on oil field development plans, but that's in the past, I guess.      Honestly, it’s why we decided to buy a nicer car when we moved out of the city. More space for everything, especially with all these trips we’ve been planning. What's your plan now, Ma? Staying in the family house or looking at somewhere smaller?      Probably stay where I am for now. But I was thinking of downsizing after this winter. It was far harder than I anticipated dealing with the garden and stairs at this age. Not a bit like teaching at the school, where I was always on my feet anyway.      That’s something I struggle with too, Di, and being off work doesn’t really help. I did quite a bit of work back in the day, mostly as a technical esports specialist—very different from oil planning—but then all got put on hold after my back gave out.      It really is important to take the time to move carefully. I remember my dad saying something about spotting the signs early when I first started editorial work. Our jobs aren’t full-on manual, but sitting all day has a way of playing up.      Ah, well, the tea and the biscuits here at home are a godsend in moments like these. I do miss the old travel days though, standing the red eye to Dubai once or twice. The old adrenaline and the buzz of that place.      You sound like my stepdad. He had that same story about Bangkok. But I much prefer a quiet afternoon here at home to the chaos of a crowded airport. Speaking of, I tried to transcribe your story last time you told it about that time in Cork being chased out by a very assertive farmer with a pitchfork—was it last Autumn?      You mean with the errant sheep and the motor go-kart I tried to use as transport? That was one for the memory books.

Mum, I just wanted to say sorry again about what happened with your bike. I know it’s been pissing you off for ages. Have the police actually sorted it yet?      Thanks, love, it’s okay. I’ve just been fuming about it, honestly. It was my old uni bike and it’s been hanging around with me for years. But actually, yes — the coppers managed to recover it through Facebook. Turns out one of my old friends saw your bike being hauled into a place in Bexhill and was like, “Lizzie’s bike, isn’t that hers?” So they went to check it out.      Wait, Facebook? Of all places? That’s wild. My friend had her bike stolen too, and they put a post about it, but no one replied. It sounds silly, I know, but sometimes social media works in strange ways!      I know, right? I mean, I didn’t expect it at all, but it just goes to show, even if you don’t use it much, it can still help. I posted a few details on my page, just asking people to be on the lookout. Someone must’ve shared it further, and that’s how they found it. They’re giving it back first thing tomorrow.      Oh my gosh, no way! That’s so good! I wish my college experience was more like that. Honestly, half the time it’s just boring lectures and the toilets always out of order. How did you get on with yours?      Honestly, it was chaos — hotter than hell and I ate nothing but sandwiches and takeaway noodles. But I met some amazing people, and it all made me stronger. I wouldn’t trade it for the world. Although, I had to cycle 40 minutes every day because I was too poor to get a bus ticket, so I kind of wish I had your energy levels back then!      Hah! I could cycle 40 minutes any day, I love it. I just need a decent bike, which I obviously can't afford. But maybe I’ll get one once I've finished my GCSEs and start working part-time?      That’s a solid plan. I’ll lend you some goody money on the sly if you're lucky. But for now, just stick to your old bike. And maybe, while I’m getting mine back, we could go for a ride together?

Rather annoying when the train’s perpetually delayed, isn’t it? I was just trying to work out if it got us on time or not. Otherwise, we’d miss our tea by an hour.      Not to worry, the game’s as likely to throw things off timing-wise as real life! I always liked the idea of a board game that tried to simulate the chaos of actually making a train journey. A lot of fun!      No idea how they thought it would ever be accurate. We’ve had three different people.Fatalfanstay chase the same express and still end up on a frozen platform.      Well, it is the holidays, and Herford is nowhere near well-known for being a transport hub! The eccentricities of a small town! I’m half convinced the Dodsley-bound express is just a legend now.      Catsfield! Wait, does anyone actually know what this town’s like? I’m thinking a posh seaside spot, but we never get to find out. Always a mystery.      I do tell you—my nan used to say the Catsfield express was quite a gem to be on. It took twice as long, but they gave out mini shortbread. Absolutely divine little biscuits.      Oh, now I’m dreaming of shortbread on a train. I miss that sort of thing—homely bits and bobs. Like the tea we were planning to make, which never arrived because someone got stuck in Catton.      Catton’s a classic one—everyone’s always lost there. Or wants to pause and look at the view. I once counted six people who refused to move until they’d drawn a map of the field!      And I suppose you found out where it was in the end?      You’re all thinking of it wrong. I’ve always said the real charm of the game lies in creating your own tale. Last time, I insisted I was a disgraced pianist escaping Herford station. We had to rush as the conductor came to arrest me!      That was one of the more engaging stories. I far preferred it to the one with the dog that started a derailment. Mournfully faithful thing if you ask me.      I’ll stick with the food. Who remembers arranging the catering? I distinctly recall Speaker_1 saying something about making it special.      And so I did! Except, well, I expected it to be delivered over the platform.

Rather annoying that the beer’s all gone.      That’s it, is it? I suppose I should’ve stocked up before this marathon game of  Catan .      You were the one who said we’d finish in an hour.  Again.  We’ve been at it for nearly three, and we’re both twitching.      Sorry, sorry. I’ve only ever been halfway serious before. Why do you think I always suggest  Chess  instead?       Chess  is what you called when we were kids. You know I can’t abide it now.      All right, fair point. Still, I miss that everyone My parents still play it after tea. Fun for them, not for us, I think. You know, they’d probably say the same about us playing all evening with board games instead of working.      I think they’d say a bit more than that. Our planting schedule is in tatters, and Ruth’s already asked me twice why I’m still in my work trousers.      Oh, let them ask. It’s a beautiful summer evening, and the house is quiet. This is probably something we won't get again until December, buried under Christmas lights.      I agree, and I know they don’t really mind. They’re quite used to us by now. Silly really, how much we’ve stayed within the family orbit. Our parents’ house in Norfolk is practically our second base.      I do wonder what our friends from university would say now if they saw us—still drinking tea all day, eating too many scones, and arguing about board game strategies.      I imagine most of them are already wondering if we are still alive. I mean, it is a classic British domestic picture. My sister texted me the other day about how my flatmate is dating someone and all they do is go to parties.      That’s them for you. I don't know how they keep up that pace. But then again, you've always preferred a more sedate pace.      Sedate, yes. Productive, no. That's the go-to argument I get from Ruth. She does wonder how I manage to balance teaching and, I don’t know, randomly box sets or board games.      Well, I suppose we’re both postgrads now. We’ve broken into the higher professional life, right?      True. We've got the lectures, the salaries, and all that academic malarkey. But I still can’t help wondering, is it enough?

Rather annoying the new bins haven't arrived yet. I remember they said they'd be here by Tuesday. We're running out of space in the downstairs one already.      Yeah, I mean, it is a bit chaotic. I was trying to sort things at work, but the timing was pretty awful on their part. I've been keeping a few things aside just in case.      I've been through all this with moving before. Honestly, I'd send them a polite reminder. They always drop the ball somewhere when people are moving. You're never surprised when it happens.      That’s easy enough. I can write something. I've got the confirmation number still. You know, like everyone else, moving is madness at the best of times. It doesn't help if the usual systems are slow.      Fair enough. But to be honest, at least the fridge is here. I thought we'd need to borrow ice packs or something in the meantime. It’s the oversized white goods that always cause the most trouble.      Oh, I remember when we had to get the old one out—there I was in a land of cows with a hire van and no jack. Nothing like a bit of country chaos to warm up your blood, right?      Mate, I wouldn’t mind, but I barely remember how to use a screwdriver. Still don’t know how you all have these DIY skills. Me and a nail seem to end up in hospital at someone else's house.      That's the professional for you. I manage people, not walls and ceilings. So while I can be calm in a meeting, I panic in a shed.      Ah, well. You can learn! But first, I'm going to make sure you've got your coffee cups and plug sockets sorted before we start unloading the rest of the furniture.      Speaking of which, passed by a friend of mine at the chemist. She told me she's reconsidering her Foundation Degree. I suppose waiting till 30 to retrain is not that unusual these days.      No, I mean, I’ve got friends doing it in their 40s now. It's a bit late to get goody-two-shoes life sorted sometimes.      You’re just in the interesting age bracket. I remember doing mine in my 20s and thinking I could have done it better 10 years later.

Rather annoying this traffic, isn't it? I mean, do we need this many cranes and roadworks in North London in 2025?      I've been over this with you, hun. Construction is booming since the Olympics site turned into a residential zone. It was unavoidable eventually.      Unavoidable, sure. But if people just drove slower, they might not hit the car in front. I saw that woman nearly rear-end him for no reason. Classic road rage.      You're too hotblooded for your own good. Still, I'd rather not talk about that. I've made us a nice stop at the bookshop before we go to visit Grandma.      Oh! The new store’s in Crouch End, isn't it? D’you pick up the TLS again this week? Or did you just hand me the print version for breakfast, as usual?      Haha, you know me, love the oversized desktop hides, even if the digital is so much easier to carry. But nothing like the feel of a print edition on a rainy Sunday. And I can never keep up with both.      Fair point. I’ve been using Substack for most of it, then. But I still like the pretentious cover of TLS. I almost read it because of the cover, to be honest.      You and your wit. Still, you should read more. What's up with you this week at uni? Lectures go okay?      Yeah, it's fine—job's looking better now. I think I want to split my time between creative writing and editing, maybe even try a small press like you worked for all those years.      That's great news. Maybe your father will stop stressing that you’re "not ambitious" if you end up editing the next big literary sensation like I did once!      Dreams, dreams. Though I did write a short story last weekend set in France, of all places. You know, your favourite. It's about your uncle Henri’s vineyard and how he refused to sell a new AI wine-dispenser he calls “perfectly algorithmic.”      Oh, he still remembers that. That machine choked on cheap Burgundy and destroyed the first bottle.      I based it on that, actually. You said it your way and you made me promise never to repeat it.      Well, your mother never had the stomach for gossip like that. But if you can write it into fiction, go ahead. I’ll read it and give you tips for the publishing pitch.

Rather skip to the part where you two tried to build a tent in the hurly-burly of Halton park and ended up with no minge clue what you were doing. I've heard it a thousand times, but I can't help but have a giggle at it.      Oh eeny weeny, I swear it was one o' them big grey tents with all them poles, a'ight? Me n' Aysha tried too be clever, but we had nae idea wot side o’ t’ pole was supposed t’ go where. Ended up wi' it foldin’ in like a scone.      That was the best bit, only Rob n’ me made that MySpace blog about t’ tent fiasco. Remember we tried to put photos on it an’ Darcy, he thought I'd gone mad? We had t' spell out everythin' proper for breakfast, no slang allowed 'cause he’s still a bit in his own world, you know?      Blimey, I still laugh when I remember that—n’ Darcy, all serious, saying "Do you have tent specifications or is it one of those DIY grief things?" as he stood in the shop pointing at it like it'd bite him first. Was Rob sarcastic or just?      Yeah and then it rained and the tent collapsed like somethin' from telly and Silas was stuck under it like a worm in the mud! Honestly, what a state. But we survived. And Darcy was a prat, thought we had a proper out-of-doors experience.      Anyroad up, I say we plan a bonnie little adventure soon, just like yon trip. Camp out the other week near Runcorn. Bet it be nicer this time, know that we know better now.      Aye, and this time we do proper lesson plan, no fancy tents, just basic sods. Maybe a bit of a fire and stories, like the old days.      I could stick to my good boots and that raincoat of mine. Heh, 'cause I think it's been the same pair since 2010, but they serve t’ purpose, innit?      If you lot start talkin' about tents and fires like it’s nothin', I'll go with boots an’ raincoats all da way. I have a fluency in navigation and survival roles after that trip.      It's a pity we can't have a holiday this summer, but at least this lot can tell stories 'gain like we did at t' Poacher, where it started, innit?

Rather unusual to talk about wild winter camping in a conversation, isn't it? But it's a hobby that brings quite a lot of benefits. You've got to find the right kind of solitude out there, a place to yourself where you can truly hear the silence. It's a unique experience in a way.      I can understand the appeal, but I haven't tried it myself. Winter camping? That sounds ambitious. What with the cold and the wind and everything, I'd probably freeze into a wobbly statue. But you seem to enjoy the challenge. Didn’t you once get caught in a blizzard?      Aye, that was a memorable night! I found myself stuck in some glen well beyond the light of sunset, with enough daylight left for a few hours more, but the wind had picked up, and it was not long before snow came in thick and fast. My tent was better than breakfast, no doubt about that!      The stories are what usually draw the interest! I, on the other hand, have a more practical view of it. I mean, it's not just about braving the cold or enjoying solitude; it's a great way to reconnect with the real, non-man-made nature. The stars are just... extra sparkle in that sky.      I suppose I could see that, and I know the therapeutic benefits of nature. I have clients who find that just walking through the woods helps immensely. But stepping out at ten below, dressed in layers just someone at home would dress in summer—that sounds tough.      It definitely is, but it's not about being tough. It's being smart. You plan, you prepare, and you make sure you understand the environment. That's the key. And when the sun comes up, and the whole world is dusted in snow... well, it's worth it. There's a peace to it.      That calmness is something I'd love to experience. I spend so much time indoors these days, confined to offices and intense academic settings. A little bit of time in the wild would do wonders. Though I'd probably misplace my tent pegs or allow the wind to steal away my hat. My balance for such a serious hobby is tenuous at best.      I think it's wonderful you're encouraging us to think about these active hobbies, but I will probably stick with tending the garden through the seasons.

Rather than going out an' gettin’ a takeaway, do we no’un think we could cook up a storm tonight? I’ve bin lookin’ at that new Jamie Oliver recipe book an’ thinkin’ “blimey, we could knock somethin’ up summat like that.”      Sounds a bit more invigoratin’ than just sittin’ on the sofa eatin’ pizza. Aye, but I’m more a George Clarke fan than Oliver. Gave me some interesting ideas once. What you thinking, then?      Well, he’s got this recipe for butternut squash and feta lasagne. Allrighty, no’ sommat you’d contemplate on the turkey, but I reckon with a bit of red wine an’ a decent playlist, we coo’ld replicate it quite nicely.      Lasagne’s a classic! Wait, does he actually say “feta”? Sounds a bit posh for a lasagne.      Aye, but that’s why I like it! Feels fancy without bein’ too daft. Y’know I’m always up for a bit o’ variety. An’ besides, we’ve got summate for the lasagne sheets in the cupboard.      Allrighty, I’m game. Just don’t throw me into a sommat too complicated, eh? I might end up burning the halloumi!      Haha, don’tcha worry. Just stick to chopping the veg and let me handle the rest. Though I’d better have a red wine to hand. Anywine under £10 is alright by me!      That I can manage. But whilst we’re at it, let’s flick on somethin’ decent to watch afterwards. I’m thinking The Great British Bake Off? Lightweight but hits the spot.      Aye, nuffink wrong with a bit o’ flambéed drama an’ disappointed gingerbread. Just don’t expect me to crack my knuckles and become a professional baker out o’ this.      Would do you? Probably. You’d be churning out soufflés in the village by now goin’ on your own show!      You’re just in denial cos I’d be sittin’ in the front row with all them cake critics!      Oh aye, I’d be hecklin’ you like it was a football match! But, ‘onest, I do like the idea o’ cookin’ together. Reminds me o’ uni when we used to mess about in the kitchen.      Me too. Though I fancy we used more Tesco Ready Meals before Oliver waded in! Still, this is much better. We could even make a bit o’ a dinner party feelin’.      Aye, let’s just add a bit o’ jazz an’ we’re good to go.

Rather than share a story, I’d rather request a story. I need one for the Brownie Promise evening... What's a tale you'd love to share, love?      Let's see, we were building a rocket out of Lego the other day. Maybe we can combine it with that and create a magical space adventure.      Yeah! My rocket flew to Saturn with a pizza that was actually a spaceship! That's a good one, right, Mummy?      That's perfect, love. You can be the captain, and the rocket has a specially coded control panel using Excel.      Wait, the control panel only lets people with the right password fly the rocket. The password is made up of numbers and letters just like in Excel.      And I used a typewriter to type the password, because the old typewriter makes a really loud CLACK when I press the key...      And the typewriter hides a secret map to Saturn. Also, the clacks help tune the rocket’s engine into just the right frequency for space travel.      What about the pizza spaceship? It needs something special as well.      The pizza has little ingredients like “pizza stars” – rocket fuel made with cheese! And it needs a really good game system to help us land on Saturn.      Oh, right, we can bring your PlayStation along and use it as a landing guidance system. Let’s say you plug it into the control panel and start a race with the other space ships using a game you both love.      We can end the story at home, with you both finally eating the real pizza from the kitchen and watching the stars from the window. Maybe even write about it on the typewriter before bedtime.      And just like that, we baked the perfect story for your Brownie Promise evening. Can I use Excel on it tomorrow for any code snippets I might want to add?      We could talk about that over bedtime stories as well, love. How about that?      I think the best part of the evening would be the shared stories and imagination, with a little go at using my keyboard tomorrow if you'd like.      Then, let’s finish this with a hug and say "goodnight, all," and dream about space missions made from pizza and games.      And maybe even dream of better typewriters and Excel tricks for adventurers in bed.      Sweet dreams, my little rocket scientists.

Rather do this'n've rather than be scrubbed up for breakfast. I know it's not  normal , but after the conference, I'm bleeding knackered and I'd murder for a decent cup of coffee and toast with jam. Charming spread, Denis. You've picked a great morning to pop in. Hasn’t it  been  a trisht day on the roads? Almost as bad as the time I missed transcription because I got stuck in that  wretched  construction site near Pudsey.      Indeed, indeed, Eleanor. Those roadworks are right childish. Still, preferable to sitting in silence sipping lukewarm tea and reading a paper. What I wouldn't give for some real clotted cream and a bit of homegrown jam. Speaking of, you mentioned growing herbs the other day—what on earth is it I need to grow? Mint? Basil?      Mint, breakfast, mint— useful  but pesky if you don’t police it. Basil is better behaved, though not as good for the tea. I'm determined to have herbs fresher than what you get in the supermarkets. Though I have to say, your property in Bradford is nicely positioned. You’d think someone might buy it and knock it down for a little  luxury village  complex. Ha – but then you wouldn’t have the old stories to whisper about, now would you?      Stories like the one about the  deserted medieval village  nearby, huh? Our garden backs onto the skyline of one. I often tell people it’s just ghosts looking sour at the modern world. Also, I've been meaning to talk to you about this – I had a colleague, good bloke, about forty, who suddenly decided to sell his manor just outside York. It was a tidy house, and not too old that it put people off. But it’s  full  to the brim with junk mail and treacle memories. All passed on to sundry relatives now, I believe. Unedifying, really.      Aye, I expect your average 40-year-old can’t stomach the old orthodoxy of living in a  proper  English house with no WiFi and a sink that you  gotta  clean by hand! Still, I reckon goin' on about life improvements is our job now – at our age, we're the ones that  should  be telling blokes like Tom what to do with their latest phone or their  messy jumpers . We're the stewards of the moral garden now, Denis!      Perceptive as ever, Eleanor.

Rather annoying I had to take my paracetamol earlier. My back's playing up again since that first snow last weekend. Never mind, it is nearly Christmas after all! How's the cat settling in, Clara?      No, I mean, it's been great. He was a bit shy at first, but I think the cat's beginning to enjoy himself now. He actually curled up next to the TV last night when I was watching that nature show. Still, easier said than done getting some time off to do anything fun before the big day. Speaking of, when are we wrapping up the last of the Christmas presents?      I've nearly finished. Just the socks and another few books left. But what’s on your list, Mummy? I heard you mentioned something about wanting to try the new Dandelion and Spoon cafe in Ashford? Is it an actual restaurant or just a place to grab breakfast, Grandpa?      Haha, funny you should mention. I looked it up, and it’s both. They do great hot lunches too. It’s got four stars on TripAdvisor—personally, I’d take that over most restaurants around here. But let's not forget, we’ve still got parties on New Year's Eve to plan for. Have you got plans yet, Stella?      I was thinking, it might be good to meet the others and maybe go somewhere new? Maybe something with a view? I remember we talked about that weekend in Brighton last time. Who said anything about Brighton? Let me check my calendar. It just popped up because I was thinking about the sea and some fresh air.      That sounds lovely! We could even take my parents with us. I’m sure they'd be up for it. Although, I have to be honest, my phone fails me quite often when we’re out and about. I remember last time I got lost, I tried to use Google Maps, and my phone had no signal. I had to ask a man in a surf shop for directions.      A little bit like your Mummy, back in her time. Let me tell you, trying to find her way back from the hospital in the snow the other night—it took ages, and I had to shout at the GPS to get go straight rather than turning back up that hill again.      Oh, don’t remind me. I had a bloke on his bike zip past me and ask if I was alright!

Rather skip the tea and just go for a pint, me. This place does an alright half-price deal on Thursday afternoons, don't it? It's been  far  too long since we last met, Bek. Too long. You’ve been off the grid!      Jess! I saw that!  I’ve  been very much   on   the grid, actually. Just very busy with that transcription job I picked up part-time and my social life disappearing under a mountain of postgrad reading. Still, nice to see you’re still very much the same when it comes to glorified tea rooms...       Obvs . I've got to keep traditions alive, Bek. You know that My nan still refers to these places as “the lounge” and constantly tries to nap on the cushions if we stay past halfway through the scones. Speaking of which, aren’t you working better than breakfast, now?      Haha, yeah, sort of. I’m actually doing freelance transcription for a group of sociologists. Basically, I listen to recordings of people’s conversations, and I write it all down. I mean, it’s not as glamorous as you might think, but it pays better than odd weekend shifts.      Sounds riveting. Does it come with weird accents, fairly? I mean, it's  England , after all. Would you get someone from Newcastle next and have to work out what ‘che’ means ten times?      Oh yes, and I’ve had to deal with accents from all over. I once had a recording from someone in Liverpool, and I thought they were reciting a poem  for  a second because it was about how ‘difficult’ the weather was. And the other day I had to figure out what ‘I’ll be cabby’ meant. Took me five minutes.      That’s   coding   you’re doing. All that grammar, all that decoding? Honestly, the future is going to be all scientists trying to preserve the way people sound when they talk. We’ll be hearing queens and commoners being academically archived by robots.      That’s not the future—it's   now  . I had a course on the sociolinguistic implications of dialects during my PhD. If I go through this properly, I’ll probably end up analysing stuff like ‘unreal’ being the new ‘lovely’ or something. The way people speak is evolving faster than I can update my app.      Tell me about it. My job is the same, just backwards. I’m the one who  replaces  the weird stuff.

Rather annoying the wet weather isn't it? I was supposed to do a bit of running this morning but couldn't be arsed with slipping about. I’m more of a gym kind of gal anyway, gotta be honest.      No, I hear what you're saying. It's put my dog walks to the test, I’ll say that for it. But if it's not all that great for a run, I prefer to hit the gym too. I got a new administrator job last month and it’s taken it out of me. My legs are like jelly most days when I get home.      You're telling me! Sitting all day, filing, sending the odd supply request, and then trying to cook what’s left in the bin! The eccentricities of a semi-retired life, if I dare say. But I used to run every single morning. Living in Edinbugger and working from home doesn’t exactly inspire physical rigor anymore.      Oh don’t I know it! I thought I'd start looking for a transcription job that might actually give me more flexibility. I do like the satisfaction of knowing I listen properly and I don’t struggle with accents as much as most people. Old job felt like someone chucking a dictionary at me.      That does sound like a good move. I often wish I could be more vocal about what I'm interested in, but an admin role has its place and its limits. Still, it pays the bills and the odd rainy day coffee out. House prices are up so much I can’t just consider buying just anything.      Just the other day I considered the possibility of being able to rent out a house to someone, or flipping it in about five years. That would be gold round here! But my old property in Midd’x was a proper nightmare. I love cooking and I really like the idea of having my own little café, but for now I stick to guest cooking if I'm lucky.      You would make a great chef, love the idea of that! I miss your beef stew. We could talk about starting some sort of community cooking night if you fancied it.
