I think it would be brilliant to do something creative like that.      Now that’s the spirit! Imagine go back to my parents’ place and trying not to fight over the microwave!

Blimey, the sun’s out today innit? Thought it’d be one of them grey Cambridge mornin’s again. It is actually! Not a cloud in the sky — a proper treat in this part of the country, I’d say! Aye, eeny harm in a bit of sun today, eh? Still, better out here in them gardens than stuck in the office compiling data. I feel you. I was inspectin’ a building site early this mornin’, got drenched in the rain, but now I’m just grudgingly thankful I’m not back there. What’s new with you? Still in that posh postgrad job o’ yers? Yeah, works out well. Doin’ some architectural reinforcement in the city centre. It’s tricky, but the old buildings here are a joy to work with — proper history. Sounds posh. I’m stuck in my day-in-day-out nonsense of taggin’ words, checking context— you know the drill, corpus admin is a nightmare. Aye, it must be grief. Havin’ to label every odd phrase people use these days. Still, it’s got to be useful for some cheeky AI project. That’s what I tell meself somethin’ to keep me goin’. Oh, I went to see  Wicked  last week in London. No way! I was a bit gutted I missed it when it was on before. I’d have loved to sing it through in my head all week. I about did! My wee cousin dragged me there, and now she’s on about going to see  Waitress  or some such. Got me thinking I might need a night out in Manchester. I’ve always fancied  Waitress  actually. Bit more… gritty, I’d imagine. What with it being about a kitchen and stuff. You mad I’m stickin’ with queens and yellow-soundin’ musicals? Aye,  Les Mis  is a grand set of songs, but this new lot are the ones makin’ waves. I think it’s more our age, y’know? Hopefully the government budget gives us blokes a bit more to spend. The latest summin’ I heard was all about givin’ tax breaks to the big corporates, not to mention a forgotten lot of grads stuck in grad’s jobs. S’all so skewed. I’ve done my time in uni, now I want to be able to get on. Still, at least I ain’t stuck in a job I hate, you know? That’s the half of it.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh, lad? Thought me back garden’d be dry 'fore I started paitin’ the fence proper. Still, better to get it done than stared at      Aye, can’t knock the view from here wi’ them drizzle drops, eh? eeny harm in a bit more dawdle 'fore I reckon me shoulder's all better from liftin' that concrete from the flat last week. Proper back-breakin' bleedin' job      Know what you mean, me and this old brush of mine don’t see eye to eye these days. Tinkered wi' a new method me lodger showed me, only paintin’ in layers 'stead of one big go. Cuts the dry time in half, he says      Knew one of them blokes once down the housing estate, could’ve died ‘inש breakfast, he was so proud of his render job himself. Pulled a crate from the skip and loaded that muck on the spare room wall thick as gruel      Naa, lads, I’m not up for that sort of dramatics. Me and this grief of paint, it's a dance best done proper. Over to thee, lad, from what I hear, you're about to rent out the flat, still plannin’ on that film project, yeah？      Silly as I am, I’ve juggled the two and then some. Fancies in one hand and bucket o’paint in the other, thought I’d do some acting alongside paintin’ it up. Got some blokes down at the community centre castin’ for a romantic comedy, about a man tryin' to date a man whilst still passin' for a thug      Proper laughs you’re after, lass. Still, I'd have recommended a ‘cosy drama’ if you wanted to act proper, not that I’m criticin’ it. You any bloody good at it, I wonder      Didn't crack my first scene and I swear to the good Lord, me with 'split shots and big whiskeys, took the director no less than ten takes to get me head back in the scene      A life o’ risk, eh? Not much else I'd chuck myself into, between teachin' t’lads and whatnot. Reckon I'd take fluency to the grave if I tried moviewise      True to life, Prof. Know where you're at when it comes to gutters？ Had the problem my missus got at the flat, the renter next door fell foul of a half-blocking flume, poor devil. Got soaked and the wall’s flaked      Aye, I’ve got me mate, Tony, on speed dial for that lot.

Rather lovely this stretch, isn't it? That view of the fields and mountains just makes it all worthwhile. I do miss the English countryside, though—nothing like the rolling hills of Cambridgeshire, even if it was mostly muddy.      It's quite something all right. I always get a bit homesick for the Northwest, you know, the heather and the moorland, but I’ve grown used to this area over the years. I’ve brought friends over here once or twice; it’s a nice change of scenery from the norm. Didn’t it cost a bob or two getting over here, though?      Oh, goodness yes! I had to dip into some of my savings—never been much for living too extravagantly. The campervan was a bit of an impulse, I suppose, and I think the fuel and tolls are coming up to a fortune. Do you get any sort of reimbursement working this in TEFL or is it all on the personal cost?      Not many perks when working in TEFL, I'm afraid. I do get some satisfaction from knowing I’m helping people learn, though. A few students from this area and Turkey sent me gift cards for the shop and a few books. But it’s little things. You’re not too bad about it yourself, are you? I mean, you seem to be making the most of it.      Well, what else is there to do? I’m retired for all intents and purposes. I never really got into a proper career line, just odd jobs here and there—jobbing as a private teacher now and then. But this trip is a good excuse to clear the clutter, quite literally about packing up my flat back home. I’ve been living out of a suitcase most of my life, and not always by choice.      You're not the only one with a ‘start fresh’ kind of vibe. I passed a couple of hitchhikers on the side of the road before we departed—had a bit of a chat. You ever hitchhike while you were younger? I did as a student once, trying to catch the Trans-Siberian Line. Not the smartest thing, but it opened a few minds and wallets!      Hitchhiking wasn't something I ever got into. I was always cautious in my younger days. But I can see the appeal, especially when your budget is tight.

Rather annoying this, naa? These train strikes messin’ everything up. Mums, ‘ow did y’learn t’navigate them bobbies at the Hay Festival last year anyway?      Oh, it was utter chaos, I can promise you that. But the books make it worth it! I went with a friend last year an’ we just got lost wanderin’ round the tents. Found a little poetry stall an’ got so lost in a chapbook about rivers. It was quite lovely, truth be told.      Didn’t it rain too? Middlesbrough lad I knew near enough drowned in a puddle. Bit of a muck-up, if y’ask me. My da took me once as a nipper. I remember this rallyin’ geezer who read Oliver Twist aloud, and I nearly wet me pants from laughing an’ crying at the same time!      I’ve never been! Hattie said she saw the Queen’s granddaughter there once, or somethin’ like that. Oi, Granda—did you know she got a book named after her?      What, the Queen? Nah love, that’ll be Alice in Wonderland… although, I reckon the Queen’s had a few “wonderful” tales of her own. He, he, that was a good one. Let me tell ye about the time me mam and I moved to Bolton. ‘Ad a lorry packed to the ceiling, an’ halfway down the road, the steering packing in an’ we had t’sleep on the side o’ the motorway.      Oh no! That’s awful. Did you make it in one piece at least? I can’t even imagine trying to move house as a child. I remember my family moving from Kosice to London when I was small. It was strange—I still have a fondness for the baked goods from that little Slovak shop near our old flat. They used to do the best kolache. Do they even have those in supermarkets here?      No! Why d’ya think we’re goin’ t’Sainsbury’s after this? They’ve got the best chocolate squares for after-exam snacks. Mums, you owe me one goin’ on this wild goose chase after chocolate.      I’ll remember that, don’t worry. I can see it already your revision notes will be all doodles and chocolate-related equations.      Ah, don’t bellyache love. I had t’study ‘neath a bed when I was younger! It wasn’t Sainsbury’s then, it was Woolworths an’ it didn’t even have half the treats.

Rather annoying this newfit lot o’ technologies, I must say. I was just trying t’message Hal when I crashed out ‘n’ went an’t pressin’ all them buttons like a bleedin’ madwoman.      Oh, now Grandmum, you’ll get the hang een it if you give yersel’ a moment. I reckon it’s not as complicated as it seems once yo’ kno’ wheer to look. I’ve had me kids teach me quite a bit as it is—nearly got me usin’ Zoom during the lockdown.      Yeah, easy enough really! Just pressin’ a square an’ then talkin’ like normal. Though if My Gran keeps fallin’ over ‘er phone I’m not sure I want to show her the Duet dance bit o’ Tik. Could be dangerous!      Now, I see no funny-lookin’ daft dances for me! Ho ho, you think I’m fallin’ for that lot. I’ve had enough bleedins’ problems—nearly lost me Bobbin book, I did—sorted it out though, quite a rummage job in me drawer for two old cards. Good job I didn’t chuck it.      Clearing out – that’s been on me mind, leastways. There’s tonnes o’ old photo albums an’ bits and pieces in the attic. If we all got together, I’m sure we could whittle it all down in one day—proper family activity. Hal, you could have some fun through the bits you chuck’d out.      Er, sure—I mean I don’t kno’ if I about chuckin’ anythin’ out. But I can pass it on to me mates if you like—that failsafe “archive it then bin it” handle. Though, I dunno, binning ‘em feels odd. What if somethin’ is important?      Important? Hal, all I had left were a few odd socks an’ a spoon stick. As for mental state… well, I seen enough to knows the sad bits a lonesomeness. Not sayin’ nothin’ here, mind yo’, but if you feel all low or go bad thoughts on your own, you talk to someone – don’t go bottlin‘ it all in.      You're right, Mary. It's all too easy to get stuck in a loop of thinking things are wrong with you. Just like with technology, it helps talkin’ ‘n’ askin’. Or, if you can’t—write ‘em down like I do. Helps clear yer mind so y’can focus on things that matter.      Like, I used to write all me stress-angers in a Moleskine.

Right, lads, here we go — I’ve just bought this brand new laptop, and I thought it’d be a good idea to show it off properly. Blimey, it sure does look sleek! Got it on a £200 discount from that site you recommended, James —DealsForBlokes, was it?      That’s the one! Glad it worked out for you. Let me have a look at the specs too — got an SSD, a decent Intel i7, and it’s light enough to carry around. You're gonna chase your friends into the past with how modern it is, mate! Still, have you downloaded any essentials yet?      Cheers, James. Just the antivirus and browser for now — still waiting for the week to finish installing, to be honest. D’you reckon I should go for the Windows updates straight away or wait?      I’d wait a bit — I mean, my last PC went into a boot loop the minute I let it auto-update. Still have to drag my old clunker out for gardening season. I swear, if I had a penny for every time I’ve cursed computers, I’d’ve bought my own allotment by now.      Ha, yeah, been there. Mind you, I miss the old CRT monitors with the green screen and chunky keyboard. There’s something about that satisfying “click” when you press the keys. Still, I can foresee this thing getting clogged up in six months.      Fair point. I reckon you should run CCleaner once in a while, and make sure you back up your stuff through Google Drive or something — your grandmother’s photo of your cat about to fall off the table does not deserve to disappear again.      True. Speaking of pics — are we going to share the trip photos from the Cotswolds to the group album today? I just backed up my phone before syncing.      Only if the one of you both stuck on the wrong side of the train is edited out. I still can’t unsee that.      Ah, classic Mark. You keep the memories while we do the hard work. By the way, have you tried this new YouTube app I showed you? It's really intuitive for editing workout clips or retro tech reviews.      Nope, haven’t even opened it yet, but I’ll give it a go. So long as it doesn’t crash on day one, we’ll call it a win.

Rather do I a lovely place this is. That logo, though— looks like it's been designed by a... What's the word? A dreamer.      You think? I think it's rather clever. Modern with a bit of character— you can't really beat that for a bistro opening in a place like Tarnow. Having said that, it  is  a bit on the retro side.      Of course, it is. If you're going to dump someone in a new city and hope they'll stick around, you give them a bit of history and a hell of a decent coffee. Though honestly, I don't think we're here for the decor.      No, I suppose you're right. I just feel like there's something... I don't know, restless about the whole thing. Like we're all looking for something we can't quite describe. Or maybe we just need to feel  seen .      And what is it we're seeing in each other, then? Are we just trying to avoid the silence? Because tell me— are we really here for the occasional smoothie or is it because it feels good to say we've seen the world a little more than we did before?      Hmm. I suppose it's a bit of both, isn't it? You know, I had a student the other day— talked about addiction like it was the most obvious thing in the world. Like she never even questioned someone needing help beyond a lifestyle crisis. That made me a bit uncomfortable.      Because it is a lifestyle crisis, sometimes. But not in the way she might think. You know, most people I know who've struggled with it started out the same way: chasing this vague feeling of being  alive , not knowing it would cost you everything.      I never thought of it like that. Maybe that's why I started teaching TEFL—to feel useful, maybe to believe I had a purpose beyond my own struggles. I tried to lose myself in fitness, honestly. Joining gyms and that kind of thing.      I think it's noble. Not many people would reach out like that, even for other people. I started with the TEFL work too, but life had other plans. Still, I think I'm just in the waiting game between jobs.      And your dreams? Do you still have any?      Oh, plenty. I just don’t know how to get to them without selling the house over in Cambridge.

I just discovered the Dorset Steam Fair is on next weekend, do you both know about it yet? Oh, I haven't heard a thing about it! Is it like a Victorian steam engine exhibition or something? No, it's more than that—it's a big fair on wheels and steam-powered machinery. It's very popular with the families. Yeah, you should come along, but I think they might be doing a ticket pre-sale. It gets quite busy otherwise. I don't drive so getting a ticket isn't the big issue—we can use the bus. Still, is everything accessible for me? I'm not too mobile these days. There's a section for disabled facilities—they've got specific parking and path access from the main entrance. But I’d say go early if you can. It gets really crowded as the day goes on. I agree. They've got food stalls and lots of old tractors and hides, you know, working steam engines and the like. Sounds like a nice way to spend a sunny Saturday. I don't get out much as it is. Do they welcome pets? I might bring Tiddles—my cat. No, no pets are allowed on-site, sorry. I asked last year because I had to leave my dog with a friend. Silly me, I should've known! Though the cat’s never been out of the house in his life. It's fine, Dad. You can pop over to Mom's later in the afternoon and be back in time for the rest of the day. She said she's refurbing the back room and could do with the help. That's true! She's been rearranging everything and worrying it won't fit through the door. My, that old house of yours is mighty tight in places! Well, the property round here is bloody pricey now. I don't blame you for waiting till you find a better place. Those prices in Bournemouth are out of control! They told me the same last week. My landlord just hiked the rent again by like 10 per cent. It really is getting ridiculous if you're not working or earning much. I suppose it always happens when big cities get too popular. Still, you two are lucky—you get each other and live close by. We don't take that for granted, do we?

Rather a lot’s happened in the last week, what with that business about the internet being down ‘n all... What was it, some giant server glitch in London?      Oh, that! It made teaching quite chaotic. I had the kids in Year 6 spending half the morning trying to log on to the online spelling tests. Kept twitching about saying “we just c’nnae get a clean signal up ‘ere!” just like one of those radio dramas off the telly.      Yeah! My teacher was like "are you lot paying attention, or just doomscrolling on TikTok again?" Honestly, who  uses  TikTok? It's just videos of people eating weird foods like that Mynta guy with the melon and lime bursts...      I reckon you're missing the point of the platform, lad. Half the charm is in the chaos and the raw authenticity. Besides, I’ve been toying with using it for a poetry series. Posting little five-line verses every mornin’. I called it “Five O’Clock Fog”—just me and the Thames, lads!      I never thought I’d hear  you , grief of a typewriter, wax lyrical about TikTok! Though I’m not sure the poetry “verse” is the most… stable genre there. Last night, I saw a man recite the entirety of “Macbeth,” line for line, for 27 minutes.      There’s more wrong with that than just the time. If you read Shakespeare like it’s a TED Talk, you’re missing half the sparkle. It shouldn’t be  performedy , it should be  lived . Prime example? I did Lady Macbeth once at the church fete. Only got to “unsex me here” before my son ran in with frost bite and a boiled egg stuck to his hair.      That must’ve been  hilarious .      Well, the pantomime was a different story. We did “Cinderella” at the school last winter, and you  didn’t  see me bursting into verse with egg on my son’s head! That was proper theatre. My students set the whole thing around this old chapel in the woods by Knaresborough. They even had a stagehand using real candlelight.      Sounds idyllic—like a Wildean picture. Though if we’re talking about stagecraft, I’ve been writing a one-act where the protagonist talks to their Twitter feed person to person. One night, she says “What’s the silence of a like,” and the feed responds like a ghost. Very moody.      Listen, I see enough silence on mine from the kids now that I’m not living with them.

I can't believe today is the day for both Elsie and Lucas’s hearing test. Do you think it's worth worrying about, or am I just being a bit of a worrier again? I don’t think we should worry, Miss Turner—some kids just like the whooshing noises and all the wiggly things. It’s like a little adventure! But I didn’t like the loud beep last time! Why do I have to listen to that again? Lucas, it was just a very loud tone during the test to make sure your ears are working properly. It helps them make sure everything is okay, like when the doctor listens to your heart with that rubber thingy. The stethoscope! I know! I had one for school, remember, Elsie? Lucas, dear, you’ve got to stop shouting when you talk—maybe that’s why everyone thinks you need a hearing test! That’s not true, Elsie—and please, not shouting, Lucas. By the way, Elsie—your friend Ashaad texted about that school trip to the museum. He said it’s about something called ... Monet. Do you remember what that is? Monet—he does those flower ones with the water, right? The ones that look like rain or something. Oh, those are cool! I went to an exhibition once where they put the posters on someone’s back and played music. Super weird! I remember that one—quite something! Speaking of weird, I think the Easter chocolate is still hiding in the veg basket, under the radishes. Did you try any yet, Elsie? Nope! I said no until after the test because that was the deal. Lucas even helped me remember, didn’t you, Lucas? Yeah, I told him, Elsie, if you eat the Cadbury egg before the test, the doctor gets mad! Lucas, please don't scare your sister. Let’s not talk about scary doctors—we’ve been over the dentist enough this month! Anyway, speaking of things coming together—Elsie, Lucas, your birthdays are in the same week again this year. How does it feel to officially be teenagers? It feels amazing, I can do more things! Like maybe get a part-time job, or help out with the library afternoons. Me too! I want to start learning how to fix things. Maybe be a mechanic like my cousin. I can even do math problems about cars now.

I can't believe it's been ages since we last met! Life’s been so hectic with work and everything. How’s the new job going? Honestly, it's been a bit of a whirlwind, but I’m loving it. Speech and language therapy in the adult acute setting is challenging in the best way. Every day feels different. How about you? I’ve been completely swamped with writing campaigns for a new brand. It's all social media content, but honestly, it's pulling my hair out! I'm just so glad to be catching up properly, even if it's just over a frozen pizza. Haha, I've missed the chaotic freezer pizza nights. Remember when we used to visit our parents and they’d always make us eat proper dinners? Oh yes, my mum absolutely used to make me feel like a failure if I was eating a ready meal! Wait, does yours still do that? Definitely! Though she’s got more sympathy for my career now, even if she still thinks I should be a full-time homemaker. I swear she reads those lifestyle blogs and thinks that's the way to happiness. Classic! It took ages for my parents to properly get on board with my work as a copywriter. They still don’t really know what I do all day, and I barely do either half the time. I promise it’s not as glamorous as it sounds. I don’t doubt it, but I also know someone who could make mending a sentence sound like climbing a mountain. Speaking of, do you think you’ll ever move out of the flat share and be ‘properly’ settled? Eventually, I suppose. I’m saving up as much as I can, but rent is brutal. I keep imagining this little cottage with a garden and a cat who treats me cruelly every time I step on the mat. Do you think it’s too much to dream? Not at all. I used to have the exact same dream. I even made you draw little illustrations of your dream flat to make you feel better when you were stressing about space. That was you! I had completely forgotten. That's why I have a scribbled picture of the 'Kitchen Of My Dreams' on my fridge from seven or so years ago. I’ll admit, it was a bit boxy, but I think your cat would approve.

Rather do a long cycle ride as a child, I remember going from Almondsbury to Bristol with my uncle when I was about eleven or so. He said it would do me good, and I’d have a “proper sense of achievement” when I got back. By the time we reached the top of Coombe Hill, my legs were like jelly. Not sure about sense of achievement just yet!      Aye, cycles and hills! I'd never attempt that in Manchester. It was quite a reasonable flat journey from my house to the university for lectures. But when I think back, being a dental surgeon like you, Speaker_4, made life a lot easier. What with all the NHS perks, I daresay you had a bit of everything.      Oh, the perks back in the eighties, and I do mean the perks! I remember one dentist who took his surgical team out breakfast, and then suggested they sail while he gave a lecture in his boat. I asked him if we could, you know, spare a few hours for drilling, but he said no—he was giving a full lecture on root canals all at sea! Bah, quite a character.      Honestly, we’ve got nothing on the past. These days it feels like we’re just booking trips for very little: Prague tickets are almost cheeps these days. I went last year and found an exhibition about Bohemian architecture at a place I’d never heard of before. And, they gave in just before the full booking deadline—must’ve been a friend of the curator.      Oh, is that how it’s done now? I wish someone would let  me  in when it’s nearly about to close. That reminds me of our local planning last night. They approved the solar project on the old factory site. Properly necessary, I say. The town could do with that. My, it used to look like a ghost town after the 90s.      And it was all because of bad architecture and no maintenance. You could see the signs. But good move to rebrand as well. The converted barn next to the cricket club is going to be used as the venue for our jive event next month. Popping it on the calendar as go-to-place for dance-offs if you ask me.      Finally, some life into it. I’ve got an anecdote about your rebranding. I have a cousin who bought a property in France in the most peculiar way—had to attend a village fair and dance the night away with the mayor to get the keys.

So do you think an online learning platform focusing specifically on communication strategies would work? I mean, with so much reliance on remote interaction these days, there’s definitely a need for it.      It sounds promising. I can see teachers, like myself, really benefiting from modules on how to structure virtual classrooms or use social media more effectively in their teaching. But where would we source the content? Would we create case studies ourselves?      Exactly, and we can start with case studies from education professionals we know—people like you, maybe even some from outside the UK or NZ. Imagine how diverse those examples could be!      That’s a good idea, and if we can add video case studies, it will help learners understand best practices in real-life scenarios. I know some teachers who are already using micro-lectures in their training programs.      Right, moving images are really powerful for learning. I was thinking of a subscription-based model at first, but maybe we could offer a few modules for free and upsell the rest. Or partner with schools for bulk purchases?      Bulk subscriptions might make it more sustainable. I’ve seen similar models with other educational platforms. Also, if we offer mini courses or workbooks in PDF format, we can give users some additional downloadable learning materials.      That’s something we could develop as an extension of the platform. Think about it—someone could take a module on social networking principles and then get a workbook with exercises and case study questions. That way, the learning isn’t just passive.      I agree. What about the branding side? If we call it something like “Connection Hub,” it keeps with the theme of social interaction and learning. And the logo could show people connecting—maybe overlapping circles or something symbolic.      I like the sound of that—“Connection Hub” for education. Let’s put together a short proposal for some partner schools or educators to see what they think. Maybe you can approach some colleagues from your school for feedback?      Absolutely. I’ll also see if any of my professional network on LinkedIn might be interested in supporting such a venture.      Then once we get some early support, we go back to the drawing board if necessary. If not, at least we’ll have started the conversation and will know what the market might need.      Exactly. Education is always evolving, and this could really tap into that growth—both for people like me who already work in it and for those who are just starting out and need guidance.

I can't believe we've never taken a weekend trip to the sea. I know it's not that far from here, and I've often thought about how nice it would be to take a walk along the coast. I know! We've talked about it before, but things just keep getting in the way. I've actually been meaning to suggest it again. I reckon it'd be a nice change of scenery. Yeah, I've been craving a seaside escape for a while. It would be so peaceful. We could pack a picnic, and maybe even chase the sun down. That sounds brilliant. And even if it's a bit cold, we could just sit by the beach with our coats on and watch the waves. I remember when my cousin lived in Brighton and he told me the best spots for walking and the cutest little cafes. Brighton, you say? I've been there once with a group of friends a few years ago. The night we went, the weather turned for the worst, and we ended up stuck in the train station with no shelter—so funny. Oh, that's the one I was thinking about! He told me about it when we were having dinner. He was so entertained by how it turned into a little sea-worthy adventure. How did you all end up with no shelter, anyway? Long story short, we got caught in a downpour and couldn't get back to our B&B in time. So we all just huddled in the waiting area with our wet coats. At one point, one of us started an impromptu singalong—of all things, sea shanties! The conductor ended up laughing and giving us all a thumbs-up from behind the counter. That’s classic you—always managing to turn chaos into fun. I wish I'd been there. But it does sound like something to remember. Oh, it was. Though I wouldn't personally recommend eating fish and chips the day before a train journey. We had to spend half the journey restricting our movements... Ugh, that's the one downside to the English coastal lunches, right? So what are we waiting for? Let's pick a weekend, pack a nice thermos of tea, and set go for a little sea-voyage of our own. Sounds perfect, let's do it. Who knows, maybe we'll end up with our own seaside story to tell.

Rather annoying this new season’s trends, innit? Seems like everything’s trying to be ‘vintage’ yet got naythin’ of the real charm, eh? I mean, sure, chunky knits is nice… but them wide-leg trousers? Feels like I’m about to trip over my own eeny weeny legs!      I know what yer mean, Sophie. Honestly, I’ve been wearing trousers so baggy I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve watched me nan’s old VHS of  Mean Girls  to check what “normal” jeans look like. But innit funny how fashion cycles back around? I still can’t get over the comeback of scrunchies and ugh, leg warmers again. I swear I’m getting left behind in this fashion merry-go-round.      Oh, I think it’s all very fun, actually! You’ve got to admit, when done right, these trends can look very chic. I’m teaching a GCSE class on fashion history next term, and looking at the parallels between the 80s and now is fascinating. My students are into vintage Y2K crop tops and metallic fabrics. You’d think they were human disco balls!      Oh, blimey. I dunno if I’d want to wear a top so short I could sneeze and it’d fly off! I prefer a bit of coverage meself. Practicality over glamour, if you catch me drift! Though, I will admit, I did enjoy experimenting with neon eyeliner a few years back. It made me oddly popular at the local pub quizzes.      Pub quizzes being crowded out by fashion? I hadn’t noticed! But y’know, I’m trying to embrace it. New year, new me sort of vibes. I’ve already ordered some faux fur coats and dip-dye everything. The problem is, my stepmum thinks I’m dressed up like a guest speaker at a 90s health seminar.      Oh, I love talking to someone who’s into reinvention! My nan told me the other day that she’s doing a fashion space in the lunches she makes. “Cake buns with lemonade liners as belts”—ya know, avant-garde stuff.      Honestly, I think it’s wonderful how everyone’s so expressive now. I just started incorporating sustainable design into my lessons—upcycling jumpers, using off-cuts. It’s about making fashion accessible and personalised, not just following those glossy catwalks.      Oh, that sounds very proper, Alice! I wouldn’t half enjoy a homemade wardrobe; I could probably make a skirt out of an old tea cosy, couldn’t I?

So, I just got my college acceptance letter today, Mum. I’m going to do media studies with a photography pathway. I’m so excited!      Oh, that’s brilliant, Liv! Your father would’ve been so proud. Photography is such a beautiful art form. You know, when I was your age, I wanted to do something creative, but I got distracted by bills and… well, life.      I know! Why don’t you ever tell me more about what you used to want to do?      Oh, it was nothing too grand. I used to write little short stories, even won a local competition once. But then the real world hit, and I became a receptionist. Stability, I guess you could say.      I get it, but what if you pick it up again? You could write for my college magazine or something. You’re really inspiring, Mum.      Maybe... I’d like that. I’ve also always been quite scared of the dark. Used to have the brightest lamp in the house—still do.      I know! Sometimes I catch you with your phone as a night light. It’s funny. I’m scared of… well, basically everything. Spiders, heights, even loud noises at the cinema. But at least I can take pictures of the fears and laugh about them.      That’s the spirit. If I could go back, I’d photograph everything—this old cottage, your father in his garden, you when you were a baby just staring at the ceiling. Some things make the fear seem smaller in the frame.      That’s such a good way of looking at it. I’m thinking about trying to do a project on different people’s fears. Maybe a photo series and some interviews. I love comedians who talk about fears too, like Sarah Silverman. She’s hilarious and so relatable.      Sarah Silverman? She’s a standout. I was a fan of Victoria Wood back in my day. You’d love her if you ever got into older British comedy.      I’ve heard a couple of her songs. I’m going to look her up after college. I’ve also been reading the "Harry Potter" books again—they make life feel more magical, even now.      Oh, that was a nostalgic time, wasn’t it? I remember reading them with you at bedtime. I still keep all the first editions we had. They’re dusted under the bed now, but they’re like hidden treasure.

Rather annoying this new application form they've sent us, ain't it?      Oh, I don’t know, Harold. I’m more cross about football these days. Did you see Manchester United last night? Not a patch on the glory days, if you ask me.      I won't pretend I’m a fan, but I reckon it's not all their fault. The kids today—they’re too soft. Got one this week crying because I told him to go pick up a football properly. Not with his hands, mind you. Didn’t even want to play with the others. Gettin’ shabby even!      That's just it, Richard. Everything's like that now. Even my cockerel's stopped crowing on cue. Probably woke up one morning and thought, “Bugger this, I'm off.” Living with it for about a year now.      I've been thinking about a new baby bird in the shed. Put it in a little box to keep it warm—and I swear, I heard it walking around this mornin'. Nothing but trouble, those feathered wee rascals.      It must be awful, then, if they don’t sleep proper. I been sleepless lately. Nightmares about my 3D printer messing up, and I barely had a wink.      All that noise and all that heat. Bit much for poor old bones. And heaven knows what's going on with the houses. I saw a new build in Norwich the other week—what a shamble! They’d dropped a drain in the wrong place and filled in the trench all crooked. Workmanship these days, I swear!      Oh, the building lot is an adventure. I once had a childminder that let the kids draw on the walls. No one mentioned to her that wasn’t for little ones. Got guest bedrooms looking like they did a paint battle at nursery.      Do you know, I tried to make some little ones help me stick the birthday card up and they just laughed. No sense of contributing, but to be fair, what are we left with these days? Even you can't get a nice birthday card!      That I agree with, love. If I was building a house, I’d say no surprises between us. But with all the rules and whatnot, it’s like playing football with gloves on both hands and a blindfold on.      It's a right laugh though. I wouldn’t be without the lot o them!

Rather than share a text, how about we have a proper chat over the phone? I would love to hear more about what's going on with you now that your daughter is coming from abroad.      A phone call would be lovely, I've been meaning to catch up sooner or later. She's beginning to study at the university here, you know. I reckon it's quite an adjustment for her.      That's so exciting and a bit daunting for a young woman to move abroad like that. What's she studying?      She's beginning a history course. I suppose it makes sense since I've always loved history and learning about the past, and she was quite the scholar at school.      I remember her school days well; I had her for several subjects. Rather bright and quite inquisitive for her age. I was proud to have her in my class, no doubt about that.      Oh she remembers me planting the idea in her, you know, persuading her that university might suit her. It's rather monumental for both of us - for her, taking up the challenge and for me, as it is my first grandchild, in a way.      That is a rather significant moment. I must remember to say hello when she gets here, and wish her the best of luck. You're her rock in all of this, and I daresay it's not an easy decision for a woman her age to make such a big move.      It's quite oddly therapeutic, knowing what you had to contend with when you finished your career here. I know you missed education when you stopped teaching, and I do hope she brings you back into the fold, talking history and watching documentaries together.      Aye, that would be a joy. The house could do with a bit of company, for one. I rather miss the young ones here about the place. I could be a bit of a helper too, I've had a fair amount of education waiting on me. We could run into queens and kings over cups of tea and biscuits.      That sounds like quite the schedule. I'll be calling in after work with the first lot of her luggage, go ahead and get your kettle on. It does sound like a plan worth making.      I shall, I can't wait to meet her. It's nice to have something to focus on, and someone to talk to those days I feel quite stir crazy at home.

I can't believe the polls showing a growing pro-independence support in Scotland. It's like nothing they said after 2014 has stopped the tide. What do you think, David? I follow the news quite often, James. Some things never change—people still want independence in some shape or form. But I don't think they've really thought out the consequences of all that. Though I suppose that's not too different from the rest of us, honestly. To be fair, the political climate in the UK makes it easier for people to want out. Still, I worry about the economy. My wife does too—she works in finance and the idea of another independent nation with its own currency is a nightmare. Yeah, she'd be well placed to comment on that. She sounds professional. I think I remember her from the last staff event at uni. Good company. I, um… actually need to ask you something a bit more personal. Go ahead, David. You always say the most interesting things over tea. My daughter—she's applied for a job teaching in London, quite a step from her current school. I was wondering if you might help her out. I know you've been doing interviews lately. She's good—really passionate about what she does, and smarter than most candidates I’ve seen. Of course, I'd be happy to. When's the interview? And what’s the name again? Let me check my phone. It's Emily. The interview is next Tuesday. Would you have a spare ten minutes? That’s fine. I’ll make sure I do. I always like to support good teachers, especially the kind who are genuinely looking out for what's best for the pupils. Not like some I've met. That’s a good way to look at it. Honestly, I'm just trying to make sure she doesn't fall between the cracks. With all the changes in education, you never know where you'll land. You're doing a good job trying, mate. I think it's partly the same with the recent referendum debates—people are searching for stability and purpose in the mess we're in. Exactly. If we can give our kids a line in the sand, it's always worth doing. Time to head out, I suppose. Thanks again, James. No worries at all.

I can't believe we've never done this before, Christopher. We've got the mousetrap game up and running in the garden, and it's the perfect way to keep the children entertained. I must say, Margaret, I'm bemused as to why you never considered it earlier. It's practically an English tradition, isn't it? Having these little games on the lawn as the sun warms up. A shame I missed out before. Oh, I watched one of those American videos online last year and was like, "I wish we had one of those!" But watching you two fiddle with it now, it's so much more fun in the real world. It's like a jungle gym but with tin! I'm going to be the mouse, right? You're all too old and sad to be the cat. Oh, hush, Isaac, and don’t look at me. I'm merely in charge of the refreshment table and keeping the mugs full. Good, someone has mercy on us bones and tell the lads what it's like working in the States, Christopher. I’ve read your emails, but we’ve only got a vague idea. Do tell. I find it most fascinating – how it must differ so vastly from our way of life here in Stratford. Yeah, like do you use British English or American English there? And what's up with those food labels? Spaghetti is pasta, not a meal in a can, surely. Touché, Thomas. I can imagine the mouths gaping at the supermarkets. No, in the office, most people about me spoke American. Oddly, I found it quite different to hear “schedule” said like “shed-yool.” Oh, cruel! No wonder I never quite caught on. And the children – are they well-behaved, or were they all eager to become the president by the age of six? A little bit of both, Margaret. The children were certainly bold and academically ambitious, but they were also outrageously well-fed. I took the liberty of bringing you some peanut butter cookies with me. I think their version of goody bags on birthdays is about seven pounds of candy and two action figures. That's serious. That might warrant a diplomatic mission one day. I must say, Christopher, I'm quite envious of the experience. But don’t start planning a permanent life among them over there – we’d be lost without you at the library.

Rather annoyingly, I've bought us a whole bunch of new pyjamas. We do need to get a couple more wardrobes in here now, honestly. I can't believe how much stuff we've built up in this tiny flat.      Pyjamas, again? Do we not have enough already? I mean, I'm very grateful, but if we're not careful we'll have a wardrobe that only contains sleepwear and t-shirts from conferences abroad.      It's not just pyjamas! Oh, I also got this new scarf when it was on sale. You'd like the pattern—it's really fetching. And I picked up a couple of skirts, only because we’re attending that black-tie university event next week, you know the one. I just needed a decent alternative to the same old boring office separates I wear every day.      Fair enough. How about we do a wardrobe swap then? I mean, I'm not in the market for any more shirts, but we can reorganize things. Also, the scarf—if it’s that nice, I do deserve to see it immediately rather than just hear about it in the middle of the night while trying to make tea!      Yes, yes, it’s quite a statement piece. You’ll see it later. And speaking of the event, I think it would really be a good idea if you got a new jacket as well. Silly as it sounds, we don’t want to look like two old professors someone forgot to invite to the dress code meeting.      I can definitely manage with the stuff I have. But fair point—if you're going out with a new skirt, I can't show up in flannel. I'll pop into the shops the next time we're out. Honestly, I just wish this flat had another bedroom. We barely have space to hang a coat, let alone do something halfway like planning an outfit.      I know. The Chinese have no idea the minimal space a lecturer couple needs to unpack a wardrobe. I’m starting to consider getting a storage unit down the road.      That would probably do it. I think it's time we start thinking about a slightly bigger place. We might run out of room before the end of term. Though really, I wasn't expecting our pyjamas to cause such a dent in the closet space.

Rather a brilliant game we had last night, wasn’t it? That try by Kelleher came out of nowhere, and I’ll not lie—me heart nearly stopped I was laughing when the ref saw it! Got me lad Oisin all hyped up, and now he's spending half the night trying to draw on all the cards I brought over last week for the birthday. Ay, I swear the poor boy thinks a birthday should be all prizes and no cake!      Dad, you should’ve seen it! My school’s team was doing the same drill last week when we played the county under-12s. We scored even! Not as good as Kelleher’s, but still!      My word, Oisin, you lot are not starting school rugby just yet, are you? You're still too young for the full tackle game, I hope!      We’re not! Just touch rugby. It’s proper fun, though. The coach said he’s planning to teach us how to line up properly for the first time next week. I told him I was going to tell you—personally, sir—what I learned if we land a big tackle!      Honestly, Sean, he’s watching us like we’re rhythm masters when we walk him to bed at night. Sometimes I swear he doesn’t go upstairs because he’s tired, but because he wants to impress you with his new moves! You know what it is, don’t you? It’s the old man influence at full tilt!      Now, now, Deirdre. You give me enough credit, but mind, I’m not being accused of turning the boy into a ballet dancer! He just likes about the challenge, is all. Right, the touch rugby’s a start—let’s see what he goes for next. Table tennis champion? Boxing? Or is it up for galloping with a horse over the hills like he once said?      I’m just saying, it’s a lovely thing, all this talking about sport. I miss when he ran out after the Saturday morning match and rushed over to say hi to grandmo with his pockets full of chocolate frogs! Now it’s "Where’s grandmo?" and "When are we going stargazing again?" as if he were some life-and-death matter!      Well, I’ll not see it coming. The box I brought in from the attic after retiring was still at the door.

Rather annoying when a sock’s pair finds its way into someone else’s laundry, isn’t it? I swear half of them are lurking in Anna’s drawer at the moment. Not that I've gone over to ask for them—she’s only borrowed a few things when we first started living together. Seems like we’ve accidentally merged our sock collections!           I know exactly what you mean! I only had to borrow one t-shirt from my cousin last summer, but now she says it’s her go-to one and insists it belongs to her. Didn’t even want to give it back when I saw her three months later. Honestly, when you're moving house and the chaos of sorting stuff out is in full swing, you'd be forgiven for thinking you've left your entire life back in the old place.      It’s not just the little things—my sister was at the house the other weekend, and she practically turned up her nose at my choice of baby names. Statements like, “No one hides behind initials anymore,” or, “You want to call your child that?” As if it’s not a perfectly lovely combination. Honestly, I don’t know what she’s so bothered about. It’s not like I asked her for approval—it wasn't even a question in the first place.      Sometimes family can be a bit like that, really. But I get the impression her critique was more to stir things up than anything else. She probably didn’t mean it. Anyway, changing the subject—have you thought any more about learning a second language? It just occurred to me the other day that you’d be a great fit for some of these weekend classes at the university.      Not really, to be honest. I speak fluent French from years of holidaying in France with my mum, thanks to her sister. But I know barely a word of Spanish. Still, I'd quite like to improve for the sake of travel and for work. I did see that the press has a few initiative papers on bilingual cognition floating around.      Perfect! I’ll pop one on to you as soon as I can. And if you ever want company to keep you motivated with your study, I’m more than up for it. I’ve been dabbling in some basic German myself.

I just did a new mural in the town centre last week, do you lads know it yet? I saw it! You painted that one of the football team by the library, yeah? Got to say, it looked alright. Was it in oils or something else? Nah, acrylics, more vibrant that way. 'Course I reckon it'd stand out better if the wall didn’t look like it’d just been soaked! Haha, yeah, dump 'em in a fresh coat and you'll be on the front of the local rag within a week. I like to paint on my property too—houseplants, mainly. You know I’m doing an accent analysis workshop for year seveners soon. I’m trying to gather some examples from mates—what do you pick for the features of the Eastern English accent most of all? I’d say the 't' in words like “castle” comes across more, you know, clipped, not so rounded back as say the West Country. And we don’t say “fella” often—person, mate,老爷 up here! We might say “lud, innit” though. Me folks are still proper working rhythm in speech. That works. Also, I’ve got a question for you both: what are the cheapest ways of setting up a homestead? I’ve been reading up on smallholdings and land ownership and all that. If you’ve got a shed and a bike, you’re halfway there—get a chicken and some seedlings and call it a weekend reprieve. Haha, I about did that once—got the chickens, the seedlings, then I had to work a gig 150 miles away and came back to a chicken-free garden! That’s tragic. Maybe chickens need less hands-on care than cats. Though I reckon cats suffer the most in terms of being confined to the house. My own is a little mad, honestly. I know what you mean—my cat bites me when I’m writing English exercises. Not the ideal working partner. Still, I’m into teaching it like a hobby—had some go at martial arts once, if you've ever seen a bloke in his line in the UFC, it's like poetry with punches. Reckon I’d take fluoxetine to handle the punches, not against em. I stopped taking meds for anxiety a while back, been doing better with diet—trying the low-carb lark. I'm on the board game lark more these days, less the pills, more the patience.

Rather annoying driving today, isn't it? That car in front of mine was just moving so slowly. I had to wait forever at that red light on the way home. Honestly, I've been saving up for a reliable car. £2000 is all I've managed so far. Do you think it's worth the wait? I don't want to get stuck with another one that's all trouble.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I had a similar thing this morning. To be honest, I haven't even thought much about saving up for a new car myself. I drive my old one like three times a week mostly. I can't afford to replace it just yet, but it's beginning to worry me a bit. You know how expensive repairs can get these days. Maybe I should start setting money aside. But how exactly do you go about doing that? It's not like there's any spare cash when you're working part-time.      Exactly! It's not easy when you're both commuting, ordering online for essentials—and then the groceries. I’ve actually been using an app that helps me automate savings. It transfers small amounts each week straight into a separate account. It's only ten pounds at a time, but it adds up—and it's out of sight, out of mind. You might find it useful, actually. I mean, it's not much, but at least you're making a start.      That actually sounds like a good idea. I've never thought about that before. I guess I'm more of a live in the moment kind of person. Anyway, while we're on the subject, wants to cook something later? I'm thinking spaghetti Bolognese? Kind of about time I attempted something a bit meatier than the usual noodles and tomato sauce.      That sounds brilliant. I can barely cook myself a decent lasagne, but Bolognese I've made before. Just need to make sure I actually cut up the onions without crying. I'm told it's all about the chopping technique. Maybe you can help me practice your knife skills while we’re at it?      Oh, I'm a complete whiz with the veggies, but let’s be honest, I’m more likely to burn the pan than anything else. Look, I’ll chop if you promise not to laugh at my attempts at fine dicing.

Rather chilly this mornin', innit? Thought me ‘n the lads 'ave ‘ad a mince pie an’ brew before the visit today. D'you need a cuppa, love?      Yeah, please, I’d kill for a hot drink. It was proper cold on the way here, I swear the wind was like a frosty hooligan.      Oh Aye, this wind's got a bite, it 'as. I remember me nan used to say it was 'cause the North Sea was playing up again when it gets like this. You'd fetch the rug from the bed, mind—those legs o' yers, Steve.      Legs 'ave been fine for years, Dorrie. ‘Course, back o’ the other leg—well, it's been a bit slow this morning. Blamed the floorboards, mind you. Old buggers shift when you step wrong.      You two’s stories ever gettin' any less mad? I mean, nan and gramps, I thought I was gettin' the full book on York’s ghosts next!      Here now, don't be bein' like that. Steve, you reckon you've got time for a mince pie? I’ve just made 'em with the same recipe me mam used to—crumbly top, proper pinches of clove.      Oi! That’s your mam, innit? You someone who found an old box of recipe cards an’ a time machine?      Ha! That is a fine lad, Steve. Anyroad, Margery, I was thinkin’ we could have about five chairs ‘round the fire this evening, see the lads can have a chat o’ somethin’. They be havin’ a laugh while Steve does ‘is maths homework. My, ‘e must be clever, doin’ A levels an’ all.      Aye, ‘e'll be runnin’ the country soon enough. I bets ‘e’s good at figurein' out how many tins o' 'grub' we need to do the next big snowfall.      ‘E’s good, 'e is. Though I'll tell you now, our Steve’s real keen on probabilities—if you chuck a snowball at ‘im he'll work out odds it lands ‘pon yer hat. Proper pest sometimes.      Yeah, okay, you're all right with the insults, I’ve had it in for ‘Probability' since the start o’ this half. It’s like my brain’s got a laddu in it an’ won’t work right.      Oh, no laddu, nothin’ like that, you ‘ave to let it sink in. Like me first wedding—I thought I 'ad it worked out. Thought love was on a 110% chance, turns out it's more like a risk assessment, love.

Rather do share a drink and tales of our misadventures. I was just recalling the time when Hal and I, rather foolishly,決定 to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus.      Goodness me, that seems like ages ago now! I remember you were teaching in Saudi at the time and thought, perhaps we could use the sea as our holiday. But of course, not with a valid permit.      Oh, I remember that; you were teaching quite a bit of history and English to young men who were very keen on their literature, but not so much on sailing regulations.      And what happened, dear Hal? Were you caught red-handed?      Yes, indeed! The local navy caught us off the coast, and I still remember the look on their faces when they saw the bottle of wine we had for the journey. They were very polite, but firm. I think they were more shocked about the wine than the fact that we were unauthorized sailors!      I still laugh when I remember that—after being jailed for the night, we were allowed to take the boat back with a stern warning to apply for proper permits in the future.      I've heard quite a few of these sorts of tales from my days as a university lecturer. Once I was giving a talk on British literature in a small town in the North, and the local library was run by a man who had once been a retired sailor. He had a dental magazine collection that filled an entire room!      Funny you mention that, David. I had a similar encounter in my practice as a dental surgeon. One colleague, quite the sailing enthusiast, would bring back these magazines from every port the boat touched. We once had to document a case where a patient fell overboard and then barely survived the day.      My, what a series of adventures! And speaking of wine, did you know that in Saudi Arabia, it was a different story entirely—alcohol was non-existent for us when I was teaching there. We had to bring our own to the hotel every week!      Yes! They had such strict policies back then. I remember the first time I was caught with a bottle in the hotel room on a weekend, the concierge was so confused!      I suppose it all goes to show that sometimes our journeys can lead us into the most unexpected situations.

I can't believe the amount of time my son spends in the bathroom. Half the house is shut off when he’s got the shower on! It’s like he’s down there doing a gym routine I hear you! When my granddaughter gets like that, you swear you'll have to put in a eeny weeny passive solar thing to keep the heat from the shower! But honestly, it's a phase with that age group, isn’t it? Oh yeah, it's just worth it to have a private bubble bath after a hard day at school when your friends keep asking you why you're not coming out of the shower. That's just it, Rob. It's like they think you're doing something secret! The other day I overheard him persuading one of the school kids on the phone and I think he turned down a chance to go for a trip with the team. I just don’t know what to do. Well, I would say it's worth a chat to see what's going on. One time, I noticed my niece was getting really closed off and we found out she'd written in her diary about a crush at school. I tell you, it's like they live another country for a while. So is that why my Mate Laura stopped coming over? I mean, it's not like she’s the one who's in trouble, but like, I dunno what to say to her anymore. Laura? Well, I think she might’ve been stressed about a work experience week at a magazine production house. They’d arranged it with the school as a sort of opportunity for the kids to see what it’s like out in the world. Her essay about the trip picked the area of proofing services, so they said what the heck! That's really something. I remember when my stepson wanted to ‘referee’ the local guest speaker event at school, he ended up baby-sitting the speaker's child instead. Complained about it for weeks, but when he started doing it, you’d think he was a professional. So what do you do with your free time if you're not in the bathroom, not going out and not at the work experience thing go? Well, there are so many opportunities out there. I’ve seen that some parents team up with schools or scout groups to give some virtual tours.

Rather annoying driving up here in this traffic, innit? But I reckon it's worth it for truffle hunting tomorrow, yeah? I mean, I’m more of a football kind of gal, but this is mad exciting.      Oh, love truffles — wouldn't say no to a good cheese and truffle board, especially if one of 'em chefs we met yesterday's dishing up. I reckon that Anežka’s got more flair than half the chefs in Bolton. Imagine what she could do with a TV show or sommat. You lot never chase that kind of stuff, love watching telly like I do?      I do watch telly, Gran. There was this one show that My turkey watched, called Marco Polo. Fun to watch, even if I didn't get half the accents. But this place is cool. They sell American snacks in the stores — like M& Ms and breakfast cereal. Bucks more 'n in the UK though.      And the American snacks — felling indulgent now. Also, the cigarette situation is dodgy up here. Can’t see smoking being aloud in too many places. I’m not even a regular, but it’s annoying.      Smokers are always risking it. I remember when I got into stem cells at uni — it was all about preventing these addictions, really. But that’s the past. Now I’m more into management and strategy. Still, it’s interesting how education and health principles carry through in different careers — especially in a place like Croatia where everyone's a chef, midwife, or football star in another life.      Hey, football is big here too — saw loads of kids playing out in the village square. That My lad of yours, do you play?      Yeah, I do. My team got promoted last year. But it’s nothing like this — the fields here are like pitch perfect. Envy.      A bit of class on the football field never hurt nobody, love. Speaking of class, you know your stem cell research? I think it's time that type of academicky stuff comes with lunches like truffle risotto. Perks of the job, eh?      Pfft! Don’t get away goin' on about your job like it’s some big fancy thing.      I suppose it is a bit bloated compared to what your lot do. But at the end of the day, we’re all in it for growth — football, people, or businesses.      ‘Course, growth’s not all about fitting in new roles.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to warm up the stone steps properly. I got the feeling it's going to be one of those days where you can actually feel spring on your skin for once. Not quite like summer, but enough to make you smile.      Yeah, it  is  a treat for this time of year. I was actually out on a morning run before coming in, and I swear the air smelt sweeter than normal. It was quite inspiring, to be honest. Kept me motivated for the whole run through the park.      That’s nice, I mostly just made sure I left the flat at a decent time so I wouldn’t miss my lunch meeting. Although I must say, the weather’s a much more agreeable bonus than I expected. It makes this place feel altogether more welcoming somehow.      Cats are better than breakfast, no doubt about that. Well, not always — in fact, more usually, the milk is quite important, to be truthful. But I suppose once you've built that bond of trust with a cat, it's like a whole new world of affection opens up.      I'd say that only works if they're domestic cats, though. Stray ones are more likely to bite than to curl up in your lap. Though I've had the odd stray respond to the tap of a finger on their forehead like it's a command to roll over.      There’s also this funny thing with one of the office dogs. He just insists on fetching his tennis ball at exactly 3:00 every day, and honestly, it’s surprising no one has told him off for it by now.      That does sound quite the reliable creature. We have an office plant — no idea what kind it is — that's barely survived the attentions of the interns, to be honest, but for some reason it always waters itself right at 5:00 p.m. No one can figure it out, but it works.      I sort of miss the days when you had that sprite of vitality at 8:00 in the morning and you thought you could do anything. Now, you’re lucky if you can make it to the printer by 9:30 without your eyes closing.      You’re just not getting enough sleep. I always go to bed by 10 these days. It's all postgraduate fluency, really.

Rather annoying this new European traffic system, isn't it? I swear they've made it more complicated than it needs to be. But at least the campervan handles it all well, or so I'm told by the owner. Not like I’ve driven one often—just picked this up through a cousin in Manchester who’s into holidays like this.      Yeah, it's all digital these days. I’ve taught a few classes on language tech too—nothing beats face-to-face, of course, but you can't ignore how systems are moving. Still, the roads in Poland don't seem too different from what I’ve taught about in driver’s ed. Though I've never actually driven in Europe, strictly on the theory side.      Oh, left-hand driving takes some getting used to—even for someone who doesn’t pick up the stick often. But I suppose you're far more likely to be better at this, given your training and all. I still can't believe you're a teacher. Only looked 17, to be truthful.      Well, I was one of those who finished university early and got certified quickly. I like the structure it gives to my time and the real-world benefits. At least in-country—it's fun getting work placements in other countries. So is Tarnow?      Yes and no. It’s a bit of a sleepy town, don’t get me wrong. But for a weekend break and some company with our friends, it’s perfect. No hustle, no hassle—just peace. Perfectly normal for someone who’s had a rough time with work, don’t you think?      That’s all right. I’ve seen plenty of people about your age who’ve gone the same route. Some just take a different direction. I suppose what matters is not where you end up, but whether you have the freedom to enjoy it.      Exactly. That’s why I’m here—with a friend, and at least a bit of independence. If I can’t afford a mortgage or a decent job waiting at the end of the road, I can at least afford to live simply. Sometimes the best plan is no plan at all.      Defiance or acceptance? Hard to tell. But the points you make go hand in hand with life improvements sometimes. If nothing else, it makes for an interesting conversation when I’m planning group dynamics with learners.

Rather annoying this, innit? They’ve got the telly on but it’s muted, an' we’re just stare oot at them players runnin' abou’ like lunatics      Aye, can’ hear the commentary, mind you — wouldn't be surprised if it’s eeny weeny  McDonald's  advert again. They’ve basically sponsor all the lads these days. A lot o' red shirts in this lot, innit?      Aye, and you no what? They’re wearing the new strip, the one with the big yellow sponsors' logos down the side!  Mate , it's like someone's spag 'o' on the shirt front an’ back. You c'n barely see the club crest. Ten o'clock on a Sunday an’ them shirts look like a bloomin’ advert for takeaways an’ cars.      Aye, I've noticed. They're gettin’ a bit outta hand, these corporate sponsor bits. It’s not the football we came to see, it’s the ads. Like, why are we watchin’ the side mascot in a McDonald's uniform doin' a little dance on the half time break? It’s not what football used to be about.      Mate, I know right! Used to be it was just a bit o' red an' white an' you could see the player’s name. Now it’s like they been paid to look like a walkin’ billboard. Honestly, I’d rather just have the old classic strips. Look at what they did to this lot's red and white. Now look at 'em —  they’ve gone Prime Sports at Appleby Road Club .      Oh come on, it’s part of the business now. Clubs need the sponsorship to plug the holes in their budgets. No one's investing in grassroots, so for the big clubs, it’s McDonald's here, Vodafone there — they'll take it. I mean, think about it, it's not like we're not getting our telly feed for free.      Aye, but why do they have to plaster the adverts all over the place? Still, I suppose it’s better than some of the foreign clubs goin' on about their 'traditional patterns' an’ ramming sponsors into the design, making it look like a bloody box of Smarties.      True. I mean, at least this way, we get a cheap burger after the match for half price. Still worth it in the end, innit?      Oh yeah, so all that nonsense at half-time was worth it

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what it's like – trying to get eBay orders tracked and it's like they've vanished into the ether.      Yeah, I mean, where is it? £20 spent, and no sign of it. No wonder people lie about it on job seekers now, eh? You just sit there wondering where the cash is going.      A lot of people would rather lie about benefits than face reality, but I'm not one of 'em. I've been claiming for a bit now, but it's not the worst. You just get used to it, even if it's dead boring.      That's the lot of us at the moment, isn't it? Sitting around with no real plan. I had this idea about a day trip with the kids in the spring – somewhere with a train, you know? Made it sound like it'd be loads of fun. But with the state of the trains nowadays, you're as likely to get stranded as not.      I remember that! Mum was getting annoyed, thinking we were taking them all upriver or something. Like a week to organise and it only took two seconds.      Exactly! But it was all good fun. I miss them – Matey's got a sneaky knack for making slap-up meals off a George Formsman or whatever it's called. You couldn't even call it ‘fixin’ your dinner, it was more like someone else did it for you.      He's oddly good at that kind of thing, is him. So much better than being able to hold a conversation! Most people are better off just buying about five meals off Deliveroo.      Oh I know. And cooking on that George failsman is like telling you’re a competent person. Either way, I'd rather be cooking than staring at the wall for another day.      I remember when you would always complain about bills, though. Gas and elect, you know? Like there was some conspiracy to make you poor.      There  is  a conspiracy, innit? I took the kettle off, for chrissake, and it was like the system was set go up £100 if you blinked once.      I don’t see it. I'm a bloomin’ student, and I’m managing. It's about priorities, to be honest. I mean, you can’t really argue with people spending money to pay off the inheritance or whatever they call it.

Rather annoying when the sat nav goes wrong, isn’t it? I was driving up to Chester last week and it got me completely lost in some village I’d never heard of! Kept saying we’d arrived long before we actually did. Charming cows, though.      Sat navs are eeny weeny, I say. I use the good old map on my phone – yes, most a the time I can find me way. Course, I don’t go far from home. Last trip worth mentionin’ was to Kettering. Gave me chase through them roundabouts. Tore me nerves like.      Aww, technology today! When I was younger, we relied on letters an’ postmen. Still, best to have it, I suppose. I had me own warts on me legs and I used to patch round ‘em with band-aids. Now they’re gone. Health is a prime thing to worry about, after all.      I agree, especially with the way we eat these days. One minute it’s healthy meals, the next it’s a Mars bar and a Diet Coke. I try, honestly! Still, I’ve taken to cooking on weekends. Freezing meals helps—very organisational.      Freezing? Oh no, I don’t fancy last night’s swill for dinner today. I’m all convenience stores for me. Pop in, grab a packet of fish fingers, slap it in the oven. Straight out again with the bin. Life’s short.      I remember when meal was a proper affair. Meat and two veg, and no ‘silly’ dietary nonsense. My George used to cook a fine pie. I miss us suppers round the table, passin’ the grace and a good chat.      I’d love to do that more often. Work has me on ‘edge’—I’m constantly chasing targets. It’s tough. But at least I don’t have a boss giving me side-eyes like yesterday when I misspoke about a client’s budget!      Aye, always trying with your workin’ life, I know. Some days, I’d be laughin’ so hard by the end the day I’d go home breathless. One man wanted antiseptic cream at the shop, and I tripped and dropped a whole basket of nappies on the floor. He was in fits.      Romans, we’d say those days, never had belly laughs like that. Tell me about that ‘plane crash’ the papers were hyped about last month—close call all over the world, they said.

Rather annoying when half the students bring up social networking when they mean social engineering, if you take my meaning. No, I take it back,  never —I’d rather sit in here and read the Dewey Decimal system by candlelight.      Same here. I tried to explain once that citing a Facebook post is as useful as citing a dream. Next thing you know, we’re debating the credibility of memes versus academic journals. Exceptionally creative, bordering on alarming.      That’d make for one hell of a thesis, wouldn’t it?

Rather than going the traditional route of converting a serviced office, I think we should consider building purpose designed facilities. It’s the wave of the future. Otherwise, we’ll end up with something that doesn’t quite meet the needs of the patients or the staff.      That’s an interesting point. We’re beginning to run out of space at both the existing locations. If we use an estate agent to help find a permanent site now, we can ensure that this project isn’t rushed. But are you sure it’s reasonable to ask for private funding to buy the land when the NHS is already struggling with budgets under political pressure?      I’m not sure it is, but the rationale for choosing a new location goes beyond that. It involves optimising access for local patients within the health service and building closer relationships with the existing hospices, which are already stretched. A central location—something in the Tunbridge Wells area perhaps—would give us a prime position to serve everyone here.      I hear what you’re saying, but building something new is a costly and time-consuming process. The consultation will need to include the local patients, of course—perhaps I can begin drafting a health impact assessment and business case. We need to present this in a way that shows how it will improve existing services without disrupting what is already in place?      Exactly. And it won’t be long before the local authority will want to know how this will affect their provision and budget allocations. If we don’t act now, there’s someone else in the area who will try to step in and build something different.      That’d be a shame. What I want here is a structure that brings more nurses in, provides a safe and serene environment at end of life, and supports the families of patients. I imagine something modern and modular, possibly even part of an estate that includes shared facilities with other care providers?      Something like that. If construction is part of the future, we’ll want to use modern building techniques—sustainability being as important now as it is for our organisation. I’ll get one of my contractors to reach out to propose some building concepts once we've got the business case finalised.      That sounds like a good plan. Just make sure that the proposal is backed up with details on how it ties into our current organisational goals and how it will benefit the community in the long term.

Rather than share a passion for books and travel, perhaps we could talk about something else, such as work or current events. I've often found that poetry has more depth than straightforward narratives, don't you agree?      Hmm, I understand your point about poetry, but I can’t lie — when I read fiction, I often feel transported somewhere new, like I’m actually walking the streets of Paris or a bustling Moroccan market. Isn’t that the best part?      I suppose it is, but it’s always been more important to me for literature to chase a feeling or an idea. Would you even consider giving it a go?      If you insisted I would, I suppose, but I’m more convinced by a crackling good story over something cute and whimsical. Then again, I do keep meaning to revisit  Dubliners  — it's set in a city I’ve yet to visit, and I reckon go there armed with James Joyce, you'd be a real charmer.      I’d be behind you with a dram and a sandwich — all part of the literary tourism package.

So, I just wanted to run through the whole job application with you before I hit send tomorrow morning. It’s in the City, at a firm called Arthouse Design. Rather annoying to be honest, the amount of work needed in that old warehouse space. Well, if we can drum up enough additional income via the furniture sales and the kiosk proposal, perhaps go back to the directors and suggest a more flexible pay or part-time arrangements.

Rather lovely to be here in Hereford, isn’t it? A bit chilly for this time of year, but the cottage is cosy enough. I was just admiring the garden from the window. It’s a shame we couldn’t have a fire going outside, like back home in Cape Town.      That would be something, wouldn’t it? Having a fire on the beach with all that sun? I reckon that sounds like paradise. Not that this place isn’t nice. Warm cup of tea and all that. Still, haven’t had the best of luck with the outside chill yet today.      Right, I’ve sorted the soup—tomato and basil, the classic, only with a few bits of crouton on top. Thought you lot might fancy something a bit heartier, given the weather.      I think it turned out rather nicely, actually, considering the lack of proper culinary breakfasts—this morning I just happened upon some odd-looking eggs, and they were charred by 45 seconds in the pan. Still, the soup smells like something that might actually hold your attention, apart from the cold beer I cracked open earlier.      I’ve been volunteering for a charity today in nearby Hereford—it was fun, really. Met a few local folks. Nothing too taxing, though: mostly just sorting through donations, making cards for children. Some of them were quite adorable—bright, optimistic things. You know what it is, don’t you? It’s the people that make places come alive.      That sounds very inspiring, love. I remember working in something very similar a few years back—supporting older people at a care home. Nothing as lively as your lot, mind you. They liked the same stories each day, which had its ups and downs.      Let’s not talk about stories and volunteers. Let’s talk about food. My sister once tried to make treacle tart for a family meal, and ended up creating something that looked more like a brick than a tart. We haven’t spoken about it since. I still stick to my recipes as written. Fool’s errand otherwise.      That’s what I do with bread recipes. My first loaf was a disaster. Took three tries before the bloke even go so much as a sniff from the dog. Still, I think I’m on the upswing now.      Time to lay off your ego and pass the soup ladle over.

I can't believe we've never done a weekend trip together before. Sheffield looks nice for a day out. We could grab a bite, maybe catch a film later? Blows the cobwebs away after another week stuck in the office. I'd kill for a day like that. My in-laws came round at the weekend and it got a bit much. Full on tea every day, not a bit of peace. What time you thinking? Got a car sorted, so we can just go as it suits us. Yeah, and no need for the hassle of trains. You up for getting the wander on after breakfast? Say ten? I reckon there's a quaint little café in the city centre that sells the best scones I've ever had. Nothing like a bit of carb to start the day, innit? Scones and adventure, sounds brilliant. Got a bit breakfast envy now. You up for a coffee before? I'll grab a cup, you grab the snacks, and we'll hit it. Also, we might pop into that vintage record shop I mentioned, if we've time. Saw some new vinyl in there yesterday. Now you're speaking my language. Bet they've got some vinyl that'd make a nice addition to that little collection of yours. Should we check the roads, though? I heard something about traffic on the M1 this morning. Should be okay. Last I checked the traffic updates, they said it was all clear. Best to drive with a grin and just hope it stays that way. I'll also pop a crate of some fresh fruit and veg in the boot. Can't be slipping up on the healthy stuff now we about to live off scones and brie! Oh yes, definitely need some balance. Let's not let the healthy stuff handle it all, though. Got some of that lemon drizzle cake left from last night if we are going for that sweet hit.
