You know, I'd walk through fire for you and your cake. Just stick the key in the ignition and off we go. Let's make the lunches, keep the snacks ready, and hit the road. Manchester's just beyond, after all. Popping into the record shop can go hand in hand with a quick bite or two. And that's the line in the sand, really. Ready when you are.

Rather annoying the queue at the surgery this morning, wasn't it? I had to get my blood pressure checked before the scan. Never mind, it is what it is I suppose. Have you been in recently?      Aw, yeah, I had to pop in a week ago after missing my period and beginning to feel a bit off. It was all right, if you know what I mean. Though I didn’t get anywhere with the diet I tried this month. Still feeling under the weather.      Please! You and diets. They never work for anyone in the long run. You know what my sister says? That it's just a matter of not overdoing the takeaway, and keeping up with the exercise. My GP keeps saying I need to get my levels checked more regularly, but I’m terrified I’m already on the way to diabetes.      It must be tough, having to think about that sort of thing when you've got other things on your mind. Like my mum, poor thing. She's going to be buried next week, and I'm still trying to help sort out the arrangements, which is easier said than done when I’m short-staffed as it is. grief is hard, ain't it?      Yes. Absolutely. When my father passed last year, the whole estate was in chaos. My brother, he just shut down completely. Barely spoke to anyone for weeks. And the whole will was a mess. You don’t talk about these things enough in this country, in my opinion. But you carry on, don’t you?      Yeah, you do. It's just life and being there for each other. I suppose it’s better when your kids understand how you feel. My girls are quite the handful still, but at least they showed a bit of compassion when I was upset.      That does mean a lot to have your family support you. I’ve always told my class that emotions are important. And it's strange, it's a funny thing, love and loss.      I reckon. We lost my grandad not that long ago. Even though he was 92, the whole whanau was in shock. My grandad used to tell me stories by the fire, and now it's just memories on the mantelpiece.      You know, I was just thinking about how we go from blooming blossoms to these piles of dust.

Rather skip ahead a bit here. So I've done a few days proofreading for a publishing house in Leeds... got to say, it's a real change from marketing campaigns! How's school treating you lads these days?      It's alright, I guess. Loads of writing and all that. But I don't think I want to do that when I finish school. Maybe something a bit more... practical, like Dad's doing.      Practical, eh? Like pulling levers and pushing buttons in the office? Just want to keep it real – marketing can be brilliant, but it does involve a lot of PowerPoint.      That's very kind of you to say, love. Still, enough about work. It’s the weekend, and I reckon skiing in the Alps is far more fun than the office. Or did I mention about the trip to the Austrian breakfasts and fondue?      Fondue? Really? That sounds, like, mad. I mean, why would you put that cheese in one pot and, like, dip bread in it?      What’s to like, like? It's proper fancy, innit? You reckon I'd work it in then?      Oh Mate, you wouldn’t last five minutes. Far too keen on the après-ski and not quite so keen on the early mornings for glaciers and all that.      There’s also this funny thing in the Alps called the “avalanche simulator” they’ve got at some of the resorts – something to do with a skier named Alf being scared of snowmobiles! We all laughed there because it made about as much sense as marketing jargon.      You're going off a bit, aren't you? But seriously, I've got this project at school on cars and the future, like electric vehicles and all. Do you think that’s going to be the next big wave in the business world? ‘Cause I fancy talking about that instead of ski stories!      Electric cars? Yeah, of course. The future’s with that tech. I’ve told my team at the plant, no more road trips in the company vans by 2030 or go out of business. If I was building a car, I’d go for that green hydrogen stuff – but nobody ever remembers to change your diaper when you mention it at dinner.      Yeah, I'm into that, too. I've been to a farm talk about zero-emission vehicles – the farmer was more into cows than cars, I reckoned.

I just found this old box of photos in the attic — remember when we went to Japan for that photography trip? It feels like another lifetime ago. Oh my goodness, I remember! That was such an incredible trip. Do we still have the photo of us at the top of the mountain — the one I insisted we pose dramatically for with the badgers? You mean the one where the badgers were clearly not impressed with your dramatic side? I don’t remember quite that clearly, but I know someone once mistook you for a character in a horror film during the festival because of that photo. Horrors! I  was  a character in a horror film, only minus the make-up and actors. Remember when we got lost trying to get to the temple and ended up following a pack of badgers for half the day? How could I forget? They were oddly friendly. Wait, is that photo of the badger family still in the box? I swear, that photo looked like they were judging our wedding planning notes. Yes, that one’s in there, along with the one of you trying to sneak food to the temple cats as if you were supplying an army. Honestly, you’ve got a heart for animals, but it’s only matched by your inability to remember the name of a single species. Okay, okay, but the photo of the baby badger rolling in the leaves still managed to go viral back home! I swear, those pictures could’ve paid the rent. That was only because the captions you came up with were so ridiculous. Also, I think the internet enjoyed the contrast between your serious journalistic photos and your badger selfies. Fair point. I think I prefer the serious stuff — but I have to admit, watching you try not to laugh when I dressed as a local photographer with a kimono and mismatched binoculars for the festival was worth every awkward shot. And I prefer to believe it was a homage to traditional culture. At least no one tried to charge us for tour guide services after that. True. But speaking of the photos, I think it’s time we made a photography-themed book out of these trips. Then we can truly capture the magic of Japan — badgers included. If we include the hilarious captions, it’ll definitely be a bestseller. Who knew badgers could be the literary sensation of Norfolk?

So, I heard you lot were in Ireland last summer, Sarah. What was it like? I passed through Dublin once and thought it was mad—full of music and green! Any craic?      Oh, we had a bit of fun—definitely one night when it was raining so hard, we went skinny dipping in a lake near Killarney. Of course, all the locals thought we were mental!      Honestly, I’m terrified of cold water. But I did get to try this incredible Jewish food from a family running a little deli in the west. Smelled divine—like Claudia Roden’s cookbook made real.      Claudia Roden? You like that one? I’ve read her too. Fun fact—I lived in Sydney for a while and I cooked a lot, mostly for mates in the café I worked in. Jewish recipes aren’t common Down Under, but I tried a few things just for laughs. Haha—terrible at it, to be honest.      Oh, I once tried to make that famous brisket recipe she recommends—personally, it was absolute chaos in my kitchen. But as it turns out, the real killer in my place is my neighbor—it wasn't the food, it was the snoring.      True story—my least favorite part of living in East London is my roommate's snoring. It’s so loud, I've considered wearing headphones to sleep. What's up with people just starting at full volume without warning?      Haha, I definitely prefer baking in silence—especially at 5 a.m. being quiet is essential if I’m to get customers in by 7.      You bakers should come over to Australia—there’s a café culture there that leaves you speechless. Everyone loves coffee, it’s kind of in their DNA. But personally, I’d rather be sipping something than making it.      I’d swap any bloody zombie apocalypse for a café in Bondi or something. I could stick out the apocalypse as long as I had constant coffee and good company.      Well, if the apocalypse hits, I’m calling in the poetry. I like writing the odd poem—keep it up on my own if I ever need to go off-grid and find some catharsis. You know, poetry lives forever.      Now that’s something I can get behind. Oh and one more thing—someone taught me a Jewish joke in Ireland: “Why don’t Jewish ghosts haunt houses?”

Rather annoying when a bar’s peanuts run out, innit? I was just in this little place in Leeds... no peanuts, no crisps—just a bowl of boiled sweets. I was nearly in tears!      Hah, I know what you mean. I had a night in Coventry once and there  wasn’t  one bloody nut within miles. But I’ve got to say, I’ve taken to bringing my own bag in now. Old habits, I suppose. It was easier when you were a kid and they just served the peanuts automatically.      Told you my mates, I said. I mean, imagine going to watch a film and no one can do a pop corn machine properly. I went to see  Ready Player One  last week and the lot was like rocks, them and the salt I think was turned to salt bricks.      Yeah, I see what you’re sayin’ but still... Game in there at the end, the way they rendered the arcades, near had me shoutin’ at the screen. I mean, do you remember playin’ Space Invaders back in the day? Like a week to earn credit and only ten pence.      Aw, yeah! Ten pence got you nothin’. My nan had one at the back, like, that old Texas machine. I had a go on it once and nearly fell through the floor. Still, ‘80s games been a big hit in this research I’m doing. Strictly for nostalgia though—no rush to buy ’em at auction prices.      You’d want a weekend at Margate if you fancied a good retro arc  about now. I hear they’re putting a whole area together near the pier—mainly 90s games, but that’d plug me in for a day. Still, I bet the security there’s tighter than the new EU guest worker rules passed last week. They’re all dossin’ round on any ‘open border’ talking now.      Honestly? I’m with you. I mean, I live in Cambridge, with people coming through the door from everywhere. Not sayin’ no one should be allowed in, but it’s a man’s job to go out and get your own if you want a job done. Gave my line in the paper last week. Said it was bloomin’ high time we stood our ground.      You and me both. I’m startin’ to wonder what this PhD’s gonna be for if I end up doing reports on food and them alone.

I can't believe I've never rowed before. I remember watching the Cambridge v Oxford race on TV when I was younger and thinking it looked absolutely brutal. It's not like football, where you can just kick a ball for 90 minutes and feel like a legend later! Oh, it's not that bad, honestly. I took it up about a year ago and it actually helped me with a bit of balance from my kayaking before that. I got a blisters on my hands at first, but once you get used to the oars and the rhythm, it's like second nature. You'd probably like it. I'd love to try it out, only my sister Alice managed to get me a membership at the club near Grantchester. She's been doing it for years now, and I suppose it's good I'm finally getting round to it. I was about to ask you if you know, do you actually need to wear special shoes or anything in case it gets wet? Actually, yes. You can wear flat-soled trainers or walking boots. I do both, depending on the day. And if I’m going out in a storm like last weekend, I tend to wear my old gear: a waterproof jacket, proper walking shoes and then a pair of neoprene socks just in case I capsize, and trust me, it does happen more often than you think. Ugh, I can already foresee me slipping and falling into the water in just my gym shoes. But anyway, I suppose my real issue is just getting out of the house with all this weather. I had a phone call from my mum recently—do you remember when she spoke about my great-uncle John? Oh right, she had this story about him cooking what he thought was a roast that was actually some kind of preserve. I remember laughing about that. My sister had visited her just the other week, actually. Said your mum was holding up pretty well. I'm told it was quite an emotional moment when they met for the first time in a while. Yes, it was. He passed away recently, a couple of months ago. It took the whole family by surprise. But something amazing happened—I was told the funeral was really gothic and my cousins ended up playing some kind of jazz at it.

I can't believe today's results day! You think they'd do something better than just post it online at like... midday an' all. I know, I remember when I got me 'O' levels. We had to wait outside the hall wi' our fingers crossed an' everything. een't like now, where we can just scroll 'n see if we passed. Aye, but I still got t' wait for ages for my friends. We were texting each other like it was Morse code or sommat. That's the new Morse code, innit. I still don't get these emojis. Me daughter sends me a face wi' a tongue and expects me t' know what it means! Dad, that's the confused one! D'you even know what half the ones I send even mean? Not really. But I know if I see a frowning face I’d better start panicking. Anyway, we're supposed t' meet up wi' the rest o' the family for dinner. Let me tell you—my phone's acting up again. I think Vodafone’ve gone to their holidays early. Try turning it off an' back on again. That always works. Or call customer services. I borrowed Mums' last night, because mine was on charge. They weren’t funked up to answer anything. Aye, I might. I’ve got an order from Amazon in an' it’s not arrived yet. I wish they’d just chuck it on the door like they used to. Or at least send it through eBay—those lads are alright, they make it in about five days. Have you still got that glass water bottle from a few years back? It leaked water all over me shoes last time. Aye, I've put it in the guest room. I'm not daft. I remember where the bin is. Good, 'cos I'm waiting till we get t' the dinner an' then I'm doing a load of shopping with lunches and veg and stuff from the Co op. We need proper meals for once, not just pasta and beans! Aye, an' if you're going, you might wanna pick up some more pens. I’ve filled out the student finance form an' I can't find a biro. Oh, I’ve got em in me bag. Just like new ones. I had t' buy ‘em yesterday cos the last pair wouldn’t work when I was applying for uni.

Yo, mate, long time no see! Thought you’d still be buried in books or working that bar shift every weekend. What's been up?      Nah, man, uni is done for now. Just finished the summer term—  massive   relief, I gotta say. Passed every single module, so I got some time to breathe before I panic about next year. But I’ve been working a bit to save up for this trip I’m planning.      Honestly, I’ve been stuck doing the same. Didn’t even want to touch coursework ’til the last minute. I’ve just been chilling, eating takeaway, and watching the dumbest netflix shows. You like that My Hero Academia one?      Bro, I ain’t watched that in a minute, but I   did   just buy a ticket to Tokyo. My cousin is moving there for work and invited me up to visit. I’m flying in October. You’d be amazed by how much I’m ordering online for the trip—just looking at ramen, bento boxes, and, yeah, inappropriate anime.      No way, you’re going to Japan? That’s insane. I’ve been saving up for a little trip too. Was thinking about booking a hostel in Kyoto or something. I’ve read so much about Hayao Miyazaki and anime culture there. You gonna recomend any restaurants for me?      Ain’t you just someone? Keep it up and you’ll be fluent in Japanese by the time we travel. Anyway, you should try this place my cousin wants to take me to in Shinjuku—it’s like a ramen festival in about five square feet. They fly you round the world for different bowls. Man, they even serve black garlic butter ramen there.   Yawns and licks lips.        Mate, you’re not even expressing how weird that sounds. I’m into it, though. I was just saying to my mates I dunno how people eat ramen every day. Feels like overkill after being academically fried all term.      Honestly, man, it's like after a serious run with a snack bar. That's how go-to it is for life after exams or boring lectures or just generally when you feel dead inside. Anyway, you need to start planning your trip soon. Financially, you might be slimmer, but not wiser.      Fair point, but I’ve been on the lookout for budget stuff—hostels, group tours, that kind of thing.

Rather annoying when Facebook just won't play ball with the old phone. I was just trying to upload some photos from our trip to Buckfast Abbey the other week, and I ended up on the ground where my phone and I were both left quite confused. Was the abbey at all well maintained in your opinion, Speaker_2?      It was lovely, quite atmospheric. I enjoyed all the stained glass windows and the quietness too. I think that place has a certain peace about it. It was quite interesting as it was one of the first places I visited when I arrived in the South.      Yes, young ones. I've made a few visits there in the past, and I do remember the stone walls and the calmness. I must say though, I find this obsession with photos on Facebook rather odd, but maybe that's just old-age speaking.      Fair enough Speaker_3. I, myself, actually find this whole concept of a cruise in the near future quite thrilling. I remember Speaker_2 ordering a group photo when we went to the pub last week—vibrating like mad—personally I think taking up occasional space in the land of digital memories is quite human of us, old-school or not.      Ah, cruise then. That might be a good move. I remember David Cameron making some comment on tax avoidance once—it certainly created some ripples in the press.      Oh yes, and we were at that point, huh? Our car just wouldn't start last week. I had to ring a friend to give me a jump. Some mechanical problem, but it's now been fixed and being diligent about insurance is all I can say, really.      I hear you. I had the same problem with my car last month. To be honest, I think it's easier to fix a car than it is Facebook these days.      Well, you young ones should take care of your vehicles. And if you're thinking of a cruise, make sure it's fully covered. I remember my wife passing on some tale about visiting the Mayo Clinic. Though I don't recall the full story now, I think it was related to various preventive measures. That's where you get serious about your health.      Actually, I've been meaning to ask about that. Maybe one of these days you can give us that full tale. But back to the main point, your suggestion of a cruise could be a great way to relieve the stress of everyday life.

Rather skip the new phone for now. You know, me and mine had a right old time with SAT Nav when we crashed in Mons by mistake. Otherwise, Belgium was brilliant! The markets were packed, and the waffles—absolute £20 spread, I tell you! But motorway tolls nearly broke us; all the Euros and the reader not working properly 'cos I'd forgotten to clear the UK memory. Had a gelato from a little stall in Belgium too—cheaper than Brighton but not by much, interestingly. Pity we couldn't cycle the whole way; the roads are too full with lorries. I like to think of it mostly because I can talk about it when the people at university ask where I've been. My lectures are all online these days. Oi, Mum, when you go to the shops, do check if the milk's in the chiller. I need it for my oats.      Buckshee? Cheaper ice creams? I'll not believe it, love. I remember we got bottled-in at Brussels. Kept taking wrong turns, and that phone of yours wouldn’t switch off the UK maps properly—had half the motorway gridlocked as it tried to recalculate for us. Nothing like a Dutch farmer watching us fumble. Still, Brussels was alright. Excellent beer at the Mate Real café, fairly reasonable, and the food was fresh-off-the-truck, no doubt. All that said, the phone’s memory is a bit temperamental at times. Lost our hotel in Charleroi once. But the chocolate! That stuff was a rush of nostalgia, sour and sweet—piece of my childhood wrapped in a truffle. Anyhoo, I’ve had enough of Belgium for a lifetime, about time I’m rooted back in Harlow.      Not much cheaper in Belgium—that fails to surprise me. Still, I’m jealous. I’d have loved to have seen a farmers’ market with you lot. All right, I did manage a few weekend breaks to the local farms where I work, but it's not quite the same. You mustn’t stick too much trust in your navigation apps being 100%. I’ve delivered a couple of patients to the wrong location because of it. Still, I did find this lovely snack shop the other day— go there on my day off if you like creamy cheese or Belgian chocolates made into dentists’ nightmares. You might like it, bloke.

Rather do this than watch telly, innit? Bit easier than the hurly-burly in town... What d'you think about starting on that pie?      Oh, absolutely! Got it in me mind to do a bit of mince pie — wouldn't you fancy a bit of eeny weeny  jam  on top?      Aye, that'd be a grand idea. I've got some Christmas cranberry stuff I bought last year but forgot what to do with 'til now! Put it in the fridge for later.      Mithose? Get the mixing bowl ready. I'd also be grateful for a short cut on the crust, do you have that posh turkey one left over?      Aye, there it is – I've saved it special, thought I'd be the only one to take it for granted. Mm better than breakfast, no doubt about that!      Aye, posh stuff. I remember that fella down the pub told a tale the other day, said that man of yours with the big booming laugh, what's 'is name again? Adrian?      Oh, Adrian, that fancy one from York… Sounds like fun, by the way, he told you that he used to be a bus driver?      That’s the one. Anyway, back to our pie—should we spritz a little perfume or no?      Perfume in food? Well, no, but I’ve got a vanilla one that smells divine, leftover from some Christmas gift—maybe a tsp in the batter? For an extra zing?      You know I love how you always think outside the box. But talking of different, I had a chat with Ron yesterday—he said he caught that new BBC show about accent differences. Rather up for watching that later?      Aye, well if we are going to speak up at me grandkids one day, better know all the lingo.      Haha, good crack! Speaking of which, have you noticed how Monica always knows the first to pop on Facebook with those dozen flowers? Was it daisies or daffodils last time?      Mithose? If I see daffodil, I swear I shall tickle her, she's always the first blooming on her birthday.      That's the spirit! While we’re at it, we can set the fire going for Atmosphere to come on—like that ‘Harry Potter’ film or whatever.      Oh go on then, that's brilliant! Clarissa always says the fireplace's romantic.      Likewise! Oh, and I fancy taking a trip to Fleet Street after this—heard about a few good conversations brewing out there.

Rather unusual to find oneself in a room full of utter strangers, isn't it? Though I've lived in Bristol all my life, I've never much ventured beyond the south, myself. I think I might be one of them Southerners you hear so much about—very posh, obviously.      Aye, I understand the sentiment. Having grown up in Manchester, I've always been a bit of a northern chap, but I fancied a bit of a change and spent a few years in Australia. That Queensland! Hotter than the pits and crawling with more redbacks than I cared for.      Oh, I've been there too! Queensland is the real deal, if you ask me. But what’s strange is that I met an eccentric gentleman from Sheffield—what a dialect they’ve got there, can’t pick it up in a week! Half the time I was about to laugh at what he was saying—like when he said “bairn” in place of “child.” Makes you remember that dialect can separate people more than the distance between continents.      Indeed, it truly does! I must say, I always found Sheffield's accent quite charming. Though, I only ever got as far as Bristol on a train, never further. Still, when I got offered a job at the language institute in Sheffield a few years ago, it was a riot listening to the locals—some of those phrases would have confused the willow trees!      And let’s not forget what someone wears in business. In Australia, you can just turn up in a pair of preferably tattered flannel trousers and a shirt with the sleeves rolled up—though I did manage to scare off a few Aussies in about five minutes by appearing a bit overdressed from their perspective.      To be fair, I wore proper business attire to my lectures and it helped a lot with the students. Though, I tried to keep it rather less formal toward the end of the term. Still, I remember one student told me I was “classy” in a way only a Northern Englishman could. It was as mysterious as a bank loan system in the 1970s.      Was it really that complicated? I remember once trying to get a small loan to set up a language school in Bristol, and it required about ten letters of recommendation, a doctor’s note, and a detailed family tree.

Rather annoying, the amount of time people spend swiping on that social media lark, don't you think? It's rather like watching paint dry, honestly.      Oh, I know what you mean. Though honestly, I find it kind of necessary these days. It helps keep in touch with students and colleagues, especially with the time zones and all. Plus, there's all sorts of interesting educational stuff that pops up too. Not that I'd call social media inspiring, mind.      Well, you're in the business and might need it more, but still. I'd rather fetch the newspaper from the corner shop. Proper news, not whatever someone's spouting on a platform with a like counter.      The corner shop’s a bit of a relic, I reckon. D'you know, I used to read The Guardian online most days, but now I prefer podcasts. I've been listening to 'The History of English' one in my car. It’s fascinating, actually — how the language evolved from dead old scripts into what we speak now.      Oh for goodness’ sake, I might have known you'd turn it into a lecture. But fair, I fancy history too. Still watching that BBC documentary trotting around with all the “relevant national monuments”? Mate, I got the gist, and I know the difference between a castle and a cathedral. It's enough to make you want to chuck the remote out the window at times.      Well, it is a bit slow. But there's something to be said for a bit of fluff, is there not? I mean, it’s not all history and education for me, either. I binged this sitcom about dating gone wrong — “Bridget Jones’s Baby” vibes. Honestly, you could write a better script with a pen and blindfold.      My, you've gone hard on the waters. All that post-grad work and you can’t write it off a blindfold? I once tried it — wrote about a cat persuading a biscuit to come off the shelf. Nonsense, but it topped the lunches of a couple of whippersnappers at the next table. Still, I’m more of a TV snob. Don’t go wasting my time with trash if you don’t mind. Show me something with a bit of meat, not just filler.      Okay, fair enough. I have been watching this true crime docu-series about poachers in Romania, though. It was pretty gripping.

Rather than going out today, we might do a bit of swimming. The pool's closing time is in a couple of hours. What do you two fancy doing?      I want to go and see ANON's Travelling Circus! I saw it on the motorway the other day. They have a horse there, daddy said.      Yeah! And they have that donkey with the funny hat too. Do you think we can see it again, Mummy?      We can definitely pop by the circus later. Let’s get changed and then we can head there. But first, let's finish our sandwiches. Then, we’ll grab our swimming stuff.      Can we take our new jellyfish floaties, Mummy?      Of course, and I think Pippy might be quite jealous of you two splashing around! Wait, I nearly forgot—before we go, let me get in touch with ANON. She looked after you last week and showed you both the Great British Egg Experiment, didn’t she? I do hope you thanked her properly.      Oh yes! We told her she was the best babysitter. We even got a photograph for the Blue Peter Badge.      Yeah – it was of us feeding ducks, and ANON took it on her phone. She printed it out for us later.      That’s lovely! She always loves those kind of things. Now, before we race off to the pool, shall we talk about something else? You both mentioned something the other day about passports and how old ANON is. I think she’s in her twenties, but I’m not sure.      Oh, she said she had to get a new passport last year because her old one had gone out of date.      And she told us she was born in Manchester. Do you know what year that would have been, Mummy?      If she’s in her twenties, she was probably born in 1994 or 1995. Do either of you know what year we’re in?      2024!      Yes! Now, let’s get our swimming stuff so we can go. Oh, and remember that joke about the Chinese eating old eggs?      The ones that are over 1000 years old?      Exactly! True to life, it isn’t—a very silly one, but ANON told it to you the other night, I think. Always keeps things interesting, doesn’t she?      Yeah, we made her laugh when we told it back to her last week.      I know, she does them all.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what me an' the lads get up to when we're off the leash, but them bobbies are more nosy than ever these days      Aye, we do try an' keep things low-key, but sooner or later someone spills eeny beans      Not 'ere in Leeds, I hope! Everyone knows everyone round these parts      Yeah, I got me 'ead in me hands last week when someone mentioned a party me and the lads had at me cousin's barn      Gettin' caught with some dodgy cider and a fella's hand up a lassie's cardy? My word, you lot are too flashy!      I ain't the one who shouted it from the town hall steps. Some of them lads, they’ve got no tact      Tact? Who still uses that word? Me da’s the only one in the felling who still speaks like he got a dictionary up 'is sleeve      Aah, I know what you mean. My ma says it’s like listenin’ to Shakespeare on the telly      You'd expect it from Cambridge types, wouldn’t ya? All po-off with their long speeches and fancy verbs      Yeah, but don’t get me started on their tea times and bookish vibes. Still, we manage to find common ground somehow      Bet you two have a good laugh at the end of the day      Oh, we do. Even if we're speakin' in different codes, most o' the time I know what the other's on about      Bet it’s somethin' to do with schoolin’ and all that univalley stuff      Univalley? You mean University?      Aye, that's where you got all them big words, ain't you? You musta been stickin' your felly into books as a nipper      I was told I was quite the bookworm back in Cambridge, but I come from a working class place      I get it, you've got your feet in both worlds, like me, I suppose. Me da’s a bloke who'd rather your conversation had a punch at the end, and me mum, well, she’d sooner you spoke earnest      Exactly, it’s that mix of where you come from and where you're at. You know? The roots an' the rise      That's it. Roots 'n' rise. Me and my crew, we may be rough around the edges, but no one denies we're livin' life to the full      Same.

Rather annoying I can't take any of the sw01 syns sticks on my own, they’re like... What was it, bitter flavouring or something? Blows! I saw someone on Slimming World saying they were sweet with a nice texture, but not for me. Just like the sugar free lemons and limes they give you in the Fruit & Fibre mug if you use the Token… they don’t even taste like real stuff. Honestly, I’d just rather have a kiwi and tea.      Ugh, I know what you mean. I tried the lemon sweets too and they just went straight in the bin! Not even funny. I've been using the 0 calorie syrup for tea like you said, but I miss proper sugar. I think I’m going to do a "treat day" on Saturday, and I’ll get the little packet of "gold" Syns and do something decadent, maybe even normal sugar just once.      Ooh, do it! Maybe even get indulgent with the double peas in the freezer, or that spicy Quorn we bought, and try some of those spices we got in the veg box. Want to go to Tesco for ingredients? I heard they have a brilliant Quorn range.      Yeah, maybe – but we have to be sneaky and not let the other flatmate see the shopping basket or she’ll start making comments about my targets. Speaking of, I’ve set my 8 kg target in the Slimming World App. Honestly, I think my scales are broken – one day I’m up 3 kg, the next day 1.5 kg down. Can’t trust them for anything.      Mine’s worse! I used to check it 3 times a day and it showed different things. I think it needs to be calibrated or something. But listen, while we’re doing the roast and cauliflower cheese, you can tell me how to make your tea better. I remember you said it was a special mint one from the Supermarket.      Yeah, the one with fresh mint. You put the fresh mint in a pot first, add the boiling water, and leave it to steep. The bag ones are a bit harsh and artificial. I get the mint in the veg box usually, if you don’t mind chopping.      No, I don’t mind, I can chop anything. But can we make some plans for Saturday? Maybe we can do a full roast together with those spices, maybe even take photos and post them on our blog or something?

Rather than going the usual route of booking a swanky resort for our holiday this year, I've been thinking... What if we try something different? Like road-tripping through France? I've always wanted to explore the countryside at our own pace.      A road-trip through France sounds adventurous. I'm up for that, especially if it means we get to avoid the usual tourist traps. But don’t you think our car is starting to show its age?      To be honest, I think it could do with a servicing, but for what we're considering, I don't think it'd hold us back. And even if it does, it's part of the adventure, right? Besides, I like the idea of finding quirky cafés and local markets along the way. What do you think?      I'm game. A bit of uncertainty can be good for us. Now, if we’re talking about perfect days during this trip, for me it’d be a relaxed morning, some oversized baguette, ordering croissants from a local bakery, maybe some walking by vineyards.      I can get behind that. My perfect day would be writing by the river with a cup of coffee in hand, local birds chirping, and maybe a little picnic spot nearby. How about – no plans at all?      That’s a bit much. I reckon some structure would be good. You know me, I panic when we don’t have a destination in mind. But someone has to be your balance. Just not overly planned, okay?      Fair enough. Also, have you considered the possibility of being split up temporarily – like if one of us gets lost trying to find a village?      Now that you mention it... It might be a good idea to take a satellite phone. Speaking of which, have you thought about the domestic implications of this trip? Burglars could be less put off if they know we're gone for weeks.      Oh, I had a friend suggest we hire a cat-sitter. We could run our trip and feel less worried. And also, maybe take lunches to a couple of the less-lucky folks in our building? That could help.      I support the cat go-between idea, but let's see about the other – I personally find politics off-putting, especially these days.      I can't blame you. It's exhausting. But perhaps we can focus more on culture and those smaller, personal stories we came across during our trips.

Rather lovely to have you here for dinner, old chap. I do confess, it's been a string of rainy afternoons, and having you over has put some colour in the week.      A pleasure, honestly. No one I'd rather dine with than you on a night like this. Right, now, I assume the reason you've handed over the spare fork is to have me help plan your granddaughter Alys' 12th this weekend?      Precisely. I do consider you to be the expert on these things. Nothing too childish, mind you – not that I expect 12-year-olds to be mature, but we mustn't go overboard with the pink and My Little Pony nonsense. Something with enough eccentricity for a young girl but enough class for the ears of a professor, if you take my meaning?      Got it. Now, breakfast, no doubt, at this early age, after some outdoor activity at the park, and then an activity, say, pottery or sketching? Perhaps a few friends over for tea? I do tell you, being a technical analyst is less about creativity and more about coaxing it out of human systems – but that still might pass for something reminiscent of fun for a twelve-year-old.      Baptism of fire, I suppose. And it's all in the cause of a very kind child.      If I might add, you should keep the homework minimal. Our modern children have enough on their plates. And regarding my own? It's been oddly sour on the stove hotter than the kid's mind. I have this theory she's been using the house Wi-Fi as a distraction tool in about half her schoolwork.      Ha, I had a student precisely like that once! Going into that university with barely a blink and out the other side with three theses, two on the Poetic Enigma.      And have you managed the one you sent? That one I had with the curling enthusiasm for the Archeological Compositions of the West Country. He’s doing a PhD now – with lunches to keep up with your digestive rhythms, if the recent card from Brighton is anything to go by.      He's rather taken to life in Brighton. And thank you for the card, by the way. I had a nostalgic week with all the sea winds and your well-sent postman.      You're most welcome. And now, I had not anticipated this to come up over dinner, but over this one’s weekend, I was hoping we might go over my reading of the latest on Scotland.

Rather than just a chair, Arabella, I think you did something incredibly kind for the Syrian refugees when you drew that design. What made you want to make a special chair?      Because they are people too. Not only do they have to leave their home, but they can’t make chairs when they don’t have a place to do it.      But what is their place? I mean, I thought Egypt was just one side from Syria, so where are they going?      Well, some go to places like Jordan or Turkey, but many come to the UK too. Arabella, your chair even won a prize at school last week. What did you call it again?      I called it the Cuddle Chair. Because it makes you feel safe and warm like you're hugging someone and you don’t feel scared.      That’s amazing! Wait, does it look like a throne?      No, not really. It is soft and has some cushioning for the back and the bottom. I told the teacher that I wanted it to have a place for a blanket too, in case the floor is cold.      That’s such a thoughtful design, Arabella. You remember Mr. Khan from our local community centre—he showed your drawing to his friend who builds school chairs in the refugee camp near Amman.      Wait, so you will know what it looks like when it comes out? Are the people going to enjoy using it?      I hope they will. I had a dream about it once—there was a young boy named Faris who smiled at it and told me in his language, "It feels like I am finally home."      That’s quite an imagination. I suppose you found out about it because of school? Mr. Hindle told us you mentioned it in your science test on structures?      Yeah, actually. The test was about types of chairs—like rocking chairs, dining chairs, and office chairs—and I thought about how your chair is not just for comfort but for safety. Even if it’s not special, a chair can make your day better if you're in a hard place.      I wish I could draw something that special one day. I like chairs too, but I think I might design a chair that becomes a bench.      A change your chair’s function depending on the need? That's quite advanced for someone in primary school.

Rather annoyingly, I haven't seen Sophie and Nathan in ages. I know her baby is almost six months old, and I hear she's starting to sleep more than  that  one.      Which one do you mean? Their son or our baby? Because  my  son hasn’t slept through the night  at all  since he was born.      Oh, I meant Sophie's baby, but now I feel a bit guilty for even saying it. It's just interesting how different their experience has been. I heard Sophie's baby starts the day at the crack of dawn, but otherwise seems relatively chilled.      That's the thing, right? Every child is like a new experiment, isn’t it? The manuals are all useless. I tried following the guidance for co-sleeping, and I think I turned into a human hammock for about a month.      You look like a very tired human hammock these days. I pity the poor students we teach, stuck looking up at a man who once fell asleep mid-lecture while I comforted him quietly from the back of the room.       Laughing  It wasn’t that bad. Okay, it was disastrous, but we’ve both taught from the same point of view – exhausted academics with new infants trying to still fulfill their roles. How long are you planning to do baby drop-in sessions next week at the department?      For two afternoons this week at least. I also invited a lactation consultant a few colleagues wanted to meet. You’d be surprised how many of them have experienced real difficulties with their early breastfeeding – even after such thorough parenting books and groups we were encouraged to join.      That’s why I admire our friends so much. Sophie and Nathan are such proactive sorts. I mean, Nathan even  created  that parenting app, so for him, it’s less about guesswork and more about analytics and baby data.      Do you think they’ll start hosting baby analytics conferences once the kid is older? “Presenting at the EuroBaby Websites Summit” – with lunches and a keynote by Dr. Sippy Cup?       Laughing  That’s the spirit! Anyway, seriously, I think it’s great our department supports these sessions. You’re really doing a good job leading it. People need to feel less isolated, especially after maternity and paternity leave. The pressure to jump straight back into it is high.      True, but we talk about that in supervision too – the need to balance everything.

I can't believe we've never done this before. The countryside around Norfolk is just as beautiful as they say. It's so peaceful, not like the hustle and bustle of London. I'll say. I grew up in London, and this—this is a whole world apart. The quiet and all the green, I understand why you chose to live here. Yeah, I love it. Being a lecturer tends to keep me indoors, so getting out into nature like this is a real tonic. Speaking of which, I heard from a colleague that the university's considering new publicity campaigns to attract more international students. That's interesting. What's the plan? You know I like a good bit of comedy, but I'd hate to see the campaign be more of a joke than an effective tool. They're playing it safe for now, but I suppose it'll get sorted out in committee meetings. Moving on, did I tell you about the bizarre superstitions I encountered while teaching in France? No, details, please—especially if it involves anyone dressed oddly or doing something equally odd. I find that fascinating. It wasn't that fancy. One of the students always crossed themselves before handing in their exam. I asked about it later, and they said it was to ward off bad marks—like some evil spirit that haunts failed tests. It sounded a bit far-fetched to me, but I suppose if it helps them stay calm, who am I to judge. It's amazing how some traditions manage to cross borders, don't they? I remember growing up, my grandmother used to make a special broth every time it rained on a Thursday. She swore it was the best way to avoid the flu. That's quite specific! Speaking of which, have you thought about our holiday plans next year yet? To be honest, I haven't. I was thinking maybe a getaway to a place where there are no automatic traffic cameras, you know, just a small town where you can drive freely. Though being pulled over by a policeman with a speed gun and not a computer screen would be quite a novelty. You're a regular man of law and go. But I'm up for anything as long as it's together and away from the digital world. I need a bit of traditional charm in my life these days.

I can't believe the amount of stuff we need to move, Dad. I was just looking online at vans—some of them are renting out for nearly a hundred quid a day. Have you got a clue where we’re going to get the money from? Cheapest things are always the best when you find 'em, luv. I was down at the garage this mornin’ and old Graham said he's got a flatbed lying around from his son’s last move. He’d be happy to lend it if we can give him a few hours on the outside of his house. That’s brilliant, really. I mean, I don’t mind helping you out, but paint? On the outside? My hands are definitely not made for that. I’m more of a mobile, nap-time sort of gal these days, not a handymen type. You’ve got to stretch out a bit, yeah? Can’t just be stuck behind a screen like a possum. Go on! You'll get the hang of it—and besides, once we've moved, I was thinking we could pop down to Dorset Steam Fair next week. You did quite a bit of computer game grief when you were younger, but there's something to be said for a little real, steam-powered fun. Oh, that does sound nice. I’ve seen pictures on my phone of that sort of thing—red carriages and clattering wagons. Bit like a proper old-timey theme park, just someone forgot to add the balloons. And regarding my computer gaming days, let’s not brag. Some habits don’t die. Hey, you weren't so bad when your grandmother came round last time and about half-chewed your tablet trying to win the touch-screen fish game. Both of us lost what little dignity we had left that day. That does sound like my nan. My sister texted me the other day about meeting up at my aunt's place. She's been trying to get a few cousins all together again. I wonder if you’d like to come along? It’s good to keep in touch with family, especially when you've lived alone for as long as you have. That sounds good, luv. Haven't seen the lot of you go at it on pond life since you were all about ten. Gave me a chuckle when that boy of yours tried to catch the goldfish with your nan’s hat.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? The council wants to knock down the library. I would've thought they’d be more sensible with heritage sites. I mean, it's not like it's a Victorian eyesore that's blocking progress.      You're not kidding. And it was renovated not five years ago! I remember we even got an invite to the reopening. Do you remember that stained glass they added? A real touch of class, in my opinion.      It certainly was. I do wonder how many important documents are still held in there though. The librarian told me recently they’ve been struggling to digitise older records because funding’s been cut. What’s the point in knocking it down now? My word, if only they’d skinned their knees a bit back in the nineties like the old grammar school, and I’ll tell you now, that building is still standing, even if it’s a Health Centre now.      That's true. People usually protect the places they once used, even if they've turned them into something else. But that library was one of the few spots where we’d reliably get the Sunday papers in decent condition. I’ve still got grief with the  Guardian  delivery on a rainy Sunday morning.      You’re telling me – I swear one of theCourier’s still got it in for me. Anyway, enough of the bad news. Speaking of which, did you pick the fabrics for the couch? I’m telling you, this velvet in the online sample book is a dream.      I’ve got three options still, but I’m skirting between the bottle green and the camel-coloured one. You know, the one about half as thick? I don’t want the thing looking like it’s had a thimble for a pillow.      Doesn’t it depend on the weight? Lightweight fabric, heavy use. Maybe you ought to check if they’re machine-wipe friendly? I'll go log in on my mobile, I might’ve seen something about maintenance on the site.      Do that. Let me just fetch the latest printouts of the new layout from the study. I swear, no matter how many times I run this by the council, their feedback is go back and pretend you didn't do it. They're practically preoccupied with just tickling the budget between council welfare and box sets of "proper" investments.

Rather annoying this new Spotify algorithm, isn't it? Seems to think I like pop songs by Ed Sheeran or some lightweight bloke with a bad case of vowel stretching! Honestly, I prefer jazz or a decent bit of Elbow.      Lmao, yeah, I get that on mine too! Keeps playing me some bad indie sh t I definitely didn’t ask for. Honestly, I just want Alesso to keep dropping that dance stuff I used to listen to. It gets me in the right headspace when I'm doing a client's extensions.      Honestly, I like to mix it up! I’ll be listening to electronic stuff at work, then go home and play like Taylor Swift’s folklore album. It’s calming! Speaking of, I just bought this vintage vinyl player for my flat, and it’s been the best little addition to my room. Gave me something better than flicking through old/current TikTok trends.      Blooming hell, vinyl! That's what I’m saying. I got my daughter one for her birthday—set it up, and it didn't work properly. Got halfway through the setup, said “I give up” and sent it back. Far too fiddly for my standards.      Hmm, I remember trying to get one to work, and ended up just listening to the radio. Binary choice really: old tunes or new sh t. Still, I got Mark a Christmas present the other day: a decent camera. Thought he’d get some good snaps from it. It's his hobby, isn't it?      Oh yeah, Mark’s got a decent eye! We went away for a festival in about July, and he took all these amazing shots of the crowd and the stage vibes. Honestly, you could hang them up like art. I gave him a scarf—unisex, black, with a bit of pattern. Thought he’d like something practical for when he's out at 6 a.m. shivering on the hills trying to catch the sunrise.      That’s such a good idea! I gave Mark a bit of a weird present too—this little Japanese tea set he mentioned wanting. The set came with a cute little travel tin and some premium leaves. He's really into that stuff, you know? Said he wanted to "practise the ritual" between jobs.      I can't be arsed with tea rituals. I’ve been obsessed with one of those BBC crime dramas, though.

Rather annoying this new car tax eh, lad? Thought me old Escort would've lasted another few years 'fore I got to splash out agin.      Nah, I think it might be worth it in the long run. My mate said electric cars cost less to run in the end. Got eeny weeny bills and no road tax an’ noVed. But I dunno, most a' em look boring.      Aye, easier said than done though, pulling 'em. Especially wi' the insurance. You're never paying when you're young. Tore me up when I was thirty-whatever. Payed double me wage in the first year I got me licence.      I’ve already got my provisional. It cost me over a grand just for the provisional insurance, and I’ve not even turned 16 yet. What about collisions and stuff if I get into a scrape? Do I just pay for a new bumper or what?      Oh, it’s Compulsory Third Party, son, so that’s all it covers. If someone else is daamin’ up I’m covered, but if it’s me own grief? Then you’ll fancy a nice long chat wi’ the insurance company and a trip to the garage. And remember – no claims bonus until you’ve done least three years accident-free. Bet you’ll be glad of it after that.      So if I don’t shag it up for three years someone at the insurance company’ll say “well done” and give me a discount? That sounds fair enough. Also, what’s a Group Rating and why is it sod all to do wi’ me driving?      That’s the category your car falls into. Group one are daft little hatchbacks and group fifty are pickups and off-roaders. The lower the number, the better. My Escort ‘ad group four. Got less points against me than a Ford Galaxy.      So if I want to keep my bills low, I should get a station wagon? Not one o’ them cool sports cars or something?      That’s whippin’ the smart o’ it for once, lad. Smart cars like that aren’t just more go-faster on the road, they cost more to insure. But if you choose summat sensible, you might be in with a better chance when the big day arrives. So long as you don’t kill me and the neighbours in yer first hours on the road.      I promise, I’ll be good.

Rather than share a recording of this, I request that anyone present consent to this being recorded for archival purposes. It's merely an ongoing project of mine involving family discussions and capturing their narratives on specific themes.      So we're speaking about workplace stress as well? That can be interesting. From what I saw at my old school, even with the transition from education to possible work stress, it's a big change. A lot of people just panic when they first start working. Oh, and what was it called again? The thing you do to test how stressed someone is?      You're referring to stress assessments, tests mostly used in clinical or managerial settings. We've found that such tools can be very useful for identifying individuals who might benefit from some intervention. The age of eligibility for the Irish pension is also a closely related topic and I think it's important for all of us, regardless of our age.      I've been thinking about this for a while. When I hear about things like the Equality Vote in Ireland approving the marriage of same-sex couples, it's like a monumental moment, you know? But then, when you're stuck in the everyday grind as a parent, it's hard to remember those larger events. Speaking of larger events, have any of you seen the suicide squad movie? My brother made a joke about it last night, it was  hilarious .      It's all about trying to capture the moment and preserve it somehow. Like those podcasts people make. I found one last week that discusses accents from different regions. Pretty fascinating stuff. It reminded me of something my Mom always did, trying to sound more posh when we went to London.      My granddad does a bad impression of the English royal family, it's part of a running joke in the family. But seriously, I've noticed it's a lot harder to understand some of the words that appear infrequently in Google. For example, did you know the word 'windpipe' is a common technical term but sounds very intense when spoken?      This is such an awkward silence we've created. Let's talk about lunches, Chinese takeaways? I’ve had such an interesting curry chicken experience recently, the quality of the chicken left the context of the gochujang sauce far behind. It was… bland. But at least the facade of deep, emotional conversation kept the box checked off on our list today.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think for once we could have a decent day without it pissing down the whole time.      I know, I've been walking about with an umbrella in my hand all morning. Look at the children! They wouldn't be out playing in it if they didn't  have  to.      I wanted to fly my remote control plane but I had to put it away 'cos I don’t want it electrocuted by some dump rain cloud. We had to leave the car boot open once during a storm and the bloke next to us like, literally screamed.      All this talk of rain and wet things — have you ever considered turkey twizzlers as a dehumidifier? I haven't, but I reckon Bear Grylls might. I think he turned maggots into an omelette once.      He turned ants into jam. Honestly though, I think he should cook for the Queen. Maybe he'd even do it.      He’d probably try and do it wearing a wetsuit.      Right, as if! You remember when Terry Wogan passed away? It felt like we lost a whole rhythm of light from the national conversation. I remember sitting down with a cuppa, and suddenly it just felt like something was missing.      Yeah, I still get the shivers thinking about it. He’d have said something funny about the rain and then done a deadpan read of a tweet from his cat.      Speaking of things in the news… Any of you curious about the  Law conversion courses ? I nearly did one after university. My dad kept bugging me to become a solicitor.      Going into that line of work now? Don't you need a PhD to do anything, like, useful?      I did fine on just a LLB. Thought about going for LLM, but life gets in the way. You know, management consulting.      Auntie Zoe mentioned once you've got to keep on writing exams to do it? Wasn’t that like  The Office  with the course on the ceiling?      That was more of a Roald Dahl metaphor made into a sitcom, but yes, law is a box of chocolates sometimes.      I’m planning to go to that conference in one of them hilltop villages, like in the Lake District. Do you think I should get over there via the M6 or try the scenic route? I reckoned I could save on petrol using the ring roads.

So, I just read an article today about lab-grown meat. I know it's controversial, but honestly, if it stops animals from being killed, I'm down. I mean, sure, it might taste weird, but at least we wouldn’t have to kill as many cows.      I get where you're coming from, but honestly, I'm just not convinced. I’ve tried fake meat a few times, and it feels like chewing plastic! I don’t want to eat something that was grown in a lab. What’s next, me eating spaghetti grown from broccoli cells?      That’s not far off, actually! Have you seen the meatless burgers now? They’re starting to taste like the real thing. Just last week, I watched a YouTube video on how they make it. It’s kind of gross, but cool at the same time.      Yeah, and it’s not just about taste. Think about the environment. Raising animals in abattoirs is so damaging to the planet, you know? I mean, isn't it time we start thinking about something better?      I agree—climate impacts are a big deal. But to be honest, I'd rather hunt. At least then I know the animal didn't live its life in a confined space. Yeah, it’s still killing, but it’s more respectful, in a way.      That’s just you and your hunting trips! I can’t imagine shooting an animal, even if it feels ‘respectful.’ It also doesn’t solve the problem of agriculture scale. I mean, farming’s bad enough—hunting a few deer won’t be able to match the demand.      Exactly. I mean, I’m not against eating meat per se—I’m just vegetarian now. It’s easier for me not to worry about the ethics and the environment. And honestly, the side effects of meat, like heart disease and all that, well, I don’t want that.      But you mentioned vitamins before—don’t you need B12 or something if you’re not eating animal products?      Oh, yeah, I take a supplement. It’s easy enough, and it makes me feel good, knowing I’m not contributing to the system that oppresses animals or the environment.      Maybe one day I’ll try it, but I still dream about a good steak or something.      So, have you ever seen  Curb Your Enthusiasm ? It’s wild how Larry David handles animal cruelty on the show, and over meat pronunciations and all that.

Rather annoying this new phone, eh? Constantly wants updating. I've had it 'bout a year and it's already starting to lag when I scroll through more than one app at a time      Aye, can do. Me mum got me a fancy one for my birthday last year an’ all it’s good for is taking photos an’ watching telly. But I tell her not to get me another ‘til I save up      I know! Mine started going off when I played a game last week. I got so far through the level, and the blooming thing crashes... like, literally right at the finish line. Bloody typical      That’s the lot of apps these days, innit? I swear, if I scroll through Tenp, the lot of ‘em crash and pick and I’m stuck with little ads poppin’ up while I try to watch something.      Fair play, though — in my opinion, the best part o’ scrolling on the phone is looking at the costume drama recommendations. I watched that new Pride and Prejudice reboot last week and it was absolute natter      Oh, I’ve seen that! Have you seen how much watching shows costs nowadays? I tried to stream the Christmas special from Netflix – Mate, I got a sting in me gut because the buffer was huge. One time I nearly had to switch to my laptop just to get the film to load      Honestly, this all reminds me of my grandad. He kept saying the new age's full of fancy things but you still need to weigh up the cost. Mind you, I still like watching the telly, Prime or not      I reckon you could do better than watching telly for most of your free time. I mean, there are plenty of games and things out there, decent bits to do with friends ‘cos they don’t always wanna sit in here mucking about on the phone      Aye, I know. I tried getting them to play that new Zelda game. It's a bit of a player of a game, mind, but we all agreed it was fun. Not as much fun as when you remember those board games with tuppence pieces      I remember them! We used to play Cluedo at my cousins in the holidays, had a team of three blokes on one team and all of us girls at the other. Me team won, though      I never had that, but I’ve had games like that where you either get the lot o’ answers right or you go entirely wrong.

Rather annoying the queue was taking so long for coffee, don't you think? I mean, it's like everyone got the memo about Alumni Day and now they're all here!      Aw, it was worth it, wasn’t it? That cardamom latte from the café was so good—reminded me of my uni days in Bristol. Still, it's not as if we don’t enjoy a nosy chat with old classmates in the line, eh? Oh, how was your trip to Spain last month? You said you were going for a short research exchange, but I bet you managed to get in a decent holiday as well.      Oh, it was brilliant. I managed about a week of work, and Marco—a fellow researcher from the University of Granada—toured me around the countryside, which was just lovely. Think I may spend longer there for my sabbatical if we get the funding sorted. But enough about me! How was your trip to the Baltic last summer? You mentioned something about ordering puff pastry and getting a flat tire?      [Laughs] Oh yes, that one was absolute chaos! So we land in Tallinn and decide to bike around, since everything looked so cute and picturesque. My friend ordered this massive tray of pastries from a lovely old lady in a market, and, of course, the bag slid off my handlebars and vanished into the canal. We spent twenty minutes catching the eye of a fisherman who ended up saving the day. Disaster with a side of charm.      That's oddly British of you—resorting to awkward charm when in crisis. Hey, speaking of jobs—I heard the Language Research Foundation in Manchester might have about five new roles available for research fellows. Have you thought of applying? It'd be a good step up from your current admin work.      Honestly? I've thought about it. But I'm still wrapping up this current project here, plus I want to spend a bit more time with my family before I jump into something new. I miss my sister's little kids. Last time I saw them they were both learning to ride their bikes.      That sounds lovely. And no pressure—just a thought. You're always brilliant at these things. I remember when I helped your dad translate some legal documents for his barrister cousin in Leeds, and that was genuinely fascinating.      Oh yes, you made all the legal Latin sound poetic.

Rather annoying me a bit, eh? You know how me lectures are goin' on, they’re like... nonstop. Never had no luck this week, eh? Just need a bit of time to breathe, is all. Not to mention this neck o' mine—feelin' all tense an' awful eeny. Proper  bodacious  sore, mate. Could really use a good massage.      Aye, love, that sounds like a proper right bleedin' nightmare. I know you said you were stretchin' your timetable for them psychology lectures, but don’t you think you’re gettin’ a bit overworked? I’ve been meannin to ask, are you thinkin' about that uni visit again? You’ve mentioned it a couple o' times now.      D’you know what I think? I’m just stuck in a proper rut, and it ain't gettin’ better. I've been workin' on me placement at the social care centre as well, and, to be truthful, I’m feelin' like I'm walkin’ into a brick wall every single day. I really fancy that short course in health studies at the uni in Leeds, but it feels like a step too far. I’m not even sure about the cost.      Well, love, I’d say, take the leap if you feel like it's the right thing to do. You always said you're goin' for it, and, from what you’ve told me, it’s a smashing course. And don’t rush your decision—just do what’s right for you. And whatever you do, don’t you forget to take a  proper  night off, eh? I’ll sort yeh a nice back rub the minute the sun sets this evening.      That would be gorgeous, mate! I really appreciate it. Honestly, I'd do just about anything for a proper lay-in and no lectures. I feel like I'm at me wit’s end. And yeah, I'll think about it—the uni, I mean. I just need to talk it through with them funds thing. It’s always the money that gets a lass down, innit? Even with grants and things, it still feels like it's stretchin'.      I get it, love. If it’s at all possible, just give it a go. And if it's bloomin’ money what your problem is, I could have a word or two with my Uncle Gary—I’d bet he’d lend a hand or two.

Rather lovely to have you both over for lunch. Thought we could talk about a few things, like the recent news from Calais. Sad business, really.      It is, isn't it? The conditions over there are just… I can't even put it into words. I’ve read a bit about it, and it's heartbreaking for the families.      You're a teacher, Aimee. Do your students talk about it at school?      A little. We've had lessons on migration and what it means when people come from distant places. It's clear to see that even at their age, they understand it's not just a distant issue. It's about people—just like us.      Well said, love. We should be supporting, not turning away. I think the world is moving in the wrong direction at the moment.      Totally agreement. It’s easy to get scared when people talk about change, but we have to remember to be kind.      That's a thoughtful way to look at it. Speaking of which, I might take up some volunteering work in the area. I’ve got too much time on my hands anyway.      That sounds like a good plan, dear. Maybe you could help out with school events or support local initiatives. I know a few staff members who are already involved.      I’d like that. It’s never too late to make a change. Although I’ve not read extensively on the topic, I’d definitely like to learn more before I weigh in.      That’s all I ask. Staying informed makes a big difference. I’ve pulled together some resources from reliable sources if you’d like to look over them sometime.      That’d be very helpful. Thank you. Now, shifting gears—how do you both feel about cooking tonight? I was thinking maybe something more interesting than the usual fare.      I’ve got some lovely vegetables I bought at the market this morning—tomatoes, zucchini, and fresh basil.      How about a pasta dish with a fresh tomato and basil sauce? It’d be a nice change of pace.      Sounds perfect. Any chance one of you could help in the kitchen? I might be a bit slow these days with the old legs.      Of course. We’re a team, remember?      True to that. I say, let's get cooking. We've got everything else sorted. Tonight, we just need to make memories.

Rather annoying the new plumbers we had in last week, do you know? Entire team, they claimed they’d be in and out within four hours, but more than eight! Messed up the tiles, left paint pots in the hallway. I’ve shown them the door after that.      A een, I know exactly what you mean. We had a similar tale at home not too long ago with a kitchen fitter from Newport. He promised the world and got halfway through before abandoning the job. To be fair to the lads, sommat like that doesn’t come cheap, but still, professionalism counts too.      Indeed. I’ve no patience for incompetence at my age. Still, at least now that Myra’s refinishing our kitchen, it left us with a chance to go the DIY route. D’you know, I think I’ve managed to spend most of the annual lecture fund on flooring and breakfast nooks!      Haha! Sounds like a posh charlady! No, you didn’t spare the expense? I once overheard Nancy saying she’s decided to install some of that new white tile—modern, I suppose, quite a contrast to her mocha countertops.      White tile is always a safe option, in my experience. Though it does show the grime more often than not, and with two grandchildren who seem to treat the kitchen as an apple pie topping factory, it’s a minefield. Last week, I found the cat’s pawprints all over the backsplash!      Children and cats, a deadly combo. Mary’s just had the shower replaced in the upstairs bathroom and it’s supposed to be energy-efficient, she says. High-tech and about five grand richer. I think she’s the only one who thinks it was worth it.      Oh that Mary. I once met her at a garden party in Cardiff. My, she hasn’t lost the habit of outshining others, has she? Invited to the event by a mutual colleague, Dr. Evans I think his name is.      Ah, you mean Dr. David Evans, the one who moved from Aberglasney to Exeter last month? Wasn’t that a bit of a blow for the course? Still writes the odd goody-me on pond life if you ask me.      Precisely. Last I heard he’s cultivating moss gardens on campus. Passes for environmentalism I daresay.      Moss gardens? Sounds eccentric, but I’m not one to judge. For now, I’m content with my crockery and the new microwave—close enough to the height of my left hand.

Rather than share a text, I’d rather describe the scene. Picture the table set in a cozy corner of a home in Cork, with four of us gathered, ready for dinner. I've fixed us a proper madras curry. Not too hot, mind, but spiced nicely—my lad Liam here can’t take the heat anyway, eh Liam?      Ay, I’m all for heat, but you’ve got to start slow or your throat will be crying uncle. Oh, and Grandad, are you gonna pass on the wine again? I swear when you chase curry with red, it's like lighting a firework in your tongue! Not that I don't like a dram, but only if Ma lets me.      Oh, you best not push it, Liam. And I’m watching you, Darcy, pick and choose what’s good for you. It's bad enough we've got a toddler breakfasting off metal toys and thinking they are "flavours," don’t remind me of what happens when he starts ordering lattes with a shot of bronze.      [Mime of chewing something crunchy, then proudly declaring in short words] "Crunchy!" Pauses for dramatic effect, then belches dramatically—very mature for a little lad, from what I hear most kids his age don’t know the meaning of belching with flair.      Would ye look at that? That’s Silas alright, the future chewing on every door handle he can find. Last week at the park, he tried to eat a climbing frame. Rudely sour metal, but you know—childlike adventure, and all. Anyhow, speaking of adventures, did I tell ye about the birthday I had as a wee lad in Dublin? I had the craziest plan to get a night deposit box as part of my toys. I fancied it as a secret superhero lair. My da had to explain that it wasn't for kids.      That’s the craziest idea I’ve ever heard. I tried to read about night deposit boxes in one of my science books. I swear it said they were like treasure vaults for people on the run! My history teacher calls it the  Horrible History of Money . Pfft! Maybe it's because goons used it to hide from the cops.      I just chuckle when I hear these tales of box vaults and capes your dad used to dream about. I mean, if we had super powers, I’d start with the ability to not feel pain—and magically feed Silas without having to bribe him with silence from his metal phase.

I can't believe it's nearly Halloween again. I used to scare the children with my jumping out when they knocked on the door. Never had no luck now, more people dressing up than ever. Oh, I remember quite well. Me and the children would go trick or treating every night in October een when I was a childminder. Not many people do that now, more all them fancy dress parties with cocktails. Yeah, I've taken my classes out to do a Halloween hike in the woods. Put in som' ghosts and ghouls in the trees and told ’em to fetch the ghouls without touching. They loved it, even the shyest child was screaming with excitement. I did that too! My horse’s name is Balthazar, and I told the instructor I wanted to ride in a Halloween costume. She said she’d help me find something. Oh, clever girl! What did you wear? I wore a cape, and a mask. Everyone was laughing. I felt real spooky like a vampire or somethin'. I don’t rightly know why as much as you like riding, but it's grand to see you enjoying it. I used to ride when I was young. Not much for it now with my old legs, but I miss the fresh air. It's brilliant for them children, building confidence and all. I’ve had quite the few students who've become real proficient in no time. Let me tell you, a teacher never forgets a good lesson—especially when the kid's got a horse between their legs. We should take a little trip soon, all of us. I’ve not been to Norfolk for ages, but I've heard it's quite pretty. Speaker_4, you’re from Norwich, is it as grand as they say? Yes, it’s got lots of trees and shops and historic buildings. There’s a castle too, all old and grey. My nan took me when I was small. Costessey’s not far from there, but we keep more to ourselves these days. Some grand oaks there too, if you’re into that sort o' thing. It'd be a fine idea to go. I could even line up a riding session if they’ve got a stable near the place. I’d bring plenty of snacks. We could take it easy, enjoy the fall colours and not worry about work or school for once.

Rather annoying the traffic is, eh gran? I mean, do they need to close the whole dual carriageway for a roadworks or something? It's not even peak time yet.      Aye, quite right luv. Seems as if half the county’s heading to the fair een! I can't remember the last time the 'A' roads were this clogged. An’ I reckon that motorway underneat the village too.      It's quite interesting, actually. We've had a few service users at the home who get frustrated with how hard it is to find parking these days. Especially if they've got a Blue Badge and people are parking in the bays like it's a fashion statement.      Oh, I agree, I was at the supermarket last week and there were twos of Blue Badge spaces with no one about, and cars just waiting to park in ‘em anyway. Should be a bigger crackdown in my opinion.      You'd think the government would do something about it, would ye? I mean, with more and more of us getting older, the need for proper elderly housing is as much as ever. And not just for fancy private flats in cities—more basic, nearer to nature, like here.      That’s the real issue, isn’t it? There’s a big divide between the private and public sectors. I see it all the time in the care home. Families pay through the nose just to have full-time support, meanwhile the council housing just doesn’t have the resources to do the same for those who need it most.      That’s so right. My nan used to live in about five different council flats before the housing crisis really kicked off. She always had to move because they couldn’t make adjustments for her mobility. I mean, it's unbelivable in 2024 that we can’t plan for elderly people better.      Aye. Used to have a nice little bungalow in Croydon, bless my wife’s heart. But when she passed, they wanted to redevelop it. And 'course, the new build was all luxury flats aimed at young professionals—makes a mockery of it, if you ask me.      It's symptomatic of a real lack of thought into the needs of older people. It's not just housing—education, healthcare, all of it. It's like we're all expected to manage roles we're never taught to prepare for.

Rather annoying the new council rules, isn't it? Seems like everything's getting more complicated with an allotment...      Oh, I know what you mean. I've been over this with my father-in-law. He's got one and tells me you need to provide a two-year-old site map now if you want to apply. It was simple enough when he started twenty years ago.      That does sound tedious. I was just thinking, I've had this old bed in my back garden. We've been removing the brambles for weeks. It's beginning to look rather lovely... like a miniature forest even!      That's a lovely way to put it! So you're thinking about an allotment too? I think starting one could be a good next step for you if you're getting used to the idea of growing. Living in London, I’ve never had the space.      Well, with a garden in Torquay, planting and growing is quite easy, even if I say so myself. But I would love more space. I dream of growing a tree or two. My crop last year was decent, a few carrots and tomatoes and the like, but I want something more… permanent.      That gives you a reason to look at an allotment fairly soon, then. I remember my father-in-law said he found an apple tree to grow surprisingly easy. You know what they say - plant a tree for your grandchildren. Our kids will inherit the skyline of trees.      That's oddly romantic when you think about it! But I suppose the practicality of it is what matters. I had a colleague, Laura, who nearly gave up on her allotment because of the man next door. She says he let thistles and blackberries take over. It was like a jungle and it drove her up the wall!      Oh, yes, shared spaces can cause such dramas. I have heard similar tales. It's probably best to set some expectations early on, you know. I always thought one day my father-in-law could hand me over a plot if he ever retires. It would be a dream to do something creative there.      Now that's the spirit! Imagine gothic ivy snaking up your rails or a wildflower meadow brimming in the summer. You might be the queen of the allotment, your own queen of the patch.      Queen of the patch!

Rather annoying I know, innit? You know what me mates are like – as soon as they see a mince pie they’ll forget about the cake I paid good money for. But anyway, where are you off to this weekend? Chuffed you’re not busy?      Aye, it’s alright if they liked the mince pies more, right? At least they’re easy on the budget. As for this weekend, me and the fam are off to Cambridge. Oh, and me mate Ellie’s having a do in the evening. I were wonderin’ if you want to come with us? It’d be nice to get out, innit?      Oh, Cambridge? Cheers for the invite! My turkey still hasn’t finished defrostin’, so nothin’ lyin’ around for me either. But a party? Yeah, sounds like a good idea – it’s been ages since we had a proper laugh. You need me to bring nothin’ in particular?      Nah, just you and your good vibes will do. Ellie’s got all that sorted. I do like the way she thinks, arranging all the food and drinks.
