Right, as long as you’re sure – we’ll pick you up on Saturday afternoon. Doesn’t feel quite right, but I mean… we’re stuck with it, innit?      Dead sure, luv. Truth be told, I needed a bit of a change after all this back-and-forth with me younger sister. She’s at full song about who she’s seeing at uni and who she’s not. It’s all a bit much at times. So yeah, this comes at a good time.      Blimey, I know what you mean. My b嘞ther still can’t keep his gob shut about his new flat. Says it’s got plug sockets in the right places or some bobཀock. Honestly, I’d rather just listen to Ellie play vinyl and not think about sodding plug sockets.      Luv, that sounds heavenly. I’ll pack a hoody just in case it’s one of them rooms that’s colder than a chicken’s bottom. I miss havin’ lads and lasses over, you know, where no one’s shoutin’ their feelings at goon hour on a Sat night.      True, true. It’s all that therapy stuff these days, bloomin’ marvellous if it’s for someone else, I suppose. But yeah, Ellie’s po잉y will be solid. You’ll be there to laugh it up, and maybe even shuffle up on the deck later.

Rather annoying me today, innit. Tried to get me mates together for a bit o’  Elden Ring  an’ they all bailed at the last minute! Typical, eh?      Oh don’t start grinning like that, Matt — you'll just end up being moaned at again.  Elden Ring  is   tough  , I had to put me controller down last week ‘cause I was just getting so stubbily stuck.      Honestly, it’s just me and the fact I.Fatalfanstay outside when it's cold. Tore my jeans like three times already trying to climb these towers. I swear the devs just put those slopes there to test us. My turkey, I’d give up.      Probably, but I reckon you're all too picky. If it was me playing with you lot, I’d be saying how we’re all just wimps 'cause we all still need Gamefaqs open. I cracked the Great Rune in, what, 32 hours? No clues, no nothing. Waterfalled it, lads.      You're quite a rude toot, Kris. Anyway, what’re we all going to be doing tomorrow? We should probably do something off-game. I miss just doing normal things, y'know?      I were thinking somethin’ to do with the phone’s upcoming film adaptation of that Liam Gale series — y’know, the one with the futuristic pubs and suspicious roosters?      Ohhh, you mean the one about   time-roosters being money-launderers  ? That’s the worst plot I’ve heard in years. I skimmed the first book once — it was like trying to read what my nan thought about her life in Brum in the 70s, but with robots.      Well, if you passed it by once, Jake, maybe leave the film to folks who actually give it a chance. I reckon it’ll be decent, honestly. Not sure about the casting of Greggie Hart as the space-drummer, though — he tried to do mime last year and it was like watching a gorilla with tinnitus!      Yeah, man, if you don’t get real drum action, I   will   mime that boy harder than he did last Time.      So, what about after the film? Thought we might go out for those nachos at the new cafe nearby. I heard they've got ‘dynamite’ on the menu now.      I'm in if they’ve got guac. Let’s be honest, half the reason we do anything is whether or not we can deep-fry it with cheese and slap it in a wrap.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to shine through the shutters. Mind you, I've always preferred Cambridge in the spring more than I ever did Essex.      It's beautiful, yeah. Look at the garden! The roses are coming out so well again. MUM, I brought over the printouts about that little film festival they’re having in King’s Parade—figured we could pick something to see this weekend.      Oh, a film festival, now you're talking! I remember when you used to want to act in school plays—we saw everything, didn’t we!  Oh, what a tangled web we weave…  Still do love a good bit of turkey, if I’m being honest though.      You mean like  Jurassic Park  and that kind of thing? Half the festival is for family, and they’re even showing  E.T . I thought maybe you could come for that one.      Well, you didn’t have to ask me twice. That ET and I—oh, we grew up together! I’d say I still have that scarf with the glow in the dark stars on. Hiding it still in the draw…      Oh, brilliant! So is Sunday good for you then? We could bring some popcorn, take the dogs if you like. I’ve been telling Jo and Liam about it—they said they're free too.      Now there’s someone who knows how to have a good time! Liam's quite the animated conversation, I remember—piece of toast dropped in my tea and he thought it was some great social comment!      I about died! Anyway—let's not bicker over the past, we have vibes to make. So, Sunday?      Sunday it is. Now run along to the garden, check on the tulips for me.      I will, but don’t start arranging any ‘corny scenarios’ I hear! I’ve had enough of your soap opera scripts from when I was a kid.      Ha! That was your father’s invention, love. Me, I’m a serious dramatist. Now, get! And go talk to the pond life if you must—always soothed me!      Alright alright—see you in the garden. Pass the strawberries will you?      Oh you, you’d think those were the only garden fruits that exist! I’ll bring them, and maybe some mint. We can make a lovely iced tea for the showing.      Sounds perfect. Sundays just got an upgrade, thanks to you!

Rather annoying the new DVD player we got isn't working, isn't it? I mean, it's like... barely a month old and already it's skint. I was going to show you  The Undateables  series with all my mates the other week—some truly cringy stuff in there. Hasn’t been  this  eventful since Brexit.      Oh come on, you’ve only had it for a month! Maybe just give it a clean-out, you know, dump the VHS and give it the full service. Those new-fangled things don’t last forever if you chuck everything at ’em. I mean, I still use my 12-year-oldDVD player from Argos and it’s still going strong. Possibly smells a bit like cheese, but hey, works for me.      I think the world is moving on, dear, far faster than our gadgets. I, um… actually just had a very luxurious spa visit in Brighton and they showed me the  The Undateables  on Netflix. Very different vibe to the usual dramas, I must say.      Whoa, really? I never thought about it as a binge-watch sort of thing, but I might’ve to… watching it at home while pacing in bath slippers definitely is. So – have you been binging series, Spa Belle?      Oh, no no, not that much. Just one episode. I was there for a weekend catch-up with some old friends. We don’t get to see each other often. Magazines and spas are oddly therapeutic when you’re surrounded by people who weigh ten stone and have the energy of a sleepy penguin.      Sounds a million times better than my weekend. I had the most awkward board game night with my partner and his friends. Someone kept trying to ruin the fun by pointing out every unspoken rule in  Catan , like he was the bloody referee. Honestly, passed out by 9 and missed the grand finale. Unforgivable.      Catan is a waiting game, honestly. Not my first choice when I’m hosting. I prefer  Balderdash  or  Cards Against Humanity . Now  those  are guaranteed for some good laughs. Just last week I told my sister that goats really do make life improvements if you raise them properly. She believed me.      Honestly, go with  Pictionary  and your family. It’s less likely to cause a family therapists conference post-game. I once drew “abracadabra” and ended up on the verge of tears over a chicken’s wing and a badly sketched wand.

Rather annoying this new washing machine eh? It's done more smashes than washes in the first week. I swear it's trying to announce it's from Cambridge by being all posh and faddy with settings.      No, I mean—some people wouldn't say it was trying hard eenough if it  wasn't  making all sorts of weird hissing noises in the evenings. I reckon that A listing by itself would put more ghosts off than a whole spooked village.      You're not wrong. Still, the chase when it's done with a big grumble like it's been working twenty years straight is always nice, isn't it? That first warm rumble like it's shrugging off the stress of an overdressed wardrobe week. Ten more, and I reckon you'd get some sort of sad acoustic poetry out of it.      Probably better than breakfast, honestly. You need to try some of these micro-roasted coffees I've been getting in the uni canteen. Richer, harsher than anything we had in Birmingham—though, if I had to choose between this coffee and that washing machine, it’d be a toss up.      Coffee… brilliant. I tried something last night, from this little market near here – Mate’s been raving about it and, let me tell you, I’ve never seen an apple pie that talked back. Silly little thing, went on about education and the principles of crust in equal measure. Spent half the box trying not to laugh. It just thought we were a  normal  family, is what it thought.      A talking apple pie in Cambridge! You know, about half the university is made up of people trying talking pies into intelligence. It’s a whole movement. We should start one. Breadwinners and Pudding Scholars, I say to the lot of ‘em.      A proper club. Baking shows, logic puzzles. Last night was bloody hilarious though. We watched that new sci-fi cult film – you remember the one with the planet that only dreams of oceans? He comes with lunches, right, and one day the ocean decides it’s fed up with reflection and goes around trying to be a man. Yeah, go on then. But it was wild. If it was at the cinema, you’d say they’d had a midnight snack box bloating on dahlias and ketchup.      Yeah, and the ending where it adopts those three earnest Martian gardeners as adoptive dad?

Rather annoying this VW business isn't it? I suppose anyone with a car these days is affected in some way... What with the emissions scandal and all that.      It does seem shocking, honestly. I read that they fixed millions of cars without telling anyone. Just like the banks, really. I'm surprised more people didn't notice earlier. Having done a bit of editing on reports like that, I can tell you things slip through cracks all the time.      It was a mess, that’s for sure. Back when I was working in development planning, we dealt with big companies too... Not to compare, but you'd be surprised how much data is massaged, only not for emissions but for profit targets. Just shows you that you can't always trust the numbers.      D'you think it'll make people look more at green cars in the North? I suppose if we’re moving up here, I wonder if car prices are affected in places like this, Hunsonby. No, you didn’t hear that from me. Good God, I’d like to get out of the South for good.      Well, property prices in Cumbria are more reasonable than London or Brighton, that’s for sure. But it does depend on the village. I remember my nan’s house in Birkenhead sold for barely half what a similar home gets here. Still, the pollution factor is lower, which is a plus if we're thinking about the car issue.      London and the South: everyone wants a piece of them but no one wants to admit the cost is through the roof and the air’s not so great. I’d be lying if I said it pains me to leave behind the clubs and pubs of the West Midlands, but this place... It’s peaceful. At least you know that VW plug-ins won’t handle the snow up here in winter. My, they’re cutting their losses rather fast.      And at my age, I’d rather not worry about whether the car I drive is legal or not. I just want to live quietly and not end up being fined out of retirement by the government over a dodgy engine!      You think they'll get around to testing every single car? I can go out of my way to check mine. If nothing else, it makes me question how much I really know about what I own these days.

Rather annoying when a new housing estate goes up right on the edge of the village, if you ask me. Ruins the view, and no local consultation at all. I’ve seen these plans, and they’re built higgledy-piggledy like.      Aye, it’s all the same, isn’t it? Not like it used to be. When I was a lad, you couldn’t build a new house without the vicar or the town clerk knowing about it. Now, it’s all paperwork and consultants, I suppose. Funny how things change, but not for the better.      Honestly, I can’t get used to the idea of people thinking they can push everyone around just because they’ve got capital somewhere. I left my last job back in Harrow, I had a good feel for how things should be done properly. Living in bed and breakfasts doesn’t leave much room, but I always tried to keep everyone happy.      And the pensions! That’s another topic that’s got folk in a stew. I sat through a few lectures at university, and I remember learning about vested interest and how short-changed a lot of us were left when the government reformed the system. It’s not right, and it’s only getting worse.      I often wonder if people still value politeness these days. I’ve seen young staff in places that would never dream of offering a smile or a hello. It’s been a long time since I worked at the factory, but I used to know what a good work ethic was. Funny thing—job security, is it gone now or what?      I’ve been reading online, trying to understand how I’m supposed to use these gadgets to check the papers or keep in touch. I’ve got a tablet now, but I plug it in and it just does its own thing—slides and scrolls like it’s got a mind of its own. I miss the days when you could leave a letter by the telephone box and it would reach someone in a decent time.      Computers, ha! I tried to get to grips with one recently to keep up with the family. I took the kettle out of the socket, I pushed this button or that button—finally gave up and bin it. My daughter says I’m a complete muppet, but I’d rather read a book than stare at a bloomin’ screen.

So, I just read this article about evolution and it made me think – why do people even reject it? It’s like, fossils and all the DNA stuff back it up! How do you feel about that?      honestly dude, i think it’s because some religions can’t wrap their heads around it? like, if humans evolved then what about the idea of being “created”? it’s not easy for everyone to let go of those beliefs, even if they don’t make scientific sense.      Yeah, and you also have schools where they barely teach evolution properly, or they mix in creationism with the facts. My older brother used to swear he was learning both like they were equal theories. That’s like saying the earth is flat because some website says so.      I didn’t know that happened in schools. We’ve only just started learning about it in biology, but the teacher made it pretty clear it’s scientifically backed up. Like, with the examples in mammals and the whale fossils and everything.      I mean, I get why people would feel confused—especially if it clashes with what they were brought up to believe. But if we’re not even allowed to question and think for ourselves based on facts, then what’s the point of education?      Exactly. It’s about respect too, right? Like, you can support science and still respect people’s beliefs—but don’t shut down what the evidence says. It’s one thing to debate it, another to deny it just because it makes you uncomfortable.      And it’s not just religion. I think a lot of people just don’t like the idea that their views might be wrong. Look at the anti-vax people, climate change deniers... it’s all the same pattern: stick to what you know and reject facts that make you feel stupid.      Dude, that’s so true. My sister got into an argument online once about vaccines after someone called her a “sheeple.” She was defending them, but all comments just spiraled into name-calling instead of real discussion.      Yeah, the internet’s a bit of a joke when it comes to that. People go hard on their views, but don’t even know the facts. I mean, I got goated online once for saying I like math—not bc I’m weird, but because I was making a joke about algebra being easier than boys sometimes.

Right, who’s ready for a fun weekend project? I found a little model kit in the cupboard the other day—it’s a miniature of George Stephenson’s Rocket. I thought maybe we could build it together! Now, if we’re going to build this model, we’d better get started in the next few minutes, or it might take us all day.      I like building things—especially when it involves Harry Potter! Rather annoying when the Wi-Fi drops while I’m in a Words With Friends game. Someone always takes advantage and racks up the points!      Blimey, I've been too busy with the bakery to play that app recently. Far too much kneading and sifting to do instead. Got a supper club to cater for this weekend, you know. My café’s website crashed once, and I had three online bookings the next morning that go straight to my pond life if I don’t get it fixed quickly.      You know what’s weird? Time flies when you're all gossiping and laughing. I made the lentils and rice, we could start supper now, if people stop chatting about work problems?

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I needed a bit of fresh air after cranking through that first-period shift. I always take my break now at the park benches by the gym.      Yeah, it's nice. Sounds like my stepson — he'll breakfast, lunch and dinner on just jam. Not a bit in his sandwich unless it’s the red stuff.      Oh, he’s got taste for that, then. At least you get the kids fed. Rather annoying this, naa? D’ya think we'll get lost again if we take that road like last time?      Nah, I don’t think so, love. But this isn't about me; you were saying earlier about teaching in Barcelona. How's that going?      It's brilliant, really. I get to wander around Segovia at lunch breaks. Though, sometimes the teens are only thinking about their phones and not the grammar, you know? I swear my left hand is allergic to taking photos on the phone now, from all the zooming in.      Oh, the joys of youth and breakfasts of laptops instead of proper eggs. Reminds me of when my boys were at that age. Used to follow me into town and demand a gelato like it was mercy from God himself. My, those days were sweet. Do you have any plans for Christmas yet?      Not set in stone yet. The kids are excited about trotting off to Tuscany with their grandparents – Baptism of some relative I can't remember. Though I imagine it'll be a sombre gathering of questionable cassati and Silvio Berlusconi references from the elderly. What about yours? Family tradition someone at the cricket club?      Oh, heavens no. I’m out in the Cotswolds with a couple of old muckers from the university days – those are the ones most likely about to fall off the proverbial bridge. But it's all very civilized, mulled wine and stories about fails at research that are now barely considered fails. And a reminder for you to have your eyeliner applied before the lesson, not during.      Classic me. You know, I was thinking about bringing some of the family friends you knew when I was small – the ones from Torquay. They’ve written to me about coming over to keep the whole English spirit alive with their red meats and rampant patriotism.      Now there’s an idea. Though I daresay if you start a disagreement about regional accents, half the lot of them might end up in the box room by dinner. But your lot do bring the warmth. I can't help but think though, after all that tea and earnest moralizing, someone will end up on the floor, metaphorically speaking at the very least.

: "Dad, it's so good to see you! I can't believe it's been two years... What's been going on with you?"     : "Oh, son! It is good to have you back. Look at you—get a bit larger in the cheeks, haven't you? Still, I understand—living on takeaways and fast food. I’ve been alright, a bit under the weather a couple times, but nothing serious. Still working in customer services, though it’s getting to be a bit grinding these days. You on the run from another job?"     : "Ha! No, I’m enjoying teaching English. It’s different, but satisfying. You know how it is, trying to get people who don’t really want to be there to engage. I’m moving to Brighton in a few months—smaller crowds, fewer rules, at least according to the internet. What about you? I noticed a lot has changed around here when I pulled up."     : "Brighton? That’ll be quite a culture shift—warm sands and young, loud crowds, I hear. Yeah, it’s different around here. They moved the park across the road for some reason, and they’ve been building that extra roundabout, of course. Constant building here—roads are getting better, but with more speed cameras than ever! Bet you’ve seen them on your way in."     : "I’ve definitely seen the speed cameras. And I got pulled over last month—thought they’d read my camera off my car, but it turns out my license was out of date. What a nightmare being back in the system."     : "Heard that story—poor you. But it’s all systems now, mate. I remember when you could speed without consequence. Speaking of systems, have you managed to remember to record the family stuff like we asked? Aunty Julie will want to know if she made it into the edit."     : "She better hope I remember when I sort out all the footage. I had that trip to Tanzania last year, by the way—absolutely incredible. Would’ve asked if you wanted to come, but I thought you’d prefer to sit on the sofa with the TV on."     : "And miss camping in the Sahara? No, I’ll take the boxset any day. I saw all of Game of Thrones before it ended, and let me tell you—I had my hours counted, my theories all set. But I’ll talk about that another day.

Rather annoying day today, really. I had to go into town for a bit of last-minute shopping before the weekend. You know, one of those days where your computer decides it hates you, and you have a deadline for a seminar tomorrow. I ended up managing it, but just barely.      That sounds familiar, honestly. I had an absolute nightmare with the university's PR department today. They sent out a press release with a typo in my name—misspelled by two letters. It's not like it’s a private email either; it was on the front of the university website. Utterly mortifying.      Oh no! That is the worst, isn’t it? You put that much effort into your work, and then something like that happens. I can only imagine the flood of emails from students and colleagues: "Is this Professor Smith or Professor Smyth?"      Exactly—there was one from a student asking if I was "Professor Smyth, the famous baritone singer, or if I had wrongly adopted the name." I nearly died laughing. I do tell you—personally, I’d take singing in public over spelling errors in press statements. Do you ever get that kind of thing in your area?      Not often—I’m more of a background person in that sense. Though I did have to confirm to a student the other day that I wasn’t “the music lecturer who was meant to teach the jazz course.” He’d clearly never seen me. Well, to get back to you—do you have any plans for the evening?      Not much, honestly. I might just stick in a film and maybe continue grading. What about you?      I was going to cook something finally—mainly because I’ve been living off pasta for the past week. But if it goes wrong, I’ll have to chain myself to the sink. Unless you want to make it a duet and play me a tune while I’m chopping vegetables. I might need it to keep calm.      As tempting as that sounds, I’m not quite brave enough to perform live while you whack vegetables with a knife. But maybe I’ll set a playlist for you instead. I started a new one goin' on jazz-via-classic—I think you might find it interesting.      That would be splendid—and thank you for all the musical enrichment. If only I could manage the cooking part quite as professionally.

Rather annoying this, isn't it? You think they'd have decent tension on this sewing machine by now. I got the beanbag project from a magazine last week. I’ve been meaning to start it for a week now.      That does sound like a good project. Is it much like knitting? I remember my gran doing something similar with an old jumper once. Of course, all she used was a needle and A4 paper. Not exactly efficient.      Haha, well, not as complicated as knitting, no. I got some cheap cotton fabric from the store the other day. It’s not the best, but it'll do. I plan to stitch the sides, then stuff it with recycled filler that Myra gave me. I’m thinking of putting it in the living room, to match the new cushions.      A beanbag? Blimey, aren’t those things better for when you're 12 than 42? I suppose if it helps, you could always throw a decorative cover on it later. Also, the colour scheme would match that new shower curtain we bought, yes? Speaking of, I still have that short length of curtain pole to install in the bathroom.      Oh, brilliant idea! Green and beige will tie the whole room together. I remember we agreed on that fairly cohesive, warm-toned scheme. It’s much better than what was there before—ugh, that bright red was hideous.      True, the old one screamed “I bought this on a whim at a warehouse sale.” Moving on, are we making what you had planned for dinner? Or shall I add something to the menu?      Let’s stick with what I scribbled down. Roast chicken, roasted sweet potatoes, and some thyme-baked parsnips. I got the chicken from the farmer’s market, so it’s quite fresh.      Lovely. I can preheat the oven. And while we’re at it, I was thinking—now that we’ve done the curtains, the beans, and the bathroom, perhaps we could tackle a new set of towels? There’s that nice set on sale at the Co-op if you fancy it.      You're a regular room designer now, go you! I’ll see if I can find some matching bath mats as well. Nothing like making that final flourish before the boxset binge on Sunday. Pass the thyme when you're ready, will you? I need to toss it with those parsnips.

Rather a gray day, isn't it? That sun's been hiding all week. Don't think it's gone to be a bright one today. I’m more used to the countryside, you know, with a little more open sky. Mind you, the view from our window is quite nice all the same. Got a bit of a garden, don't we?      Aye, yes, it's a lovely little outlook, but I do miss the hustle back in Harrow. The park was quite a place to watch the world go by. Children running about, people chatting, the odd bloke walking his dog like he was on some grand adventure. Still, I suppose we're well taken care of here.      I must say, I’m not too fussed about the weather, to be honest. Drove into town this morning to pick up some supplies for the week, and the drizzle didn't get me down in the slightest. There’s something about getting in the car and just driving that always lifts my spirits, even if it's only a short trip.      Supplied, have you? I say, I might take you up on a trip to town sometime soon. Never did get much chance to shop much when I was living in Costessey. Mind you, most of my shopping was done at the same corner shop, same bloke behind the counter the whole time. It was nice, like a proper community place.      That does sound lovely. Our shops here are full of chain stores. I often feel like a stranger just drifting through. Funny thing, isn't it? We live in the same place for years and still feel like we don't quite belong. Not that I mind being left to my own devices, the peace and quiet is quite something.      That's because you choose to be left alone, Nellie. I'd have found a whole group of friends by now if I lived here. There's always something going on in the local community center. I've been trying to get a gardening club off the ground, mind you. It's been slow going, but I'm hopeful.      Grappling with the community, are you? That sounds like a grand idea. Popping along the community center one go, I'll make a point of it. Mind you, I expect I shall spend the entire session figuring out where the bloody thing is.

Rather annoying the queue at the supermarket today, to be honest. I was trying to get home before it pished down again. Never mind, at least I got the mince in for Sunday dinner. That's always reliable.      That's the spirit! Sunday dinner is the one night we all get together and actually  eat  the same thing. I tried to pick up some sprouts on behalf of everyone but only found half-a-dozen in the whole shop.      Honestly, who needs sprouts? Put some sweet potato or chestnuts instead. Just want to keep it vegan-friendly too these days. I’ve even taken to making little mini meatless pies to bring along.      That’s a good idea, love! The kids like that sort of thing more, to be honest. D’you think we could make a patchwork of dishes this year, instead of the traditional lot?      I’m up for that, if only to avoid the usual tray of soggy hides, you know? I’ve never got the knack for Brussels sprouts—always overcook ‘em.      Fair enough. If we spread the dishes out, we might even be able to avoid the annual argument about watching football during dinner. Janice from the staff Christmas do loves a good cheeky match while the rest of us try to talk.      Would she not just shut it off and have tea? Bit old-fashioned, don’t you think? There are people out there who have never played the bluddy game. Should appeal to the global vibe a bit more—maybe something with more culture than muddy trousers.      Aye, fair point. Maybe we invite in about half the people from the health centre round the corner? Might broaden the mix.      That would be lovely. Could even do some dancing if the space allows. I do know a couple of local bands playing stuff that’s not quite chart rubbish. A bit more soulful, you know?      Now I’m intrigued. So long as there’s a crack to the side for the sprite of the family to space out with his computer game nonsense during the evening.      Defo set a couple of corners aside for that. Let the kid go wild with his zombies or whatever while the rest of us have a rumble on the floor. Sounds brilliant. Definitely the kind of vibe we need at your place with the big windows and that big garden.

Rather lovely to sit out here on Sunday mornings, isn't it? The coffee's a bit strong, mind you, but I’ll take it. So, how are you finding Northern Cyprus, Mr. Hargreaves?      Oh, call me Philip. And yes, it’s peaceful out here—quieter than I expected. I was born in Bushey, just outside London, and most of my life was spent in the bustle of the south. This is quite a change. It takes time getting used to. You seem to be enjoying it, though. How long have you been here?      My name's Ruth, by the way. I’ve been here nearly two years now. Being a teacher, I’ve always liked new places to visit and learn. I moved here to teach at the British School, and honestly, it’s turned out to be an excellent decision. The students are curious and bright, and the town has this lovely Anglo-Cypriot vibe.      Really? That sounds interesting. I always thought the political situation might make it complicated, but I suppose it doesn’t get under your nose too much if you keep to your own.      It doesn’t for the most part. The locals are very friendly. I remember when I got here, I was a bit nervous about how I’d be perceived, but they were welcoming. I even learned to dance the Cypriot  tsiftetelia  at one of the village feasts, which was quite a sight at first.           I can imagine! Some habits don’t transfer well across cultures, but I suppose you make do. I had a colleague back in my youth who about broke his hip trying to waltz the  tsiftetelia . Not much of a dancer—he thought he was doing the right steps!      That does sound quite comical. I must say, though, the food here is a revelation. I’m not used to it being so light on the herbs and heavy on the olive oil, but I’ve grown fond of it. Have you gotten into any of the local dishes yet?      More or less. I’ve tried the  kleftiko , which is a bit of a hit among the go-to dinners I usually share with my grandson. He comes over for weekends, and we go out exploring. It’s the only thing keeping me from what your lot would call early grave. I used to manage a conference centre, mind you— early  mornings and all that nonsense!

I can't believe we've been working in Beijing for six months already. The pace of life here is so much more intense than I expected. Yes, I know what you mean. It's a stark contrast to the quieter streets of London, and even Norwich! But at least our departments here are pretty supportive. Definitely. It helps that we both got offered lectureships in the same institute. I’ve only had one problematic student so far this semester, which is easier than I thought it would be given the language barrier. Same here. The teaching staff are pretty well-integrated too, like Sarah from the philosophy department. She's been a great support and introduced us to some lovely colleagues and local friends. Oh, she mentioned a weekend trip to the mountains, do you want to go with them? It could be a good way to spend some quality time with the team and breathe fresh air, away from all this pollution. That does sound nice, thanks for letting me know. I didn’t know they planned a group outing. I’ve noticed the air quality getting worse, and being outside in the city doesn't feel as pleasant anymore. I know, and it's worrying a bit. I always check the pollution index in the morning before heading out. We're doing our best with the air purifier, but the nights are long and the city is thick with smog. I've been wearing a mask at work too, just to be safe. I miss the brisk walks outdoors with no worries about the air quality. I wonder when the worst months will pass. I've heard from some locals that the winter months can be particularly harsh. I do hope the government is investing in clean energy to improve the situation long-term. Yes, I think it's heading in the right direction, but it's going to take some time. In the meantime, treks like Sarah's will help us stay active and at least momentarily escape the hustle and the haze. Let's make a night of getting our gear ready this weekend then. I'm also planning to invite some of the people we met on the first night. It's the perfect opportunity to strengthen bonds and share a nice experience together. Sounds like a fantastic plan. I'll start prepping for the trip and let you know if I see anything about team dynamics or academic opportunities on campus.

Rather annoying the new oven’s taking so long to preheat. I blame this damp weather, it slows everything down, don’t you think?      Not a bad idea if you fancied a rest before we eat. I’ve read somewhere that modern ovens take about the same time as boiling a kettle and making a cup of tea. Not that I know much about tea-making—Liz? Normally you’ve got a good grip on the best brews.      It is interesting you should mention tea, Mark. I got a photo from Amie, the kids had a picnic in the park. Horrible photos mostly, but one’s editable, I reckon. I’d shown her some bits about photo editing apps on my phone, you know, the basic ones. Ten minutes, and now she’s sent them all through and I’ve got the lot.      Cats on the back breakfast, no doubt. I’ve been messing with a new show on Netflix this morning, ever so addictive. You should check it out. Also, the cookies I made earlier were a bit overbaked, maybe the oven was too hot. I mean, we all make mistakes.      Oh, we’ve got plenty of cookies, Claire. I saw you put them in the tin earlier. Mate, you got the cinnamon mixed in, that’s a plus. The kids like them better with a topping, like something Silky or chocolate drizzle, you know?      Silky sounds an odd name. I’d read about a chef once who oddly had a recipe with nutmeg and something called Silky cream. It was an odd match but oddly good.      I mean, I’m not the chef round here. But I did sort out most of my emails this morning. Going to be easier with new dishes and stuff. Liz, you mentioned that the herbs are ready for cutting. Shall I do that while the others cook?      Oh, a great idea, love. We could do with them for the salad. Got some lettuce from the grow bed that came through well.      I think it was your care, Liz. Earlier in the day, I saw you with tongs and the watering can, goin’ on for ages about each row. Anyhow, I made calls to the department today, had a team update, all well on schedule.      That sounds big, Mark. Thought you were going to miss those meetings, what with all the holidays coming up?

I can't believe the new bus route’s taking so long to get implemented. It’d make such a difference if it got to the Press bookshop quicker, y’know? I’ve stared at those shelves long enough to commit them to memory. Honestly, I wouldn’t be surprised if the site eeny meant to prioritise anything that doesn’t involve   profit margins  . I’ve been trying to grab a book on industrial ethics for one of my projects and got told they’d reordered it  three times . Oh, I heard about that! The student protester outside the Senate House last week? Right, I saw them holding that big sign saying, “Knowledge shouldn’t cost blood.” My lectures still scoff at that sort of talk. “You want free education, go work for it,” they say, and I’m like,   eh  , most of us already do. Aye, I’ve been thinking about how I’d’ve rolled my eyes at the uni I went to, ordering flash new facilities while the printing stations die of neglect. You ever been to Sunderland, luv? I passed through once, near as to Manchester. I dunno, it still sounds a lot like watching a machine that used to be in motion. You ever consider comparing us? Sometimes, I think it’s like trying to compare the weather—Cambridge’s got all them   blazers and forecasts   and we’ve got hills made of smoke. Our libraries had books chained to tables! That does sum it up oddly well. You ever think about the irony? You catalog and I recalibrate—measuring the same thing from different ends. It's kinda like us trying to pin the shape of clouds, innit? I tidy what you untidy, you break what I fix. Doesn’t sound unromantic in that comparison, though. To be fair, I did once get asked at open day if I’d ever considered being a civil servant. I stared at them for a bit, then said, “No, and I’m being asked out by a clock with lunches.” Ah, I took the more direct route—applied for a job by mistake and the interview was in gothic room with man who looked like he’d just stepped out of a college line in a history test. You’re telling me what your actual job title was at the time? Library monkey, yes. And I never got that paid promotion to “seasoned data prisoner.”

Rather lovely to finally be out of the house and away from that old classroom, dontcha think? The first few days since I left teaching have been a bit more than I bargained for, I must say! Got to keep my mind off things, so I thought what better than a nice cheerful lunch with my two best friends?      It was my idea to come to Cheshire actually. Thought it a change from our usual haunts in Birkenhead. And honestly, Patricia, seeing you smile again is like sunshine. We've missed you so much. Those chalkboards probably kept your kids well under control too!      Mary, darling, I kept them in line well enough, but heavens, I miss that buzz of a classroom. Still, enough about me. How is work treating you, and how are things with Marcus?      Oh! Before you get to me, let me just say breakfast with my sister Winnie this morning was something else. She mentioned she might cook for the weekend when our little boy visits. She's so helpful, isn't she?      My, yes! Winnie is always up for cooking! But honestly, as much as she loves food, she’ll still mix up salt and sugar. I swear!      You’re not alone – I once boiled a whole pot of coffee with salt instead of sugar. The kids weren’t too pleased! But hey, it's all part of the charm, don't you think? We all have our quirks.      That sounds like a chaotic but hilarious memory. I remember with my son, James, when he was little and being fussy with his food. We finally gave in and made a "mystery plate" where the vegetables were the main dish and he didn’t even notice.      Oh that is brilliant! I might have to steal that one from you. My grandchild eats like he’s been told he can’t eat dessert unless his plate is clean. Good grief!      Oh Patricia, that’s how my little ones started out too. Persistence is key. But seriously, how are you dealing with the 'retirement' phase? Any new hobbies? Arts, maybe? Still remember those after school drawing classes?      Actually, Patricia, Mary and I wanted to talk about something. While you’re off in the land of no schedules anymore, maybe you can start a bit of volunteering with us. We have a few projects with the local community center in Hunsonby, and I’m sure your teaching background would be a big help.

I can't believe we've never done this before. Walking along the Thames—it's just beautiful, especially this time of year. I’m more of a coastal kind of person, personally, but this is nice. Not to mention convenient, since we're on our way to the O2. Got a ticket to a comedy show we bought on a whim. Still reckon it was a good choice? Absolutely. Much better than doing this all by car. Oh, and don’t get me started on cars. I'm still getting used to not owning one. Feels like I made room in my life for more walking—and fewer parking tickets. I get it. Honestly, I like that car-free life too. Less stress, though I do miss the freedom of popping to the shops whenever I want, even if I only buy the odd sandwich. But I’m far more thankful for better air quality, no doubt about that. Exactly! And being out here, getting some fresh air, even if it's a bit chilly. It makes me wonder—after this show, should we book a holiday? Maybe take the kids somewhere with no traffic, no noise. Somewhere real, like the countryside or even a country we’ve never been to. Now you're speaking my language. I’ve been thinking the same thing. Places like Norway or maybe even New Zealand—somewhere where you don't even notice the passage of time unless your phone shows it. Speaking of someone not noticing time, remember when my sister visited from America and asked for a coffee in an "8-ounce cup"? It took me five minutes to explain that 8-ounce cups in the UK aren't nearly about to fall off the table. Ha, I remember that. Honestly, some of the little cultural differences are the funniest parts of it all. Maybe we should do something like that for the kids. Enroll them in a cultural swap with some American friends. Just so they can see both sides. That’s a great idea. Makes me wonder, though—how do we even define what a good life is? Or a meaningful one? I’ve been thinking about it a lot lately. Truthfully, I think it's in the little things—the walks like this, the shows at the O2, the quality time with our kids. The everyday moments that pile up and suddenly, you've made a life.

I can't believe the weather’s still so bad today — it's pouring sticks and stones! I came in like a drowned rat. I had no luck getting a signal on my mobile phone, either. It’s a proper pain in the bum trying to video call my sister as it keeps dropping. Hasn’t it just been absolutely drenched the moment you step out the door? I tried making a pot of tea earlier before I popped out to work this morning, and my kettle refused to go on. I think it’s one of those days where the weather decides the whole household can be at war with kitchen appliances! Honestly, I can relate. All I needed was a drink, and I ended up boiling the kettle on my phone because I couldn’t be bothered to wait. Probably not the healthiest habit, but it beats having no tea! I was about to say something similar earlier when I was trying to sort out the kids for sports day in the park next week. Mega oversized rain boots, you name it, they’ve got it. I reckon we’ll all end up with puddle-sized socks on by the time the day is out — quite a spectacle to be honest! Oh, I remember watching sports days when I was a little. Wasn’t it lovely – even though it often rained, and none of the other mums brought the right gear. It was all just chaos and laughter. That’s true — it’s all in good fun at the end of the day. Although my sister insists on dragging one of her ‘Build a Bear’ ones out for every occasion. I swear it’s as essential as a mobile phone in her world! Ah yes, the cuddly toys! She’s had one for years. I remember doing that with my teddy when I barely left the house. These days, I just do with a ‘knit and create’ guest speaker at work — not quite the same, but keeps the hands busy! At least someone knows how to keep themselves entertained. We’re still trying to figure out potty training with our youngest. Between that and a new swimming class starting in the local pool, it's like trying to multitask with three left hands sometimes. I remember your stories about trying to get mine to go in the water in the first place.

So, I’ve been doing a bit of thinking, love. We need to set some personal goals before we dive too deep into this new chapter. I’m feeling ready to commit to something long-term, but I want it to be with a plan. What do you think?      I’ve been thinking along the same lines, actually. It’s easy to get swept up in the easy rhythm of life, you know? But I think now is the perfect time to step back and really think about what matters most. Career-wise, you seem to be enjoying the entrepreneurial vibe. How are the plans with the new café?      Honestly, I’m excited. The lease is almost sorted, and we’re in the early stages of sourcing materials. It’s a bit overwhelming, but I feel more prepared this time around. I suppose it's partly because of the structure we’ve had with assembling the team. But I want to know, what about you? How do you see your career in the next few years?      I’d love to keep teaching, but I’m also thinking about taking on more leadership roles, maybe even PD work in the next couple of years. I’ve enrolled in a few workshops, and there’s something about guiding others that really motivates me. I just want to make sure we’re both supporting each other, and not spreading ourselves too thin.      It’s that balance, isn’t it? I understand completely. And I’d love to join up more with someone at the café who also has a teaching background—maybe they could run some of the training with us. Also, about family planning—have you given any more thought to where you see us in five years? I know it's early conversation, but I’m starting to consider different areas we might settle down in.      I love that you’re laying it out like this. I imagine us with a small family, and ideally living somewhere with good schools and a community vibe. I remember talking about it before when we were house-sitting in England. Maybe even starting a school garden or some sort of sustainability project.      That would be amazing. I can see it clearly—us working together, our children helping set up a garden, with our careers moving forward in sync. I’ll make it a personal mission to keep the café as eco-friendly as possible to support that sustainable living vision.

Rather annoying when people can't get my accent, innit? I was trying to book a hotel in Leeds last week and the bloke on the phone kept mishearin’ me words.      Aye, Leeds do have their own sort of tongue. Me mam gets it wrong all the time when we're talkin’ on the ‘phone. I reckon it's worse than Wigan vs Warrington.      Honestly, I thought it was funny. Imagine me nan pulling her hat over one ear and moanin’ cause me accent was too thick. Still, I'd fetch chips to keep 'er happy.      What’s that you were sayin’ about accents? I still can’t get my head around the Yorkshire one. Ten minutes in Leeds and I’m lost. But I used to think it was like a different language altogether, to be fair.      You need to go to Costa after for a bit o’ calm. I always tell me mates, even if I can’t understand the lass, I can always rely on getting a flat white right.      Bah, I’ve tried to read the menu when they’ve got fancy names on it and I reckon I asked for something wrong about ten times. Once I ended up with a caramel something or other, and I just wanted a latte.      You know what gets me? If I go out and don’t smoke for a day, I feels all twitchy. But I’m tryin’ to use the Fitbit to remind me not to pop out for a fag. It’s strange being told I’ve been inactive when I’ve been out the whole day about nowhere.      Have you tried blinking at it or something? I once forgot my phone at home and wandered off and I was like, “Might as well do something, ‘cos the bloomin’ thing’s tracking me anyway.”      You know, I was out camping once and left it in the tent. The bloke told me the Fitbit was like a sprite of some sort—keepin' 'im up nights wonderin’ if I took the tent down. Still, I did run into a dog that looked like a cross goonie on the lake, so it wasn’t a waste of camping.      Aye, fight or flight, innit. Me brother’s got a dog that’s like a small bear and one time I was scared to approach ’im because of the way ’e barked, soundin' like a cow and a chainsaw had a baby.

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun graced us properly after such a blighty of a wet weekend. Never mind, a nice Sunday dinner and a football game on the telly’ll sort us out.      Oh, George, you and your football! I was in the kitchen all morning making a nice chicken pie with some leftover vegetables. Margaret, you’d like that, don’t you?      That sounds lovely, Margaret. I've had a mad week, pulling together lecture materials and grading essays. Sometimes I wonder why I chose teaching, but the blokes on the telly are hardly a better alternative.      What are you talking about, love? You like that Myke Mordecai bloke—you were telling me last week about how he made you obsessed with stats. Never got tired of a little sea shanty here or there. Mind you, I preferred the old-timey ones—now it’s all pop tunes and electronic noise. Don’t forget the politics! We’ve got Prime Minister Johnson in about five days doing something baffling. Yesterday the papers said he’s considering another referendum. Mind you, I’m just glad the Wi-Fi works. Sue, you blokes on your laptops must get it sorted in five seconds flat.      We do, yes. Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what me Mam’s like—she's always ‘clean socks, no nappies on the floor, no more than one pair of socks left after Tuesday’. But this is 2024, not 1984.      Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive notes on the door from me auntie. Thing is, they don’t clean that A4 under me door, so every time I open it, it’s just there, pulling me back. Know what I mean? "Dear Elsie, when are your shoes going under the bed again like three years of age?"      Oh no! Funnily enough, I didn’t tell me brother that I might drop out… I reckon I might have to drop out. I mean, I can’t even afford rent with the part-time jobs, let alone eat and survive. Going to be easier to drop out and handle it all together, but I do feel like I’m letting someone down. Probably Ma.      I reckon me Ma will say something like, ‘Elsie, I tried to make a little madhouse out of the shed so you had somewhere to study. Even wired it up with proper lightbulbs and told your dad to do the plugs properly, you remember that? Then you told me you wanted to study away go on then I said, if you don’t get a first, I’m going to go out and purchase a sable.’ I’m like, what?      That sounds familiar!

Wait, does your sister know you’re meeting up with her best friend ever and not inviting her to lunch?! I tried to stop my colleague taking the last biscotti, but you know how they are — once they've clocked it, it’s gone!      Exactly, you try to plead with them and they just smile and derail away. Look, on another note, do you fancy going for a pre-lunch walk in the park? I need to clear my head before the weekend.      That sounds brilliant! Let me just finish this coffee and we can off, I’ll make it a proper scenic route — I’ve missed this city so much lately, with everything remot        I love that, brilliant plan.

Rather than going out an' getin’ swamped in tha shops, I’d sooner hop ‘pon me ‘puter and pick wot I want on Amazon. D’ye ever give it a shot, love?      Nah, I mean, I’ve used it a bit, but it een’t really me thing. I’m more the 'go an’ pick it up in town' sort a' lad. What if it’s the wrong size or colour, Miss Ferriby?      Well, that’s where the reviews come in handy. Most of the blokes up north use eBay to sort out their older tradeshall kit, but I reckon Amazon’s better for day-to-day bits like My turkey twizzlers or new jelly slippers. See, when I need to get hold of a calculator, or one of them A4 folders for all your GCSE mocks, Amazon ‘as it all, no trouble.      I suppose, but what’s the deal with eBay then? Ken Wright told me he scores a tidy buck off it by sellin’ his Nintendos 'n’xbox controllers. I never thought about sellin’ stuff.      Oh aye, eBay’s the place if thee ‘as a few bits lyin’ bout no one wants any more. I sold me old vacuum cleaner on there last week, and ‘bout £20 in me pocket for a load o’ cables an’ that. Saves carryin’ it all down to the jumble sell in Malton, aye?      Yeah, that'd be smarter. I mean, it’s not like I’ve got a shed full o’ stuff, but I ‘ave a couple a’ bangers in the loft. Gotta be th’ old ones though, innit? Not like new games and stuff.      That’s ‘ow thee gets the bobbies on yer back if thee dares sell sommat new as it is. But ‘old onto them used bits, and you’ll be fine. Just stick a good clear pic and description on’t listing.      I s’pose I could have a go. Me Gran set me up with a ‘voc account the other day, goin’ on aboot 'carbon footprints' an' 'sustainability'. I don’t see it. But if it means I can get what I want without trudging all the way to York, why not?      Exactly! Just make sure thee read the slots o’ info ‘fore thee hit the ‘buy now’ button. There’s some cheeky Arry out there wi’ a dodgy rating. Treat it like a shop in town but wi' a bit more adventure and slightly fewer bin bags.

Rather a cold day we've had, isn't it? I've been trying to get the old heating sorted all week and I've had no luck. It's not like it used to be in the old days, is it? Not quite the same feeling as when things were simpler.      Yeah, it is a bit of a shock with the weather lately. I tried calling someone in town this morning—it took me forever to find a decent plumber! Why can't things be easier? I was going to sort it for you, you know, if you like. Didn’t your cousin Jerry used to do some of that kind of thing?      Oh, Jerry's long gone, moved out to some boring town up the coast, I think. I’m not sure. Doesn’t come by anymore. I reckon he got fed up waiting for things to get fixed round here. But I’m not complaining. Got better things to worry about than a bit of cold. Although... I suppose if it keeps up, the pipes might freeze, you know?      That would be a nightmare—especially with the prices of contractors these days. Honestly, I sometimes think if we’d stuck with the old electrical and pipework, things would be better. At least we’d know how it all works. Mind you, most of the old estate is being knocked down, and none of the new build is much good.      Aye, I've noticed that. Bit sad, really. Families like yours are in this area now, and they deserve something better. You’ve a good career, I hear. That’s something to be proud of. Not like some of us who never got the chance. My day’s filled with deadlines and meetings, but I like it. It’s something I chose to do. You told me once, it's about choices, and I think that sticks with me.      Oh, I’ve seen you grow up with your head full of ideas and your eyes full of the future. You set your mind on something, and you make the best of it. That’s more than I ever could.      You’re just not giving yourself enough credit.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what airports do on Christmas Day. Filled with mums with kids and grandparents with tablets. Still, at least it's straightforward flying, right? No gotta worry about hating the train or anything.      Honestly, Andrew, I don’t get how you lot  want  to be on a plane on Christmas. My bakery’s shut of course—it’s the only day I actually get off in this year. Still, I'm seeing my folks inchester, so journey’s going to be long. Might drive instead. Less hassle. Not to mention the usual roadkill deers, foxes sad in the middle of the road with everyone honking. Cats would have been breakfast, no doubt.      Yeah, yeah, sounds like you lot have enough wildlife on the roads to make a proper feast. Good Christmas dinner for you—vibrating tyres, maybe a mushroom or two from the side of the road. What about food itself, though? You all having the full gear: turkey, sprouts, trotters, mince pies? It’s fancy, feels someone at least gave a thought.      That’s oddly enviable. My Christmas bake-off is going to be marshmallows and gingerbread—compared to your wild game, it feels like I’m baking porridge.      Ha, Sarah, let’s not be too humble. You know that your cinnamon rolls are the stuff of legend up in Birmingham. I’m hosting this year, so you’re guest cooking my guests’ dessert. Baking? Done. No need to thank me.      Ah, now that’s a proper Aussie crack at good eats. I’ll come over with mulled wine and a barista tip-up—you know the chocolate ones the size of your head.      Now you’re talking! Just don’t get your Aussie hat stuck trying to beat mine at pre-dinner line dancing, mate.      Time to lay the invites out. Shawna, you planning to fill up on kina’s leftovers or come down to Birmingham?      I’ll come. Anything for overcooked sprouts and silence from Shawna during carols. Deal?      Done.

Rather annoying driving up from Birmingham eh? You know, me being from the midlands, I always think the M1 and the A14 are the main runways between everything. But sure, Cambridge’s a nice pit stop. Not quite as spread out as London mind you.      Got a point there. I’ve been to Cambridge for uni open days before, and it all feels like a very clean version of nowhere. Like they wiped out every other town to make space for colleges. Makes me miss London’s clatter and clutter, even the noise pollution.      You’re not getting the full Cambridge experience if you don’t venture into a pub and ask the locals where the best "planty" jokes are. Although I’ve met enough eccentric mathematicians in this city to fill a library. You two should try the architectural bubble in the Kettle’s Yard building – it’s like a gigapixel photo breakfast, no doubt about it.      Oh yeah, I hear the architecture here hides a few secrets. I mean, I drive past university buildings all the time in Birmingham, but you get the impression they were just slapped together in short order. Cambridge’s like a living sketchbook for historic blueprints.      You'd expect a little from the “home of crumpets and cleverness” though, wouldn’t you? Speaking of, are we stopping for lunch before the game shop appointment? I haven’t eaten anything useful since yesterday at that bap and bacon place just outside Wellesbourne.      Only if it's a sourdough kind of lunch, not some preprocessed wonderbread. Oi, I may be from Birmingham, but I promise you I can switch between a Cockney duster and a poshh Cambridge professor voice at the drop of a hat. Give me a mic, a coat, and a bit of sprite and I'm off.      Don't forget the “I’ve read every book you’ve ever opened” voice, like you’ve personally met Walter Scott and he gave you life improvements. It does sound convincing though, which is the main bonus.      You two could lend your voices to virtual barons and tutorials in The Game Of Ages and still leave critics perplexed. Now, anyone got objections to recording a third character tomorrow in that sound booth behind the station?

Yo lads, you’ve gotta hear this new album I downloaded the other day—the bass hits so hard it feels like my earbuds are vibrating through my skull. It’s by this band called   Middle East  , genius stuff. You into indie rock?      Deffo, I'm obsessed with  Arctic Monkeys  and   Frank Turner  . I actually saw Frank live a few weeks ago in Camden. The crowd was wild, but honestly, the encore was  fire . Middle East sounds a bit… different though. They like playing with rhythms a bit more, right?      Yeah, I’ve heard a couple of their songs. They’ve got this mix of like electronic and lo-fi elements. I’m more into orchestral rock—  Mogwai   or   Sigur Rós  . There’s something about the massive walls of sound that just pulls you in. But hey, if you said it’s got a good bassline, I’d be lying if I didn’t say that’s always a plus in my book.      Roights—personally I listen to music I can headbop to. But I’ve tried getting into orchestral stuff too. I watched this documentary the other day where a conductor from the   London Symphony Orchestra   explained how string sections can mimic almost any emotion. Like, if you want the feeling of dread in a movie, you just have to know what combinations of violin and cello notes to use.      Yeah, I remember my physics teacher talking about resonance and overtones. Some film scores are specifically tuned to trigger emotional responses.   Hans Zimmer   does  that  so well. He uses about five different frequencies in a single note just to touch the different areas of your brain. Wild stuff, really.      Hah, bloody hell, I never thought of that. I thought it was just about how high or low a note sounded. But maybe that’s it—why some music just  hits  you harder than others. You ever notice how some songs make you feel like crying even though you’re not?      Totally. I remember the first time I heard  The Social Network  by Trent Reznor—it gave me the  chills , man. It wasn’t even emotional in the traditional sense. Just this really brutal piano loop with a blooming synthy texture. It was like… unnerving, in the best way.      Worth doing that, man. I had the same reaction when I watched  Inception  for the first time. The music and visuals just worked so well together.

Rather annoying I had an email from my daughter's school about Balanceability they had her in it they said first... So Becky said you need to test the water first. Like, throw a stone in and see if it makes a splash or just goes in slowly.      That's a good point. I did something like that when I was your age, and the water was too shallow. It's important to be careful. Speaking of water, I noticed you two were talking about cats in school the other day. My teacher told us about it and showed pictures of cute cats in costumes.      I told her about our cat, Micey. She said something amazing: Micey's favorite food combo is tuna and chicken — it's like our own special sauce.      Oh no, don’t give it to her every day or she’ll get fussy. It's like humans and pizza — you can eat it every now and then, but not all the time!

Rather annoying I’ve just got aching knees from the gym. I blame that spin class, ‘ow much I got to pay for a pain in the back more than I can take, innit?      Oi, I know the feeling. Sounds better than the usual lot. I’ll message you the link when I get it. Need to at least take a look to see how it’s different from the usual flim-flam.

Rather than share a text, I’d rather describe the scene. A lanky lad in his teens, piling bits and bobs into his satchel, ready for another tumble on the old Domino Drive! “Alfie, love, don’t forget your thermos — you'll be out in the cold een all that running about,” I say with a chuckle. “And tell your uncle Harry not to let you’ve the lot of sausages in the van again, unless you're promised stew as well!”      “But aunt Liz,” replies the boy in his childish, thick Tyneside brogue, “we sorted twenty boxes last week. That’s more than last term, innit? You like that My turkey and cheese quiche you made though left me belly feelin’ rummy!”      “Blimey, the little ‘un’s back again!” chuckles the taller, older, somewhat ruddy-faced gentleman in his cricket cap — Harry — at the cooktop, oversized knife in hand, ordering the pizza. “You want pineapple on that or not, Alfie? Cos if you do, I’m startin’ to think we’re not as much uncles and nephews as old-school gangs goin' to war with stickers and rhythm games.”      “Now Harry,” I cut in, with a bit of slap on his back — the old geezer tries to dodge it like a Silly Stones fan dodging press-ups at a weekend bash — “you just ‘big up’ your lad. He’s got promise, and if he’s doing Domino Drives hotter than the summer sun, then I say give it ‘im a break!”      “Yeah, about promises,” Alfie says with a grin, leaning on the fridge “So, Uncle Harry, you said if I done that extra shift last week, we’d watch  Captain America 4  at ‘ome. PoIze tell Aunt Liz here.”      “Oi, it's a Marvel ‘espect he talking about,” Harry replies, waiting till I spooned the last bit of garlic sauce on to the base before continuing. “I told him and it's a promise made, innit? Even if Marvel’s lost their way by now! Alfie, set goin’ on your own mission while I cook up a legend of melted cheese.”      “Right,” Alfie bellowed, lifting his satchel with puff, as if to declare war on the stairwell. “This time I’ll finish first and get more slots for ‘Number Ninjas’ at the food bank drive! Cos I’m the fastest ‘ockey player in Year 8!” — he paused at the doorway, “Even if I did lose my hat!”

I swear, I could drink tea all day. That’s me sorted. But anyway, I was thinkin’... got any plans for this weekend? I fancy a few cathartic pints at that little ale house near the station. Y’know, the one with the carved oak entrance. Got eeny weeny barstool stools, an’ the barman always remembers folks. Aye, love that place! Got that stubby booth, where we’d used to spill cider and someone once drew a moustache on the mirror. Didn’t even get cleaned. Haha, I still recall! Reminds me, I need to ask him for that kale recipe Alice mentioned. She said you could practically taste the melon in it or summat ridiculous like that. Aye, and I think it turned out alright. It was kale, a bit of garlic, breakfast lard from Marks and Spencers, and a bit o’ lime. I charred it in the pan, didn’t take long. Sounds complicated, like me trying to tell you how to change a spark plug. I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like food, but when someone says “charred kale,” I’m like... is that healthy? Oh Mate, health is relative! I mean, it's not like we are chowin’ down on fried squirrel like the Silly Stones crew. Although, Liam Neeson made me laugh the other day. He appeared in this ad for some cheese substitute... a man of his age doing a TikTok challenge over cheese! Aye, you know, I actually had a colleague, Laura, who nearly flaked out seeing him at the coffee machine the other week. She was fangirling so much, and I nearly spilled my smoothie! I mean, it’s Liam Neeson; the guy could read the phone book and still look like a movie star. Aye, it's a shame he's not drinkin’ ginger ale with me in that ale house this weekend. Still, we can’t all be out fetchin’ the lunches of a new generation of politicians. That's for certain. You know what, let’s just get the tea goin’. I think it's more of a social event than a necessity at this point, innit? You’re on! Kettle to the boil. I have that big mug with the koi carp on it. The one that looks like belly flopped! Oh, that’s the one! It's fitting. I’m goin’ to make mine with a shot of ginger and a slice of lime, like always, 'cos I'm very posh now, and slightly eccentric.

Rather annoying when no one’s paying attention. That happens way too often.      Okay... What was the word she said again? It rhymes with “teams” or something.      “Brazilians,” I said—get on with it! Come on, it’s beginning to get a bit stiff in here if we don’t get moving.      I’ve only got one brain cell left after this game, honestly. Oh, and she was joking about the rules. We can chuck the directions out and just go by what we think.      It is a bit daunting if you take it all too seriously. I found it easier to just have a bit of a laugh. You know, play it left or right.      You're all too picky about the rules. I came here thinking rules were about guiding and giving better clarity. But no—maybe I just happened to have a bit too much to drink, you know.      I say the rules are made to be followed, like in life. My, I had some funny times when I got it wrong with the children as their support worker and ended up on YouTube.      Oh, really? What was the best one?      True story—this young lad asked me to explain the word “courage.” I thought to myself, easy one. I said it meant doing what you fear the most and then led him out into the hallway to face the school cats.      [laughing] Did the kid have a nightmare after that?      No, in fact, he developed a fascination with them. That day the goldfish watched the whole thing, and now I can’t go into that room without it staring at me.      Maybe we’re all just a bit over the top about words. I happen to know Welsh has a word for “complaining” that means being mildly irritated.      You must be speaking of the word “cynnal.” That’s what we always used with lunches—“cynnal” the chocolate cake but let the pudding be forgotten.      I think the most fun is when it’s all about guessing. If someone gives two clues and you just tick, tick, tick away.      And your team’s counting on you. I used to play with my charity group in Cardiff. We’d all dress up like characters from the ’70s for competition over this. Only nobody remembered them! It ended up looking like my cousin’s birthday party.      Right, so the real game is trying not to get distracted.

Rather annoying that the Wi-Fi still isn't working, isn't it? Although it's given us a rather... charming excuse to play this old board game I found down in the bottom of the loft. Okay, that’s enough scheming for today. We crack this one as soon as we figure out whose turn it is with this cursed game.      Wasn’t that you, delivering the “I’m feeling a bit ill” routine go? Worked for you about seven times at uni. Not today, Mark.      Honestly, maybe I will go for the ‘I’m allergic to honesty’ card. That feels more safe than dancing in the shop.      True to say, we’re going to have to shuffle the pack and see if luck is on our side.

So, I just finished watching this new series everyone’s talking about. I know it's been on for like...ever, but I’m finally catching up! It’s properly intense, by the way. I’m definitely applying for psychology! I’ve always loved learning about the mind and why people do certain things. It helps me be a better friend and, you know, avoid the drama that happens once Christmas is over and people get overexcited about presents!      I’m seriously going to laugh at you if you tell me you’ve still got no idea what to get me for Christmas! I was just told by my mother-in – no one – that I’m getting a Dyson vacuum cleaner again. Like, really? We don’t even have carpets anymore!      You should be grateful, huh? Our family just got full sets of board games every year. I tried to sneak one out of the wrapping paper last Christmas, and it was a Rubik’s cube. I still haven’t solved it in five years! Not that I’m bitter or anything...      Ha, I had to work a double shift last weekend at the shop to save up for some gifts. I bought my sister a bunch of eyeliner for her beauty obsession. To be honest, I think she’s just pretending she likes it. She told me she's saving up to go to university too, but I sort of doubt her. Like,  she  also said she’d never break up with her boyfriend and wears the same jumper to school every week.      Ugh, I know the feeling. I have a cousin like that. She breaks up with her boyfriend every six weeks and then fake cries in the food aisle of Tesco. It’s exhausting.

Rather lovely evening, isn't it? Perfect for a bit of a stroll after dinner, if it stays like that. I've always preferred walking to driving, more peaceful I think. Clears the mind, don't you agree?      That does sound nice! I wouldn't say it was my first choice, mind you, I'm more of an 'on the go' sort of person. Cycling's a bit more up my street. Plus, it's eco-friendly, right? If I'm going to dump someone it might as well be the planet too, what?      Honestly, walking or cycling sounds far too much like hard work to me. I've got the car, and if I can drive there and back, then fine by me! Besides, left-hand driving is ridiculous – I still get confused.      I think it's important for all of us, at some point, to get out and enjoy the scenery without the windows whizzing past in a blur. I remember the days when we used to drive into London and get lost for hours, just for the sake of it.      Yeah, I'd love that sort of adventure! I’ve read about people bikepacking, covering hundreds of miles in a weekend. Doesn’t sound quite my thing, but I respect the dedication – it's a bit more my older cousin's kind of thing.      Now don't go making me feel lazy for preferring the car, okay? I might not live far from the shops, but in no way should I have to cycle there. It's bad enough doing the school run without getting all out of breath in the process.      That's your prerogative, love, I just find there's a type of clarity to walking or even cycling. It gives you a chance to really take stock of life and enjoy the little things around you. No pavement in sight, just a breeze on your back and your feet steady under you.      Well, as much as I enjoy being all philosophical about it, I do have to factor in getting somewhere on time to start my shift. Retail being the chaotic place it is, I'm a little behind schedule as it is today.      Ah yes, with work like that, it's even more important to get some exercise if you can. Any chance of a walk at lunchtime? It might do you the world of good!

Rather exciting to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty today, isn't it? I'm Laura, by the way, working on language research out of Oxford now.      Nice to meet you, Laura. I'm Joanna. I handle the administration side of things for a similar field. I recently came across a fascinating dialect survey from Lincolnshire — very different from where you're from in Buckinghamshire.      My name’s Charles. I’ve been teaching here for over thirty years and it’s always intriguing to hear how different regions shape the English language. Do you, for example, speak any other languages apart from your native tongue?      Yes, I dabbled in Spanish during my Masters and have since been captivated by the Basque language. It’s fascinating how it doesn’t seem to derive from any other known language in the world. Have you ever visited the Basque Country, Charles?      I have, indeed! Hmmm, it must have been about five years ago. Spectacular region, both culturally and geographically. I spent some time in San Sebastián, and had the pleasure of attending a local festival there — quite a contrast to the highland rugby festivals back in Shropshire.      That does sound like a treat. I remember my first visit to London fairly well, still, because the journey involved changing trains at Euston three times and missing my original one. Still, it was worth it!      Oh, London — one of the most linguistically diverse cities in the world. I had a friend from China who’d moved there a year before I met her, and she used to speak with such a distinctive accent it made about half the people walk away trying to figure out where the heck she was from.      Going back to languages, I once met a colleague who could switch between Mandarin, Spanish, and Basque with alarming ease. It was quite the sight. Though I have no such gifts. My wife and I, however, have always loved Wales for its Welsh language culture. We visited there last year and stayed in a small village where everyone still speaks Cymraeg.      Was it in Mid Wales or Gwynedd? I’ve always wanted to learn some go iawn on my own if I ever head up there. I find the preservation of language interesting, especially with English being so dominant.      Absolutely. Language is so intertwined with identity, and losing a language is like losing a part of history.
