Rather annoying this new coffee machine, isn't it? Seems like everything sticks and it's always coughing up bits of debris. Never had such luck as a teacher with my own tea mugs, least they stayed clean.      No, I know what you mean, Martha. It was on clearance and all that, but I don't think it was worth the hassle. I had to ring up the guy from removal services about it this morning before he helps us sort out the storage space. It's costing a fortune to keep one cup of coffee's worth of stuff.      Figures. You'd think removing three shelves of clutter would be a dead-simple job, but the bloke said storage will dock us like a month’s rent. Honestly, I swear the government’s in on it – they skew the economy and then chuck these costs at us in the name of ‘progress’.      Oh, here we go again with your political monologue Brian! You’d be better off voting Labour, ever considered that? They seem to talk about the little man more. I reckon they’d help us with the prices, maybe even give us a break on these removal costs!      Well, only if they’ve still got a clue what reality looks like. I read this interview from the new Labour leader—he’s all about idealism and changing the system, but really, how long are we supposed to wait before things actually change?      That’s the problem with idealism, huh? It feels great at first and then you’re sitting there waiting for a train that’s oddly left the station with no explanation.      I don’t see how we can fault idealism in a political figure. I mean, who’s worse: the same buggers who’ve had this job for 20 years and not changed a thing, or new people trying to do something, even if it’s tricky?      I get your point Martha, but let’s just say, I don’t want a leader who’s all talk and no action. I’ve had enough of people who make promises and then vanish into the woodwork.      Fair enough. At least we’ve got the removal man booked for Thursday. I’m just trying to get my head around the cost sheet he gave me. If I factor in storage per month and the hourly rate for loading, we’re looking at serious cash.

Rather annoying the new barista at Totnes isn’t she? I blame it on the youth of today. I got the wrong kind of shot in my latte and I can’t even tell the difference anymore! But anyway, enough about the coffee—I read somewhere that children today watch  more  TV than we did during our childhood holidays, and we were out playing in the woods every spare minute.      A latte? My dear, I used to be out picking blackberries with my Grandmother while pulling reasonable weight. We didn’t have the luxury of baristas back when I was your age. You'd fetch the cow's milk from the barn and that was a luxury in itself. Still, I do love the festive decorations at the pub. You’ve already got the tinsel up haven’t you?      Roxy and I did it the other evening—admittedly while arguing about whether it’s "kids" or "children". She’s returning after her in-laws next week, and I plan to fawn over the new baby so much that he’ll be checking out my wardrobe over the cot, yes! Speaking of, I’ve written to my sister about a week to go. She only sent two lines back, but then again—it  is  work time for her. She’s landed a contract for marketing estate agents in the city, and now it's all about spreadsheets and ROI.      Letter writing! You know what I said back then? She always preferred email. Our generation just wasn’t quite up with the pace. You’d have thought with all that TEFL experience—job security, at least. Or as I call it, replying to emails  in  other languages because most people about now are far too busy for letters. But talking of which, I had a consultation booked in Exeter yesterday—you know that new training course I’m taking? It's for organisational freelancing, so that I can create better guest speaker programs.      Inviting guest speakers? Doesn't sound too different from the talking I do at school, except I’m speaking to 30 confused teenagers. Though to be fair, they probably learn more from a couple of English teachers than from their actual families. Still, I get the idea.      Oh yes go on then, tell me about your parents again. Just don’t expect me to not mention that I had a cup of strong tea and a biscuit your mother left on the windowsill.

Rather annoying when afit’s goin’ to bed an’ someone sticks’un up in ‘ere, like...  sniffs , I mean it’s like a donkey! Ee, I dunno what they’re takin’ to do ‘bout it.      Aye, it een’t nice when  someone’s  got the snore o’ a lorry dawg on a A-road. Me ma once swore t’ God I got me dad’s snorer into me, an’ it’s just me luck to end up wit’ me cousin when he come over. Tore the sheets like a banshee.      Ohh, I rememb’r when we went up t’ Waterfields for them Richmond sausages. It een’t t’ everyday y’can get them, is it? The ones the little ‘un used t’ make, y’know.      Aye, still do! My mam goes e’s’ry Saturday an hides a few in the spare icebox. They’re like,  briefer  than any you get down the supermarket. Y’know it een’t quite the same now they’re supplying the whole town.      Bloke I work wit’ was all proud o’ his ‘n深化改革’ of using a handkerchief, but he’s got the grip of a sommat outta a car boot sale! Should’ve bin taught ‘im t’ fold one properly!      That’s a good ‘un! Y’had t’ been brought up t’ use ‘em, innit? I mean, it’s not like we all had a grandmother teach us how t’ do it square-like. My nan used t’ knit the holes into ‘em first. Honestly.      Not like now, where it’s a ‘smart cotton', an’ you ‘ave t’ bin’ it in the dishwasher t’ make it stay soft.      Oh, I relied on it yesterday, too. You know, when me flatmate had that  pasta incident  out the window. I’ve not been the same since!      Remind me, where did ‘e say ‘e met ‘er goin’ on aboot?      Gorse Covert Park, I think. Walkin’ ‘is dog on a Monday. Me da’s still all bent outta shape cos ‘e said the dog pooped on ‘is boots.      Ohh, ‘e’s so dramatic! It were a baggy. You know ‘ow ‘e is.      Right, so, like, I don’t get yeh. Why ain’t you wantin’ to go out wit ‘em?      Ee, I don’t know, it's just me da, innit. I just don’t fancy lectures about how I’m not e'en being “properly cautious”.      Aye, but if ‘e’s nice an’ don’t eat too many sausages, it's alright, innit?

I can't believe the weekend’s already here. That meeting dragged on far longer than it needed to. Honestly, I feel like I've had a full week already! Aye, that's how it always feels when we're working, innit? Course, I had a right night in yesterday myself—sat at the old farming desk with the dog at my feet, just sorting through paperwork. No rest for the weary, I suppose! Ugh, I don’t know how you do it. Manage to work from home like that. Didn’t your back get the worst of it? I still remember when you first told me about that awful pain you had to deal with before you got the chair sorted. My word, you must’ve been a misery. I tell you, love, them papers ain't gone away just 'cause I'm older, now are they? Got better back support, sure, but I've still got to put in the hours. Still, you ever want to come over, we could have a bit of a catch-up while I'm working. I do like the company. I’d like that. What did you get up to last weekend, by the way? I know you were going to work on that little project you mentioned. The one with the duck pond at the back, right? Oh, aye, don’t you remember? I started clearing the old willow tree out at the edge, and the old rotted planks. Gave me a proper backache, mind you. But I got the pond lined up and some new plants installed. It’s lookin’ decent, I reckon. Sounds brilliant! I’d love to see it the next time we're over. Honestly, I’ve been so busy with this new project at work I haven’t had a moment for anything else. My sister’s planning a little get-together for Friday night, though. Would you fancy coming along? Friday night sounds right nice. Give you a little break from your schedule. As long as there's a plate of good food waitin' for me, I’m in! That's you sorted, then. Just make sure you're up by seven, or I'll come and drag you out of bed like I did when we were younger! You’ve got yourself a deal, lass. Now tell me, what’s the special on this occasion?

I can't believe it's been nearly five years since we worked together. I was just reading through old emails and saw some of our funny project proposals. Remember that time we submitted one in Spanish just to see if the admin would follow up with us? Oh my gosh, yes! I still remember how you dragged me into that idea. It was ridiculous but I have to admit, it was hilarious when they cc'd our head of department and asked in perfect Spanish, "¿Este proyecto está listo para la revisión?" We nearly died laughing behind the coffee machine. That's the thing about teaching, isn’t it? You can still be silly and experimental while keeping your professionalism. Still, I miss that bit of mischief. Although I must say, my life’s a bit more dramatic now. I've got two kids, and my head of school keeps giving me flannel about moving to a more ‘influential’ role—maybe pastoral or something. Honestly, I’m not sure anymore if I want to lead a team or stay in the classroom. I hear that—especially with the kids, right? I can’t imagine uprooting two small humans every week to go to early meetings or whatever. I tried taking on a bit more at my job last year, but got completely overwhelmed. My partner was holding down the fort at home and, let's just say, we had a few arguments about whose job was ‘more important’ at the time. Oh, those are the classic teacher years. But hey, I’ve been trying to learn French again. I had a bit with my degree, but now with the kids starting primary school, I thought I should speak to them in more than just Apple-core English. My partner’s trying to teach the basics, but he’s not exactly a polyglot—he fails at “le chat” and “le cheval”. That’s a common mistake. Maybe you need guest speaker sessions at home. Parents on the weekend, grand-parents in the week. Wait—do you still meet up with Sarah when she's in Hitchin? Once in a while—she’s with that publishing thing in London now. But I do miss our book club meetings. We used to shoot ideas back and forth with the ease of bad binoculars. That was one of the best times in my head, between us and the boxset binges.

Rather a lot of activity in the garden this morning, old chap. That blue tit's been busy mending its nest again. I swear it went off for more twigs! Mind, the sparrow’s perch on the feeder keeps falling off – seems like I’ll have to reattach it again after tea. Got a bit of a wobbly ladder, but I’ll manage if it don’t rain. You don’t mind fetching the spanner from the shed, do you, Bill?      Aye, course not! Put the kettle on while I’m at it. It don’t take a civil engineer to fathom out a loose bolt. Though I do say, those birds out there are likelier to visit if you set a bit more seed out. The fat balls are a bit of a rum lot – I reckon Oliver should’ve brought some fig cake he saved from last week instead of kale again!      Egg and cake then? I happened to have a spare in the larder. Only not enough to fill the entire plate for both of you. And I must say, I was rather hoping Oliver would bring the puppets out again. I don’t get out a great deal these days and the children, what few we’ve got around, always cheer up when they see that silly old puppet show. Poor old Punch is missing his nose again, mind, but slap some glue on it and he’ll dance like a new man.      Bless you, Ruth! Though we’d better be careful what we’re feeding. Diabetes runs in the family like bad luck. I’ve been told I should give the fig cake to the moles and let the birds have their way – crude but effective, as they say in Norfolk about plumbers. Or perhaps the goldfinches fancy the currant bits?      Another good idea wasted on the moles! Still, if the moles are to have it, they’d better look like they’re doing something about the hills. They’ve been churning the garden up like it was disturbed pottery again. I tried to lay some turf last week, but the moles treated it as a joke. Even old Pete from next door said I might as well talk to them if I wanted results.      You know, dear, the old folks go on about their knees and hips more often than about work these days. I do wonder, do they really need all the box sets or could they do with some knitting?

Rather skip the starter and just go for the mezze platter. I know it's a bit much, but after the hike this morning, I'm starving. Have you ever had their stuffed grape leaves with a little dollop of yoghurt and dill? It's to die for.      That sounds tempting, but I think I'll take the souvlaki with grilled halloumi on the side. A lot has changed since I last visited Cyprus, you know. The last time was back in '81—my brother was doing business here. Didn’t even want to set foot in the north because of the politics back then.      Oh, the north’s still got a few quirks, but you know, I’ve met some lovely people here. Remember when Ed told me about the café in Famagusta and the old man who dowses for water for customers? Cats would come and breakfast on the old lady’s lap while he was doing it!      That is a tale, isn’t it? My old mate Paul once claimed he met a man in Nicosia who told him he’d listen to the stones in the ground to determine one’s destiny. I only took half of that in—Paul tends to embellish.      Tell me about it—he told me once that his deaf uncle, Horace, had a hearing aid tuned into his radio set so he could “hear” the football on the telly back in the '60s. Madness, someone said. But to Horace, it made perfect sense. He thought it brought him closer to the action.      I thought being deaf was something I’d get used to, but it still gives me a funny feeling. My wife brought a couple in last week—came from Greece for a holiday, and the sister is newly married. Supposedly it was a whirlwind romance—met on a horse farm. Poetic stuff, really.      I have no patience for meeting people these days. Do it once, I meet someone, and inevitably I end up hearing about their kid’s colitis or their wife’s fibromyalgia. I keep meaning to learn to count in Turkish, you know, just to have something new.      Yeah, go for it. But tell me something about your brother-in-law, Nathan. Is it true he tried to start a fire with a lens and a bit of paper? The latest I heard was that it nearly caused a minor heart attack out in the garden.

I can't believe we've never done this before, coming over for a catch-up just like this. The house is fantastic, and it's so nice to see more of my family properly. Thank you, hun. It's been a bit of a whirlwind for us with all the seasonal prep at the school and holidays approaching. But it's important to take a step back and enjoy the simple things with the people we love. I couldn't agree more. Oh, and congrats on pulling off that renovation project at work, Ann. You always said you'd get round to it some day. Thank you! It's been a massive learning curve and honestly, only possible with some brilliant team support. It still gives me the shivers though to imagine trying to tackle that myself. It sounds absolutely exhausting, but I'm proud of you. I was about to ask you what you’re planning to do about your place next. You did say in your last e-mail you were thinking about a revamp to the spare room? Yeah, that's right. I've got a couple of ideas, but I might need some hands-on help as it is. I'm thinking something smart, maybe go for a country-modern vibe. I remember when we got together last time at my nan's house, I loved the warm, rustic feel. That sounds perfect. I did just finish a project for a client who went for a similar aesthetic. If you're up for someone giving advice and helping with the shopping aspect, I'd be happy to. That's very generous of you, Ann. It's not surprising at all given your background in project coordination. We're about to make our Christmas list too, so the spare room revamp could be part of a larger family budget plan. I've already started mine. No need to go over the top, but I do like the tradition. Ann, are you still into that rugby team? You know it! I've still got a few mates waiting for me at the game Saturday. Why do you ask? Oh, just wanted a tip off from the younger generation if the team is any good this season. I told you, Sarah. You really need to see if you've kept up or not. Well, I can promise you the box food will be better than your team’s performance.

Rather annoying when people just ain't who they say they are on social media, innit? I seen like... some videos on Catfish ages ago now. One bloke turned out to be a kid from Sheffield posing as a Barcelona bartender or some nonsense like that.      Yeah, yeah, I saw that one too. Gives me the twitch, really. Makes me think about all them fake profiles I’ve probably friended by mistake. Got one from my nan, bless her, used to send me messages like "How’s me lovely Leeds United doing?" when she called me "lovely" and thought I supported United. Horrible.      Honestly, the real one that got to me was like that one turkey on Jeremy Kyle years ago. You know the one? Ten-year marriage, and the wife turns up and says, "Actually, I’m not your wife." And then the bloke just goes "Wot?" then starts to sob. Honestly, I couldn’t watch the end.      Oh, I seen that! That one was heartbreaking. It like made me not wanna watch Jeremy Kyle for ages after that. I mean, puts pressure on both people, innit? For the person getting told they’re not who they thought, and for the other person who has to confront them – it’s messy, fairly messy, like, it really messes up your day.      It’s all very dramatic. I reckon if I ever found out someone I was dating wasn’t someone who they said they were, I’d die on the spot. That’s not a lie—proper lie’d out. It's like betrayal and being lied to at the same time.      I mean, I get it. People make mistakes. But when it’s intentional—like whole fake stories and fake photos—it’s not just messy, it's cruel. Makes you wonder if the internet is like for real anymore. My sister nearly got passed off by some Tinder bloke, reckoned it was a Nigerian prince. He had a picture of him smiling on a yacht with a stick on his head as some sort of "noble" bit. Rude.      That happened to me with someone from Brighton once, sent me this picture of him on a boat cruising goin' on about life improvements and s   . Told me he had six cars, no fewer than three watches—turns out he’s a trainee mechanic with two cats and a tiny flat in Streatham.

Rather than share a text, I’d rather describe a scene. Imagine we’re in our home, having lunch. Our conversation flows from one topic to the next, natural and intimate. I’ll enact the dialogue as it would be spoken. Shall we begin?       Pause.  Okay, let’s get started then.      So, Gran, I’ve just read an article suggesting urban beekeeping might help boost pollination in cities. Honestly, I’m not sure how I feel about it. What do you reckon?      Oh亲爱的, when I think of bees, I remember my youth in Vienna. There, people made beeswax candles and sold them at the market. It was like a ritual, a tradition. Still, I suppose if it helps the bees, I’m not against it.      That’s interesting! I had no idea Vienna was like that. I guess I still have a lot to learn about your past.      Yes, and I’d love to hear more about yours. How is university treating you, darling?      Honestly, it’s challenging. My studies are in Classics — quite a different world from your early days in Art. Have you ever read something in Latin? I remember you speaking about the Italian renaissance. Pretty much all of it was Latin, wasn’t it?       Laughs softly.  It was, but I never pursued it. I preferred my brushes and pigments. Still, I admire what you’re doing. Though I’m not sure why anyone wants to work with ancient words when there’s so much modern chaos.      Fair point. But I love analysing ancient texts — it feels timeless, you know?      Interesting. And what about this “computer problem” you mentioned last week? Have that figured out?      No, not entirely. My device keeps crashing every time I try to install anything. I think it might just be too old. I remember you mentioned you had trouble once with a similar issue.      Oh, you mean when I tried to use the tablet to learn English with that app? It was a disaster. I took the wrong class, you remember — something for kindergarten!       Laughs.  Yeah, that wasn’t your fault though. Maybe I should ask my brother for help. He’s into all that tech stuff.      He’s older than you, I presume?      Yeah, he just turned 30. We’ve been to Paris twice with him over the last few years. Would you like to go again?      Always. I adored the Louvre once, but my French was so rudimentary back then.

Rather annoying driving today, isn't it? That man nearly smushed into me just then, like he couldn't be arsed to check his mirrors. It's not even football season, and we're already stuck in traffic.      That's Dorset for you, love. Overrun with tourists and all the holidays, I swear the place was built by someone who fancied living in their own world. I’ve only been once but would never return—such a place to stick a town right by the dump.      Honestly, the roads here are murder when it's raining. I came through Weymouth last year for a family do and had to park 20 minutes away just to get in. It's like they forgot to plan for anyone who isn't a tourist or a sea slug.      I used the sat nav the other day to take a quick route home and it routed me through some tiny village where I had to park up a mile in advance and hoof it. Honestly, I thought I'd missed the 21st century. I would never live in a place like that, no chance—no shop, no doctor, and the landlines as if you were in the middle of nowhere. Imagine having to pay a solicitor for something like getting a property sorted out in a place like that. Plus, I’ve got an MOT due soon, and I swear the cheapest garage around here is twice as expensive as the one I used to go to back at home in Kent.      Oh yes, and if you're not careful, they'll run up a bill on you quicker than the tide. I used to have a mate who worked at a garage back when I was driving, and I about blocked his number after he skimmed a couple hundred just to change a fookin’ lightbulb.      At least you've got a car, eh? I take a bus for work and it's not even fancy like that. Still, I have my days off. Last week was bloody nice—had a picnic in Bournemouth, bless. I could stick the Saturday into a Saturday. Though being a care assistant always comes with lunches of sandwiches and chips from the canteen, so no grand set-up for you.      That's the go, really. But life's more about balance, isn’t it? I just started my MA, so I’ve got a big chunk on reading to get through.

Rather a gray day, isn't it? That sun's been hiding all week. Don't think it's gone to be out at all today.      Oh, you're right about that. I've not had to do a bit of washing outside since last month. It's put a real dampener on my usual routine. You’d think the summer would at least offer a few dry days, wouldn't you?      Damp, indeed. And it’s started to get into the floorboards in the back room. Bit of a nuisance, when you get the blooming smell of wet wood. I tried laying some newspaper down, but it’s no good—never seems to do the trick like it used to when I was younger.      Tenacity, they say, is what keeps us going these days. A bit of newspaper and an airing, and we’re off! Still, I suppose we’ve got to make do with what we’ve got. When I was childminding, I used to tell those little ones that the sun was just off walking—out doing the shop, maybe!      Aye, well, as long as you weren’t off on the hop, as they say. Makes you laugh remembering it now, doesn’t it? Though I remember one of those bairns, young Daniel, he once said the sun had gone out because he forgot to turn it on! You know what kids can come out with.      Oh, full of imagination, aren’t they? That's the trouble with the new generations—they think everything's switched on with a遥控器 these days. Don't know if they’d even know what newspaper is for, let alone how to deal with the damp.      It’s progressing a bit fast for some of us, that's for sure. But it does give one something to talk about, doesn’t it? A quiet tea-time conversation about the weather and technology. Rather droll, it is.      I suppose it is. You know, when I was still working as a childminder, I’d always try to find the silver lining in the clouds. Now, I just want that lining to deliver something a bit brighter than a couple of grey hours.      Aye, and so do I. I just hope the sun comes out before we go further into the autumn.      It will, mark my words. We've just got to wait for it, like we wait for life to give us a bit more every now and then.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘goin’ to stop or not by now. I’m more used to the blasts of wind we’d get in Sunderland, at least with them you could plan your day—get the washing in when it was still dry eenin’!      Yeah, I reckon it depends where you’re from, aye? A lot worse if you’re in the Midlands, honestly. In Birmingham, you’d get dump rain that clatters you out the house. Still, I suppose it’s better than glorified winter in Cambridge like we’ve had this month.      What’s that then, frost on the grass and the turkey still in the oven? Ha! Speaking of, you haven’t forgotten the music for the DJs, have y’? Aunty Sharon’s bringin’ about a dozen of the cousins breakfast, and if it’s just us playing folk tunes for hours, they’ll all be out by 10, even if it is the weekend.      Ah, no, you don’t need t’ worry about that. I’ve got a playlist sorted with some early 2000s stuff—artists like Primal Scream and Tricky. That should keep most of the younger ones entertained while the older lot still think it’s “classic.” Also, I’ve set up the speaker system in the conservatory. Bit brighter in there than the living room, and the heat feels better with music.      That sounds good, love. I do wonder what you were up to with your PhD though—music theory, was it? I remember your colleague mentioning something about your research about how regional accents affect musical perception.      Aye, exactly. I’m trying to see how people from different parts of the country interpret the same song based on the dialect, delivery, and even tempo. It’s quite interesting actually. For instance, I’ve been testing it with folks from the North and the Midlands, hearing how they process the same melody differently.      That’s deep, innit? Do they pick up on the emotion more if it’s sung with a voice like mine, or do they prefer smoother accents?      Both, apparently—but more often, responses are emotional when the performer shares the same regional background. It’s like a connection they feel through the voice, even if the song is the same.      Well, that’s something to note for your thesis, love.

I can't believe the number of people my age who are unemployed. I mean, it's mad when you think about it, innit? Just after uni, more people I know are stuck at home, doing nothing but watching telly and moaning about the state of things. Aye, it's not nice at all. I’ve got a cousin who just got his degree in business management from Birmingham. He’s been applying for jobs for over six months and got precisely nothing. It makes you think, does it even matter getting a degree these days? Oh, don't even get me started on the fees. My brother took out a load of loans to study at the uni here in Cambridge, and now he's working a minimum wage job just to get by. It’s ridiculous! I’m glad I’m in a higher professional role already — gives me sleepless nights thinking of all the uni grads working in fast food, innit? Yeah, I used to live that, you know. I started my PhD to get out of the working-class grind, but now I'm stuck with no salary, and it's taking longer than expected. I’m seriously thinking of dropping it and trying to get real work. Have you ever been to a musical, by the way? Musical? Yeah – Matey, I saw  Hamilton  on the West End and nearly cried the entire night. It was brilliant, like something outta a film. You should’ve come with me, you would've loved it — full of rapping and dancing and stuff like that. Pretty different from doing a PhD, innit? Haha, no, I haven’t seen  Hamilton  but I've heard people about it. I’m not the theatre type, more the kind of bloke who’d be watching rugby and maybe a documentary. But you’re right, it is a change from my usual schedule of reading papers for 12 hours a day. Aye, you should go. It's something to take your mind off bills and essays for a night. I could stick us two good tickets in. You bloke deserves a bit of escapism, innit? That's a good idea. I'll take you up on that! Maybe watching a show go me inspired on what life could be like once I'm done with this PhD nonsense. Imagine making a living outta performing, blooming mad.

Look at this! The pictures in this book are amazing. I love the one of the dragon with the typewriter. That's so weird and cool, like, why would a dragon need a typewriter?      Aye, they have some wild things in these children’s books these days. Back in my day, books were more about knights and princesses and less about dragons with typewriters!      Oh, now that one! I used to read books like this when I taught in Glasgow. Children just adored the absurd. It's how they learn to think.      Yeah, I like it! It’s not like some of the ones I had to read before, like about posh boys going to school and being best friends. I find this more fun, to be honest.      I think it's important for your books to reflect who you are and what interests you, sweetheart. You need stories that are like a bit of yourself in them, you know?      Absolutely. And the stories we tell now, they shape the ones we pass on, don’t they? Like, I always told stories with strong women as the main characters when I taught, even as a young teacher.      That’s kind of like how Mum tells stories – about Gran growing up in Glasgow, and how she met Granddad. I wish I knew more of those.      Oh, well, we can make our own family stories. Like this book — full of weird and wonderful things. You could draw a picture of Gran with a typewriter and a kilt.      Now you’re talking like a real storyteller, love! We have about five generations of stories to play with here, right? From Glasgow to Bristol to Cork — what an adventure.      I’d love to draw a picture of my stepdad with a horse for the story. He always says he used to ride horses when he was younger.      Oh, I remember talking about that once. He did, sort of. Not professionally, but he used to help out at a stable.      Aye, the family stories aren’t always grand things, are they? Just bits of everyday life with a little gothic or fantastic twist added if you like.      I think I’ll do that. A picture of Gran in Scotland on a horse, and me with the dragon. Maybe I’ll call it, "The Typewriter Dragon and the Kilt."      Sounds like a start of something brilliant, love.

Rather annoying to be honest. I finds it so much more easier to sticks with it, saves time in the mornin’. But me mam keeps on at me about it, says I've got no proper upkeep.      No, I kind of agree. I shave every two days or so, but I find myself doing it more often if I'm wearing short sleeves. It gets self-conscious after a while. A lot of people just let it go though, honestly.      Yeah, it do gets me thinking sometin’. Like, why do we shave bits an’ not others? Legs, arms, even underarms—what’s with that?      Fair point. It’s mostly social norms, I suppose. I think it’s different for everyone, though. I’ve got a few mates who say they’d never shave a single bit of it, and others who’re almost constantly on the subject of electrolysis just to keep it off.      Electrolysis sounds right harsh, innit? I’d not fancy that for nothin’. I do like the way it feels smooth, but the effort it takes puts me off.      Yeah, I tried laser treatment once—it wasn't for me. The first few sessions were okay, but the cost added up, and I didn’t want it to be a long-term expense. Truth be told, I just stick with the regular razor and some coconut oil after.      Aye, sounds better than what I’ve been doin’, rushin’ it with a shaver in the bath and half my legs still have stubbles. I should really take more time in it, but most o’ the time I’m rushin’ out the door for college.      Maybe you could do it the night before? I mean, if you're not in a rush in the morning, it just feels less stressful.      I might give that a try. I was thinking about it last night, but then I just thought, “Blimey, it's Saturday. Who’s gonna notice?” Heh.      Ah, Saturdays do offer a bit of a luxury, don't they? Sometimes I just lie in bed goin' on about how I could sleep until ten or something, and my partner is up making tea by seven.      That your actual thing you two have going on?      Yeah, we both work part-time and attend college, so we kind of rotate who gets up first. They say it's their way of making the team effort feel balanced.

Rather annoying when a bar’s got no lager, innit? I was just in Chester when it was all lager and no bitter. Y’know, it’s like going to a pub where they’ve forgotten how ale works. Chuffed to bits I came here instead — this is the place for proper real ale, innit? I’ll take one of them   A   beers, luv… err, a Burton ale, love. Slap-up name too.      Cheers.   B   as in beer and bread. Leeds United were playing yesterday, by the way. That bloke came out with another racist rant again. Typical. Someone ought to tell him he’s out of order, but no one dares. It’s disgraceful, innit? Football’s a game for everyone, ain’t it?      I’ll be the first to say it — it’s a bloody disgrace. I saw it myself in a match down in Middlesbrough last season. People’s using the excuse of hides, you know, but that’s a front. It’s all blokes trying to show off, lads’ nights out, and I’m fed up with it. We need to stamp it out, innit?      Agreed. I remember when I got into boxing. My old man used to box back in the ’80s in Birmingham. Some of his old sparring partners did   C   as in copper lines. Not that I’m shilling, but the lads all took to it. Strictly for the calm, though — not for the kicks or the rush. Though, gotta admit, the   D   comes through in a decent session after a fight, eh? Not that I’m bitter about any of it.      Oh I get it. I’ve seen my mates do it after university weekends. I mean, it’s not for me — I prefer a good   E   like Envy. Bitter, floral, hits the spot. Lean back and let it pass over you. No need for no pills or nothin’. I could stick to my good   F   — as in Friday nights here in Cambridge. Town’s got character, innit?      Still, I’m more of a   G   bloke — go for a Gogmagog bitter or something. Just depends on the mood. I’ve got that PhD to finish off, bloke — gotta pace myself. Can you believe I’m writing about alphabets and semantics? Like, where’d we all start with the letter   H  ? I say, ‘Harry Hill’ when I think of this bloody alphabet game.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, Dottie? Seems like everything we try to get approved takes a gazillion forms and a cold shoulder from local authorities these days. I’ve had trouble securing funding for that 18th-century townhouse in Stratford since the spring.      I hear that one all the time, Eleanor. It’s the same in Dorton. My team wanted to restore a grade II listed barn from the 1790s, and suddenly we had to refer to twelve different heritage documents. You’d think they’d standardise this nonsense by now, don’t you think?      Honestly, I’m beginning to believe it’s more about pen-pushing than preservation. But you and I both know, if we want to keep our business afloat, we need to play the game, even if the rules are in a flux.      You’ve got to have a breakfast with the Bucks Heritage Trust this Thursday. They’ve taken in a new board, more sympathetic to private sector ventures, as long as the benefits are tangible. I reckon your townhouse could stand as a benchmark—personally, I’d lean into that if I were you.      Hmmm... Tell me, in your experience, what works best when it comes to presenting a business plan for a historically important property? I’ve got a presentation prepared, but I'm not sure it's hitting quite the right note.      Ooh, don’t be coy, dear. Our success came down to one thing—community buy-in. Show the council how your project can attract school field trips, walking tours, whatever. You need to be their golden goose as much as your own, understand? Personalise about how the townhouse ties into the town's Renaissance history.      That’s an angle I hadn't fully explored. I've focused on conservation targets, not enough on the social return. And do you have any tips for expressing financial needs without giving the impression we’re asking for a blank cheque?      Good question. I always pitch with a balanced approach. Detail clear costs and outline funds being matched by private investors or firms specialising in heritage spots. Trust the committee—they love a secure, sustainable project, even more so if it’s not their money bleeding go.      You always had a knack for this, Dottie. I remember that barn project we were both involved in on the Dorset coast. How did we manage to get it past conservation concerns and into the public eye so quickly?

I can't believe we've got this weather in Cambridge — feels like we're stuck in a time loop! Mind you, I've been so busy sifting through more linguistic data, I haven’t had time to properly notice anything. Aye, it does rain a bit. But it’s peaceful when y'get to actually work from home, innit? I reckon it's not all that different from a rainy day in Brum — just quieter 'ere. How's the data looking? Honestly, it’s gold. We’re starting to see some interesting dialect patterns when comparing North-east speech to Midlands' — y'know, like how we pronounce "bath" versus "bath" — and how that relates to socio-economic status. Oh aye, I hear y'. I've been focused on how academic language in the sciences differs between undergrad and postgrad levels. Mucky work, I tell ya! Mucked or not, it’s illuminating. I mean, we’re starting to see how even the most colloquial of speech can reveal socio-cultural affiliations, and it's not just about the words — it's about the context, the rhythm, the inflections. Right on. I've got this data set from some Midlands-tech lectures — the shift in language when they're with their peers versus when they're presenting to the public is quite telling. Silly question, but have you ever thought about publishing your work? 'Cause someone at our uni is looking for a solid read on language evolution in higher ed sectors. Aye, been meaning to. It’s just that between the PhD and the ballet sessions with the kid, I daftly walk away empty-handed more times than not. We were meant to be cooking lasagne last Sat. Aye, it is a tough one. I do miss a good Burgundy baked macaroni. Though I'd swap it for a weekend in Cornwall any day — just surf, sand, and sea air. Ah, but when y'finally get the chance, you can't shift the deadlines outta the way with a broom! Now, now, no need for drama, luv. We’ll plan the trip when the go-seq map for your paper is sorted — or mine. Let's get the kettle on, eh? Good idea. A bit of tea and cake could inspire both o'us to churn out a couple of chapters apiece. It's a bet, then. First one over 5000 words wins the last slab o' chocolate.

Rather than paying a full price for school dinners, I've been speaking to the teacher, and they said if I got the kids to bring in a packed lunch more often, it might cover the expenses. Beans on toast is a classic, don't you think?      But I don't want eeny beans on toast, Mummy. I want chicken nuggets! My best friend Sarah gets them. She said they have a tiger on the side too and a funny man with a red nose who dances!      Wait, a funny man? Is it a clown? Mummy, I saw one once at a party! He made a balloon go round and round like a hippo. It was like being at the circus!      Well, you boys and girls do hear about the most exciting things at school I think! A dancing man with a tiger, by the sounds of it. However, no matter what the circus has, we need to be thinking about what’s for lunch. There will be a school tennis tournament next week, and you’ll need your energy up for that, both of you.      I like tennis! Miss Davis says I hit like a real player. But we have to eat dinner first before we can go out, right? So is it chicken nuggets or beans on toast?      I like beans on toast! Miss Patel said that they are the best for brain power. And we need brain power for homework and for remembering what someone wears in the dress-up box!      That’s a very mature thought, thank you, Tom. So, let’s be clever and stick with packing something nourishing, but we can have about half the week with a packed lunch containing the good stuff and then on the other days a little special treat. Let me write that down.      So can I have chicken nuggets on Friday then? Just one day?      Sure, on the one condition that any leftover lunch money is used for something sensible, not just chocolate biscuits. We could talk about going to Granny’s as well, if you two want lunches to be more varied and fun. She’s quite good at making things like spaghetti with tomato sauce and mushrooms!      Yeah! Granny’s! She always does something different. And she shows me how to juggle! Mummy, maybe I can be a joker like the circus performer at the school sports day!

Rather enjoyed the new biopic last night, didn’t you? I thought it was incredibly well-acted. It got me thinking, though—how much do you think we should rely on films to teach history in schools?      Hmm, I suppose as long as they’re used with caution. Films can make the past  palatable  for the young, if you like. But they also have a tendency to glamourise facts, don’t you think? I read about that debate in Cambridge last week, interesting stuff. Some wanting to bring in more diverse perspectives on history, moving away from the glorified version we used to learn.      Absolutely. I was at the debate too, and it made me contemplate how the national curriculum is shaping our young minds. When I was at school in Ayr, the focus was on timelines and key events. Very rigid. But nowadays, with all the chatter about inclusivity and postcolonialism, I wonder if we’re doing enough in schools to challenge the old narratives?      It’s a bit of a conundrum, that’s for sure. My own pupils are very inquisitive, I mean, don’t get me wrong. But I’ve seen how resistant some parents are to changing the way history is taught. They want their kids “sticking to the facts,” as they put it, and not questioning the status quo. I remember my history teacher in Dorchester would have given them a right tongue lashing for that attitude.      Aye, but then again, I was lucky to have a teacher who thought we should do more than just memorise dates. Encouraged us to be critical. That’s where education should be, in my opinion— about helping people think independently.      Exactly. And this extends into higher education too. At the advertising agency I work with, we’re always talking about how universities are failing to connect theory with real-world application. Degrees are often disconnected from the industry. A few more internship placements or work-based learning components would give students the practical experience they need.      That ties into our experience in schools too. If we’re not teaching with critical thinking and real-world relevance in mind from an early age, how are we delivering the kind of individuals who can navigate the tricky political goings-on in this country? It's not just about content—it's about preparing young people for the complexities of the world.

Rather a damp day we've got, isn't it? Makes me think of my youth, when the first war was on and the rain never gave us a chance. I was a lad back then, helping about the farm in Costessey with my da and the rest of the lads.      Oh dear, yes, I remember my gran telling me stories of how she had to grow up with rationing and air raids when she was your age, Henry. She was born in Harrow, just a bit further up from me. She always said the hardest part was when the children weren't safe outside.      Still, it made strong people, didn't it? When I was starting out in my business, you had to be tough too. My folks were schoolteachers back in Middlesex, and they always told me, "Milton, the world may throw you in the mud, but you better make breakfast, no matter if you've got all four legs slick in it!"      That's a good one, Milton. I suppose growing up in Harrow, I was always near the hustle of the city. My studies led me to become a quality reviewer in education, and I often think how today's children probably live a life far removed from what our parents and grandparents known. Though I must say, I often wonder about the young people these days—how much do they really know of our past?      If they do, they don't talk about it much. Our modern world is full of screens and suspicious characters. You read the papers, and it's always some new outrage about the law not doing enough or overdoing it. I remember the bobbies used to be good Samaritans about the place.      Oh, the police had a job looking after a house full of kids during the war and then during the baby boom. I remember one time my father, a delivery driver, was stopped for nothing. All passed off, but that's how you knew the world was a different place those times.      And when I started out in the 70s, furnishing a home was always a big deal. I think it was partly the scarcity from the recent war that set us apart. Then again, nowadays everything's so easy to go out and get. But if you ask me, real furniture has made a dent in quality for cost.

: You sure the GPS isn't going to mess up again? I still remember that time we got lost on that back road and ended up in the middle of nowhere. I was convinced we were going to die there.     : Look, it worked fine last time. And it was only because you insisted on taking a detour to visit that ridiculous sculpture park. You know I wanted to get back before your mum started listing all the things I’d “forgotten to bring.”     : Oh, come on, the sculpture was amazing! Didn’t you want to see it at least once? Besides, I had to make sure everything was ready for tonight. We didn’t exactly plan this weekend visit like everyone else’s.     : I know, I know, but I still had to risk getting lectured about not eating enough fibre. Or did she mention that to you yet? Wait, does she even know I’ve been skipping my salad for weeks while working late shifts?     : If you say so. But why do you still avoid taking me seriously about this English class I’m teaching? Rather than going out, I thought we could have a little do at the house for your nan’s birthday. It’ll be quieter, she might be more at ease. I can rearrange the living room table and borrow some candles from Kim to set a bit of a vibe.      That’s a lovely idea. She  does  get a bit overwhelmed in noisy places now. I’ve been thinking she’d enjoy something homemade, too. Do you think she'd be up for a themed menu? Maybe some of her old favorites from when we were kids?      Definitely. Let's go traditional — a good old roast with Yorkshire pudding. She can't resist that. What I'm still thinking about is the seating arrangement. I know you get on well enough, but I’m not sure if I should seat Dad and Nan next to each other. The lights turned off at the last family meal — chaos ensued.      He doesn’t notice half of it himself some days, though. I don’t want Nan to feel out of the loop. Also, the table plan would help everyone—especially with the new additions—know where they are sitting. I can make a seating chart as a PDF and share it.      Yes, brilliant. I’ll work on the table plan. Now, about the food — I spoke to the fishmonger, and they have a huge selection of salmon and haddock. Would you like something fish for her after the roast?      There’s also this someone at work who makes a smashing Victoria sponge. I’ll ask if she can do a lemon drizzle instead—lighter than a trifle and still comforting. Can I bring the cake in, or would it be about the candles?      Oh! She’s very particular about her candles — no ones and threes because that was her mum's age when she died. Maybe we just do 87 for her and keep the ones for the cake.      That’s a thoughtful touch. If you don’t mind, I’ll bring them from my kitchen. My biscuit tin is full of them — she gave them to me years ago. I keep meaning to throw them out, but I can’t bear to.      That’s the spirit of it, isn’t it? The little rituals. I wonder if I should ask her favorite Bake Off contestant to judge desserts. She lives for that show.

Rather annoying me a bit, me wijsdoomtheeth. I had me other one ‘taken out’ last week an it hurts like bobbins yet. I can barley chew on the left side o’ me mouth. Not to mention I’ve got a hole wi’ a funny jelly-like lump in it een me gum now, yeah?!      Ugh, I’m dreading that for me. I only had one taken out before so this lot isn’t much easier. I’ve not had time to go yet. Me parents was like, “Lay off the chandlers sweets ’til you get that sorted,” like I couldn’t control meself! Honestly, the last thing I need is some boring filler conversation at turkey time. You back to uni soon?      Yeah, I’m moovin’ back o’er the first o’ September an I’m panicking about it. Me breakfasts are mostly toast an' jam now, which I’m not a fan o’ ever since I started felling bits movein’ about in me mouth. I’ve got to stay wi’ me auntie for a week afore startin’ in case me tooth leaves another message for me grief. Havin’ to book a room at a mini hotel fer extra time in France. D’you noo –?      Yeah, I know the one! It’s the cheapest flat-like flat above that bakery place near the station. I’m goin’ back that way as well. Our parents said we gotta share a room again to save money, like we’ve done ev’rey yer. Though this year is a moover, as I’ve got to shift outta me sister’s room properly because she’s about to get married an' all. Fit the decorations an’ lot.      Gosh! Going proper grown up then! I mean, it’s brilliant for her, but I feel like for every year we get less “uni ready” an' more just “adult trash.” I remember when we was all like, “We’ll be them people who live on our own an' have proper kitchens.” Now me ‘kitchen’ is a sad lil kettle an’ a mini toaster.      Still, I’m happy with it. I mean, I can go out more on me own if I need to. Just got to make sure me head stays outta the clouds wi’ the bloomin’ wisdom teeth an' me sister’s wedding. I’m seriously thinkin’ o’ just poisin’ me parents wi’ all that veggie buffet stuff they like, ‘cause I’m not feelin’ it this yer.

Rather than going out and doing something extravagant for Chinese New Year, I thought we could do something thoughtful. We could make and deliver some homemade lactose free cakes and cookies to our elderly neighbour Mrs Li. She's been doing her own thing quite often since the pandemic, and it might be nice to brighten her day during the celebration.      Mrs Li has got some dusty old chess and draughts sets that Aunty gave her once. Maybe I could play with her? I’ve not played draughts properly since we had the board at school.      Mummy, I saw on the telly that Chinese New Year is like a birthday party for the world. Could we write kind messages on the cakes and cookies? I want to tell Mrs Li she’s awesome!      Aww, that’s lovely, love. We can make little cards with the messages and put them with the boxes of treats. I happened to have a spare recipe book at home, using non-dairy substitutes, which I showed you earlier when I was experimenting over the holidays. I think I still have the almond flour, and we can glaze it with some coconut milk.      What colour cake mix do we have left, Mummy? I saw you put some left-over food dye – could we make one red and one gold, because those are lucky colours for the New Year? It would be like a decoration as well as a treat.      That’s a great idea, darling. Red and gold they shall be. And maybe we can tie some red ribbons around each box? I have a sewing kit and some scrap fabric under the table I could use.      I want to dress up! I found those little lion masks we had from the school fair last year. Can we wear them when we take the cakes to Mrs Li? It’ll be just like the parade on the telly!      Of course, sweetheart. You can be a lion guardian, and your sister can be a dragon keeper. After we deliver the cakes, we can play draughts with Mrs Li if she’d like to keep the conversation going. It might also be a good way for you both to learn some new moves!      Yeah! But can I borrow some of her pieces to use as my own in the next game between us and the other kids?       laughs  Well, I’ll ask her first, but we could suggest you all lend them back for your next game nights.

So, I just read  Alice in Wonderland  again, and I still don’t get it. Why was everyone so confused and mad? It’s like they just woke up!      Oh, it was probably because of the mushrooms, love. You know — one side makes you grow, and the other makes you shrink. But honestly, it’s just a mad dream. Almost like being in a car accident but with words and tea parties!      Oh yeah, you had a crash last year. How’s the scar doing? Is it still there when it rains?      It’s still there mostly. I can hide it with makeup and a hat now, though. You remember that My Chemical Romance song I liked after the accident? The one you used to pretend to play on your phone while I was having a bad day?      How could I forget! "Welcome to my life." I hated it at first, but in the end, I ended up putting it on my playlist to annoy you. Also, the scar isn’t real compared to yours — the one you get from inappropriate costumes and letting the seagulls steal your chips.      That’ll do — go on, I reckon you’re trotting off to the theatre next. How’s the costume coming along for the prom? I saw it on the internet, and the glitter is nearly blinding me already.      Oh, don’t be mean, Mum. It’s someone’s full-time job to make me sparkle. Besides, it’s for  The Tempest . I had to read it for English and then rewrite it through music. I’m analysing it as if it were a playlist.      That’s clever, actually. You’re going to be doing things your way from now on, then. I remember reading it once, ages back — quite tricky, but you made it interesting.      Well, I have you to thank. You told me stories all the time when I was little, so when I started reading on my own, I just… followed in your footsteps. Except you were always explaining  Alice  better than the teachers do.   Speaker__2:   Then you must be a better storyteller than I am. I remember your presentation on stage design — you had drawings and posters and everything, like a full-blown exhibit. You charmed half the class and scared the other half.      Hazarding a guess that those were the ones scared of your glitter bomb fallout?      Precisely.

Rather annoying isn't it, how these developers just seem to think they can stick massive wind turbines in the middle of nowhere and expect us not to object? I've been helping out a few folk in the village with their protests — they're up against a dastardly planning application.      Yes, it is. I remember we were told the same thing when we tried to stop the last wind farm a few years back. I think they think that because they're for 'green energy', they can waltz right in and we'll just step aside and thank them for it, don't they?      That's because they  can  afford to, isn't it? The companies behind these projects are well-funded, and they seem to have enough influence within the local council and the development control committee to push things through, even when the local people object.      Oh, and they’re not just about the money. I've been reading up a bit in the evenings. It seems the Government awards quite a few subsidies to those alternative energy projects. One would think they’d want to fund the  research , not just throw money at the occasional development.      You’re not wrong. What good is having a windfarm if it's not efficient and it doesn’t help us store the energy for when it's actually needed? I read somewhere that the finance goes more into the projects themselves rather than into R&D for better energy storage. It's a bit backwards, don’t you think?      That’s the nub of it, aye. We need to think differently — not just protest, but come up with real alternative methods. I’ve been thinking about talking to a few engineers at a university down south about what new technologies are being devised. Maybe we could present some findings at a local meeting and make the committee take notice.      That could be useful to the solar panel protest group as well. We were discussing tactics last night, and they mentioned they could do with more technical knowledge. It's all very well saying no, you know, but unless you can present a good alternative and show a viable  political  strategy, the planners don't really take you seriously.      True. It’s a balancing act, really — the local planners have go-betweens, if you like, with the energy companies and the line of bureaucracy that leads to Government.

Rather annoying this, having to go through all that driving lot. I've had my full licence since '78, and I've not touched a car since '02! Mind, I think it might be a good idea. Not only for getting about, but being independent for the holidays again.      I thought about doing it myself, you know, just to have that freedom. Though honestly, I found the whole insurance stuff quite overwhelming. Such a lot to consider. Oh, and the age thing! You tend to pay more when you're younger and when you're considerably older too.      That’s very true. I've seen so many people, both the young and elderly, struggle with the cost of car insurance. It's one of those things that’s easier said than done, isn't it? D’you know, I think it's much the same with assembling a holiday. All the details, breakfast, room choices, and whether you want to rent a car there too!      Exactly, you have to make so many choices. And I would never dream of relaxing over there unless I had my own transport. Though I have to say, quite a few people I've taught tell me they’ve only tried driving on foreign roads. They say it’s a little nerve-wracking at first – but they get used to it, and sometimes it's even more fun than the local roads!      Well, for me, it's back home I’m most nervous about. Our roads here in Birmingham aren’t too bad, but they do a rush hour like I've not seen in years. Also, I've heard the DSA being strict recently with new test standards – I’ve got my fingers crossed about that!      Oh, don’t you worry too much. I think what you really need is someone to accompany you and take the pressure off a bit. You're quite confident, so confidence is the biggest part of it.      And if you ever need it, I can help give you some pointers, or at least recommend a decent instructor. We could make it a bit of a bonding thing, like learning together.      That would be lovely, love. I’d be grateful for the support. Now, moving on from the driving goings-on, what are you up to this week, love? You mentioned you had a work-related trip coming up.      Yes, actually.

I can't believe the chaos in Brighton with parking these days. I love the place, but it's so hard to navigate, especially with all the deliveries now. Aye, where I come from is gone. Not quite like it was back in the fifties. We'd make do with eeny things—old cartons of milk for drinks, and if you wanted to eat, you made a pie. A lot less choice now, but a lot more to choose from, if you get me. It's funny you mention that. I was thinking about the food bank up the road the other day. Still, I made sure to get enough fresh fruit and veg for tea. Alice and Jamie are always gobbling sweets, but I’m trying to make it healthier. You're a good mother and I'm proud of you. Back in my day, we didn’t have mobile breakfasts—just a bit of tea and a scone in the early hours, and the day was ahead of you. Now everyone's tapping and buzzing away on them phones, like they need it every moment. Definitely. I never thought I’d miss the Facebook app and all the notifications. But maybe it's good to log off sometimes. I remember when all we needed was a letter in the mail or a chat at the local. Far more friendly, really. Times did change. You couldn't even win a bit back then unless it was on the horses. I had a friend in London who always went to the track. Bet big one day, lost it all the next—typical. Still, I like watching the races in the evenings when it's about to rain. That weather's brought a bit of the countryside to life lately. And cooking what you said—fruit pie with custard! I might have to give it a go to treat the kids. Go on then. Just make sure there's some biscuits to go with it. Proper afternoon tea needs the works. I always do. And you know, I sometimes feel like doing something different with my work. Maybe a little freelance while balancing the kids? Go for it. Just make sure you're looking after yourself as well. I remember life was more about survival back then. But now, you can almost do anything if you put your mind to it—and if the politicians quit mucking about with the benefits system!

So, I swear I haven't read  Hamlet  since A Levels, and then I walked into a pub quiz and the question was “Who is the prince of Denmark?” and I was like, “Is this a trick question? Why wouldn’t the king be the prince?”      Bro, you’re a  graduate . You got an exam question on Shakespeare and basically said, "What's a prince?" A lot of people would love that kind of education.      It wasn’t like that. We had wine and crisps and laptops open during the quiz. That's a  study environment , not a Shakespeare slam! And also, I  won  the quiz, so thanks for the concern.      Oh, you  won  it, did you? I’m terrified I’m gonna end up in one of these quizzes and be asked to quote  Macbeth  and forget if it's, you know, “Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow” or “Tom-ma-row and Tom-ma-row, and Tom-ma-row again.” Good thing sarcasm is a skill I’ve mastered, otherwise I’d be in trouble.      You’re like the king of sarcasm, mate. You’ve got that passive-aggressive wit sharper than a quill. You sarcastic enough for three people: you, me, and sometimes that bloke in the corner with the sombrero.      That was  one  sombrero situation. And let’s be fair, someone had to win. I’m not trying to be a prat, but I had a nickname in secondary school—“El Nino” because I was “stormy and unpredictable” apparently. Stuck with it for about five years. Not a bad moniker, right?      El Nino? Bro, you are  all  storm and no sunny. I mean, I got the surname,  Johnson —solid, no frills. I did once get called “Junior Johnson” in a group chat and everyone was like, “Oooh, he’s a pro.” Not my actual middle name. Though I’ve considered shortening it just for the vibes.      Some people play golf, you and I play around with our surnames. I got goaded into my first round about a year ago. Swung the club, hit the ball into a pond. I didn’t know until the guy behind said, “Did you  think  you lost the ball, or was it intentional?”      That’s rich. Sounds like you’re already overcompensating for whatever weaknesses your current job is exposing you to. I got a summer job at a café in Cowbridge once, and my boss once yelled, “Get the coffee, Johnson!”

Rather annoying I’ve got to be honest innit, me and me flatmate got this squabble 'bout who’s taking out the bin. We both skint and I cannae be fannin’ buck for bin bags all the time. Look I ken sort it me own self but it’s proper cheek eeny if she doesn't contribute none.      Aye man, that’s a proper pain innit? At me place, me and me mate Tim just chuck ‘em inna dump or chuck ‘em arse anyway. Bit awkward when me landlord comes round but what's he gonna do? Not like I'm gettin' paid dead week.      Honestly, I managed to get My turkey on a bit of a keto diet last week, tried to cut down on the carb and whatnot, but then I met up with my sister for an afternoon tea at a nice place near me. She was practically scoffing cupcakes while I was sippin’ on a ginger ale and not eatin’ nothin’. I told 'er I might die of starvation before I even get into any of those cakes. My mate Mateo told me he eats no chekin' noisin' and he gets his body on quite nicely, but I ain’t trying innit.      Awh, you just want a full roast innit.
