I’m actually organizing a product launch in Central London next week. Proper busy with it, guest speaker and all that jazz. Can't wait for a weekend off though. My mate Jess said we could catch up at her place or something, just stick on some good tunes and maybe have a few drinks. What d'ya think?      Sounds grand. Me and Tom usually bash something around with our bikes on the weekends, cruising goon various routes. If I get some spare pennies at the end of the month, I might head to Brighton with a bloke from work. He told me there's summat about chiap' on offer and a bit of a bar crawl, proper messy bellyache type of weekend.

Rather annoying this new TV licence regime, isn't it, George? I had to fill in a form like I were still in school. Just because I’m retired and I don’t even watch much telly!      Yes, the rules are as thick as a Norfolk field after a November storm. My dear Margot, we’ve both been victims of this madness! But what d’you think about that programme on black holes? Phenomenal! I never thought I'd find space so terribly romantic.      Oh, the "Cosmos" series, don't you love how they talk about the beginnings of space! It made me think about how we once painted our small summer house with flowers like that Myra on television. Still, enough talk of outer space—what did I tell you about the bamboo in the garden, Henry? It turned into a green army in one summer!      Indeed, if I’d known it would spread like that, I might not have ever planted an olive tree, to be truthful. George, we might need to speak to Mr. Barnes about the fence—his cat keeps missing into our side of the garden.      And that deadly cat of Barnes’s probably thinks it owns the owl box we put up. Mind you, I remember the days we moved with just boxes, and now it's all about buying a proper moving company. It's enough to make you want to chuck the lot and go back to living in a caravan.      But remember when we first moved in? It took us weeks to unpack! Some things don’t change—only now we have more politicians wanting us to speak nicely about everything. You know, it nearly did make me want to take the verbal barge pole the other day at the shops.      Oh that was you! I nearly fell out of my chair when I heard the shop assistant say 'could you refrain from...' I thought I was in a foreign language class again.      Speaking of talking, yesterday I tried to speak on Skype with a cousin from Australia and halfway through I couldn’t work out if it were a conference or a conversation!      That's just technology for you. But it's good the sun is set goin' on an eclipse if you ask me. Just don't forget the plant in the window that needs watering.      And your cat forgets to water the plants in the window?

Rather than going up The Cob, mate, I’d take the A19 out o’ Sunderland. That’d be faster an’ we’d avoid the traffic up by the football ground. Course, if we miss the turn at Horden we’ll be stuck in Bishop Auckland again —  still  haven’t got that een mind.      Aye, I know what yer mean. Last time we tried goin’ up through Durham, we got side-tracked by that weird new café on the roundabout near Spital. Know the one — the one with the dragon outside? It looked like somethin’ out o’ a comic book!  Mate , I reckon it’s the only place where you can get a scone an’ a doorstep pint at the same time.      I didn’t know they had them anymore, o’ course! They should make it an unesco world heritage site — better than that cathedral up in Durham anyway. All gloomy an’ in a castle. I’d rather have a decent felling than some old dead folk sittin’ in pews.      Aye, I hear yer — I mean, don’t get me wrong, the place is grand, but still, there’s something to be said fer a good curry in a humble little takeaway. Y’know what I mean? Sometimes, leastways, the  best  bits o’ somethin’ are the bits you don’t expect.      Absolutely — like those little old buses that still run in Gateshead. They’re like time machines. Rattle an’ roar an’ you still get dropped at a bus stop named after a hill that no longer exists! Look, as long as we get about half an hour walkin’ time round the area, we’ll sort ourselves out. I’ve already found a place in the cathedral quarter — the Black Bull. Know it?      Should do. I’ve been there once — passed out in the loo at 10pm after a few too many jackets. Owner still tried to charge me fer a pint o’ water to clear me out. Typical of the lot o’ em, really. Still, it was a good night — ran into someone who knew my uncle.      Oh aye? goin’ on then, if it’s that friendly, I reckon we’ll do alright. Just don’t mention the water, eh? I’ve already had to cancel a meeting at the planning office for today — and that’s after I begged those folk to give me a new schedule to work on the data for.

Rather annoying this newfit alarm clock, innit? Seems like everything wants to beep at us ‘fore we're fully awake these days. I’ve tried switching back to a wind-up one, but where d’ya get them? Not like we’ve got a fella at the local DIY centre who knows what they’re talking about.  laughs       I reckon it’s about as productive as most a’ us being up by half past six in this weather, to be honest. I’ve taken to pulling the damn plug and setting off the kettle instead. Funny you should mention, I was up at the crack of dawn to sort of feed these bloody robins. That lot round the back, they’re starting to think they own the turkey feed. You know I swear to God I can hear them calling, "Open the coo-feed, open the coo-feed!" like a bloody mantra.      Aye, I heard that too earlier this week. Sounds a bit like "Tuu-whit, tu-whoo, you!" to me. I got the field guide out last night—vain attempt, if I’m honest. These feathered blighters don’t seem as bound by the human sense o' colour as we’d like to think. I tried binning a light pink one—I thought it was a girl—is it? And I got a mouthful for my trouble.  laughs       You know what Silvia was saying the other day? She fancies herself a bit of a someone at the dentists—her own emergency services she insists they’ve become. Nosebleeds outta nowhere, and now she says the dentist’s being ‘suspicious’.  Sighs  You know Gerri’s old man—poor thing—had throat cancer. We were saying how they said no more boiled sweets or whatever that was.      Aye, I heard. My sister ‘eard someone mention he was in the hospital here last week. Silvia d’ya say? She mentioned ‘elderly women’ I think, how we all seem convinced we’re the next one in line. You seen the lady round the park with that lilac wig and garden gloves the size of oven liners? Reminds you a bit of us, doesn’t she?      I think it was more of a comment on our preoccupied state o‘ mind. I suppose it does go with bloomin’ gardening, your upper body’s in all manner o’ contortions and you’re thinking more 'bout your broken jaw than the new type of tulip you saw at the nursery yesterday.

Rather skip the new book for a sec — I’ve been meaning to ask you, how’s work been? I got the gist from Sarah about the IVF press and I can only say, I’d have a little breakdown in the local café myself. That sort of news would throw  anyone .      Thanks, I appreciate the sentiment, but really, if it wasn’t for Sarah suggesting IVF in the first place, I would still be stubbing my toe on the same old path. To be honest, it wasn’t just the biological stuff — deciding to chase it, be a single parent… it’s like choosing a whole new script.      Oh, I’d agree. It wasn’t that long ago when I was chewing my gum and left arm over this ridiculous book I’m half-finished writing. But once I said to myself — why not take the plunge, why not try something better for breakfast, bedtime and then suddenly this happened.      And social media? I tell you, you didn’t spare a second thought for why I would start bloviating over Instagram, but it’s become this odd place — I mean, sharing your pain as much as your grief. For instance, today someone commented on my post about how it’s time I write a humblebrag about IVF cycle three: “you’ve got a way with words”, and I almost chucked my flat white out of the window. Silly really, isn’t it?      Oh, someone said to me last week that they’d read my blog post and thought I had a point — you know the one about why a former teacher and a tea enthusiast should combine forces for a memoir. Honestly, it made about as much sense to me as eating a spoonful of chilli powder for breakfast.      Oh that was you! I mean it did strike a chord in that it spoke to ‘career change and lifestyle’ — well, at least for you. For me, yoga’s the new religion. I give it three sessions a week, and my little ones think I’ve lost my hearing as I’m off being ‘still’ when they want lunches delivered. It’s worth it.      Still, I’m saying this because if you started a yoga routine go along with it — life improvements are often incremental. Just don’t expect me to follow, I’m far more inclined to box a bad tomato than stretch one gently.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I’ve been meaning to get out for a bit of gardening—finally got the time off work. Life as a language teacher is all about flexibility, after all!      Aye, the weather’s as good as it can be this time of year. That’s a jolly thing to hear—you must get quite the mix of students in your classes? I remember teaching A-level English once—absolute rollercoaster, if you ask me.      Oh, you bet. I have children from all sorts of backgrounds, some learning for exams, others just to travel. One of my students is going to work in the Netherlands, and another wants to visit Brazil. My job keeps me on my toes. And you retired a few years back, didn’t you?      That’s the story. Teaching secondary in Birmingham was a marathon, not a sprint, but I’m glad to have stepped back a bit in my later years. Still, it's quite worrying, the way education is going—plenty of funding cuts, less support for teachers, and a growing need for mental health resources I don’t think the system can handle.      I know what you mean—it’s heartbreaking to see students struggling when all they want is a good start in life. Politics has a lot to answer for, really. It’s the same with crime in the area, isn’t it? I've noticed more police patrols at night.      Yes, and to be honest, it worries me a bit, being out alone at night—though I’d rather not be in the way of being mugged! I’ve had a colleague burgled last year, about five minutes from here. Poor chap lost the lot.      That’s awful. I worry for my parents too. They live up near Luton, and the older generation is particularly vulnerable. I always tell them to make sure they’re active and have someone to check in on them. It's all about community, really.      We could do with more of that. Let me tell you, when I was coaching a youth football team back in ’03, it was brilliant—giving these kids direction, a place to channel their energy. But I suppose life had other plans for me.      That’s fascinating to hear. I’ve always thought about starting a community language project—maybe at the local library? If you ever fancied coming along, you’d be most welcome.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think in Cambridge we’d know if it’s ‘goin’ to pour or not by now. I’m more used to Leeds—always sure we’d have a grey sky followin’ us about like a bad smell!      Haha, y’know, I grew up in Sunderland an’ it rained so often I actually thought of it a bit like water from the sky—like one of those fantasy films where the rain gives you magic powers or summat. We’d dance in the rain and pretend we were in a musical. Still do, specially if the tunes good enough.      Oh, the magic of rain! You know in south England it’s a bit more… restrained. I left Kent a few years back, but I reckon the sky decides it wants to open every single Thursday without fail. It’s like a calendar. ‘Four o’clock—bring an umbrella’.      And yet, I’ve never looked at the weather in the same way. As a consultant, I deal with large-scale Water Retention Plans, and it fascinates me how people take short bursts of rain as if it were a global event, when really we’ve got much bigger hydrological issues. Still, when it’s drizzly like this, it’s a good excuse to make a decent brew and talk about something more fun. Any recommendations of films to watch?      Oh, you should catch the new one out in the North East. It’s a bit grim but it’s a good reflection of the region.  The Wet Coast Chronicles —only in the region and being streamed next month.      I’ve seen about five films about the North. I prefer the grit of Yorkshire or the mystique of a foggy London. Give me that London Noir aesthetic over the sunny Mediterranean any day.      Aye, Leeds’ got a bit of that about it. Bit bleak, but the culture is solid. What about music? Any new bands or stuff from your parts getting attention?      Oh, yeah, we've got this great indie pop act called  Fog & Tide  from Sunderland. Their set at the Riverside Festival last summer was the best I’ve gooun to in years. Got that dreamy sound like it was made for a rainy, Saturday afternoon.      Now that’s your sound. Indie pop with a bit of regional charm. I like that it’s accessible but with local roots.

I can't believe the weather’s better in Cambridge than it is back in Birmingham. Stormy and damp up there... got to admit, this city’s got a more vibrant vibe, even on a rainy day. Yeah, honestly, Southport is kind of the same—rip-roaring one day and eeny weeny drizzle the next. I was just saying to someone yesterday about how jealous I am of you lot down here with your music scene and this new social place. Oh, and what was it you said about the kids’ summer camp? That sounds like fun. Oh yes, the summer camp is happening right around here. They’ve got a mix of sports, music, and art. From what I’ve seen, it looks like they’re even offering basic coding classes now! I’m actually involved in the planning, so I’ve been swamped reviewing the schedule and assembling the handbooks. That’s pretty cool. I mean, with a bit of coding at a summer camp? I remember when I was their age I would’ve killed for something like that. It helps them get into things before university, you know? I’ve written a short demo game myself as a side project and I'd be happy to design a mini-coding session if it'd help out. As for music—even though I'm into game development, I still love hanging out at the local gigs here. Cambridge’s got some hidden gems. You know what, mate? That’s not a bad idea. Our group here at the gym has also got a few teenagers in it. Maybe suggest it to the organisers—get them interested in some kind of inter-campus collaborative project through music and games? I bet it would light up their summer about tenfold. That's such a good point. The vibes from a cross-town collaboration between sports, music, and tech could really bring out the best in both places. My kids at the local school have always shown promise in creative spaces, but they just need the spark. I’d love to help facilitate it. I'm all for that. We could run it as a small pilot to see what kind of response we get. I think it would be amazing to do something creative and inclusive for the kids. Absolutely. Between the four of us, I think we could pull it off.

Rather annoying this, innit? That bloke at the back’s practically on my telly.      Sorry love, I’ll skoosh ‘em out then.      Aye, proper alright. Look at that—get in, eh?De Gea’s een total mess today, I reckon.      Naw, it’s United that’s a mess. A lot o’ red shirts in this lot but not much idea.      Oh, and we all was singing the same tune when we won that cup last season. “Magic under the lights,” they said! Rubbish.      Aye, well, we’ll see what turkey look like by half time. Oi, you fancy chips after this? I reckon the Oliver’s special is on today.      Sounds brilliant, yeah. Got a film I fancy watching tonight if we’ve got some time after dinner. It’s that new sci-fi one— Spacefarers  or some nonsense like that.      I haven’t heard of it, but sounds up my street. You think it’s as good as  Interstellar ?      Probably not, but nearer it than most of the garbage that gets pumped out these days. Though I’m not sure I can watch starships today after the mess on the pitch.      Fair point. ‘Balances,’ innit? There’s also this documentary on Spock for TV. Just sounds like a proper waste of time, to be honest.      Or you can come here and watch  Spacefarers  with me! You know I do like company.      Oh come on, I ain't th’ one who skipped out yesterday to meet that mate of yours and left me watching  MasterChef  all on me ‘lone.      Tut, you were just grumbling to the TV again. Proper ‘get me out of here’ attitude you’ve got on.      Oh ho, as if you’re always full of lunches and Easter dinners and whippin’ up the perfect bunny cake for Dessie. Then again, course you bloody well are.      Oh you sly sod, I know what you’re doing—trying to sidestep the boxset by calling it what your lot call ‘a film’.      You’re not wrong. And I know I’ll bellyache about it by ten o’clock ‘cause I’ve been promised silence and a bag of crisps I can eat in peace.      Oh, you old romantic. Alright, chips first, then the film. Deal?      Deal. But no waffling on about ethical vegans in them spaceships, yeah?      Oh fine! I’ll keep my politics to me, Mr. Film Lover.      Spot on. Now, off you go—shove that out door and fetch the lighter.

Rather looking at the photos of the lads, ay? I love the one of Fergus when he first won the race in the cinema—that laugh of his, it could bring a smile to a grumpy priest on Good Friday. Do ya remember when the film came out at the Dublin cinema? We brought the lads to the cinema, and we were both twitching in our seats.      Yeah, that was AWEsome. I wish I had a photo of me and Fergus from that trip. We did the London marathon last year, didn’t we? It was, like, miles under the London Eye. It was wild. I mean, imagine running past Parliament and the pubs, only to end up in like a MySpace post race madness with strangers. Fun.      I didn’t know you ran a marathon, Ewan. That’s amazing! I remember looking for you at Trafalgar Square, but I lost you in the crowd with all those flags and people shouting, “Come on! You can do it!” I had the baby in my arms, and I swear I saw three Ewan-looking types in that sea of people. I thought, “Is that  my  Ewan?” But by the time I got to the finish line, you were already gone. Tell me it was you who ran it in four hours flat, and not one of the random unnamed types.      Aye, and you were a credit to yourself, laddie. I remember the day you came back with blisters and chocolate on your face, and you just collapsed on the couch. I made you a nice pot of tea and stew and told you that no decent laddie in Glasgow runs a marathon in about four hours unless he’s eaten gold biccies the night before. It was a fine day for your mother and me that day.      You sound like my stepdad, grandma. But yeah, it was epic. Though I missed the fun fair that weekend. I know it was a mad place, but the lads tried to stuff me into a bouncy castle while my kid was being hoisted to the sky by space bunnies. I think someone tried to charge me €30 to drop a balloon in the bucket.      Oh, go on then! They do that at our local fair too. Fun fairs are the worst when you're with babies—no food that isn’t questionable, dodgy rides, and hotdogs made by people with questionable hygiene roles in the kitchen.

Rather lovely to have you both over. You know, ever since we moved into this house, it's felt... complete with our company. Just the three of us. I’ve been meaning to try out this new recipe for a vegetable lasagna I found online. Susan, you were telling me the other night about your grandmother’s version—something with eggplant?      Yes, that’s the one! Graham’s mum taught me when I was your age, Emma. She was quite the cook. We'd dump everything in the garden shed and just... go for it. Eggplant, tomato, herbs plucked fresh from the windowsill. Still make it when I get a craving. Of course, now I’ve got the pressure cooker to do the hard work, but there’s not the same smell of sunshine, if you know what I mean.      Oh, I know exactly what you mean, Susan. Back in my day, we didn’t have any of those fancy gadgets in Peterborough. Our planting was by the stars, our ordering by gut. Cooking was the heart of the home, like knitting was the calm of a storm. I still knit every Sunday. You young ones should give it a go—gets the hands steady, warms the fingers on a winter's day.      I’m afraid my fingers are more often wrapped around a coffee than a knitting needle these days. Though I did pick up crocheting again after Silas was born. Silly little squares that made sense only to me at first—but now they're a quilt! That child sleeps like a log beneath it.      Ah, now that's the way of it—tiny quilts, bigger hearts. You know, most people about our age don’t remember the days of the talking pictures, but I remember going to a cinema where they played films of that doll world—what was it called?      “It’s a Small World”? Yes, Ma, I remember going with my parents at the Winter Garden. Those dolls sang ‘Hi, hi, hi’ and you felt like you’d touched every corner of the earth.      That always gives me a bit of a whiff of nostalgia. Some things, no matter how many years you live with them, never quite slip away. Just like childhood games played in the sand or on broken glasses. Did you ever line up pieces of glass to make a ramp, Susan?      Of course!

Rather fine day today, isn't it? That sun feels gentle on the skin. Mind you, it's not quite the summer of '47, but still. I’ve been sitting by the window with a cup of tea, watching the garden. That bird in the hawthorn—it sings just like it did when I was a lad farming in Norfolk.      Aye, it is a lovely day. A shame I haven’t done any gardening since I retired. Oh, don’t look at me like that—it wasn’t retiring per se. You know how things are, don’t you? No one fetches you in when you haven’t made a stir in years. What I do miss is working with the children. My loo, I’ve met some eccentric mums and dads back in the day.      Always thought you were the world for what you did with the little ones. Made better sense of them than I ever did with my own, which I suppose isn’t surprising, being the milkman’s son, stuck looking after a few sheep and not much else.      Come, don’t talk like that—everyone has their own path. What did it teach you, raising sheep, besides how to recognize a good ewe? You always did have a sort of way with words, even if it showed itself late.      Well, I’ve had time to read quite a few books in the past few years. Found one about the Battle of Hastings, which I suppose feels all the more interesting now that I’ve not read anything like it in my youth. Funny thing—time’s a curious beast. It wants to pause here, and run like a scold horse there.      I agree. I sometimes wonder if the years just pass faster once you've passed a certain number. Speaking of time—I was thinking of organizing a small gathering. No one but us two and, perhaps, the occasional treble guest. A bit of food, maybe some music. Just a day to recall the stories we’ve had.      You hear that, I say to you—don't overdo it. Sandwiches are grand lunches, a little conversation over digestive biscuits, and the kettle boiling. Still, a bit of company would be a treat. I’ve go the binoculars—let me check there are no odd visitors.      Oh, don’t go getting paranoid now. A bit of company is good.

Rather annoying I had to take the bus in to work this morning. My car's decided it doesn't like the weather and broke down by the supermarket. I had to call my dad, and he turned up with this jumper lead thing and all that. Looked like he was on one of them survival programmes or something!      Oh no, that must have been stressful! My car isn't great either—it starts fine, but if I leave it in too much traffic, it pings and fumes, which is a bit embarrassing when you're trying to collect the kids from school, don't you think?      Honestly, I'd rather not talk about cars. I just had the worst time trying to find a present for a friend's birthday! I went to this boutique shop in Croydon, right? Drove all the way down in the traffic and came back with a kaleidoscope and a jar of breakfast cereal—hope she likes whimsical!      A kaleidoscope and cereal! That's, like, mad. I got my sister knitting needles and a pattern for a jumper she's been wanting to make. She's always raving about how brilliant it looks on someone else. Hilarious, really.      You'd think it’d be easier with so many shops – but it's often the opposite, isn't it? You spend ages trying to pick somethin’ that’s not generic. I was lucky—I found a gorgeous book that made sense and matched her style. She was beyond delighted!      That’s just you, Jess. You always know what to get. For me, I thought being quirky would be safe, but now I’m second-guessing about whether I should have gone all out with the Renaissance Faire prop sword I considered!      Going out with that would probably have made it more memorable, anyway. I do love a good themed party. I once guested at one called "Victorian London at Dawn". Horribly over-the-top but quite fun.      I haven't been out much. It's been so busy with school. I swear, trying to catch up with friends during the week is like trying to schedule a meeting with politicians!      I know the feeling. I work late on most days anyway. It does get so easy to push these things to the back, between work and the boxset binges.      So, have you made any plans for the holidays yet?

Rather annoying this new bar across the road innit? Seems like everything sticks out in this ‘hood these days... got to be some sort of local investment scheme, eh? I mean, sure, where we are in L8, Liverpool proper, seems like the city centre’s expanding bit by bit. I’ve only een here a few months, but even I’ve noticed more folk coming in.      Aye, love, but I know what this all means, right? More people, more tourists, more bars and cafes... and the rents go through the roof. I can’t keep paying what I’m paying now, let alone even think of buying. My son’s got to live at home another few years and that’s the truth. I’m lucky I still get the school job, keeps the wolf from the door.      I hear you. As a receptionist in one o’ them new office blocks, I see the same thing. People are still alright for work, at least, but the places we used to hang out, they’re gone now. One of my favourite cafés was replaced with a kebab shop, and it used to be the best Saturday morning spot. But still, I dunno, maybe the economy’s on something of a roll.      Dad said it’s all because of estate agents being skint, and that it’s making things hard for people like you. It’s not fair. I want to get a job already, but every job nearby wants experience. Like what? I’m still at school. And not even just a job, I want to do something with books like my nan. She used to read  Harry Potter  to me all the time.      Ah, there’s a lad! That’s good to hear. I used to teach a bit of  Harry Potter  when I was at the uni. The themes in those books—family, loyalty, overcoming adversity—y’know, they resonate even now. Though I have to be honest, these days it’s all  Policy  and  Societies  with me. We barely talk about books.      Y’know, I read a little bit of  Harry Potter  when it first came out. But after a while, I just started watching the films goin’ on. Too many books to keep up with. But I agree with the boy—there’s somethin’ in that series.      I still have the books! I read them all again after I finished school.

Rather exciting to be planning a trip to Nepal, isn't it? I've never been further east than Israel when I was rather younger—mind you, that was after I'd finished teaching EFL in Germany! One wonders what the village shop would serve us out there—definitely wouldn't be sausage and mash, I'm sure!      Yes, I reckon it's quite an adventure. Though I've been to Turkey a few times before doing this and that for school; but Nepal, now, that's something different! My husband was quite the war-time survival type when he was younger. Told me once he could survive on anything but apparently never tried muesli sticks and lentil soup!      Honestly, I’m more interested in the food themselves—especially the gluten-free stuff if I’m being honest! I used to make school displays for local festivals and religious ones about healthy eating habits. And breakfast, oh—my husband starts the morning with a full English if he remembers, but ever since we started shopping at the farm shop, he uses the free-range eggs and that helps!      Speaking of shop—there I was two weeks ago, squashed between the grief of realising my latest book on language teaching is outdated—and buying gluten-free sausages. You wouldn’t believe the prices they ask for fairly simple stuff these days!      Well, at least you don’t have to worry about glaciers and war-time food rations while you live in the countryside. Though I must say, the amount of new free school meals they’ve introduced is quite a surprise—more healthy, more accessible. My daughter worked on it through some university social project!      I do wonder what our mothers would have thought of the likes of gluten-free diets back in the 40s! My mother-in-law came all the way from Siberia to Africa in that war, and they survived on baked apples and tea. Now here I am, choosing between pumpkin porridge and brown rice cakes. What a difference an age makes!      My daughter is training for an Iron Man over in Cheltenham! Talks about discipline a lot. More than the school display co-ordinator role you remember, I daresay. I told her I wouldn’t have lasted five minutes unless I had a good cup of coffee pre-race!      And the Tour of Britain goes through near your house every year.

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me n mine lassus in Chesterfield had a baby shower and I couldn’t juggle both events at once. Not like I've got time to breathe as it is. £200k event in Sheffield on Thursday, can you believe it? Got eeny weeny budget left to even think ‘bout snacks fer the delegates.      Aww that sounds lovely, but serious tho, this ain't funny. You're working your bleedin' 'ead off! You need to step back for a minute. I get the vibe you’re not doing that. You know, even I’m stressed as sin with deadlines at the warehouse, only I’ve got someone to help me turkey out. You’ve just got to plan better, you know?      D’you know what I think? Sometimes we push ourselves too far for other people and forget why we’re even doing it. I mean, everyone here’s got a hard job, but you’re not a machine, you know? I had to have words with my manager last week—told ‘er if I had to choose between work and my mental health, well, as they say, grief. Hah!      Sounds good what you're sayin, but I ain’t in a position to take a holiday. I got cheques to balance and confirmations to send. Truth is, I did try taking a whole Saturday off once—messy week at work, toilets overflowed in the venue, chickenpox in the speaker’s daughter... chaos. So imagine that without a contingency fund or a good debrief meeting. You can’t be ‘prioritising yourself’.      Not sayin’ you should walk away from everything, but maybe just take a breather. Maybe a weekend walk in the countryside or meet us at some café and have a proper moan without planning the next thing. Burgers and bad decisions, luv. That’s all that’s needed sometimes.      ‘Eh, maybe I will. I miss when we used to stick out Saturday nights as lassus being wild. Now it’s just lunches and a couple of whiskeys if I can squeeze it in. Grew up so fast.      Exactly go out and get your life back a bit. You work too much and I do not appreciate it, okay. We were friends long before we were what your job description says. It’s about time we remembered why we’re friends in the first place.

I can't believe the council’s thinking of tearing down the old library. That building has seen us through so much over the years. I’m starting a petition today, actually. You need to sign it, Mark. Absolutely, Julia. That place is as close to our hearts as it gets. Got a meeting at work about the changes in borough budgeting today—they’re moving all the funding to shiny new facilities in the city centre, but that's where the community isn’t. Oh, and by the way, my night shift gets me in at six tomorrow, so I won’t get to the library ’til the weekend. Six pm—what a pain. That’s just after I finish transcribing for the day. I still can’t get used to the long bursts of silence when there’s no music involved. It’s not the world, is it? I was thinking the other day about mnemonics—how if I just happened to remember a certain word each week, I might manage to remember to add more to the petition. Like a kind of brain training. That’s not a bad idea, Mark. Maybe I can do the same. I’ve read enough studies to know that associating tasks with memory triggers can help with retention. I remember when we got married—even though I panicked about the order of the vows, I remembered because I linked each vow to the flower arrangements on the table. You always were the detail-focused one! Though, let’s be honest, someone at the borough office also needs to be detail-focused. It just feels oddly undignified—job titles like 'community representative' and real decisions being made in premium hotels where no one in Plumstead would consider staying about how many books we get per month. Ugh, I know. We need more people to know that the library is more than just books. It’s where we do art, where the local group treasurers sit down and learn about basic bookkeeping, where kids go to do their homework instead of video games. I tried to frame some of these ideas in the petition already, but we could use more persuasive language—perhaps from the people who actually use it. We should reach out to some of the community groups then. I’ll get the email go-round going on the weekend if you promise not to work at the library until six in the evening, okay?

Rather annoying lot, them Jehovah's Witnesses. I used to get 'em knocking on the door when I first retired, and I told 'em straight, "I don't have time for your pamphlets." Mind you, we were £20 better off for the jam tin they took.     Jam tin!  laughs dryly  You 'ad ter give it ter 'em? Nonsense. I’ve ‘ad worse. Once, one fella insisted on discussin’ the end times while my wife was mid-tea. She threw the teapot at 'im, or near enough. You don’t like to see a gentle soul riled.      Oh don’t go on about that poor Myra again. You know she still bites the spoon if someone says “holy water” at the table! But I say, if you don't take kindly ter strangers at the door, better ter plant a noisome bush or two. They shy off in a hurry.      Speaking of the door, have you noticed the clatter of Sam Pritchard over on High Street? Last week I counted five wheelbarrows full of broken dishes in ‘is back garden. Housman would say it was a domestic tragedy, but I’m more curious how he plans to park at the coast with all that clutter.      Parking! Heaven help us all. It used to be £2 at Hunstanton. Now they’ve doubled it. I say, if you want to cast a fishing line or see a seagull, just pay up and do yer worst. Though the seagulls, bless 'em, ‘ave learned to skip the chips in favour of the remains o’ our roast dinners.     Roast dinners! Now there’s a subject. Did you know Sarah Bell at the village hall treats her lasagna as if it were the Last Supper for the pigeons? They sit in rows outside, all keening for her next batch. She told me she mixes it with raisins for crunch. I say, if your taters come with a side of sprite, you’re getting’ creative with lunches.      Now if only our dentists took such a creative approach. Mine charges a bob for a glance in the mirror. But what about you two—heard anything at the election? Still sure the tax increases will be halved, Arthur?      Aye, but only in the council meeting, not the courtroom. John Peel spoke earnestly last week, said to ’im: “Tell ‘em where the taxpayers are, and they'll follow.”

Rather annoying the new neighbours, eh? You know, the ones who came from Tokyo last week? The first thing they did was install one of those log burners. I can smell their wood smoke all the way in here.      That is a bit of a bonus. We could make use of one ourselves if we could afford it. It was bloody freezing here this morning before the central heating kicked in. The budget is all over the place with this place needing a bit of love.      You should do! My husband was always a champion when it came to logs and the fire. He'd fetch the wood himself, even make fudge on the side with the toffee supply he always had stored in the kitchen. It was a bit of magic. And the cats, oh, they'd nap around the fire, purring away and ignoring the dogs.      Well, there's something to be said about a good fire and proper company. Reminds me of when I was the schoolmaster. There was always some indulgence for the old habits. One time, we even sourced some interesting logs from the antique shop next door. They'd have these quirky pieces quite suitable as kindling.      Tell me about it! I reckon the cats and dogs both enjoy the company more than the heat – but it's got a certain charm. Speaking of, have you been to the new restaurant on the high street? I heard their mashed potatoes are to die for.      Honestly, I've been working so hard with the outsourcing aspect of my job. Moving admin work to India has taken up a massive chunk of my time and energy. Between that and dealing with the house, it’s been a trial.      My dear, you'll need to take a break. Work can be demanding, but not at the cost of your well-being and family. You remember when I was the headmistress for decades? There always had to be balance.      Aye, it's a delicate balance all right. We've tried to make the most of visiting our daughter. She's been over from Edinburgh to help out with the renovations and lunches. I think it's been good for all of us.      I truly agree. I think the main thing is that we need to share more of our lives with one another, even if it is just over a nice cup of tea with fudge on the side.

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, isn’t it? I was just reading the  Norwich Evening News  and it says they're now charging more on second homes. I've been thinking about buying a flat in Norwich for the winter months, but this tax might put a stop to it.      Aye, I heard about that as well. They always seem to find a way to grab a few extra bob from folk like us. Why can't they tax the big corporations more? They dump their waste and pollute and still manage to pay less than we do. The state's run out of ideas, if you ask me.      Honestly, the government’s only thinking about their pension now. My son keeps saying I should’ve invested in a better one, but I was a childminder, for goodness’ sake! If I saved any money, it was for the holidays and school trips for the kids. I’ve never had a proper pension.      I know the feeling! I was working as a civil engineer when I was younger, but now that I’m retired, it's all about sorting out the papers and trying to make ends meet. Still, I’ve got the house, and as long as I live there, I’m not paying too much. Mind you, the cost of Sat Nav updates is fairly steep, and I rely on it to get to remote places.      Sat Nav! You know what I blame that for? Getting lost on those tiny lanes out here in Costessey. Let me tell you, a good old map and a magazine would outsmart any technology out there. Or at least give you something to look at while you panic in the middle of nowhere.      I prefer the remote places! I found this lovely place near Thetford where they recycle everything. Properly. I take the TV down there every time it breaks. My sister had one of those new smart ones, and it wouldn’t play the old shows. I said it was a waste of money, and she agreed yesterday when it stopped working again!      Those modern things are as reliable as a politician’s promise. I keep meaning to whinge about the state of our pensions, but I get lost in trying to sort out the tax forms first. Honestly, I think life was simpler when I was working.      Simpler, yes.

Rather annoying this, the laptop's playin’ up again. I've had it for six months, and it's crashed twice now. Just luck I saved my work both times. I've a ticket open with support, but they can't do much over the phone—get me sorted yet?      No harm there, Dad. I told you, these machines aren’t bulletproof. Though they should last a bit longer before needing to be fixed so much. I’ve had mine since last year and it’s still working. What’s wrong with yours?      It's the board under the screen, needs to be replaced. I’m still under warranty, so no charge, thank God. Just stressed about losing data. I’ll bring it into Cogent on Monday, they do hardware swaps.      But is it worth spending the whole morning? Or you could just hand it over to Michael while breakfast, he's got that clever touch. Maybe a bit in his head for the weekend?      [Muffled babble from the table, mouth full of cereal.]      He's busy with rugby next week, training with the lads from Ballincollig RFC, remember? Club dinner on Friday—been messin’ it up for months. So no, can’t wait. Bringin’ it in and then pickin’ up some fajita sauce on the way back. You all want some? Bit spicy, but Liam likes it.      Fajita sauce for a toddler? That sounds like a recipe for tears.      [Giggles]      Don’t listen to her, Michael. He’s a tough kid, handle the heat. Just not on his hair! Speaking of, I had to pluck his ears this weekend—something about ‘sticky out.’ Doesn’t sound unkind, but that kid looked like he got socked between the ears.      Awww, poor Michael. I did a few ‘fix it’ sessions myself yesterday, you know when he gets distracted while building lego and then goes off to dreamland. He’s a bundle of energy and static thoughts.      That's normal, I think. Just growing like a weed. Don’t go spoiling my day with news like that though, or I’ll never get to the weekend without wanting to go swimming.      Swimming!? It’s November. You're planning to go to the indoor pool, I’d assume. I can never visit without Liam hearing the splash and running in with a towel wrapped around his waist and a big grin.      I think that's the cutest thing in the world, to be honest.

I just brought a new box of frozen pizzas in from the car. Which toppings does everyone fancy, then? We’ve got the cheese, ham and pineapple one, or the pepperoni with mushrooms. I want the pineapple one! My friend Emily likes pineapple on her pizza. She says it’s yummy and sticky and makes your fingers all gooey. I want the pepperoni with mushrooms! I don’t like pineapple because it’s too sugary, Miss Alice said that once in class and she said it wasn’t proper pizza. Well, Miss Alice might know maths well, but she also said once that broccoli made her throw up, so I wouldn’t take that as gospel! So that’s turkey and pineapple for you, and pepperoni and mushroom for you – I’m picking the veggie supreme, because I’ve been eating too much sugar all week. Miss Alice doesn’t like sweet things? I once asked her if she liked doughnuts and she said no, and that they were full of “empty carbohydrates.” I didn’t know what that meant. I asked her too, and I think she thought I was rude. I didn’t mean to be rude, I just liked doughnuts. Nobody thinks you’re rude, love – but maybe next time just ask, and not take the whole box! Anyway, let’s set the oven to 200 degrees. While it’s heating, I might tell you about the time I saw a full handstand on the beach. A man did it just for fun, and said he used to do it every day in the army. Can  you  do a handstand, Mummy? Once, when I was 16 and thought I was superhuman! Now it would probably end with me laying on the pavement, sprawled like a starfish. I want to make a fairy garden. Can we do that after dinner? I was thinking we can use some of the marbles from your old stationery box. And glitter from Nana’s birthday card! We can stick it on rocks with glue and the fairies will think it’s magic. That’s a goody idea! But let’s see about dinner first – and maybe after, we can go out and look for the Loch Ness monster in the garden pond. Has it big tentacles? From what I’ve read in books, yes – but we might just see a very sneaky goose or a fish that jumps up.

Rather than share a real conversation, I can describe what a 400-word dialogue would look like. It would start with Speaker_1 ordering a drink, perhaps a gin and tonic, and commenting on the weather in Istria. Speaker_2 would respond, as a midwife with a more mature perspective, maybe asking if everyone liked the accommodation. Speaker_3 might chime in with an enthusiasm for trying the local food and critiquing the menu, while Speaker_4, coming from a different dialect and socio-economic background, could bring up thoughts on air travel and what countries they might want to visit next. The conversation could shift to more personal topics, like new technologies being taught at school and the debate around marijuana. There could be a moment of light-hearted humor, especially if Speaker_4 mentions Steve Jobs or inventions, and the others argue over whose favorite tech is better. Speaker_2 might bring in a concern about global issues like Ebola or immigration officers while drinking her wine slowly. Speaker_1 could ask about photography, being the student and possibly taking photos to share with friends back in Bolton. Speaker_3, the younger one, might have a tic or comment on tics, adding a personal anecdote as he dives into a pool for a swim. The dialogue would showcase the blend of generations and backgrounds in a warm, family setting. –      Right, and it would all be in a casual, conversational style with their dialects and personalities shining through. Speaker_4 might bring that London edge into the Bolton backdrop.      Yeah, like me saying "we’ve been doing a project on food tech at school—like, can you imagine being able to grow vegetables in the future in a totally new way?" and then Speaker_4 being all "sounds efficient, but where’s the soul in it?"      Exactly, then Speaker_2 could segue into talking about how that kind of tech might help in the hospitals she works in.      And me, as the business bloke, saying it sounds like a start-up opportunity. You know, Steve Jobs would’ve had a field day.      And I might add, “but we’ve got enough problems with the way things  are , don’t you think?” Maybe talking about something news-related or the pond life if we’re swimming. And that would wrap up in a way that shows how these different lives and voices come together in one conversation. It would be rich with context and emotional layers, despite the relatively neutral starting point of a meal in a new place.

Rather annoying this new debt collectors, isn't it? Seems they've got forms for everything now. The other day got a call 'bout some PPI I paid for thirty odd years ago.      Aye, quite right. That sort of things frightened half the elderly out of their wits. My dear Marg, I used to think they'd get me if I kept not paying them back on a mortgage that I had when I was working in this and that place. Oh but then, what would I do with the money?      Didn’t it get sorted out with some sort of regulation like three or four years back? I can't recall the exact name, but there was a compensation campaign like that My turkey shop, bless it, got involved in it a bit back in the day.      Easier to get the government to take an interest now about those sorts of things. I see it in my work as a quality reviewer; attitudes in these fields are shifting. Anyway, enough seriousness, Ken brought back some interesting seeds from the party over the weekend.      Oh yes, I heard about the seed raffle. Was it as beautiful as the orchids they had last November?      You remember that West Asian gardener? Tony, was it?      Right, he had orchids and some rare sweet peas. Now don't go making them sprout in the living-room, Mark. We might find ourselves in the business of someone else full time.      Laughter, gardening, and a good luncheon. Also, have either of you seen the latest magazine article Marg brought along?      No, Marg, what is it about?      Oh this one is about a new TV series that's going to explore the connections between the church songs and the singing in that old abbey where Ken used to go for guest performances. Fascinating, really.      Unbelievable how all those sounds have survived over centuries. I remember passing that Abbey once while visiting Harrow and I just stopped to listen to the passing birds and the wind.      Some people, like Ken for example, even find this interesting. Now, shall we set go over details on the computer about that PPI again or shall we go into the garden? It is quite a beautiful spring, after all.      The garden could really use some fresh water. Oh and while we're at it, can anyone confirm the new details to the next talk about that article over tea at the Crompton House next week?

I can't believe the amount of cases we've dealt with this week. The justice system's under real strain. It feels like the court's always full now more than ever. Aye, it is a bit chaotic to be honest, and not just at the court. Everything from transport to public services—standing at a bus stop last week, and there were at least ten people all grumbling about the same thing. It's all interconnected, isn't it? With the funding cuts and inflation rising, you can see how the pressure builds up. I was telling the new usher the other day that part of the challenge is just keeping everyone calm and patient. You know, like you said, it's not only the legal system. I've been back home, to Insch, a few times this year, and the changes there are quite astounding in a way. More cars, more plantations—there's talk about a new railway line for goodness knows what reason, but the locals are quite fidgety about it. I can imagine—especially with the Scottish weather and tourism, changes can be both exciting and worrying. Like your students, you’re teaching? How's that going? Well, trotting on, thank you. I’m at the local college in Solihull, and I’ve just started a new cohort. They’re quite varied in backgrounds, but all have a passion for travel and language. I suppose the curriculum is helping them learn English not just in textbooks but in real-life situations—something they will need when they travel. Some students had very limited formal education previously, so the motivation is intense. That’s fantastic. I do something similar with conversation classes for immigrants. It's always enlightening to hear their stories and what brought them here. Life seems easier to me now that it did a decade ago in that the funding, grants for education—there are still inequalities, of course, but there are more open doors. Do you think there’s a way for people in our station—part-time workers such as me—to have more of a say in things? I mean, the big decisions are always made in the city centres, not here in Solihull or back in the village. It's about getting our voices heard, building local communities, and relying on each other. It's the small things that sometimes make the biggest difference.

Rather than money, I often say to the children at school that happiness is like a full hopper in a cookie jar—sweet, satisfying, and best when shared. I know it's cliche, but there's something in it. When do you feel happiest, children?      I feel happy on rainy days when I can stay in with you and Mummy and draw. I like drawing rainbows. They make me feel giggly inside, like a bubble bath full of bath bombs.      I do! When we go to the park on the weekend and get ice cream. I like the chocolate one, but it melts! It made my face go all wet and cold, and Mummy laughed and made a joke about a sunshine sunset, melty me.      Ah, now I remember the rhyme! "If I were a sun, I’d shine in the sky, and giggle and breakfast, and then say 'goodbye!'" Haha, isn’t that the best part of being a little child—everything’s a giggle and a rhyme, and nothing’s too monumental.      I want to be a millionaire though, like a dragon with loads and loads of gold, with more presents than in a magician’s disappearing act. Then I’d get you both ice cream every day?      But wouldn’t that just make your tummy too full of fun? Like when you have too many jelly sweets and then everything wobbles and wiggles!      That’s a very good point. Money is helpful, don’t get me wrong—everyone needs the odd pair of muddy trousers replaced and a weekend trip now and again. But it’s not the most important thing. When I walk to the school gates each morning, what makes me happiest is knowing I’ve helped someone else feel clever that day.      Like how you taught me the rhyme, ‘Ring around the Rosie’? Although Mummy said not to play with germs...      Oh, I know, I tried to update it to “Ring around the sun, we all have fun.” Let’s not worry about germs but sing a new one with joy instead.      So, if I had lots and lots of money, I’d go to space on a rocket, and come back with real stars in a jar to give you for your birthday. And you could laugh until your tummy wobbles like jelly!      Then we could eat ice cream every day and never never run out, and we could laugh and laugh and laugh until our teeth sparkled and cleaned themselves like magic.

I just did a project on global economic trends for my economics class. Have you thought about what career you want once you finish sixth form? Maybe something related to finance or investment? I mean, with how fast places like China are growing, it feels like there are so many opportunities there. Honestly, I’m kind of thinking about becoming an engineer. Not just any kind of engineer—like product development or something. Maybe I could even start working on inventing new stuff or helping bring new technologies to market. China’s economy is definitely booming; I was reading the other day that they’ve become the world's largest patent filer. It makes you think, doesn’t it? Yeah, I read that too! And that’s wild when you consider they used to be left behind in the tech race, right? But now, they're setting trends. If you wanted to work in innovation, it could be really exciting to look into British firms investing in China or even Anglo-Chinese joint ventures. Imagine being part of the team that hides a patent or gets it filed first in the EU or Asia. That’s the kind of stuff I’m into! I mean, don’t get me wrong, I like the idea of investing as well. My uncle is always going on about financial freedom, like building a portfolio from a young age. But with the chance to be part of inventing something new, or even adapting an idea for new technologies, that just feels cool. I could foresee universities offering more joint degrees focused on innovation and international trade in the near future. Yeah, and imagine the support a school like Upton Court could offer. If you worked on a project that had patent potential, do you think they would help? I mean, I know a few of our teachers have worked with local businesses. There’s a business studies teacher, Mr. Bell, who told us last term that a student from his class two years ago had their idea for a portable water filter patented. It was based on something they developed in a school project. That’s intense! I don’t know about getting a patent while still at school, but just being involved in something like that would be amazing. It makes you realize how interconnected the world is. Even for us, something as simple as an idea can ripple out into the global economy.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is making everything look so bright—the snow's practically glowing! What d'you think?      I know, it's a proper treat! Being out of the clouds all afternoon seems like a bonus after such a grey morning. I was actually thinking we should use this weather to get the kids down the slopes a bit tomorrow. They’ve been cooped up with that awful gully rush last time.      Oh, yes, quite! I think it’s a good idea. I'll check what the run difficulty is today and see if the ones we usually go down are open. Not that I don't trust their instructors, but still, better to have an idea what’s on offer. I did mention to Sophie’s teacher this morning that I'd be back in touch with some pointers for the week ahead.      That’s brilliant of you! And breakfast, by the way? I happened to see a new little place at the end of the valley road that looked smashing—quaint and warming, the kind of place we’d like. I do think we should try it this morning—perhaps I can sort the booking.      It'd be lovely, thank you. I’ll bring the kids over at about half past nine—I want to give us all a bit of a chance to warm up before the journey down. Also, I’ve been trying to catch up with Pauline’s cousin who lives in Sofia. We might meet for a coffee in the afternoon at the hotel terrace—thought you might like to come along?      Oh yes, lovely! I’d enjoy meeting her and being able to catch up all in one go. This is such a good opportunity with our travel patterns all aligned. Have you still got her number?      Yes, I've written it down and left it on the kitchen table for you to have. She’s planning on meeting us at guest entrance B at 2.30? Let me know if you’d prefer a different time.      Perfect, I’ll pop a message to her as soon as we've finished. And speaking of the lunches, I think it's time we asked if the restaurant can serve additional veggie dishes for the children. Last night’s main course didn’t really suit them well, and I’d hate for one of them to struggle again.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, dear? These old badminton strings just won't hold up. I tried the usual knots, but it's like they're destined to snap by the third hit!      Awfully true, and it's such a pity. We could make a real go of this if we could fix the problem properly. I tried using cable ties on mine last week—they held up better, though I'm not convinced that's the long-term fix.      Cable ties do seem rather makeshift, though. But what else are we to use? The pliers I fetch from the drawer—it even left a mark on the handle, goodness!      You want permanence, then you need material with enough tensile strength. Maybe some sort of reinforced plastic or alloy wire. But the dimensions are tricky—too heavy and it'll unbalance the racket.      Precisely! And positioning is a science in itself. The angle you tie it off hides how much strain is happening. Also, the weight—if we can keep it under 10 grams, we're in business.      What about using a high-tech string made for professional use? They charge a fortune for those, but maybe we can source them cheap. Though cost is another problem: we'd have to price it affordably for schools.      Oh, don't you worry about the schools—I already foresee a banner that reads, "Badminton Revival in Primary Classrooms!" Just not secondary unfortunately; they’ve all moved to netball, you know!      Charming, as always. While we’re on the subject of words—I did wonder about your use of the word “fleet.” Do you mean “a set of rackets” or “a fast-moving solution”?       laughs  Both, really! You know me—ever the education teacher expressing herself clearly.      Speaking of education—and scissors—I think I might have cut your earlobe rather sharply just there.      Oh, heavens. And also, you've taken a lovely stripe out of my hair. Some "home haircut," you've got there!      I assure you, I meant to do that strategically. If we go on the "Dragons’ Den," I imagine a short crop with a modest scar adds to your mystique.      Mystique and a misstep, yes. Now, marketing-wise, do think we’ve got a product or merely a very personal passion project?      I think we've got something between the two. Just may need a logo, a slogan, and probably a legal disclaimer for the part where we slightly deafen our clients with string snaps before they even play a game!

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracing the garden like it's hopin' to stay. Just a spotter of luck, mind, after that sodding week of drizzle we had. I've brought over a few fresh scones—made 'em myself in the slow oven. Hasn’t got that store-bought taste, 'course.      Oh, a proper treat, love. Much better than that pre-packaged nonsense. Oh, and bless you, pulling out that nice China cup and saucer. You always go the extra mile. Do you remember how you used to paint miniature landscapes on these cups when we were younger? That was a proper talent you had there.      Oh, you flatter me. It was just a hobby to keep the fingers moving. But I used to love it. Art’s had a grand influence on me since I was a lad, really. Always thought this world’s too dull for folks not to appreciate a bit of beauty in hides, you know?      That’s such a nice sentiment, Dad. I’ve always loved that about you. I mean, we grew up in a home filled with little bits of colour and creativity—every tiny corner had its own charm. And then of course, it's inspired my own choices: becoming a lecturer, focusing on art history. There’s something about sharing those stories of creativity that just brings people together.      Absolutely. And let’s be honest, someone’s gotta make sure the next generation understands why Frida Kahlo’s self-portraits are so meaningful, or how a humble scone can inspire a tea painting! I mean, it's not just about technique—it's about expressing what words often can’t.      Exactly. And it’s not limited to the young. I see it in the old as well—how they’re so inspired, even now. Like you, Margaret. All those years running with the children, you managed to carve out a life full of love and colour, even when you had little else.      Oh, thank you. It was always trying to find beauty in the small things—like seeing the world through a child’s eyes, where a scrap of paper can become a dragon or go-kart map. And if that's not art, I don't know what is.      That connects so well with what your research covers, Matthew. The idea that art is a universal language, shared across cultures and generations, even in the most mundane of moments—such as this one over tea.

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses my name. I know it's not that hard— Claudia , not  Cassandra ! But I suppose it's their first day or something. I don’t have the patience to correct them half the time. Just nod and take it.      I understand. It’s the same with the people at the post office. They miss my name constantly now too. Not that I go there much, but when I do, it's always someone new. You’d think they’d keep notes. Didn’t your director teach you how to manage expectations?       laughs  I doubt it'd help with poor spelling ability. On that note, what’s the point of intelligence if you don’t use it for basic tasks, like remembering names or, for example, not smoking in the house? You know you did it again last night. The smell doesn’t lie.      Haha, you don’t miss anything, do you? I didn’t puff for ten years—then why did I start again? Water and wine, Claudia—personally I think moderation takes skill. You don’t see me splurging like the other blokes at the pub on a Friday.      Speak for yourself. I remember the tales of your university days— those stories  you tell every now and then. But seriously, I did read something the other day about the link between stress and vice. And let’s be honest, someone who works in your field must get a fair amount of it.      Fair point, but it's not like I want it. I just—I don’t know—revert when it gets about late at night. I’ll be round the corner lit up, then come home and immediately wash my hands. Guilt trip, you see. But it is a reminder, I suppose. My sister’s over here from Australia, by the way. Said she can't believe how open women are here—well, you—with all the talking about feminism and stuff. You must bore her senseless.       chuckles  She said 'I keep meaning to ask—do you all really believe in that equality nonsense, or is this another British thing where you sound more goody-goody than you are?' Honestly, it was one of the braver things anyone's ever said to me. But I told her it's not about preaching; it's just about respecting people's autonomy and choices.

Rather than going out and taking a walk in the park, do you both know where we're going tomorrow? It's a rather special surprise. We're visiting a farm in Comberton.      A farm with animals? No, I didn't!      Yes, eeny weeny, and we can feed the chickens and rabbits if we're very careful. You'll need clean shoes, though, so tomorrow morning after breakfast, I'll check your shoes are alright.      Can we ride the donkey again? Do they have donkeys there?      Only if you're good and don't forget your manners, and only if we can find a donkey willing to be ridden! I’m not sure. It depends on the animals, not the other way around, silly. I think there may be pigs to see, too.      Will we get to look at cows? They're so big!      There will be, and if you're very careful, you may even get to help milk one with Mr. Farmerperson, though we should be polite and call him Mr..Green.      Will we get to draw something on the farm, like Mr. Jones from our art class drew at the park?      If you promise not to throw your drawing paper away on the way back, then maybe! You know what happened last time you lost your drawing, huh? Our car smelled of chicken feathers for a week!      That was not my fault— he  dropped it!      I did not!  You  are the one who dropped your doll!      Now, now, listen up. Both of you. There was a mess because both toys were improperly disposed of. The car  smelled , so be mindful. And speaking of being mindful, how do you both think you did at school today?      I was helpful with the art activity, and Miss said I was good at sharing!      That’s very nice to hear, I’m proud of you. Now, what about you, Tom?      I told a joke to go to the toilet, and I got a warning. But it was funny!      It may have been amusing, but it might have also been inappropriate. It's about respecting the rules and others in the environment, love. Now, after we finish this dinner, we can talk about the DVDs we watched earlier. Which one did you like the best? I think  Paw Patrol  was quite the hit.       Dora the Explorer  made me feel adventure and brave. I want to go on an adventure tomorrow.

I can’t believe the Olympics are on again already, ay? Feels like it was only las’ year. I got me a cold brew from the kitchen—want one? Aye, that’d be good. Is that what you lot are doin’ now in yer spare time? Funny you should mention, I’m learnin’ too. Me Nan taught me how t’ do it. Bit squarey at the moment, but I’m gettin’ the hang ay it. Tryin’ to make a scarf for咱r birthday. Roight, I’ll be chuffed. Blimey, you’ve got better technique than I thought. I tried once, but it looked more like a bad ki e’s leg than a proper scarf, ay. Well, I reckon it helps havin’ a proper teacher—personally I think celebs are ruddy terrible at it. Did you see that influencer, what’s ‘er name… Jade Thirlwall? She tried to knit on Instagram. Rather than going out an' all, innit, me an’ the missus 'ave a plan. Thought we'd take a Sunday wander through the V&A down in South Kensington. Y’know, a bit o’ culture before we start feelin’ like we’re stuck indoors.      Right, now  that’s  a proper idea. I reckon me wife's all for that sort a thin'. A Sunday by the museum, some tea and a bit o’ peace. It beats me dumpin’ the telly in the corner an’ rotting away in front of the news. You'd fetch the bus or a train, innit? I reckon the 74 goes right past there, or maybe that My Bus app you get on the metro.      I ain't right sure, Viv, but I'll double check the 74 an' the number 148. I've heard they run 'em early on Sundays... but in me experience, the bus ever so often hides behind some building, or the driver decides he’s had enough for the day. I do tell you, it's a nightmare tryin’ to find a bloody bus in London.      Tell me about it! I reckon the last time I tried, the driver looked at me like I was a threat with a timetable in me hand. Anyway, if the museum gets a bit flat-liners, there’s that IMAX place down the road, innit? What d’ye 'ear someone said there's a 3D film on about the deep sea. I 'avn't seen nuttin’ like it. Must be real life livin’ under the waves!      Aye, I'm hearin' you. 3D’s a treat for most folk — what with the glasses an’ that lot. I've only seen it once, ages back, an’ found myself squintin’ for half the film. But if it's somethin’ the missus likes, I'll take it. I dunno, though... I sort o’ like to feel as if I'm being  challenged  with me day a museum. More glass cabinets, more art, no fish floppin’ around with virtual bubbles!      Aye, well if you end up gettin' bored wi’ the kings, queens, an’ scribes, I can see you might fancy some virtual fish. I'd take the 3D, though, mind. As long as I don’t 'ave to walk more than five steps, I'm good. Only problem is them glasses. I once took one off an’ got confused between left an' right. Found me loafing around like a 'eadless chicken in the middle o’ the cinema aisle.

Rather annoying this, having to bring our own Christmas spirit halfway around the world, isn’t it? But let’s be honest, it’s no different than back home. I’ve already got the tinsel and cards ready in the box under the bed.      Aye, it’s strange not having all the shops plastered with carols and baubles at this time of year. Still, a bit of homemade cheer beats nothing, I suppose. I got a couple of sprigs of mistletoe from the market yesterday. Thought I’d give the place a bit of festive cheer.      You’re a legend! I’ll pop round later with the crackers and supply the wine. On the subject of cheer, did I mention I’ve been meaning to watch  The Green Mile  again? I missed the last showing at the cinema in Chengdu and I fancy a bit of Tom Hanks at Christmas. You fancy joining in?      Haha, you and your movie nights. I remember that fella ordering puff pastries and a pint once, determined to re-create the American dream over kebabs in Manchester. Give me that film and a dram of mince pie and I'm in. Just as long as we don’t have the neighbour trotting in with their humble “relevant” contribution – Mateo brought his mistletoe, but he’s sure as hell not bringing subtlety.      You know what? Last year Liam turned up with a case of beer just because it was "cheery." And Kevin from the language department thought he was doing a good deed by playing the full 20 hours of  The Night Before Christmas  on loop over the loudspeaker. Not a fan of that one.      Oh come on, I had to document it for research. “Cultural adaptation through ex-pat Christmas traditions” or whatever the hell that title was.      Right, well if you’re going to be the academic, I’m the planner. Let’s give it a structure. Turkey, stuffings, wine, movie, crackers, and then maybe a toast to old friends left behind.      Aye, sounds doable. Manchester snowed on Christmas Eve last year by the way. That was something else. Hope it’s not about to start snowing on our doorstep.      Hopefully not. Although I’ve got the jumpers already queued up. Now, how many guests can fit in your flat without one of them starting a snowball?      Ha, we’ll have to cap it at eight or silence them all together.

Rather annoying when a customer leaves a bad review just cos they had a minor gripe, innit? Like... got to my face one time about the soup being lukewarm at this place I hit up in Margate. I mean, I was there for the vibe, not a thermal symphony!      Yeah, I understand the frustration. Having your hard work judged by a five-star rating is a bit harsh. I've worked in baking so long I'd think they'd know how fickle ovens can be. Once we had a heatwave and every loaf came out underbaked. Tore me up, but I had to make it work.      I get it, working in hospitality you get the turkey reviews. I had someone who demanded a free cake because their gluten-free option was five minutes late. But I was the only one serving that day! It's like customers don't factor in logistics when they tweet their complaints.      Speaking of Twitter, my mate started a new venture there, some kind of design business. Man, he's determined to convert trolls into clients with just threads and memes. I say good luck, I'll believe it when I see their credit card info.      Real gamblin' mindset. I remember when I got into baking, I just threw it all out there on the interwebz and prayed someone would see the photo of those apple muffins. Now it's a proper schedule. Still, you can't expect glowing reviews all the time. Takes balls and a thick skin.      That's oddly inspiring. You ever think about expanding, like a retail outlet or something? Even a Margate kiosk? I could do a trial run about Margate design while I'm there. New business always starts with a bit of a leap in the dark.      I've got no issues with the dark side if the leap includes cake samples. Maybe you could guest bake while I help with the design side? We'll call it a fusion event - culinary and creative.      You mad or what? Joining forces as untested as this. Websites and waitros with lunches and loaves. But hey, if we can survive the online world, we can run with it.      Let's do it then. I'll start booking premises for spring, and you two can gather your design portfolios. We go viral, or we go home.      I'm in! Just promise me one thing: no crust_ratings, please.

Rather than share a text, I’d rather describe a scene. Imagine the table set in a real home—Cork, perhaps, with mismatched dining chairs and a vase of fresh blooms from the garden. The scent is a mix of roasted chicken and the faintest hint of chocolate—someone must have brought home some chocolate ice cream earlier, and it's still lingering in the air. The youngest of the group, a bright-eyed little girl , is fidgeting with her peas, poking each one with a fork as if they might suddenly jump up.      The table's central topic of conversation is food—how it relates to everything from exams to gardening. The teenage boy , recently home from a walk around the neighborhood, mentions finding a broken bird’s egg by the garden gate, and how he reminded himself of the importance of patience when handling nature.      The teacher contributes stories about her students’ recent exams, and how some of the younger ones have been obsessed with the idea of eating berries, especially raspberries, which remind them of the tangy treats served in school lunchboxes.      Meanwhile, the stay-at-home parent is holding a small child, Oisin, on her knee. She recalls how – just yesterday – he mistook a handful of leaves for edible greens and almost ate them. Now, she’s gently guiding him to try a spoonful of mashed sweet potato while reassuring him that the raspberries someone brought in are for dessert.      The teenage boy pipes up: “Mum, is it okay if I take the gerbils for a walk after dinner?”      The teacher laughs. “Only if you bring them back before it gets too dark. I’ve seen your failsafe attempts with the gerbils and the bike—the last time, one of them found its way onto the handlebars.”      The stay-at-home parent adds: “Tell him how you once mistook raspberries for cherries when you were small and ended up with a mouthful of thorns, young man.”      Grinning, he says: “That was you, wasn’t it? Mistaking berries for cherries!”      The little girl giggles and points at her plate. “Chikelet ice cream!”      “Chocolate,” Speaker_4 gently corrects, and they all begin to eat in easy, shared silence broken by the occasional anecdote or question about the night's plans—possibly walking the dogs, biking later, or returning the gerbils safely to their enclosure. The conversation continues as the group bonds over food, memories, patience, and the little things that keep the evening alive: animals, exams, and the joy of a good dinner with those you love.

Rather annoying when the supermarket’s out of stock, isn’t it? I was just trying to get some pears for the crumble this weekend. I’m hosting Claire and the girls again.      Aye, we’ve had the same thing—half the fresh stuff gone by midday. I saw the lady at the counter say they’ve had more stock problems than usual lately. Though they don’t seem to be listing any deliveries on the app this week.      It’s not like it’s just you two, dear. You’d never believe it, but the last time I went for my eyebrow shaping, even Mary at the salon was commenting about the shortages. Said she can’t even get her tea bags turkey!      Oh good grief, I can’t imagine life without proper tea. But anyway, I think I’ve managed to get most of the ingredients sorted. Claire mentioned she doesn’t do nuts, so I’ll skip the walnut topping in favour of almond, you know, in case she’s allergic.      That’s thoughtful of you. I do like the way you think of those things up front. You don’t make as many mistakes that way. For what it’s worth, if you need any extra help trotting out then just give me a call. My Mate Laura borrowed my car this week and I’ve had to rely on the bus. Doesn’t quite get to Peterborough as reliably as I’d hoped.      There’s no shame in needing help. I remember when I first moved in a few years back, I wasn’t used to getting the groceries either. So helpful to have mouths like yours around.      Aye, about helping—have you decided on the haircut yet, Mum? We were thinking Saturday. I’ve already found a good place that gives you a free refresh if it goes on for more than two hours, like for cutting and processing colour.      Aye, sounds grand. I’d love something fresh, I’ve had the same cut for far too long. My hair’s sprouting as if I’ve got a brush stuck in it with a machine!      That’s going to look brilliant, believe me. Just make sure you don’t end up goin’ on your own if you end up smoking too much pre-salon. I’ve seen that combination go badly in the past—vaping and your reflection.

Rather than chuck a bar of chocolate at the ceiling, how do we go about weening the little mite? Our dear Thomas is five months old now, isn’t he?      Yes, and it's probably about time we started the process. I've picked up a few books from the library on beginning weening, and we can start with simple baby-led weaning or maybe smooth purees? I reckon we should go by his cue, so to speak, rather than stick strictly to a schedule.      Indeed, and I heard from my cousin in Liverpool, she said she made a lovely recipe involving butternut squash and carrots—very popular with her little one. Of course, we must make sure that the food is cooked until soft and mashed to the point of being easy to swallow.      But I was thinking of introducing single-ingredient foods at first, just to monitor for any allergic reactions, and then build up to mixing. What do you think?      Sounds logical to me, love. I shall make a note to pop to the supermarket this week and do a bit of reading on what's good for Thomas' age. Right, as to other things—our friend Nancy mentioned today that they're holding a mini family gathering next week in Lichfield. She's penned us?      Oh, that does sound nice!
