As someone still adjusting to the system here, it's quite inspiring to see so many professionals with different histories all working toward a common goal. It’s like an undercurrent of something much larger, tying everything together in about forty different threads.      Exactly! We were just looking at a new manuscript this morning that was written in Malay and translated into English. It was incredible to see the nuances, like how the translator managed to keep certain cultural phrases alive while still making them feel natural to a western reader.      I loved that too. You know, growing up in Sweden, I was mostly exposed to academically translated English with a heavy focus on fact over flair. Now, working here, there's this subtle artistry in how these books are composed and revised. It really does make you think more about the craft of language itself.      That's always the goal, isn't it? To translate cultures and connect people.

I can't believe we've got this far wi’ the plan. A charity rally in Mongolia, o' all places! You've done a mad job organisation-wise, Blaise! Cheers, Kev! But honestly, I’m dreading the visa applications. Got me head in a twist wi’ all the documents, and we’ve got to get   two   people sorted. You need me help? Aye, that'd be a relief. I'm stuck on what photographs qualify as "passport-sized," and the directions are like foreign language. Y’know the bloke up t’the shop near Anfield who shots digital ones? I've got the print taken care o' there. Oi, you luck! Me photo is this Sunday – I’m picking the café in Warrington for the shoot. They’ve a green screen in for portraits. Mucky bit o' kit, but it’s cheaper than photobooths in town. Midget, you are a legend. Also, we need to post on Gumtree for van donations, if we're going t’do the rally properly. Fiver a week to keep the van running for two months ... we’ve got t’get creative. Tell me about it! My Mate Joel's got a mate, and that's just how it begins. Let me sort the ad draft and send it through phone first. We’ll add somethin’ about the charity cause in the North West. People up here   do   like to give. True, you know the Warrington community wants to give back. I’ve considered canvassing t’the O2 nightclub in Wigan. They’ve pulled all sorts o’ good stuff for charity in the past. Going there would be brilliant! I've even got a cousin who works there. Let me text her 'bout it. Geo., if we can borrow their space and have me cousin sort it, we can dock all the van money and meet target quicker. Blooming good move. I’ll draft up a short presentation – with some of me photos from the scout trip to the Lake District. Reminisces a bit, but it’ll make the proposal more vivid. Oh blimey, you mean the camping trip where it poured all night and we soddled in the tent? Lift your legs higher, mate! You laughed when I told yer 'bout the broken tent pole and me face to the elements! But that trip gave me the passion to do more! You lot near got cold feet wi’ the Mongolian plan after that, but I see it now.

Rather annoying I had to go to A&E last night, innit? That prat in my chemistry lab poked me wi' some sort of brazier stick or whatever it were. I've got a proper contusion now.      Oh blimey! You alright now though? I were meaning eeny weeny sleep last night anyway. Lectures at the arse of eight in the morning? I reckon that's a proper scandal if you ask me.      Yeah, it weren't as bad as it looked. They just gave me some ice packs an' told me to keep it elevated. Not like I had much choice but to sit on me arse the whole night.      Honestly, you'd think they'd give you something stronger than a damp flannel, ain't right. D'you know, I think I'm going down with something too, ain't been sleeping proper for days, feel like total 'eck. Maybe a bit of chicken soup would do me the world of good.      Yeah? Maybe you should take some hot water with lemon and a bit of honey, that's what my Nan always used to do.      And for goodness' sake, pass on the watching of the lads for a little while. You lot know how much I hate talking about them, not least now because they're all off me. I reckon uni's gone to their heads and their feet alike.      Aye, they all want this someone or other in my class. Just because they see a bit of skirt hangin' out doesn't mean they gotta weigh in, you know? Anyroad, at least university's got its ups and downs. I did enjoy the weekend walk to the lake, the birds looked different this time of year.      Yeah, that was right peaceful. I reckon it does us good to step out of this flat for a bit. Although, I can't help but feel that the more we leave the flat, the emptier it feels once we come back, you know what I mean?      Right ho. Let's not talk about it with 'eck and whiffs in the air, I'm off to make some tea. Who wants anything?      I do really, just a nice cup of builders. Just don't spill it on my specs, that'd be a nightmare.      Pass me a cup too, please. I might manage a bite of toast after I'm done with the tea.

Rather do I! The grand old living room in Malton, eh? That's where we've been piling in the lot of us for the weekend—10th anniversary of their wedding, you know! Your Grandad finally remembered to wear a decent tie this year!      Baah een! Was there a fancy dress theme this time 'cos I reckon his tie's been on that shelf since the last Auld Lang Syne! What was the weather like, then?      Oh, dry enough to be decent. Not like last year when it rained so hard the cake nearly went to seed! Still, we made do. Your nan's the real hero—she baked thrice the amount 'cause she said "You never skimp on the cake when there's Hillier boys about!"      Oh, the little pigs! So who was about the old place then? Dave, James, Claire...?      Oh aye, the clans were in full flight, lass. All the uncles, aunties, and—God help me—Cousin Doris with her knitting. I swear, she turned up with a jumper and only started on it as we were finishing up. But what's a good family gathering without a bit of knitting and a cheeky glass of mulled wine?      Mulled wine! Now don't go making me feel left out—did I miss anything good?      Aye, luv. Strictly speaking: no speeches, just your Grandad doing a shanty about the Royal Navy. That and your Auntie Mavis nearly falling into the fire basket when she went to put about her birthday bark. Everyone's used to the dramas now!      Ron doing a shanty? Not sure I've met up with the  right  man. My idea of a party's playing video games.      And I'm sure the Hilliers still think you're a bit of a city boy, but bless 'em—they all adored hearing you and that sprite of yours jabbering away with your Yorkshire slang and speaking English! They're proud of you, even if they'll never say so in a room full of folks.      Oh blimey, so I ain't just a bit of a disappointment to Dave anymore? That bloke still thinks I should be playing rugby.      Dave and his rugby team—better start training, maybe! But don't you pay no mind. Look ‘ere, you been working at them GCSEs? You’ll go far yet, m'boy.      Am, always, even if I do get stuck. Got to keep up with the examiner, haven’t I?

Rather annoying when a water bottle freezes up in a car, innit? Me an' nan ‘ad to chisel the ice off one time. Like, proper proper job!      Aw, that’s right. When I was a lad, we used to take thermos flasks full of eeny cocoa. Keeps the drink warm, an’ puts a smile on the face as well. Though I reckon that water-bottle business tends t’ happen when you’ve left ‘em in the boot o’er night. Know what I mean?      Yeah, but it's not too bad now, is it? I mean, we’ve got a fridge at home, don’t we? Or like that one turkey shop near Bolton, you get proper left’s-with-chips there, ain’t right? D’you think we should make a stop? ‘Oo knows, by the time we’re back breakfast, we might be needin’ coffee!      I expect we will! That shopping centre near Exeter had a proper great chippy, or that—was it Holland and Barrett—personally I’d rather get one o’ those strong black coffees and a few of those vegan chocolates.      Aw, don’t give me all that “vegan” – nan’s been on a real kick with that irritable bowel syndrome thing. Keeps telling me not to eat liquorice like it’s a deadly medicine or summat. Still, if we carry on in this traffic at this pace, I’m not sure my stomach’ll react to anything but sour-dough crackers and still water.      Traffic’s a sod, innit? I remember us moving house in about ’99—spent all day trying to unpack the furniture, then had to figure out what the hell the washing machine button was doing!      Maybe we’ll have better luck ‘ere. I dunno, Dad, I kinda miss cat-flaping at me nan’s. She told me ‘at Egyptians had a proper reverence for them pets. Like, proper deep.      Right ‘onkey, yeah. An’ I s’pose Japanese do too, but with all that tea and polite junk. You know, I once met a Hungarian guy in a shop in Manchester, couldn’t pronounce his own name! Sounded like “Chike-hAILY.”      Aww your accent’s way worse! “Jurassic Park 3” sounds more like “Juraschick Parc Three.” True, I did talk about that ‘at Latin exams are like, them big old LATIN exams—got my fingers crossed to pass, otherwise I might have to explain the Cat in the Hat in Hungarian or somethin’.

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think by June we’d have seen some proper sunshine. Mind you, I rather like a bit of rain when I’m transcribing—puts me in a reflective mood somehow.      No doubt, Susan—some people wouldn’t dream of working in this weather, but you, I understand. It’s all about the rhythm, isn’t it? Still, I’ve been transcription myself too. Not the best when I’m trying to log into the records system, which is perpetually temperamental.      Didn’t it rain the entire week I came to fetch the children last summer? Mary  insisted  we take the children out, only to find us all marooned in a café for hours! The eccentricities of English weather—it never fails to surprise me.      I think the weather round here is an added character at the table sometimes! Still, it gives me something to plan for. Construction delayed for a week at least, thanks to this sodden muck turning into near sludge in the trenches. I’d have fancied a summer job, but no, I’ve got the occasional commission keeping me going.      It must be tougher still for you, Marcus—rain messes up rhythm in a whole different way. How are the works progressing otherwise?      Slowly, but surely. One of the clients picked up a bench I did at a yard sale—used some oak I’d been nursing from the old garden. Takes time, but the interest is there. At least it keeps the oddly satisfying side of me occupied.      You always had a head for structure and aesthetics, hadn’t you, Marcus? I do remember you making puppets for the school play when the stage backdrop collapsed—quite the savior of the day.      I seem to recall a rather lopsided dragon with a handle for the tail. Enthusiasm outshining precision, perhaps?      Unquestionably, but it had heart, and heart is often what makes a difference in the end. Those were the days of constant chaos and grandeur.      More importantly, it took the bullies out for a minute—those with opposition to Mary's proposal to add gothic details on the library ceiling.      True—still, it’s interesting that between us we cover roles from transcribing minutes to lifting construction beams. So diverse, yet inextricably linked in roles we’d never consider complimentary.      And we all talk about the weather over tea, anyway—universal topic!

Right, so today is the day we start sorting out the Mother’s Day surprise for Grandma, yeah? We’d better make a plan before the kids forget they're part of it.      What is a surprise? Why do we have to plan things? I thought we were just gonna buy her flowers?      It’s more than just flowers this year. We’re making a card with handmade paintings from you two and hiding it under a wrapped pot of lavender from the garden centre. She needs to feel extra special.      Can I write “Mum is the best tree in the forest” in the card?      That’s only if we’re going to Forest School today, Elsie! C’mon, Joel, you promised you’d help dig the pot in.      I’m not even sure what a surprise is. Is it like breakfast in bed but then you get a scolding because you made a mess?      Oh, sweetie, a surprise is the opposite of that. It’s something fun and secret, and Grandma will love it because you both put in the effort. Here’s the plan: Joel, you’ll help wrap the pot and paint a leaf for the card. Elsie, you’ll write a sentence about something you love about Mum, and I’ll tie it all up with the ribbon and some of those daisies you picked from the garden.      Can I put in a joke though? Like, “Mum: my shelter in the storm, but also the one who made the toast this morning!”      Oh, that’s  hilarious . You two have about five minutes to get ready before we head to Forest School. We can finish wrapping and stuff on the way.      I’m not going to Forest School. I have a squirrel in my pocket.      That’s not a real squirrel, Joel. That’s a bag of wooden coins.      You’re just jealous I found my treasure.      Treasure? What treasure?      Joel thinks he found a dragon under the washing machine after he flushed it with muddy socks. Don’t go there.      Well, real or imaginary, I think it’s time we head out. Who knows, maybe we’ll see your dragon at Forest School.      Can we take it with us? It’s hiding under the fridge now.      No, it’s not, I flushed it again. It’s my magical squirrelaurus.      Right, let's go. Squirrelaurus can join Grandma for Mother’s Day and then we’ll all have a laugh.

I can't believe it's been a year since Dad passed. Time really flies. I know, it still feels like yesterday. How are you feeling about it all lately? Honestly, it's been up and down. Some days are easier than others. The grief just lingers in the background. That's completely normal. I think losing a parent is one of the hardest things. A lot of people don't talk about it, but it's a big loss. Yeah. It's not like he had a short illness or anything sudden. He had cancer for a while, which made it more drawn out. I still remember the last time I saw him before he went into that final round of treatment. Me too. I flew over from London for the funeral, and it was tough being away from the kids for so long. They're still really young. I know what you mean. My daughter was only four at the time. She doesn't quite understand, even now. We try to talk to her, but it's hard. We're doing the same with mine. It's about giving them the language to grief. Letting them know it's okay to be sad, or to confuse it with being angry. Exactly. I often wonder if we're doing it right, but I guess the jury is out on that one. For sure. And we don't talk about it enough. Our parents had it worse in a way. They often didn't have the treatment he did, or the support systems. That's true. Mental health is more talked about now, in a way, but I still feel like there's a stigma around grief, especially for adults. You're meant to "move on," as if it's that simple. It's not. Grief is a process for everyone. I've been lucky with my job, actually. I have open leave policies here, so if I ever need time, I can take it. That's good. I had to take a few weeks off when it first happened, but I was worried about the business side of things. Freelancing is a balancing act. That's one of the harder parts of life, isn't it? Juggling your personal and professional worlds, especially when it's serious. Definitely. But we've both made it through, I suppose. And we've grown in some ways.

I just finished marking the midterms. Honestly, I'm exhausted. I need to think about tomorrow's lesson on phonology and how to make it more engaging for the students. What are you up to, by the way? I'm trying to sort out my timetable for next semester. I want to take a linguistics module, but the one they offered doesn't sit well with my English Lit classes. I'm so worried about my tuition fees and how this might affect my overall financial plan. That sounds tough. You might want to reach out to the department and see if they can offer some flexibility. I know a couple of lecturers who can be flexible with their classes, especially if you show some real interest in the subject. I remember when I was studying for my masters, I approached my professor and negotiated my research topics, which was a game-changer for me. That's great advice. I've heard good things about Professor Clark. Maybe I should talk to her. I'm also interested in food, you know, specifically the linguistic aspects of food preparation and culture. I was thinking about combining that with my thesis on vegetarianism and ethics in food production. That's an original twist! Have you considered how much animal treatment laws differ by region in the UK? You could compare different methodologies of food production with their respective language and communication styles. It might open up some interesting pathways in your research. That's a really useful idea. I might look into case studies in different geographical regions. By the way, I found a few computer games for sale at the supermarket the other day. Do you have a game you'd want me to pick up? Actually, there's a new title I've been eyeing off. But talking of different areas, have you thought about what you want to do after university? I'm thinking of taking a short trip to South Korea. I found out that their language processing is quite unique due to the mix of languages and the use of honorifics for men and women during festivals. South Korea sounds amazing. We could talk about that over lunch. Let's make a plan to take lunches to a new place each week. I also love studying in our back garden, the slight buzz of activity around the flat is perfect for me.

Rather than share a vibrant conversation, I'm sorry, but I can't generate an interaction with real-time typewriting and audible speech within this text-based interface. However, I can share specific details about me! I'm a 32-year-old graduate from Birmingham, currently rocking the student life in Lancaster. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive tendencies with the housemates over pizza.      Oh aye! Aye, I'm from West Yorkshire and I ad much easier time seeing differences in dialects 'cause we've got such thick accents. But when me 'n' the gang's in the uni house, we're more likely united over braving the chaos of the Sugarhouse night out!      My name is Elise, I’m studying in sixthform, and I must say I prefer the thrill of watching "The Big Fat Quiz" over playing violent party games like Hungry Hippos. Wait, does anyone remember when I bricked everyone with a Game of Thrones heads up card last week?      Heather’s the one who still clings to her childhood memory of wearing sports kit tops—personally, I favored the occasional racy reality show.      And for deadly serious quiz time, we've watching University Challenge nights. Absolutely lit when we got Charlie Simpson references right – Mate, you got the same hair as him, remember?      Y'know, when they offered the whole module on Cloud Atlas, we were like 'this'll be a breeze!' Who knew we'd end up cracking each other over the chaos of the plot?      Just the other day, Sam and I were being bad at physics – Sam ended up in a twist because he dropped about five vodkas he'd brought round from the bar.      To be fair, the Chaos Walking trilogy was like watching a windstorm. Quick, who's got the next piece of pizza 'cos I'm not donating my blood today, thanks.      Oh, and any bloody snippets of Twilight left? Guess we're restricting ourselves toأد thriller reading while the rain queens over Lancaster again.      And 'hey mate' speaking of Rain – happened last week with the floods?      Pissake, the entire kitchen go's bin on pond life! It's not every day you see camping gear line in the flood water between Stockport and Manchester.      Aye, and all the planning for the African trip postponed because of it. As long as the Cosmic Coach belly dont’ start droopin’ from ‘neath this bed’s frame, I’m content.

Rather annoying this, innit? Stuck in the car with no signal and it's pissing it down with rain again. Never thought I'd miss Sunderland more than I do now, stuck out here with you and this car full of library books. Look at this lot!      Yeah, I'm just as fed up as you are, love. But if it wasn’t for the rain, I reckon we'd have gotten halfway by now. Why'd you bring so many books, anyway?      It's not like I had a choice, was it? That bloke at the fetchin’ desk said I couldn’t borrow more than twenty, and the project’s only due in two weeks. But what’s a couple o’ late fees between us?      Hah, love, you know how I feel about the uni system—bloody expensive at the best of times. I still can’t believe I chose engineering. Reminds me of when me da’s planting the potatoes in the garden, ordering them up in neat little rows. That, and that man’s got a worse temper than the weather here.      Aye, I still credit yer dad for drivin’ you into this fancy consultant thing, eh? I remember when we got stuck in Sunderland at the Baptism of Fire festival, last summer, and yer dad rang up to see if you were out of yer mind taking the whole family.      That was a good one. You laughed at me in my da’s face. You know he still counts his pennies, right? Still drives the same hatchback he bought in the '80s.      You know I did it for yeh! And you laughed the most when yer dad wandered off looking for a free sample and ended up in that dodgy looking cider tent.      He claimed he ‘found the best treacle tart in the county.’ Still, sods law, innit? If yer not stuck in the rain with me, then you're waiting on me dad’s terrible sense o’ direction.      Aye, and I s’pose I do like it, stuck in the car and everything. I'd rather be with you than anywhere else goin' on about life improvements and whatever boring engineering work you've been reading about in that fancy manual.      You're what your dad would call 'a proper soft touch.' But I'm not one to argue with that, am I?      Oh you’re not arguing, you’re just waiting for the next round of the 'I miss dad's treacle tart' saga, aren't yeh?

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed me thick socks on before even gettin' out of bed. You lot 'ave no luck, I've seen it droppin' nearly into frost!      Yes, the weather’s being a bit of a diva, isn’t it? I went out for a run today and had to stop after ten minutes because I was shaking with the cold. A real proper winter’s come in!      I’ve had to leave the central heating on all day just to keep the numbness from my fingers. Funny how things get to you when you're older. I used to be out and about in the cold, mind you. Pushin' that pram through all sorts of weather.      I hear you, Mum. D’you know, I bought a new electric kettle last week because the old one died on me. I've no idea if it's just age, or if I'm just being lucky. But it's amazing how you start relying on bits of kit. One breaks, and you wonder how you ever managed without it.      Aye, well said. Me kettle's been wheezin' like an old man on a bus for years. I blame that stupid company—I still don’t see why they stopped makin' the old-style ones with the on/off button. Now you've got switches and clocks and all that malarkey.      It’s the same with all the hospitals and clinics—too much waiting, not enough time with the doctor. I had me blood pressure taken at the surgery the other day and it was higher than I like, but I couldn't even talk to about it. Someone handed me a leaflet and said come back if I'm feeling poorly. That's not very reassuring is it?      I think the system's under a lot of pressure. I've got friends in nursing and they work their socks off. Still, the minimal attention you get when you go in is frustrating. I suppose we all need to be a bit more proactive about our own health these days.      I agree. At least with tech, you can track things for yourself now—blood pressure, activity levels, all that. There's an app for everything if you've got a smartwatch or phone. Still, I’m not entirely sold on the idea of living off data.      Gadgets, gadgets, gadgets—never mind about data!

Okay, I can't believe we're all sat here in Sarah’s living room again, squinting at each other and trying to catch up after months of silence. I feel like I've aged ten years since we last met. So, Sarah, have you decided what you're wearing yet to Liam’s wedding?      Ugh, don’t remind me. I’ve basically had to self-restrict from buying anything new because I can’t decide between this off-the-shoulder thing and a slim-fitting maxi dress. What do you all think? Is slim-fit okay when it's hot?      Sarah, you sound like  me  when I shop. What’s the venue like? If it’s posh, then definitely go with something more refined. The off-the-shoulder one sounds cute.      I think the mini dress would be perfect if it’s a beach wedding. Wait, is it a beach wedding this time? Because last time I thought it was, but no, Liam hides details, doesn’t he?      Yes, it  is  a beach wedding—personally, I’m up for it if we get a free drink and a tan. Honestly, since my breakup with Tom, I’ve considered getting a little tan first. I haven’t looked at my skin in weeks, I’m so scary pale these days.      Oh no, not Tom again! Did you hear he’s dating one of Liam’s old mates? From the coffee roastery place in Manchester. Honestly, I don’t know why you stayed with him so long. Some people just don’t know what a keeper is.      Look, he wasn’t the worst. I dated someone who left me a note saying “you’re the sun to my sea vibes.” Honestly, that was the cap. I’m still salty about that. But listen, moving on to the bigger,  more  important question—has anyone started thinking about marriage after that?      Unhh. I think I might have a mini heart attack if someone asks me to marry them. Like,  what even is marriage anymore?  It’s either a holiday photo or a long waiting game with lawyers. I’d be terrified.      I mean, I wouldn’t say  never , but if you don’t get real first, kids are just not in the cards. Honestly, the idea of changing someone’s nappy after a full day at work sounds like a nightmare.      Wait, so are we basically all agreeing life is more thrilling without marriage or kids?

Rather a dreary afternoon, eh? You lot up for a decent cuppa and a squint at the telly, or are we just moping like cats?      Oh, I’d say we pop the kettle on and spread the scones! I wouldn’t say no to a good eeny and a bit of chatter. It’s been too quiet round here since the grandkids moved on. You’ve got a grand with horsemanship too, haven’t you, Martin?      Oh aye, nothing like the crack of a whip and the canter of a good nag. I like to take the kids out to the riding school near me. What’s that you were saying about the telly the other day, Bill?      Oh, just that I’m trying to catch up on these modern devices. The son gave me a tablet, but it’s harder than herding goats. I can’t seem to get past the bloody boot-up!      Bless you! That’s what the grandkids are for—those little ones, they can help you over the hurdles, yes? Though I’ve noticed the world these days puts quite a focus on technology. I tell you, when I was a childminder, we used to read books, play hopscotch, and – heaven forbid – actually sleep! Children these days barely know how to pick up the paper.      You’re not wrong. I teach kids and you’d be surprised, they’re more at home with hardware than arithmetic. But they still read stories, just not from books. Funny thing—books still matter, just different now.      That’s all very well, but how do you get about without any money? I’ve had a rough go of it, this last year. Expenses keep going up like leaves in the wind.      I know the feeling, dear. The ‘retired’ lot always get the short end of the stick. I used me pension as it was, and relied on charity once or twice. It’s a waiting game, honestly.      I know what you mean. Even as a 'manager', the budget gets tighter with every year. Still, there’s always a game around. Picked up the board game set goin’ on with the kids and parents—always a laugh.      Well, between us soddins, let’s make the most of it. We’ve had our time, and we’ve still got tea and company. Now, anyone got the sugar nearby to go on the scones?

Rather lovely to sit down and have a chat, Christopher. Life’s been a bit full-on with work and all, and I haven’t had the chance to pop down properly! How's everything been over at your place?      No, I know what you mean, Martha. Time’s been flying by, and since I’ve been retired, it feels like I sit about more than anything else these days. A few cups of tea and a chat every now and again are just the thing. It keeps me pulling through!      I hope so! Didn’t you say the other day you'd been experimenting with painting again?      Indeed, I have! I found an old sketchbook in the attic the other week, and I thought, “Why not give it another go?” I was obsessed with Degas and Monet back in the sixties. Living in London, you’ve got amazing exhibitions and galleries, but now it’s just me and my paintbrush in the back lounge, trying to capture the garden.      That sounds absolutely delightful. I’d love to see one of your pieces—personally, I’ve always been intrigued by visual art.      It’s not what it was in my prime, I must say. I’m rather proud of a small canvas I did of the fox that’s been coming in every evening to the back of the house. Doesn’t quite look like a fox, but it was rather expressive, if you ask me. Anyway, what's new with you? How’s the teaching going?      That’s so sweet of you to say! I have a great group of students at the moment—mostly university students wanting to brush up on their English. It's always interesting to see where they're from and what their stories are. I had one last week from Kyoto who told me about her grandmother's wartime childhood. Fascinating.      Oh, I like that. It’s always interesting to hear people’s experiences, even if it's just through stories. Speaking of, I was meaning to ask—you said you were going on holiday soon?      Yes! Next month with some colleagues. We're going to the Lake District for a work-away experience—sort of a teaching retreat. I’ll get to enjoy the scenery and recharge for the new term.      Splendid! I’ve been there once or twice in my youth—walking through the fells was like stepping into something out of Wordsworth.

So did you go out for dinner on Valentine's or just do the usual Netflix and cringe?      No way, I actually went to this Italian place in the city. It was a mad rush because half the town must’ve shown up. But at least the food was good — we had calamari and carbonara.      Ooh, sounds fancy! Who’d you go with? A love interest or just your best mate again?      Just my cousin, it’s always her. She's got standards when it comes to Valentines. Still better than my mate Sharon, who last year took  her cat  to a candlelit dinner at the same place.      Hah, I’m not gonna lie, I feel more cheated everyday I haven’t got a special someone. I just went to the cinema with my mates again — we saw that new horror flick, and then went for curry after.      Blooming typical of London! No, you didn’t have to go to the cinema over here, that’s what I do here, get takeaway, and listen to the washing machine do the washing. Here it’s either grief food or greasy kebabs.      Honestly, yeah. I swear it's like the entire estate is powered by kebab and distrust.      Yeah, but don’t knock it ‘til you’ve tried it. Last night I had mexi chicken and chilli at someone’s house and my mouth is still trying to live.      Oh no, did it at least come with mint chocolate and a tea? That’s the  British  way to make it better about things.      Hah, yeah, I had to. I’ve been burning my tongue for an hour then soothing it with digestive.      My grandma would be proud.      I think she would. Anyway, next weekend I'm going to go shopping for some new Foundation — I need to look decent for the party.      Let me know if you need a hand, I’m not the best with skincare, but I can at least remember to not run with it like a man with a paint goffer.      If you go wrong, at least you’ll go out in a blaze of glitter, I say.      Exactly! So maybe I’ll see you there?      I’ll try not to be to posh for you, ‘cause I’ve been working at the catering job again. You know my accent becomes like BBC if I don’t watch it.

Rather than share a text, I’d love to hear more about what's on your mind! How does it feel to be in this restaurant tonight after everything that's been going on with housing and politics? I feel like it's all over the news these days.      Honestly, it’s good to just sit down and talk properly. It’s ridiculous really—how people still try to act like housing is a personal choice instead of a policy crisis. I just got done writing an article on how private landlords are using Section 21 to just ditch tenants and keep profits sky-high, but the government won’t do a thing to stop it.      Ugh, I know right? You know I’m doing an extension on a social housing project at the moment. It’s supposed to be affordable, but the cost of building is so nuts. A lot of local authorities are cash-strapped, and they’re relying on private firms to build at scale—which of course means drive in costs and cut corners.      Exactly, it's so frustrating. And I don't even want to get into the racism—there's this constant narrative that people in short-term lets are “undeserving” when in reality it's often migrant families or single parents just getting by. And then the media jumps in with all this “they must want more” nonsense.      It's like capitalism's telling people to suffer quietly and fight for scraps while the big firms line their pockets. It’s all very convenient. And don’t get me started on the government—count me in for the sour noodle with tofu. Also, have you seen the way they’ve been replying to all the rent control campaigns?      I have! And you know the thing that’s p   ing me off? They always say “you know that housing is expensive because of housing demand!” as if that’s some kind of proof that the system is fair. But if housing costs are high because of bad planning and a lack of public land being used for building, then fixing that is on the state, not on us to “adapt.”      100%. I think it's partly the psychological trick of framing it as a  choice , as if it's a meritocracy of renting. But really it's a system that's designed to work against us—especially if you're not in a high earner box job or something.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, having to get the little one off to nursery so early... It's been tough enough juggling everything already, and I haven't even started thinking about going back to work yet. Do you miss her, or are things just easier with her out?      I do, yeah. It’s weird, really. I mean, I wanted to go back to uni so I could finish this year off strong, and I thought I'd be used to it by now, but she still pops into my head the whole time. Do you want to keep her at the same nursery, or is it even open over the summer?      I don’t think it is, well at least not full-time. I’m thinking of starting her on solid food earlier to help the weaning along, push her into being more independent for when I go back in September. But you better not get too comfy with your studies this summer; I’ve been looking at Spain for a family trip, maybe somewhere on the coast. I say we plan it once I’m back in the office and know what the hours are going to be like.      Spain? That would be brilliant. I’d love that. Although, I can’t promise I’ll be in a good mood if it's too hot and I’m stuck in my room with a hangover while you lot are out sightseeing. It’s not as if you have much patience for that already.      There’s a reason someone older in the family should always travel with students, love. Besides, I can do the sightseeing and the kid-sitting in the evenings and still look chic at the same time. Though, honestly, most people about our age don’t even notice what I’m wearing these days, I'm far too busy doing things they don’t know how to talk about over wine and cheese.      That, I can believe. I mean, even if I wasn’t working on assignments all summer, the TV is holding me hostage as it is. I tried Netflix, but all I see is one too many thrillers and end up being terrified out of my mind.      Agh, same with the recent crime dramas you’re into. I had a nightmare about the one called  End of the Road  last night. Honestly, cut it out, or I shall be forced to change the Wi-Fi password again.

Rather annoying day today, really. I had to give a statement to the police for the broken window in the kitchen. Just couldn't work out who was responsible, and I ended up talking for nearly an hour! It is rather draining, honestly.      That does sound like a lot of hassle. I'm assuming there was no insurance to cover it? I know if it were my home, I'd be calling the insurance company straight away. Much more efficient than waiting for the police to sort it out.      Unfortunately, the damage was below the threshold for a claim, and I’d rather not get the insurers involved if I can help it. I just wanted someone to know, just in case there was an actual incident involved, you know?      Well, I can't imagine dealing with the police for anything, let alone a broken window! But then again, it’s a bit easier if you’re, um… if you’re used to dealing with authority figures professionally. People like you, Dad.      Haha, I suppose. I deal with that kind of thing for a living—person-to-person, not really written statements and police interviews.      Actually, something similar happened to me this week—except it was work-related. I had to give a statement after a client meeting got cut short. I still haven’t heard back on it. Honestly, I’m quite used to bureaucracy by now, but even I’m getting a bit fed up with the slow reply from the someone at the office.      That does happen, doesn't it? You give a statement, and it just floats into the abyss. Still, at least you had your colleague, Laura, to back you up. She’s a gem when it comes to paperwork.      True. She was very good. Properly professional. I owe her a coffee, for sure.      Switching topics for a second—my phone bill arrived today. EE, again. I'm told it was quite high. I don't know how people can spend that much on data, honestly. All I do is scroll a bit, email the boss, and maybe watch one show in the evening.      I get bills too, dear! The kids must be streaming every movie on the planet if you're paying for so much data.      No, genuinely. I haven’t downloaded films or anything. It’s like the phone just eats data.      Maybe you should consider downgrading your plan for now.

: "Lads, haven't seen you in a while. How's the garden in Luton holding up after the snow?"     : "Mate, it's like a jungle out there. I've got more weeds than tomatoes this year. But at least the chilli plants survived. Got a few from my Cyprus relatives last summer."     : "Well, that's a good start. A friend of mine swore by chilli and garlic to kill off most pests. It's worth a try. Speaking of which, I watched an episode of  Spartacus  last night—it reminds me of Rome's obsession with spices. They'd throw anything onto their food, garlic, pepper, even mustard made from lentils."     : "Ah, you Brits always skewer Roman history, don’t you? I think the real history of spices is in the East. Cats forget how far breakfasts—like chickpeas and bread with a bit of nutty paste—got from India to China, right?"     : "Exactly, and that mortar and pestle thing, I had one in Cyprus—mom always put in some strong leaves. Bay and thyme. Smells like the garden there. Speaking of, how's your rhythm in teaching all this? Still tongue-tied?     : "You know, it’s not as simple as pressing some herbs. You have to know the rhythm of the language, like a tune. And, hey, you want someone who knows how to grind spices to explain a past participle, don't you?"     : "Haha, fair point. Still, I prefer my education over tea, not in a textbook about  malarials  in the Channel Islands. Remember that trip we had to document a house full of sea lice? Not the highlight of my life."     : "You mean that 'romantic' guesthouse near the coast? Yeah, and I told them the pestle was for ground nut mixes, not disappointed lice. Not that anyone listened. We ended up with a handmade yellow tea as well, which always comes with 'origin story' tales from the caretaker."     : "You know, it's funny you mention tea. I was testing my students on 'traditional British tea' today. One thought it was a separate room, not a drink. That bloke from China, though, he’s got all the lingo for special mixes—like genmaicha with those roasted bits."     : "He’s probably got more stories than the Cyprian nut salesman I once met. Told me herbs could fix anything—early deaths, bad luck, even romantic failures."     : "Haha, he probably used the same mortar and pestle as the tea man then."     : "Now  that  would be a show, a herbalist and a tea sommelier in a jam-packed flat in Bedford.

So did you get an A on the English test? I swear mine came out like cr p. The question about  Pride and Prejudice  nearly gave me a heart attack. I didn’t even know where to start.      No, I scraped a B—Deirdre’s eeny weeny passive voice comment cost me an A. But at least I didn’t have to panic. I’ve been revising every single weekend since this term started, so I had a clue what I was doing.      That’s cause you're literally, like,  obsessed  with everything to do with school! I still can’t get over how you joined wind band, art, and now you’re trying out for captain of the French club. I’m like,  what the hell, Gemma?!       Oh, don’t give it to me like that! Wind band is heaps of fun, even if everyone still thinks I’m a criminal because I dropped the oboe on day one. I told the conductor it was  definitely  not me—but he looked at me like,  xactly , I mean,  exactly , like,  exactly who?       Bloke, you dropped a musical instrument. You’re bound to look shady. Plus, I’m not surprised people act all weird about the wind band. I mean, you’ve got like 47 people wearing outfits no one ever heard of, blowing into random instruments at someone who might be your grandad. Like why do we have to suffer through that encore  every  concert?      Hey, their music is decent once you get past the polonaise vibe about half the time. I mean, our trumpet section lit up the whole place last week with  Wait for the Wagon . Not that I noticed because it was uncool for me to do that, obviously.      Oh my  god , did you? Like, did it happen where you got all red and then fell over mid-song or did you just awkwardly crack a smile as your face sprite-puffed out?      Nooo, I was fiine! Okay, fine for  obviously  not being a trumpet, but still! I bet you were sniggering your head off about it at the loos.      Well, I was, until I went to your house and you made me clean your flu pipes with a k  t brush. Which also made me snigger because, well, like, it was basically a  thing  we had to do! It wasn’t the  cleanest  project at school.      That's part of why I joined wind band in the first place, to try something new and real.

Rather chilly for a Saturday, eh, love? Thought we’d get a bit of sun, but it’s more of a grey, stagnant day. Still, best not to let a bit of drizzle put a damper on our tea.      Yeah, well, the forecast was iffy eeny way. I mean, it’s the North East fer cryin’ out loud—could be a snow flurry at any moment. Not that I’d be budging an inch if it started to snow, mind.      Snow? Please! We’ve had worse days in Hull when you could barely see your nose for the fumes and the fella round the corner had to guid his bus by torchlight. Anyway, Elsy, you still talkin’ ‘bout expandin’ the playgroup? D’you think o’it?      God help me, yes! I’ve nae slept since I started lookin’ into grants and childcare vouchers. It’s ever so complicated, especially with the way they keep changin’ the rules. One bloke I spoke to said he had seven different forms to fill in before they even gave him a “maybe.”      Blimey, that’s mental! You used to teach, right? So it’s not like it’s new to you dealin’ with paperwork and all that.      Aye, but this is different. It’s less about what the child needs, and more about what someone at the council thinks the child might not need. I tried to run a little community school outta my house once—only lasted three months and it wasn’t for the funding!      I did nae know that! You used to do that?      Aye, and not because I wanted to. My eldest was havin’ a bob on to the bin, so I thought I’d rather put her in a proper class with people who at least knew the alphabet.      Okay, but hang on—I thought you liked your garden. You didn’t like that idea of doing something indoors?      A garden’s fine if you’ve got no knees and don’t mind aches and pains! But no, na goin’ back to that if I can help it. Not after six hours on my knees weeding between break times.      Pass me the cake slice, love. I’ll manage the kipper scone.      It’s a “kipper scone”? Sounds like one of those weird posh teatime things I read about in one of Dad’s old books about the Queen.      It’s not posh.

Rather annoying driving up from London today. The sat nav decided to glue the car in the middle of nowhere. I got turned around at least four times before I found this road!      Aw, it happens. Not all of us have the kind of time to memorise every twisty turn in eeny Norfolk. I remember once I got stuck in these woods out near Bury St Edmunds with a flat battery and a full flatbed truck in tow. Classic.      It's easy to get lost! My brother was directions-challenged too. He once tried to drive to King's Lynn and ended up in Scotland! Not because he was a bad driver but because he’d grabbed the wrong map.      You know, I've got a theory this is all genetic. I mean, I can read a map and make sense of it. Living in London, you’ve got to! But when I was younger, I hated driving. Something about the stress of it. I even had an anxiety-related panic attack once at the wheel—and that was in traffic, not in the middle of the fens.      Yeah, I never thought about it as a genetic thing. It’s more like, you either got it or you didn’t. I learned from my old man. He was a mechanic too, before he retired, and he taught me how to fix things as a kid. It was hands-on learning for me.      That’s nice. I never really drove at all. Spent my time putting together jigsaws or baking, which oddly gives me an allergic reaction now—peanut flour in particular. It comes from my sister, I think. She had Operation because of a stomach issue. Her doctor said it was all the junk-food genes kicking in.      Oh! Going back to that then! I mean, it does seem like in families, obesity, allergies, operations—everything kind of gets passed down. There's that health gene, and the one for patience. I think I got mine.      Haha, yes. As good as your lectures are, academically speaking, your lunches could do with a bit of work. Some of your students must be trying to live off your chips and ketchup.      I’ll tell you what's not genetic—that inferiority complex you got in the kitchen, Kath. I remember you once tried to make what your mum called a 'vegetable omelette' and ended up with scrambled courgettes and broken toast.

Rather annoying that the new tutorial version of Moodle isn’t working with the latest update for our software course. I’d got the materials uploaded and ready to go for the students.      Yes, it is a right pain. I’ve seen the same issue on my end. We could make do with a bit more support from the university IT team, really. I reckon it’s not as simple as most people think. A lot of lecturers are struggling this semester.      It is pulling teeth to get help sometimes. I’ve got twelve students who are literally waiting for the coursework to appear. I suppose we need to get back to basics and talk them through the files directly, don’t we?      I’d say that’s the plan. It might be more work for us, yes, but at least it keeps things moving. I tried to make a quick handout with screenshots yesterday. I could email it to you this evening if you’d find it helpful.      That sounds brilliant, thank you. I was thinking along similar lines too, but I haven’t had the time to put it all together yet. I’m also quite stuck as to how to explain the keyboard shortcuts for the design software properly on Moodle.      Ah yes, that's one of those things that often gets glossed over, but really matters when the students are trying to set up their own projects. Why don't we schedule a trial session with a couple of students and test it out?      I’d like that a lot, actually. It would give us a chance to see where they get stuck and adjust our method as we go along. We could even make a recording and use it as a walk-through for the rest of the class.      Exactly. Another thought—you know that new plug-in I tried for the coding module? It allows the system to ‘record’ the lesson rather than just note down the keystrokes. It shows them every step. It might be adaptable for our design content too.      Oh, that does sound interesting. I’ll have to check it out. Do you think students would actually watch those kinds of videos, though? I find sometimes they only come to it if it's their absolute last go.      Fair point. Maybe we can make it a part of the weekly tasks. If it's framed as something they can refer to instead of just another assignment, I think they’re more likely to engage with it.

Rather annoying jetlag, isn't it? I mean, I've only had an hour or two in bed... What time did you manage to go to sleep last night?      Around midnight, I think. Not quite enough to feel like a functioning human being this morning. And I don’t want to imagine what  he’ll  think when we get home if his routine's all messed up after a week away.      Of course, it was easier when we started bed-sharing; someone’s always there to help anyway.      It's true. But honestly, I like to keep a bit more privacy when I’m not with you. I found myself reading for hours in bed if I don't fall asleep first!      Ten to one you're reading about D.H. Lawrence and I'm stuck feeding little William. It is a far, far cry from when breakfast, bedtime and nappies happened all at once for us!      There was something nice about that kind of chaos, though. I miss those days—when time didn’t feel like it was working properly.      You did like the early grief of real, non-school-related bedtime stories… watching him sleep, remembering it was then all we needed.      True. He's still such a dreamer, though. Barely stirs in the night unless he gets a sniff of chocolate or sees the moon!      You know, when he climbs on the bed at night, I wish I thought I had the energy to fling him out now. Or at least give it a shot!      Haha, I about did that last week! He brought a toy car into my bed and immediately started thumping on the duvet like it was the school bell. I nearly lost it!      Should've made him treble guest speaker status. I did once. He’s been banned from my side of the bed ever since.      You mustn't encourage the rebel acts, then. Though I do think we've created a proper little sociable character with interests in chocolate, the moon, and road trip singalongs.      He's our best work. If I could bottle that cuteness and sell it, we’d never need that lecture money again.      Financially irresponsible but appealing all the same. Speaking of which, though, we’d better start thinking about adjusting back to the schedule to prepare for the dramatic performance on Thursday—assuming we function at all!      The key to that is baby naps and plenty of caffeine.

Rather annoying this, innit? Moving house at this stage. I've had to chuck out more stuff than I got to keep, mind you. Still, more space for all them books, eh?      Yeah, can see that, I mean—get a bit chaotic in a few places when eeny weeny apartments go. Heard about some bloke down Ayer just had all his papers stuck in a fridge. Lost a load documents over that.      Haha, yeah, pulling 'em out one by one was like sorting through a fish 'market, but serious bloke came out with frozen documents. Still, you'd think scanners were invented for this.      On the other hand, you know, I’ve met enough people left themselves in bits of turbulence, ain't they? D’you know how I got stuck aiding someone from oil-controlled parts, far harder than you think. Copy, no documents gone? Now you are stuck.      I hear you. There’s been some to do near the area I grew up over that too, like Waterfords, you get 'em in places—somebody I know, quite a while back, trying to get a visa for her尕娃 in-country—it wasn't easy. All this about oil control and Wahhabi-style – Mate, I got no chance, least way it felt.      Yeh, quite often they tie things down for people who live in countries with oil and no toilets. Makes you wonder someone at the top is also suspicious of oil money just like they are of people.      Also, some of the folk I talk with through work—university students, people, they've all got about five nationalities. Seems the younger generation's interested in different cultures, but most ain't keen on politics.      Supposed to handle it all, but in my job, quite different. When someone has no education, can't speak, can't read? All they know it's a land full of money and threats.      Arche, I hope you didn't hear that—"threats", innit? I 've been meaning to ask—was it hard when you first moved?      Peh! Hard’s an understatement. First I got a visa, or I got none at all.      Hopefully, they'll go easier now—after Libya whatnot, but you know how it is. Still, I suppose we can do our bit—pointing people in the right direction to sort stuff out. Know where they can get the help, innit?      Fair enough. Just done for today?

Rather lovely this roast lamb, don't you think? It's been ages since I had such a properly cooked joint. Just the right amount of rosemary and garlic. I'd murder for someone to cook me a meal like this more often!      You're very kind. Honestly, I’ve had a bit of practice over the last few weeks. Having to cook for three seems to be better than eating microwave dinners day in and day out. Though I do miss a good takeaway now and then.      Well, you’ve certainly hit the mark this evening. Nothing quite like the slow sizzle of a good joint in the oven, is there? I used to cook the same way when I was headmistress. My turkey on Christmas Day was infamous—you’d think I’d qualified back then, the way the teachers would rave about it.      You had an oven, then, Mabel? Wait, I remember you saying you cooked in a microwave when you first moved in with me. That oversized desktop microwave, you remember?      Good grief, yes! I was overjoyed if it didn’t spark. But I always said if we ever had a proper kitchen, I’d be back in my element. And here we are, with a range and all. Mind you, I miss my old estate: at least I didn’t have to watch the children throw peas at each other during dinner.      You know what I miss? When the old landlord let me put in a TV in the dining room. Watching a romcom while the wife moans at me about the stove hotter than the sun—classic. Now we’re being told no screens in the house because the new tenants “prefer” about five candles and quiet eating. Blooming eccentric landlords.      I take it you’re not happy with that arrangement then?      No, I’m not. But I’m not the one paying rent. Though I will say, that and the strict no-pets rule are beginning to give me ideas about a holiday. I’ve been looking into cruises. There’s one to the Canary Islands next month—booked with lunches and a couple of whiskeys.      Oh, a cruise now? Pah! I had a cruising go in my sixties—fine if you're alone or with a sprightly partner. Imagine trying to shuffle up and down three flights of stairs on a ship after dodging the gym for three decades.

Rather annoying this newfit in eh? You know, me an’ the flat just don’t realle get on proper. I’m fed up of this whole bloody place. Not saying I've found where else to go though.      Look, John, you can't afford to move. You know eenyhow. You’ve been on benefits for ages. I reckon it's not all that bad? I mean yeah, it’s starting to smell in this room, but that's probably due to me, not you.      I don’t get how you even can be friends with someone who’s never had to worry about money! Not everything is about me, Marti. I only cook for us and now you think you're entitled to living somewhere clean! Yeah, no. Tenants need to look after their home.      Fair enough, Sharon. But I’m not the one who put the breakfast on the floor then left it there. Not saying I’m clean, but I try. Properly try, you know?      Listen, you all blokes need to learn a bit of domestic skills. I try and I don’t even live here as much as you grief. For once, could we just have a proper night without it binning in the kitchen again? I’m at the uni preparing for new term, not sorting your mess!      Yeah, Tom’s right. We need to sort something out soon. Me and Liam at uni been talking and he's going to apply full time for a course next year. That's if we can afford it. You think you’ll get into uni, John?      Can’t see it happening. Not with my record and about nowhere. I’ve sent a few apps but dunno what they want from me. I’ve got a degree but it doesn’t seem to mean nuffin’ anymo’.      That's just sad. You should use that to your advantage. I’m trying to sort it out for any bloody job I can get, but Germany is restricting everything. I don't know how we’re going to survive being here.      You keep on speaking English, Sharon, and you’ll be fine. Work experience matters more than anything. I started with nothing and go in with my best smile, and it does help.      I just think that between us we could support one another properly if we had better jobs and more stability.

I just did a quick sweep of the kitchen, and I think we’ve got everything for the baking lesson tomorrow. Flour, sugar, eggs—oh wait, do we have enough butter? I've got a bit in the fridge, but I don’t know if it’s enough for the class. I saw some butter in the cupboard by the bananas! I tried to eat the bananas but then they went a funny yellowy-brown. Not nice! Oh no, you didn’t! That sounds perfectly edible to me, actually. But thank you for the butter tip—it's probably the extra block I bought last week. I’m so glad I store it in the fridge, not out. Can I bring my Tomodachi Life plushie to the lesson? I made him wear an apron, and now I think he wants to be a pastry chef too! Well, he’d better not step in front of the oven in his Tomodachi Life glory! But yes, you can definitely bring him along—just not to the actual hot parts of the kitchen, got it? I don’t like baking. I like reading. Do we have to eat cake tomorrow or can we read a book instead? You can read after the lesson. But we do have to bake, because tomorrow’s also my half-birthday! And I thought we could celebrate with something sweet. Half-birthday? That’s like a super-duper birthday for people who don’t like waiting a whole year for presents! I got you a book from Morrisons. It was in the children’s section but I thought you’d like it better because it had about baking! Oh, that’s sweet of you. I can’t wait to read it. What was the title?  The Cake Bible ! But I couldn’t pronounce "bibble" so I called it "cake animal." That was very nice of you. I’ll read you a little bit from it after the lesson, as long as you promise to help me mix the batter first. Can I do the sprinkles? I’m good with colours. Only if you promise not to make it look like a rainbow exploded on the cake. I will. I’ll make it look like Tomodachi Life! I’ll help too. We can team up! You two better start planning your design now, because tomorrow morning, we start at 10 sharp.

Rather annoying, though—Facebook these days. I mean, do we need to know what half of my first-year students had for breakfast? It’s like they think everyone  wants  to hear about their kedgeree at 7 a.m. on a Tuesday.      I saw that!  Kedgeree  and   57   comments about how "creamy" it was. Honestly, if I wanted to know about someone’s breakfast, I’d ask   them   in person. Not interrupt my coffee with a timeline of someone called "Oliver J." being very passionate about frozen fruit loops.      Exactly! And the   algorithms  —they push this stuff at you like you’d   actually   care. I scroll through and there I am, five years ago, at this very pub in   Norfolk  , with you in the background, looking very drunk and breakfast-less.      That was the night the car broke down, remember? You picked me up in that clapped-out   Fiat Panda   and we got stuck on the A1067 for two hours. You were so proud of it.      It was a   British car  , it was from   Norfolk  . It just decided it didn't want to be in   Norfolk   on that particular day. But seriously, I did   not   want to be the person who leaves a lecturer stranded in the rain.      But also   such   a bad decision buying that car. I mean, what made you think that a   used     Fiat   from a   car boot sale   would last more than a few weeks?      Optimism, my love. Both of us buying terrible things and hoping   something   would work. I mean,   you   went out and bought that ridiculous ‘all-terrain’ bike that was basically a Segway with   handlebars  .      That bike was a   masterpiece  . I could clear   hedges   on that thing. Except when the brakes gave up and I whizzed   straight   into the   flowerbed   of a very annoyed   elderly woman   in   Cambridge  .      And I think she   charged   you for that.
