For instance, as someone from England, watching how the gym scene is in other countries gives you so much to talk about.      Yeah, it really does. And while the gym bros in Poland are more like average Janes and Joes, back home in England, it’s all 'flex someone at the gym to get girls'. That stuff just blows my mind.      I mean, is it different for women as well being English? Like, does society treat us differently there because of stereotypes about English women?      Interesting point. I mean, gender roles and stuff definitely play a part. In England, you often find that women are unacknowledged in the gym, like for the majority you're not even considered to be a true 'gym member', unless it's a woman giving you attention. At least that's how I've always seen it.      Yeah, being English, especially being English with 'British qualities' can be so odd at times. Like, there's this polite ignorance around gender issues. I sometimes think we're goaded into maintaining that status if you don't.      Yeah, I think that's because we were brought up that way. Silence your feelings and you'll be just fine.      Yeah, suppress your emotions and all that.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun's doin' wonders for the garden. The potted geraniums are really starting to bloom proper, eh? Not a hint of that overcast mood we've had all week.      Aye, can't complain much. Got eeny harm out there last week—probly 'cos I was sleepin’ in me socks most a' the time! But this weather's got me all excited to get me hands dirty again. I’ve got that clump of lavender by the fence that's needin' a trim.      Oh, I’ve been talkin’ to Jan last week—she’s taken to makkin’ these lovely hand-thrown mugs. Told me to pop by one day and see her worksheeet. D’you know, I think I might have a go at one for meself. Got better things to do than subscribin’ to another coffee house!      A’right, Jan’s got some talent, I’ll grant you that. I reckon she’d like to give it a go—personally I’d start up sidein’ with the glue as quick as look at me.      Oh, don’t be so daft. Be a good laugh. Though I must say, I got a bit of a scare last week—woke up to the power out an’ thought there was summat wrong with the toaster. Turns out it was that wind, carryin’ out all the lights in the street.      Aye, I remember one out in ‘97—only a couple blocks from here—prior to the big festival. Got so dark, most people about considered candles to walk to the bridge. But talking of scaries, had I mentioned I’ve seen this spider in me greenhouse that’s barely the size of me thumb but moved in to the bin, ‘cos it’s hiding from that black one?      A’right, it sounds like it got its own little underworld in there! I’ve been noticing a lot of the birds too—those yellow ones with the long beak, they’ve been keepin’ me company in the mornings when I feed the nuts and crumbs.      Oh, the goldfinches? I get them about me sunflower patch. Not much else grows like it, but that sunflower always brings ‘em in.      Aye, planting seeds in the spring really does bring the garden to life. I’ve never had the patience for it like you though. Know where you were at when I first mentioned this idea of a homemade cup?

So do we get to take our bikes on the train, do you reckon? I mean, they said it’s got to be folded and all, but I paid good money for a sturdy one      Lucy, don’t start bargaining the rules again—just check the train website. I’ve booked the tickets already. But yeah, if it’s folded and has a wheel cover, they tend not to complain      Ay, that sounds like a top plan. If I was as fit as you lot, I’d chuck the bike in and be off chase the hills myself. Still, I don’t like trains. Too much jumbling and clattering about, if you ask me      But the visit is all about exploring! The North Yorks moors and all, loads of trails and things. We can’t just sit in the hotel all day      Oh, we’re not—there’s a museum in Middlesbrough in the plan too, you know. You lot can cycle to it if you so desire. And I reckon we’ll visit some villages with tea shops—proper proper ones, not the fancy falafel brunch spots in Hastings      Teas in the shop… Sounds like my kind of rhythm. Be a good way to take a breather. Plus, I’ve got a bit of time to practice some tunes. I reckon the countryside might spark a few new ones      You mean your creepy, rainy kind of tunes again      Ay, why not? It’s not like I do metal—more like the slow, moody folk songs. Anyhow, what about the rest of you? Neil and Jess have promised to meet us somewhere, right      Yes, they’re staying a night in York. Going to meet us at the station the day after we arrive. They’re bringing their kids too—two of them, one’s eight and the other’s five. Be interesting to see how they keep up with all the walking      You mean me doing all the walking! I’m not a tour guide, you know      Aye, but you’re the one who wanted to explore, luv. Now you can be their hero as go guide them on your own mission      Ha—no chance. I’m only leading because I know where I’m going      So are you planning to fill up on ketchup and ice cream every night after, then      Is it not allowed to recharge the batteries a little      You’ll go all sugar rush at the theme park.

So did you watch  10 Things I Hate About You  last night? I just finished it, like... ten minutes ago! Honestly, it was way more than I expected. Patrick was kinda swoony, and I was literally yelling at Kat like, “Just go after him, you dummy!”      Yeah, I watched it with my older sister! She totally nerd-sniped me with it. She’s been listing every 90s teen movie since, so now I’m into it, I guess. Patrick was fine, but Heath Ledger as Joey? Iconic, don’t you think?      No way! I can’t believe it’s the same guy from  The Dark Knight  and My Name Is Earl. Honestly, his eccentric stuff’s better than Joker! But anyway – back to the film, the whole Kat-Patrick thing made me think of school again. Ugh! Why do we have to do that hated project everyone has to do in Year 12?      Oh, spare me the drama. At least we don’t have to give it orally, like last year’s class. Remember Emma faltering with her report as if her life depended on it? Honestly, we’ve got something to live for. But it’s such a pain. I’m thinking – what if we do a report on film adaptation?      Yeah! We could compare  10 Things I Hate About You  and the original play  The Taming of the Shrew . Oh, my teacher would  adore  that. Besides, we can definitely talk about how modern the film feels compared to the original.       Exactly.  Best of all, we can make each other suffer by watching  The Taming of the Shrew  first. I’ve already warned my sister. She says we’re deranged. But listen, while we’re on projects, I overheard someone talking about a possible school trip to London. Can you believe it?      Wait, really? I haven’t heard about that yet! My brother mentioned visiting the British Museum next month as well. What if we take the trip together and join forces to do our project? We could even visit some filming locations around London or like, the National Portrait Gallery gothic vibes!      That’s brilliant! We could line it up with our project. Imagine explaining Shakespearean adaptations in front of one of those portraits. It’d be like seriously cinematic. Oh, and we could go for fish and chips in Camden as well to fuel ourselves for research!      Or just get lost in Hyde Park...

Rather annoying this new Facebook lark, isn't it? I tried to sign in the other day, and it kept on asking me questions about old photos I’d never seen! Mind, I think it might be getting to me. Not quite sure if it's the site or me getting scatterbrained.      Oh, I understand that, dear. I haven't touched Facebook in ages. Far too many people putting on a show. Not like in the old days, chatting round a cup of tea, pulling no wool over one another's eyes. And for what? To show off or keep up with the Joneses like we're still in school.      Honestly, I found it easier before when we had to write letters or speak to people face-to-face. I remember you mentioned you used to write letters to Darcy, Dad. I think modern life is just too chaotic for some of us. Speaking of, when I was a child I hated chicken pox – I used to rub Vick’s VapoRub on every single spot to distract myself. Madness, I know, but it worked.      You had OCD traits, then! I can relate — I’ve always had to flick switches twice or something equally as insane. It’s funny how these traits run in families, isn’t it? Though I suppose it’s not often talked about, least of all with the children these days. They’re too busy swiping right and wrong.      Mark you, I always thought religion gave people a frame of reference. Used to go to Sunday services in the old church down the road. Now it’s just all about going solo, and I don’t mean in fitness – I mean spiritually. Lost me there!      That’s the same story the good Reverend at the chapel told me — no one wants to commit to anything these days. Everything's optional. I remember when we believed in something, whether for better or worse. There was a sense of community.      You know, I was thinking about that the other day. Students are so detached these days. We discuss ethics and religion in lectures, but they treat everything like a take-home exam. No wonder you feel the world’s going off the rails.      It's a shame, really. There's room for both old traditions and new ideas, but I think people are just not trying to understand each other anymore.

Rather annoying when the oven’s on the blink, isn’t it love?      Oh honestly, I’m not one for mucking about with gadgets. Just need something hot      A full £200 the sod cost me!      Right, I'm going to give the place a good tidy 'fore I sit down. Where d’you think I’ve been all day?      I’ve brought some wine, thought we might not be stuck with just bread and cheese.      Did I mention how lovely it was in the Cotswolds?      All those marble fireplaces and antique chaise longues? My word, must have been something.      And I’m guessing the sandwiches were lemon and pickled egg in a wholemeal wrap?      Oh better than breakfast, no doubt. I hated that.      When’s the last time we went on holiday to Germany together?      Let me think. I do like the way the locals there say 'Guten Tag' with quite a different twang to it.      It’s funny how accents can trot along in little groups. You ever notice how the Baptists in Brighton all speak with a kind of educated drone?      It’s not just them. Silly as it sounds, I’ve heard that the toilets in some supermarkets out west don’t always work right.      That’s oddly precise.      I mind the noise sometimes.      I quite like it, it makes it about something.      But it can be hard on the ears. I’ve seen some very grumpy people at school gates who seem to have a lot on their minds.      There’s always something going on, isn’t there. I remember when the sirens went off nearby, it was very intense.      My brother was visiting from Lagos and he just panicked.      Towns and big cities are full of surprises. Once I saw a man delivering something in a trolley!      That sounds potentially life-changing.      You’re just in the wrong house if you like the quiet life.      It’s all part of the lives we lead, though, isn’t it?      True to say, we can’t get over this one’s new car, can we?      It's alright for some.      And always remember to charge the thing. Last time, he was stuck miles from anywhere.      A fine mess, by all accounts.      But oh look, here we go on the potatoes now. That’s always a good sign.      Everyone’s practically in their pyjamas by now.      And rightly so.

So, I heard you've been up to gigs a lot lately. Any good bands jumping out at you? I got into a bit of music after uni—always thought I'd take it up properly, but then life got in the way.      Yeah, been to a few decent ones. The local indie place, The Crow's Nest, had this underground band last week—packed out completely. I reckon they’re gonna break big soon. What kind of music are you into?      Oh, a bit of everything, really. Found myself getting into heavier stuff after uni. You know, like Foals and even some post-punk. I used to play the drums back in sixth form in Nottingham. My mates still bug me about it.      Drummer, eh? You're in Devon now and I in Exeter doing this chef lark, but we both got into something. I never really played much proper music, but I’ve always loved live stuff. Watching the energy in a crowd, the way everyone moves the same. Good for the soul, man.      Yeah, man—there’s nothing like a live show. Did you ever play?      Nah, I wasn't cut out for it, but I got into sound engineering for a bit when I was younger, messing with laptops and mics. I thought maybe mixing music could be my thing, but then I found the kitchen and the rest as they say, is history. You? Any music in your future?      Not unless I start a band with my mate from uni—Dan. He plays the bass, I still have all my kit in the attic. We might do something at university after I finish my internship. Got one at this publishing place in London starting in September.      That's the stuff. Internship in London? That's a proper step up. You always wanted to do that, yeah?      Yeah, I was bloody nervous about it, but I reckon I’ll get on alright. We should come back down and grab a bite or something once in a while. Catch up on what you're up to with the bands and that.      For sure man. I can go halves on the curry and you can talk me through your drumming comeback. Sounds like a plan.      Deal. And what about some of the older lads from school? You ever see Haz or Mia around?      Nah, not since we were in that weird over-21 bar in Exeter.

Rather a lovely place, isn't it? That table by the window looks nice an' all, but it’s got the rather loud telly blaring out more than I'd like, if you ask me. Let’s pop over here to this quieter bit, love.      Yeah, that’s alright. Thought we’d pop in somewhere for a cuppa before heading over to Durham on Saturday? I’ve got A-level stuff to revise before that.      Oh, well, Durham's right up ahead of you, I reckon. Funny how quickly the time flies. Still, you'd best not leave your revision till the last minute. I remember learning about the castle, only to find out in the exam it was a bit more history-based. Fun stuff.      I know, I know, but I’ve been swamped with work. It's all about the Drive through project we’re doing—this lady at the gym’s running a drive in aid of the food bank and I’m helping her out ordering supplies for the transport and printing flyers.      That’s very commendable, I must say. I remember you did quite a similar thing for the school food hamper initiative. You’ve got a good heart, lad. Still, when are we going shopping for the – what’s it called again?      Shopping list. Yeah, her van gets refilled every week and I wrote a list—sleeping bags, tents, toilets, all sorts. She said businesses in Newcastle also dropped off a few supplies. It's amazing how folks do their bit without getting all loud about it.      Can I get another jelly bean, by the way? I mean, I know I shouldn’t be having such sugary stuff this close to bed, what with the radio reports on obesity and school kids and everything. But a little one won't do me, will it?      A little one here and there won't hurt the world, love. Just don’t go finishing the whole jar, or your poor nan will come crackin' down like that sprite player from that football game you've been watching too much of lately!      Defo, I won't. Though I do wonder—will you go with me on the actual day? It’d be good to have someone there to help, you know, with the delivery box arranging or something?      I’d be delighted, to be honest. Must be nice lending a hand, don’t you think?

I can't believe we've not caught up in so long, Tom. I was just telling my students about university... got them talking about slang from the West Midlands, actually. You know what they're like with regional differences. Haha, I bet they were thrilled to learn about it. You always did have a soft spot for linguistic stuff. So, you saying you're still living in Bedford? I miss that place, even if it’s a bit too quiet for me now. Nah, moved to a new flat in Sussex. Bit of a change, considering I’ve been in Bedford my entire adult life. It’s nice, honestly—brighter, with more green space, and easier to get into town if I visit university colleagues. Still, I miss the bursts of life back home, the real carbuncle on the legs of the West Midlands. Sounds like you’ve really shaken things up. I heard from Jen that you’re thinking of a joint bank account with someone, too. Keeping your finances on the up and up, then? Yeah, I mean, it’s not a romance or anything, just a flatmate arrangement. Makes it easier to split bills and keep track, especially as we’ve got a couple of roommates. I remember when we used to compare our student budgets? I wouldn’t say it was a comparison, more of a competition. It was always “I can survive on a packet of pasta and a can of baked beans,” kind of thing. Now, though, I’m steering toward my own career. Trying to establish a secure position with my company—salaried, and all the perks that come with it. Prime stuff. I did some teaching gigs while I was back in the area, too. You remember my old job doing form-filling projects for that data company? I’m glad it’s in the rearview. My students are way more fun to interact with. Speaking of fun, remember when we would smoke a few before heading to the student bar? Ah, miss those mad nights. We crack jokes about it now, but I’ve gone cold turkey. That’s the spirit. I took the plunge as well—makes budgeting a bit easier. I’ve been looking into goings on in South Korea, actually. If I can afford it, I might spend a holiday there. Spanish always intrigued me, but I never really had time to develop it.

I can't believe it's been a year since Dad passed. Time really flies. I know, it still feels like yesterday. How are you feeling about it all lately? Honestly, it's been up and down. Some days are easier than others. The grief just lingers in the background. That's completely normal. I still have days where I break down for no reason. A song, a smell, even a colour can trigger it. It’s like it’s part of the furniture now. You get used to it, but the pain never really goes away. I've been so grateful for the support the family has given me. It's made a difference. I agree. We've all been leaning on each other, which is what we need more than anything. Have you spoken to your sister lately? She mentioned breakfast with you the other week. I did, and it was good. She's been minding the grandkids a bit more, which I think helps her cope. That makes sense. Keeping busy takes your mind off things. It's funny, but since everything happened, I've been thinking a lot about how important it is to live in the moment – with the ones we love. That’s wise. I’ve started taking walks with the kids every evening. Silly things, but precious. It’s the little things that make life worth living. I’ve been trying to focus on work more, which definitely keeps me occupied. That’s understandable. Any news on the new clients you were chasing? I did close one deal a couple of weeks ago. Felt great to have something positive out of all this. That’s brilliant. You always do such a great job. I wish I could be as good at managing clients. You are, actually. You lead a team for a reason. Thanks, but I still worry about burnout from all the calls. My mental health has taken a bit of a hit too. I took the recent flu as a bit of a break. Sometimes stopping everything for a while can go a long way. I wonder if I should find a counsellor. I’ve read a bit about it lately. That’s a positive step. I’ve been on and off one after Dad was diagnosed with cancer. It helped me process a lot. That’s good to know. I tend to push through the pain; I need to stop doing that.

Rather than share a text, I’d rather describe what happens. A few people around the dinner table in Fradley, Lichfield—probably the family kitchen or dining room. I've fixed a bit of roast chicken with some parsnips and carrots, nothing too fancy. The kids are chattering away about school, and my partner, Speaker_3, listens with that half-smile of his. He’s a bit of a introvert but tends to open up when the conversation turns to football or referendums, topics that seem to pull him in like a magnet. Didn’t even want to start with those, of course, but somehow it all comes out—what with me talking about the upcoming referendum and how people in the village are split, then Speaker_3 asking about my thoughts on apprenticeships and business, because he’s got his eye on investing and I’ve dabbled a bit with proofing and marketing services.      Heh, this happened when I was playing in a tennis match, you know, in that local tournament last weekend near the village? I was up 5–2 in the third set, and I just totally lost focus. I mean, the sun was in my eyes, and I started thinking about today’s maths test… You reckon I should work on endurance then, not just serves?      True enough, but still, it's important to stay grounded. I remember when I was younger, my dad always said if I could handle the heat at tournaments, I could handle business too. And now I’m looking at steering investments toward apprenticeships. Not bad for a lad who was floring the lawns in Seoul as a kid being dragged out for weekend tennis matches.      I do wonder if there’s a way to make the two worlds connect, though—business and sport. Maybe your son could get into coaching. I've met a few unis who are offering courses in sport business planning. Maybe it’d be something he’d consider?      Honestly, I’d prefer something more stable. Like, I dunno, maybe waiting till I’m a bit older and figure out if I can academically keep up with what I need to do first. My mate took an apprenticeship, you know, something around engineering, and he's basically earning as goin' on holidays and learnin’ at the same time.      It’s not for everyone, but I can see it helping your mindset.

Rather looking forward to this trip, really. I needed a break from the hurly-burly of university work. You've been to Lancaster before, haven’t you?      Yes, actually, a few times. I spent a summer working as a research assistant there a couple of years ago. The campus is stunning, especially the view from the top of the hill.      That does sound amazing. I’m hoping to visit the campus, maybe see if they’ve done any interesting building work. We’ve been doing quite a bit on postwar architecture, and Lancaster's a big case study in the module.      Oh, I remember the debate around that. It was like a reaction to all the traditional stone buildings—you know, the Arts and Crafts style, the red brick universities. A bold move for the time.      Exactly! And oddly enough, it doesn’t feel old-fashioned at all now. Maybe because it's so open and built for the future. Speaking of, are we planning to go to the coast?      Absolutely, if the train is on time, we’ll make it down to Morecambe by early afternoon. I’ve heard the sands there are something else. They stretch practically forever.      Yes – but it's also fairly infamous, isn’t it? About the cockle pickers’ disaster in 2004.      Oh, that's right. Terribly sad. A full four-year gap in my memory, unfortunately. It just goes to show how easily people can ignore the tides when the wind’s pulling it back.      Staggering. I did a little bit of reading about it for the English lit module I was teaching part-time a while back. The reports are brutal to read.      Maybe we’ll do something less fatal for lunch then. Got a craving for fish and chips. There’s a dinky little place by the train station, I believe.      Perfect! After all the talk about architecture and coastal tragedies, we need something fried and British.      Entirely agree. By the way, how are you finding your MRes? Still loving the master's work? I remember how you used to talk about wanting to write a dissertation on language policy in multilingual schools.      I am, though it's all-consuming sometimes. I’ve been writing and rewriting my proposal. And yes, I’m still set on that dissertation topic. I’ve got over thirty hours of interview transcripts from primary schools in Tower Hamlets so far.

Rather annoying, innit? I’d rather be hanging about with me mates anyway. We were ‘ere like... last weekend an' had a laugh, but tonight’s a bit murder by the look of it. Got anything planned?      Nup, just thought I’d come downdown een case I got fed up me mam badgerin' me to go out. Proper ball of fun she is. Aye, but tell me more abaht your mates. Still seein’ up wiv that lot as well?      Yeah, course, but they’ve all gone different ways like. Most of ’em are still dead knigged up at sixth form still, but some have started work an’ all. You know how it is. I’m tryin’ to see if I can catch them up this summer.      Yeah, it’s a shame they’re not all still around. Me best mate Dan’s still alright — in Leeds at un’s. Mega boring compared to us, innit? Used to be the life an’ soul, now he spends all ‘is time reading books or listenin’ t’ classical music. Ridiculous.      Blimey, classical? Bloke, we used to light farts and run out the door at breaktime, an' now ‘e's off listenin’ t’ violin sommat. Mate, you done something wrong to ‘im or summat? Still, if he’s happy... what can I say? What about yu’? Got a new crew or is it still the same lot?      Nah, still me an’ the lads from ballet club — you know, about five of us. We all still hang out most weekdens. Course, most of ’em into gaming now. Me an’ mate Jamie still go to gigs sometimes, mostly in Doncaster. Had a few alright ones lately. There’s this new indie band playin’ at The Rockit soon — you any interest?      Aye, I sort of stick to my old faves mostly — The 1975, Wolf Alice. Grime and all that happened last year, but I’m trying to get into it. Still, the gig idea sounds goon. You think it’ll be our kind of crowd?      It’s rocky but not too shouty — yu might like it. Jamie said summat about The 1975’s vibes, so you’ll probably fit in like a glove. I’ll talk him into gettin' us tickets or whatever.      You lot ever go out for anything else? Gigs an’ gaming, or do you get up t’ anything else?      Nah, we do a few walks in the Moors sometimes.

Rather annoying when the red plague is spreading everywhere and no one is handling it properly. Someone needs to step up... or maybe I should have taken the Operations role more seriously. Honestly, I've been overburdened with teaching all week.      It's not like you're the only one playing, Claire.  Looks at the game board.  We haven't even cured the blue disease yet, and you’ve only had one action to move this round. I’m beginning to wonder if we should have shared the roles more evenly.      Didn’t even get the chance to play my role yet. I mean, I mostly just made us snacks and tea while the real decisions were being made. You know how it is when you’re not used to being left out of the team structure, right? I’m the chef, not the game expert.      For what it’s worth, I do see the strategy board and I agree. Maybe someone should be thinking a few moves ahead. Like in chess, you have to anticipate the opponent—here, it’s the viruses taking over the board. Claire, maybe you can assign someone next round to be the foresight person.      Honestly, we’ve been playing so many rounds, and it’s all pretty much the same. Back in Cardiff, I often play Scrabble and Monopoly with my friends, but Pandemic is quite different. You have to work as a team, or else you're literally overrun. It’s kind of like work at the charity—no two days the same, but you have to plan.      I have to say, I thought being a support worker would prepare me for this, but no. I about blocked the wrong player by accident! I mean, the severity of this game is just a little too much! I know that was you, Rhys, trying to take over my action. My, my!      All right, all right. Let’s take a moment. If we want to win, we have to start working together properly. Someone take the lead. Maybe we should review the rules again. Websites mentioned always trying to 'split tasks' according to your roles.       Laughs  Then again, if we started over, would go straight to my best friend from uni. He destroyed the other teams in college just by smiling at the board. He’s Welsh, by the way. Passes for a ghost at the table.

Rather than going out for dinner this summer weekend, what if we do something a bit different for Emily's birthday? I was thinking of throwing a small CBeebies-themed pantomime at home. It might be a hoot, and we can spread the stories out as a makeshift play.      That sounds brilliant, Mum! I've been watching   "The Gruffalo"   on CBeebies so much recently. Can we do that as one of the stories? I think George would love pulling off the leaves and pretending to be the mouse.      Do I get to be a big, bad character again? In our last CBeebies party at nursery, I pretended to be the   "Gru  " from   "Despicable Me"  . I scared everyone on purpose! You should have heard the adults gasp!      Well, let's make it something a bit more old-fashioned and clever this time, alright? The Gruffalo’s forest setting is perfect — we can even gather spare bits of fabric and old Christmas baubles to make props. We could get the kids to write short scripts about each of the characters. It’s World Book Day only a few months away, so this could be a fun warm-up!      Can we invite Mateo from next door? He and I made cards for Mother’s Day the other day — maybe we could combine them and have a little Mother’s Day-CBeebies hybrid bash?      That’s a smashing idea. I’d draw Mum a Gruffalo card. I made something very scary for her in art class and it got stuck under the fridge!      I love how excited you two are about this. Let’s draw up a list of roles and a little story board. We’ll be telling tales and acting out our CBeebies favorites in no time. And don’t worry, George, you’ll have plenty of lines. The Gruffalo’s a bit of a mouthful, isn’t he?      I could stick the scripts into a handmade story book as well. I always liked the 'Once upon a time' sayings. Some of our class stories were really good, although not by me!      Yeah, but your stories had the best names for characters! You once called a pirate   Sir Salty Legs the Brave   — that’s what your teacher embroidered on Mother’s Day card, wasn’t it, Emily?      I’ll take that as a compliment, thank you, George! Now, why don’t we discuss the string and the green cape we could use for the Gruffalo — and perhaps a birthday cake with a mini mouse on top?

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You’d think by June we’d have seen some proper sunshine. Mind you, the garden shower at least keeps the plants happy. I’ve been meaning to ask, are you two still considering moving in together properly or have you decided against it?      Honestly, I'm still on the fence. It’s one thing living together casually, but taking the plunge into a formal tenancy agreement complicates things. I mean, I adore Charlie, but we’re both quite firm in our habits. We’ve been talking about sorting it when the current place comes up for renewal in September.      I couldn’t imagine living with a partner unless the equilibrium was right. You know, like shared dishwasher turkey, shared madness, shared jelly! Speaking of, I’ve been meaning to try the new Italian place on the High Street. Do you lot fancy going with me for pizza this weekend?      Sounds good. I haven’t had a proper margherita since I last went to Naples on a college trip back in the day. As long as it’s nothing too posh or overpriced. I’d rather not be side-eyed in a restaurant.      It’s not that fancy, just a local spot. They say the mozzarella is from a local relative of the owner — it's got a bit of a cult following around here. Honestly, the cheapest slice of heaven you could hope for in the 21st century.      There’s also this someone I met online who keeps insisting they're my spiritual twin. He's oddly literal about the term — sent me this article titled  How to Be a Two-Person Temple in the Modern World . Scary and touching about five seconds in.      Oh come on, Charlie, let’s not go into this! Swiping left is fine and dandy, but does anyone ever click right? My sister’s over here with a new guest speaker at the parish hall. They’re doing this eco-Christian initiative — apparently, you can be green and grow a beard too.      Joining such a group sounds wholesome. Is it anything like trying to find meaning through compost heaps and mindfulness retreats? I almost did that for a bit after my last travel assignment.      Honestly? I think life improvements start with food, real conversation, and the occasional Netflix binge without self-judgment. That, or learning to read your cat’s body language — have you noticed how much more annoyed Hazza gets every time you speak to him in that new gruff dad tone, Liam?

Rather annoying to be honest, I’d rather be at home with a good book. But it’s been lovely catching up and I’ll take any excuse to see more of my family. I've found over the years that it's easy to get caught up in work and neglect such important things.      That is true, I understand completely. I find that I spend far more time in meetings than with my own family. Being a Head of Admin and HR isn't always glamorous, but I do enjoy it. What about you three, how was your weekend?      Oh, I spent most of the weekend wrapping up some financial reports for work. I work as an accountant, and these kinds of reports are always the turkey on my desk at the end of the month. But I did finally get around to trying out a new recipe for bubble and squeak that I had bookmarked for far too long. It honestly doesn’t live up to the name, but still a hit in my household.      Oh, I love those traditional recipes! As a sales manager, I often find myself with very little time for cooking, but I still have a soft spot for dishes that reminded me of my childhood in Boston, Lincolnshire. My mother made the best Lincolnshire sausages. I swear no one else can replicate it.      That does sound good. I grew up in Peterborough, and as you can probably hear from the way I speak, I have the East Anglian dialect. We had our own variations too. My mother made a version of toad in the hole that was hotter than the summer sun.      I was brought up in Essex, so there is a bit about our speech that is a bit different too. English can be very regional, and I think what's really interesting is how that comes out even more when we talk about food. I remember the first time I visited Speaker_1 in Lincolnshire; I had no idea that something called 'compo' was a stew made with whatever was left in the kitchen.      Ha, good one. I remember being in a pub once trying to order a 'Lincolnshire Line steak' and the man behind the bar thought I was asking for a snack! The points of difference go so much deeper than just food and dialect though.      Completely, I think it's fascinating how background and upbringing shape our lives.

So did you really just take off to Majorca without anyone knowing? That sounds like the kind of holiday we all need right now!      Blimey, I didn't even know! Your mum just popped it on and told us not to expect you for a week. Honestly, if it wasn't for the passive-aggressive texts from the dog sitter, I'd still be in the dark.      Well, we  do  have a habit of rushing into things, don’t we, Alan? Remember the time we drove to the Lake District, but the car wouldn't start? That was a right mess!      That's nothing, love. You should've seen that one visit when you tried to go kite surfing and ended up in the surf shop storeroom with a bin bag and a sad fish. Kudos for ambition, though.      I still can't believe you've been all the way to Majorca and didn't even share a photo of the sunset or something. You're a tough audience to please sometimes, Mum.      Speaking of, what's the deal with the dog? I’ve still got grief from the time he chewed through my essay on municipal engineering. That was a first-class disaster.      Don't be silly, Dean, that was  months  ago. You should be used to that by now. Silly pup! Bless him, he’s only been nipping at people’s heels since he was a pup.      Besides, we had a proper laugh while we were away. Stuck on the ferry with no Wi-Fi and no sunscreen. I spent most of it in flammable pink shorts and a sunhat trying to look the part. Jane had me covered with the sandwiches and the cap. Proper love story!      Maybe we should do something like that for the four of us soon. A quick road trip with no plan? Like a weekend getaway or a surf camp? I mean, I tried surfing once and immediately fell off the board. It didn't go well.      Do you think Jane and Alan would go for it? We'd need to set some rules—mainly, no eating the sandwiches early or go in bin bags for emergencies if necessary.      Ha! If anyone needs that, it'll be you, Dean. You might try to blame the sandwich if something goes wrong!      We’ll start with something simple—like a nearby beach or a park.

Rather annoying the newfit in the kitchen ain't it? Chez sticks it on, it buzzes like a wasp an' I jist now I'm tryin' t'boil a bleedin' kettle.      Oh, hang on! You wouldn't have used it without readin' the manual, would you? It says 'ere on the box that's all self-cleaning. Maybe that's what it's doin'.      Honestly, Simon, I wouldn't let you near my oven without me present. Remember the time when you tried to make vegan lasagne... and it collapsed like some dodgy tower block?      Aye, well, that’s 'cause you told me t"use everything you've got in one go". Probably need to stick t' what I know, and I know kettles. Blimey, this is more frustrating than solvin' a structural problem at work.      Oh don't be so dramatic! You lot, engineers, think you can solve the world's problems, but can't follow simple instructions.      Lucy, he might not be able t'read the manual, but tell me, what fancy book were you reading last night? Sounds like it was about as riveting as watching paint dry?      Rimshot, that's  literature ! I was reading about the new Prime Minister and their policies. Bit concerning, honestly. We might be heading into some austerity again.      Aye, that's summat different we can do t'earn a bit more. Maybe a side gig. Any ideas? Can't all be veg ballet sessions.      I'm thinking about trying to monetise my podcast. We were talking about it over drinks last week. Going into that data privacy gig. You up for a sound engineering side to it?      Aye, well if it's about data 'n' me, the technical side's probably got my attention. Just don't ask me to read anything unless it's on my phone and in 140 characters or less.      Typical Simon! "Innovative, but vertically challenged when it comes t'literacy."      But on that note, maybe our new engineering friend can help out. Fix the kettle, design some technical stuff for the podcast, and maybe even your dodgy vegan recipes.      You know what, after I'm done with the kettle and not set fire to it, I'll have a squiz at the podcast and see if there's a way I can plug in to that. Just don't expect me to podcast, Lucy, my mic's probably not fit for human ears.

Rather annoying when the satnav takes us the long way round. I blame it for us being late to Reg’s last weekend. Never mind, it was a lovely gathering. I can’t believe we’re saying goodbye to him after all these years.      Yeah, well, at least it’s not just the satnav anymore — we’ve got Google Maps these days. Saves money on all that satnav hassle. I remember when I moved to Saudi Arabia a few years ago, I had to print out maps because of the signal! It was madness navigating the desert when the GPS died halfway through.      That’s nothing! I once tried to reach a job site in the outback only to find the directions made no sense. Just kept driving until I saw the left-hand side of the sky go orange from the desert dust. But hey, I make a good living from all that messing around — harder than any office job I imagine.      Ah, a bit of hard graft never went out of fashion! I used to drive through those sorts of places in uniform, full kit and all. Nothing like a bit of adventure, I say. Still, I never did quite get the hang of high-tech mapping — always felt more proud just turning left when the sun set. Old school, but got me from A to B?      Right, but it’s not all about the trip, is it? It’s the company you have. Reg meant so much to our family — always bringing everyone together. I just wish we could get together more often. Ever since he decided to move out to the countryside with his new wife, it’s been tricky.      I hear you. My place in Peterborough is about an hour’s walk away — you can imagine trying to get there on foot most days. But thanks to Satnavs and Google Maps now, I can plan a trip with my stepdad and not get us hopelessly lost. Geo-tech has passed its time with me.      If you want advice on decorating the new flat, I can recommend some decent places. We just finished our living room. Took me all month but it’s coming along. I think it fits my personality more than the paint work, you know?      That’s the spirit! go for it with your own style. Always proud of a job well done, even in the dirtiest of trades.

Rather lovely to be out here today, isn't it? The garden looks like it's been through some recent care. You can tell by how the pathways are so tidy. I mean, sure, New Zealand's got its own wild charm, but this… this is continental class.      Yes, it is remarkable, isn't it? I read that the gardens have specific watering schedules depending on the species. I taught a group once about the importance of understanding a plant's native environment. It was quite interesting—my students were initially dismissive, but once they saw the plants thrive or wither under different conditions... well, they were deeply impressed.      That’s precisely the point, Alice. Being well-informed about your environment—whether you're tending a plot of land or your own well-being—is crucial. I used to think hydration meant just drinking water, but now I’ve learned to better gauge when my body actually needs electrolytes or when I'm merely in need of a mental reboot. It's amazing how much clearer your mind is when you're not overworking or under-hydrating.      Absolutely. I've been cycling quite a bit to keep active and clear my head since starting my business. It's not just about work rhythm; it's also about ensuring your mind can cycle through thoughts with the same efficiency. My wife won't stop reminding me that I should set boundaries—businesses and bodies have limits.      That's a good lesson for all of us. I think part of being a professional in a field, whether it's teaching or communications, is recognizing when it's time to step back and regroup. I’ve had to learn that there's a difference between being productive and being burnt out. Sometimes the most effective action is to simply let something rest.      Not to change the subject entirely, but speaking of rest—have you noticed the benches here? There are ones specifically under fruit trees, probably for designated rest or to monitor the growth. If I were managing this garden, I’d make a little signage there. We could run into a bit of a safety issue otherwise—imagine someone lunches underneath a cascading apple branch. Not the healthiest spot for a midday meal.      Oh, go on then, run it past me like a sample brief. What would the line be? “Please enjoy your picnic with a fruit tree in view, your well-being is our highest planting focus.”?

I can't believe how strong my accent is these days — anyone from outside the South East would think I’m speaking a completely different language sometimes! Just the other week, I was on a video call with a friend from Scotland, and I had to repeat myself like ten times! Aye, it’s all the more reason I don’t use the 'Voice Recognition' thing on my tablet — couldn’t make head nor tail of it. Not that I use it much, mind; it gives me a headache pulling out that device! Oh, I do use it occasionally. The tablet came from my son, bless him. Though honestly, I still much prefer the phone keypad, don’t you know? Being older, you still get used to the familiar! Speaking of, I just moved back to Harlow after my mum passed away and I couldn’t look after her. It was for the best really — better for her, and for me too. That’s really kind, thanks for saying that, mums are incredible. Speaking of, I remember when I was little, Mum would enforce a 'no screen time before bedtime' rule. I never did quite understand that at the time, but now, with uni workload and everything… watching shows before bed feels unhealthy in a way. Mate, I often sleep on my old mattress because the other one is broken. I’ve been trying to ignore it for months now. If I could blame anything for my back pain, it would be this. Let me tell you, a good mattress is worth its weight in gold. Though, at my age, I can’t be arsed to change mine — it’s as good as it gets about now! I know what you mean, Charlie. I work a lot of hours as a care assistant and then barely have time to rest. Still, I try to be there for patients every day. It's steady work at least, even if the pay could be a bit better. At least you're employed! You must see your fair share of good and bad things. I’ve seen a bit of the 'health' crisis during lockdowns. Now, the recent trend of obesity is heartbreaking. I had a course on the social determinants of health — it’s wild how your background can shape so much of your well-being. Honestly, with all the chips and alcohol your dad used to knock back, I’m surprised he ever made it past his fifties!
