Rather lovely to have you here, my dear. Thought we’d start the day right wi’ a proper Yorkshire breakfast, and a spot o’ tea, o’ course. Not like what they call breakfast in Swansea, is it? Not quite as hearty, I’d bet!      Aye, well, Swansegians do things a bit different here, love. But I have to say, you’ve outdone yourself. The sausages and black pudding are outstanding. I’ve not had a reasonable cooked breakfast since we last visited Yorkshire.      Oh, well, I thought I’d whip up a bit o’ home. Still, enough o’ the food—how was your visit to New York? I read online you met some eccentric folks.      Eccentric is one word, mad and sad in equal measure is another. But it was an adventure. Got to fly a proper private plane, which is probably why I’m now in the early stages o’ flying lessons! No, you didn’t hear that from me.      Oh, do tell, lass! I’ve always fancied it myself, but a certain fear o’ heights got in the way. Imagine though—seeing the world from up there!      It’s a marvel. I got fairly tipsy and tried to land in a lake. Let’s say the instructor wasn’t amused. Anyway, enough of that—what about you? Any big plans today apart from this splendid breakfast?      Aye, I’ve a lecture to prepare. Some students seem to think social media shouldn’t count as a ‘real’ form o’ communication in a world o’ email and letters. I’m baffled! I still write proper letters, you know. It’s what civilisation fails to understand.      Aye, well, I do enjoy a hand-written note. There’s something timeless aboot it. Reminds me o’ Japan, where we first met. Do you remember how I tried to write my name in kanji?      Oh aye, and how you insisted it was a new style of Japanese typography. Some people, no? Still, I’m glad we met. Now, while we reminisce, I need to tell you something.      Go on then, out wi’ it.      I had to cancel the latest bin collection o’ the week. Thought you’d appreciate the heads-up so you don’t leave your refuse outside like a forgotten sermon or summat!      Ha! Now that’s something I appreciate about you, love—always prepared. I swear, if it weren’t for folk like you, the whole world'd be full o’ rotting tat and plastic!

Rather annoying when people are late, isn't it? I mean, I was supposed to meet Sarah at the coffee shop and she turned up twenty minutes late because she thought I'd asked for the shop on the other side of the bridge. Charming.      Oh, that sounds familiar. I once turned up at a uni event in one building, but I'd been told it was in another with a slightly different name. I spent twenty minutes wandering around confused. Still, at least I got to know campus better.      That makes me think — when did the word  late  start being used to mean tardy? I mean, like, is it the same word as  late  in like  Last night was late ?      Good question! I think the origin is from Old English, and I think it meant something like "leading in the opposite direction," but then it evolved, and now it just means happened previously. Huh.      Honestly, I never look into that kind of thing. As a chef, I just want to know the word for a plate is  plate  and I don't need to spell it  platte . But in Scrabble, we’ve got to be careful with that.      Oh no, don’t start talking about Scrabble strategies again, James. You already used “quinoa” as your opening move again. Honestly, who even  uses  that word outside of Scrabble and debates about food.      I think my mum read me  The Very Hungry Caterpillar  when I was a kid, and I still say “fee-fi-fo-fum” when I see a caterpillar. I’m clearly not the verbal type, though.      Honestly, you’re not. Sarah and I used to argue over whether it should be spelled  fee-fi-fo-fum  or  fé-fí-fó-fūm . I’m with you on the simple version.      Guess what I found out at catering college? People from good A-Level backgrounds are more academically prepared than those who come straight in after school. They're often better with reading recipes and understanding health and safety.      That makes sense. I remember my A-Levels were a real rollercoaster. Thought I was going to fail chemistry but managed a B by the skin of your teeth.      Speaking of teeth, have you checked out the Chelsea Flower Show yet? I was watching a clip online and saw a guy over there pronouncing “bedding” like  bdin , so posh.      I thought the pronunciation of  bedding  was just  bending .

Rather a gray day, isn't it? That sun's been hiding all week. Don't think it's gone to be out at all today.      That's the September for you, dear. One minute it's alright, the next it looks like the sky's gone to bleed. Got me all bundled up, I have. Light jacket and thick socks if you hadn't noticed.      Aye, I noticed that! I don't much mind the cold myself as long’s as it’s dry. Wet and damp makes for stiff joints, in my experience. Still, I'd fetch the rug for you if you'd like. Can't abide someone being cold in their own home.      You're too kind. I left it on the back of the chair earlier, yes, if you’d be so kind. A little bit of company is all I’ve needed to feel warm. Not often we’ve much to do but still... I like these chats.      Oh, I do too. There isn't much to talk about these days, I know, but a bit of small talk keeps the mind going. Remember your brother as a lad, grief of a child he was. Would demand treacle toffee for tea time and then sulk if it wasn’t warm enough.       laughs  You weren’t much better, were you? All that time spent in the garden at Costessey, you were more birdwatcher than man. Fancies yourself an expert on the rooks, I reckon. Rooks and rabbits.      A man's got to have a hobby, Margery. No future in it, of course, about rabbits or birds. Just the same as the likes of you watching the children from Harrow. Gave you a proper life, you did. Doesn't sound unkind, but I do miss a bit of energy about the place.      Aye, me too. I used to have such nice times. Barely a minute you knew when one child would stick their finger in a socket. You'd think they were born trying to find trouble.      Some of them were, you remember Jack? Could shoot a bow and arrow with the precision of a soldier before he was ten. Not that it did him much good, mind.      You’re not one to talk, your legs still stiff in the morning, I hear.      Well, I never! Just because I stopped work to farm and ended up with overuse complaints.

Rather lovely to be having this last meal together before heading back. I've been watching the local news — they're finally going to open that train station now, more than a year behind schedule, if you ask me. Seems like they had to lay fresh tracks and sort some drainage problems.      Yes, it is! I’ve been keeping an eye on that too. I think it will make getting around a bit easier, especially for those of us in this area relying on public transport. The kids were quite upset that it took so long to open, but nevertheless, it’s a win for the community. I heard the new platform is even electric! Not that I understand much about the technical side, only that it should be better for the environment.      I think it is a marvellous development, but as a teacher, I was sad to hear the delays. It did make it difficult for some of the students when we had those outdoor learning days in the village last term. Though at least the planting part is coming to good use — the new flowerbeds near the station are going to help pollinators.      Oh yes, I remember seeing the pollination gardens they were installing early last year. Small ways to go green… I reckon the council got quite a task on their hands. Though I must say, I’ve been trying to track some of the news on my new app, and it’s quite informative. Very easy to use. Bit of a fiddle at first, but now I’m used to it.      That sounds like a good idea. I haven’t got round to getting one specifically for local news, but I’ve been using a fitness app more recently. Staying fit remains a challenge with such lovely food around — you can see it on my face this week!      Don’t worry, love. A little indulgence is understandable, especially after a celebration. But I do like the idea of tracking fitness — I might actually join you. I could start with a few exercises before bed, just to get the blood flowing.      We could make it a group effort. Let’s walk round the grounds after dinner, keep the conversation going while staying active. We’ve all been too indoor-bound these past few days.      I’d really like that. Fresh air and good company go hand in hand.

Rather annoying the new barista at this coffee place, isn't she? Always mixing up the orders when we're in the middle of discussing whether the latest Premiership game actually counted as a win or a stumble.      Aw, don't worry about her—we were the same when we started uni. I mean, at least the coffee's good, and it's got decent free WiFi for when we lazily log into our seminars. Much better than that place off campus, where the beans taste like cardboard.      True, I'll give her that. Although, I still say we should’ve taken the three of us to that sushi place last week instead of watching the new blockbuster thriller. You know the one that MySpace still recommends because I watched it once in 2010.      Roasted sushi? No thanks. I nearly had an allergic reaction to the ginger sauce. Wait, does Thai even count as proper food if you can't eat it slowly? I'm still replaying that stag weekend to Bristol where the group took the night bus, and everyone— everyone —decided it was a good idea to eat falafel immediately before karaoke.      Ah, classic. I was reading  The Lie  in the hostel ensuite that night. Pretty pretentious for a genre novel, but hey, it won a prize, so fair enough. Have you caught that new Shakespeare documentary on TV? It's got some decent takes on the sonnets. Our tutor said it could change your readings.      Yeah, I did. Didn't really finish it, though. Was too busy gaming with Lee and DJ’ing house music in the background because he reckons it's ‘tactile energy’. Interesting word choice, right? Both our course mates and the rest of the wider family are trying so hard to sound intellectual these days.      Honestly, I miss the days when politics was just about who was eating at 6 a.m. in the student house microwave. Now it's all about restricting migration policies or the EU being this grand bureaucratic overlord. Even the Premier League has political sidespeople coaching shots on goal now—what happened to the good old days where you just supported a team because of a shirt or a goal goonie on your wall?      True, but you can't deny that it's all a bit bloated now. Anyway, we've got to at least take in the new campus conference seminar next week.

Rather skip the new barista café near the station, old habits and all that. How’s work been? I got the email from Karen about the Oxford conference yet?      Oh, that's where we were based when we were at the uni. It frightened me how quickly the place was renovated. Hasn’t it? I meant to reply to Karen but haven't had the energy all week. The marketing campaign is taking up too much time, frankly.      Oh, bless. I know you said you were taking it easy after the London launch, but it can’t be easy being responsible for Pearson’s new branding. Still, at least you're flexible with your hours, right? That’s one benefit of being an executive, I’d imagine.      Honestly, more paper-chasing than anything, if you know what I mean. They’re moving to an entirely new digital platform and they’re waiting for my feedback from the beta launch in Manchester. Hectic, but not bad. How is your project, by the way?      It’s going well—setbacks with the suppliers and the deadline changes, but the team is keeping things moving. I’ve still got grief from my ex for not turning up on our three-year anniversary, by the way. He got way too dramatic about the missed dinner at that Michelin place in Soho.      Oh no! It was that bad? Honestly, if he couldn’t handle a work situation, maybe he wasn’t suitable. Who cares about one meal anyway? I cancelled my own dinner with my brother last week. He’s hotter than the summer sun these days and I feel like apologising for forgetting about him.      I did meet up with Anna last weekend, though. She’s got this new job in health and wellbeing, and she’s starting that fitness blog. I’m helping her out with the organisational side of things. It’s nice to feel useful for once.      That sounds lovely. I’d love something like that—less meetings, more passion projects. You must be envying us Northeners for being resilient after being cold out there all winter.      More patient with the weather, let’s say. I’m learning to be more adaptable! Still, I can go back to my parents’ if it breaks down again.      Finally, let’s talk food. You haven’t said a word about your croissant. You ordered the cinnamon one, right?

I can’t believe we've got a plant growing in the kitchen. A few weeks ago it was just a potted sprout and now it’s nearly as tall as the worktop. I've been watering it a lot, but I don’t know if that's the reason it's growing like mad. That is remarkable, yeah. I told you, plants just thrive on attention. It probably heard you chatting with it every morning when you make your tea too. I’ve heard they grow better when they get a bit of a pep talk. Oh, don't get too full of yourself – I talk to it because it helps me remember to water it, not because the plant listens to you. But yeah, well done you, it looks healthy! So, what’s on the cards for dinner tonight? I’m in the mood for something hearty. I was actually thinking about a nice curry. I’ve got a recipe from my aunt in London, she made it when she was visiting last summer and we both loved it. It’s a bit of a family secret, passed down from Mum over the years, and it's full of spices and veg. You don’t mind one-pot meals, do you? Not at all, I love a good curry, and I'm more than happy to lend a hand with the cooking, least I can do while you're studying into the night. It's not as if you have much time to cook these days with all that PhD work. Aye, it's certainly not an easy ride. It's one thing doing a PhD, but another altogether when it's in urban ecology and you're out at all hours analysing wildflowers in the middle of about nowhere. But while I'm stressing over the next lit review, I'm looking forward to what you and I can cook together. Well, if we're both going to be making time for each other between work and plants, let's make it exceptional. I remember my gran would always add something fresh, like coriander or lime, just before serving – small touches make such a difference. I’ll whip up a tray of naan as well. Perfection! We’ll have our PhD and a curry under our belt. Now, shall we set go for boiling the kettle and mixing up our ingredients?

Rather a wet weekend I've had, I must say. Spent the better part of it pottering about in the greenhouse. Never realized how fussy sweet peas are until I tried to grow them. What about you, David? Not quite as wet in Tredegar?      No, it was miserable up there, I’ll say that for it. I reckon it rained all Saturday morning, but I’ve taken up watching snooker tournaments from my armchair. Oh, and watched a fair bit of that football match between Liverpool and Manchester City. Funny how people talk about the kids of those young stars these days, isn’t it?      Oh, the glitz and glam of being a child of a footballer. I remember my students talk about it all the time. I had one who wrote an essay on the psychology of being a child of a celebrity. Very insightful, actually. Made several valid points about pressure and identity.      That rings true. People’s lives are so exposed these days, even the young. I was reading an article about entry into the armed forces and the police—there's a consistent theme of needing young people with strong moral focus to apply. Do you think university students today are cut out for that kind of mindset? Or are we just reinforcing certain stereotypes?      Good question. I mean, it's not all glamour. One of my former students joined the police and wrote me a letter after six months in the beat. He said it was more about someone being in the right environment than being a hero. I quite liked his take. Funny thing—marking all those essays these days and realising how their views reflect the world more than anything we teach them in class about Aristotle or Herodotus.      Oh, I've seen it too. Another weekend I caught myself marking late and thinking how it's a wonder these students pass. My sister’s got a lad playing for a local snooker club. Brought him around to the house once—he was bloody good at the table, but couldn't spell his way out of a wet paper bag. All that skill but academically, well, not so much.      Some talent is born, you can't argue with that. But I sometimes think we set the bar too low for life if we don’t encourage both. Still, I do enjoy the chit-chat.

Rather annoying the new schedule at work, isn't it, Sarah? I was hoping to spend more time preparing for Rebecca's big day this weekend.      Rebecca's having a party, Mummy? Can I come to that too, like when we went to Auntie Claire's last year? I want to wear my glittery party shoes again!      Of course you can come, darling. It’s your cousin's 10th birthday, so it’ll be quite a big bash. But first we need to get the Christening plans sorted properly, don't we, Lucy?      Yeah, I’ve been meaning to check the date with Jess again. We have to get the guest list updated because some of her new uni friends are flying back over, and I reckon their kids should be invited too.      Oh dear, that’s going to make it a proper occasion then. I wonder if Brian has a spare in his schedule. I know the Cathedral is quite popular, even at short notice.      I’ll give him a call, don’t worry. Lucy, would you mind if we pop round to Jess and Tom’s tonight for a quick catch-up? I want to go through the order of ceremony with them properly.      That’s a good idea. And Lucy, while you're there, maybe you can scope out their kitchen and see if they’ve run out of the emergency chocolate stash. Rebecca’s never in a good mood when it’s low.      Haha, fair enough. Some things never change, do they? Alright, I’ll pop in later. Oh, and Charlotte, there is a bit about the birthday party—Lucy’s head teacher mentioned the school trip is on the same Saturday. Maybe we should ask her if she can rearrange?      Oh, that’s a problem. I didn’t even think about that. Mummy, what do you think? Can you speak to Miss Taylor for me? I’ve got too much waiting on me at the shop to handle that right now.      Is that why Mummy wears that funny hat to work every day? The one with the tassels?      Actually Mummy works in a hat shop, not a supermarket. But yes, the hat is part of the dress code—bit blokey sometimes if I’m honest.      Lucy, why don’t you go out and play with the garden garden for a bit to give us a bit of time over this?

Rather chilly this morning, isn't it? I needed three cups of coffee just to get out of bed. I remember the summer holidays we had in Cornwall last year—oh, how I've been longing for a proper holiday since. Speaking of holidays, have we decided what we're doing yet?      Yeah, it  is  a bit on the cold side for this time of year. Honestly, I’ve been dreaming about New York ever since we talked about it. I've even begun researching flights, pulling up some options. It might be cheaper to go at the start of July rather than August. You'd think the hotels would be even more overpriced by then, but the flights are still okay. Alice and I talked about it yesterday, and she seems excited too.      I want to visit Central Park! And pick cotton candy in the subway! Is that an actual thing?      Well, no, love, but there are plenty of fun places there. When’s the wedding again? I keep thinking we’ll have time to plan the New York trip directly after—after the weather gets better and we’re not too busy with work.      The wedding's early September, and let's be honest, I’ll probably still be working at least part-time. You know how much the shop relies on me. I wouldn’t mind taking time off, but I imagine my boss will want me to cover the weekend shifts.      That’s true. It’s just such a big change in pace for the three of us to be a family of three now. I remember what it was like when it was just the two of us—priorities changed so quickly when Alice came into the picture.      I know what you mean. She’s only five now, and it feels like she’s grown so much since school started. I remember how unprepared I was to be a mum. But she’s a breeze compared to some of the kids I’ve seen at the store. I'm told it was quite the show last weekend—the way you played with the cats!       laughs  Let’s not talk about that. I think I woke up with a stiff neck from the positions I was in trying to stop her from tugging at the tail of one of the rather grumpy tabbies.      But Mittens let me rub him!

: Right, so I've got this load of paperwork from my thesis advisor that I need to work through first thing tomorrow, and I'm trying to get my head around it all before I've got to meet him again for the next revision process.     : Oh, that sounds serious. What’s on it then—another chapter to rewrite?     : Not quite as bad as that. It’s more about ethics approval documents and some data collection forms. Turns out there are a few new boxes you gotta tick now with the updated university guidelines for postgraduate research involving participants.     : Right, I guess even if it’s not like a clinical trial or anything, they still want to make sure everyone’s turkey on board with the ethics. I remember having a right old headache with the institutional review board when I did that psychology module in my first year.     : Yeah, it’s a bit of a faff, but better safe than sorry in the long run, you know? There’s also some bits about participant confidentiality and how the data will be stored and destroyed after the study.     : Do you have that sorted yet? Like, do you plan to store the data electronically, or are you using paper forms?     : Mostly electronic. I’ve already set up a secure shared drive with my supervisor that's password protected and only accessible within the university’s domain. It’s all GDPR compliant or whatever tick box they need at the moment, which should help.     : That's solid. At least you’ve thought it through. I was just chucking mine into whatever folder and hoping for the best. Not the best approach, in hindsight.     : I know, right? I watched someone get their whole thesis rejected last year because they hadn’t gone through the proper data-handling process. Don't wanna be the first to have that nonsense happen to me just because I was in a rush.     : Fair enough. It's probably easier sorting it out now than crying over it later when it's too late. How long you planning to work on it tonight?     : I’ll whack away at it for a couple of hours and then call it quits. Try and get the main stuff goin’ so I can sign off on it tomorrow and pass it back to him in the morning session.     : You're the one to do that.

Rather annoying to wake up in the middle of a good dream. I had one last night about winning the National... got to pick the numbers off a cake like in the old football pool ads.      Oh, don't start filling the house with children again. Just like the last time. Got eeny and went  'it's got to be good luck if it's on a cake!'  and you were buying lotto tickets for the next  fortnight .      Mummy, did you and Daddy win the big money once when you had the black dog? The big one with the floppy ears?      Well, it wasn't real, only in the dream. But that dog, a proper sheepdog, big and fluffy. It followed us everywhere, even into the café in Diss, and no one said a word. Half the people in there probably thought we’d won it.      That’s because you told them you’d won the National and were being generous, remember? Some man at the next table actually offered you £20 for one of the tickets—personally, I was too tired to explain.      Do  we  get a dog? Real one, not the stickers. Mr West from the park said we can have one if we promise to feed it, and not let it eat his slippers. Again.      I want a little one. Not like the big sheepdog, maybe the ones that bark at people and get cross.      Little one, sourpuss with fluff, is it? Or wants to bark at burglars at 3am?      I’m not against the idea. We just need to decide: big dog for looking after a house, or a small one that looks like it should belong on a cushion. Maybe both?      Maybe both. Got to happen before I start dreaming that I’m surrounded by a thousand dogs holding lottery tickets. I had a nightmare yesterday about them all waiting for me to feed them apples and biscuits and then demanding to know what the grand total was.      So if we do get a dog for  real , will it dream like you? That we win goonies on the National?      Well, I like to think it might. But we’ll need to teach it to count your pocket money at least.      Oh good one, really. And after that maybe we can send it to teach maths at the school where I work. Only if it can learn decimals.

I can't believe I've got a sprained ankle and now I've gotta go to the A&E in this weather. It's cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey, an' I dunno if it's worth the queue. Aye, I wouldn't say it was sunshine and roses down at the A&E last week either. 'Course I reckon it depends on how bad it is. You should be able to get some painkillers and a plaster there, but if it's just a sprain, maybe you could manage with the boot at home for a while. It's not just a sprain! I fell over on me ankle when the pavement gave way, and I've got that 'un on me leg as well. Oi, it's not funny, Rob. I know, I know, love. But if you're in that much pain, better safe than sorry. I'll give you a lift, alright? The car's warmed up, and I don't fink the lads at the surgery will be able to give you a proper x-ray like you need. Ta, I fink that's as good as any grief. I'm just worried 'bout the waiting—it always takes forrr ever in them places. You ever been stuck for three hours waitin' for a plaster, only to find out it was just a scratch an' you could've done it at home? Fankfully not, but I 'eard that happens an' more. Just 'ave to consider the seriousness of it. I dunno if you're at a stage now where you want being told it's nothing serious after your ballet. I just want to walk properly again! I can't be staggin' about looking like a cripple and not knowin' if it's more worrying. I understand. My sister had that 'appened once after her high-heeled affair. She pushed it too far and it took a few months before it was fully healed. Listen, I can wait with you while you're in there and then drive you 'ome afterwards. What do you fink? That'd be brilliant, thanks love. I'll come with you once I get me coat on. Moooooving day it is! This painkillers don't help much anyway. Just making me sleepy. I dunno how the rest of the lads do it. It's like I lost me welly and one boot.

Rather annoying this new trade policy they're pushing, isn't it? I was just reading about it in  The Guardian  and it seems like it's going to make things far more complicated for small businesses.      Aye, I read something about it yesterday too. If you ask me, it's all a bit over the top. It was bad enough with Brexit, but now they're making it a nightmare for folks like me. I’ve got a few suppliers in France; I don’t know how I’m gonna keep sourcing my materials without paying the earth.      That's a real worry, George. I had a former student—his family owns a little café near Oxford and they’ve had to lay off staff since the cost of living went up so much. It makes you wonder how much longer small businesses can hold on.      You’re not wrong, Tom. My wife says I should get out of the trade agreement business and go for a drive in the countryside more, you know, take it easy, enjoy the age. But I still enjoy running the place, even though I do tell her I might hand it over to the grandson in two or three years. He’s got a brain for numbers and a heart for customer service—it would suit him.      You’re very lucky to have good family support. I, on the other hand, have my son, and he's quite busy with his tech startup. He was down to see me last week and we had a great chat about someone who might be interested in mentoring him. He was a bit nervous at first, but now he’s talking about expanding.      That’s brilliant! I remember when he was starting out, he dropped by with his university friends once. Refreshing to see the different take on things. And it’s rare these days—you know, people still taking the time to support a youngster with dreams.      True. There’s not nearly as much community spirit as there used to be. Speaking of which, any plans for the reunion this August?      I was going to ask you that. I know Aunt Margaret’s mentioned it a few lunches back. She’s keen to do it at the old pub, you remember, where we had our first jobs after university. She reckons it'll bring back some memories.

I can't decide what I'm going to eat. The menu here is promising, but it's a bit hard to choose, isn't it? You got the chicken and leeks already, didn't you? Yeah, honestly, I went for the chicken because I thought you might fancy it too. I'm glad I liked it. The menu was tempting enough to make me forget about all self-restraint. Did you watch  Happy Valley  before this episode? Oh yes, I caught up with it a while ago. The writing is so tight, isn't it? That new character came out of nowhere but makes a real impact. I can't believe how gripping the whole series still is. On that note, what do you think of the décor here? It’s a bit of a throwback, I think, with these old tiled walls and lights. It is definitely a bit old-school, doesn’t it? But I quite like it. Harks back to university days, sitting in places like this, debating politics, or music tastes—those were the days. Oh, you and your tunes. Remember when you insisted I try that jazz-fusion band and I nearly fell off my chair laughing? Good times… although I still prefer something rhythmical, like folk music. How's the coat holding up, by the way? Oh, you mean my new one? It did pick up a bit of a smell from the bus, but that passes, and the coffee smell someone nearby had was worse. At least the cat hair wasn’t too bad. Ugh, don’t remind me. I still have to repel the idea of your colleague’s cat when it visits about once a week. I don’t quite know how the office survived it. Honestly, I thought you were going to adopt that cat yourself. Ha! Maybe in another life. But I do like the way he guest-stars in our lives now. A bit more interesting than the usual administrative shenanigans, I have to say. I think your administrative skills are unfairly downplayed. You've saved me more than once with your nuanced understanding of filing systems—my world would be a mess without you. Pfft! Maybe, but even I have my boundaries. If I see one more broken highlighter, I might just chuck the whole lot into a bin. Fair enough. Now, back to food. Let’s get the fish and chips, shall we?

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? Hard to get a decent snap when it's continually dreich. Mind you, I've been out with the camera more since I picked it up again.      Aye, we do love the view when things dry up, but the rain’s not altogether eeny-minded. Raindrops on the lens make for good texture if yer careful. Got me thinking on a recent trip I had to the North York Moors. Ded, but absolutely worth seeing.      North York Moors? That sounds like me chase when I was younger. Tore around with the camera more like. Lakelands? No, forget the name, but there was hills and blue like you wouldn’t believe.      The Lake District? Probably, aye. You'd get some great shots up in the hills there. I took a course while there and managed better pictures when I stopped trying to capture the whole landscape and focused on little details — a stone path, leaves in motion, you know?      That’s sound advice. I tend to just point and hope, I reckon. Got one decent short — a shot of the trains in Berwick-oh-Tweed. One of those country ones, screeching past then fading into silence.      Aye, there’s beauty in the mundanity sometimes. One time, I was waiting to catch the sunrise at a place called Selkirk, but it ended up pouring. Rather than chuck the day in, I wandered into a local man's garden and he oddly had a collection of floring plants arranged like a scene from some strange play. Made a decent photo — he gave me permission because he reckons I looked like an art type.      You're daft — what's your failsafe when the weather's barely up to it?      My go-tos are the treacherous spots — like the hills near Jedburgh or maybe a scenic spot by a ruin nearby. If the clouds lift for a second, you can get some heavenly light through the gaps. I've also picked up a bit trying with a drone. It's whistles the breeze if the wind picks up too much, mind.      Oh, go on then — show me if you've got a real gem in yer memory line.      Alright, I will — picture the wind-swept plains at dusk near Melrose, the light gilding against the sheep and the hills in the distance. I couldn’t talk about that without over-romanticising, but it's up there near the top of the best shots I've ever taken — kind of makes you forget the cold, I reckon.

Rather annoying the new layout in the living room, isn't it love? That coffee table squinting like it got the hiccups from the dining room. But I suppose it gives the place a bit of variety, don’t you think?      It's a bit much, to be honest. That paint job on the nursery wall is very 'interpretive dreams,' if you know what I mean. I’ve only just started organizing the shelves and this colour is giving me quite a migraine. It's not like it’s pastel or sommat soothing for a baby’s room, no.      Oh, I like it! It’s so vibrant and modern. You know, only another few months and you’ll look back on all this mess with a big laugh. It’s just the prep, is all.      I know, I know. It's just, with the nursery gig and teaching breakfast, bedtime feels more like therapy time. Honestly, I’m running on about six minutes of sleep a night, you'd think I was still a university student.      I do tell you all the time, listen—nap when you can, even a squiz is better than nothing. You’ll thank me in hysterics later. Speaking of work, what about the staff? Are they at least trying to make your life a bit easier, or just making things up as they go along?      Honestly, half of them seem to think the word 'system' is a curse word. I found one of the supply teachers trying to count the number of children we had by shouting out numbers like it was some kind of code-breaking mission. Anyway, at least the kids are alright, they make it worthwhile about half the time.      Oh come now, I remember when they used to walk all over you. But that school! I mean it is a proper hive of action. My, you've made it through your first trimester like a champ. The rest will come easier, I'm told. What about us this week? Still gardening on Saturday or will I be reading the Saturday paper as usual?      No, the lunches on a stick are over! Saturday morning we plant some herbs, you remember, the ones with the odd names the bloke at the market insisted on? And if you don’t mind, I fancied watching some of that baking show you like. The one where they jump through flaming hoops to make cake.

Rather annoying I had to cancel last minute innit, me event’s gone a bit pear-shaped ‘n Yorkshire... got to sort it out before it’s too late. I’ve been on the blower non-stop since I got up. Chuffed they allowed me to rearrange the venue though—it’s gonna be so eench if it all goes off without a hitch.       Proper jealous of you job you’ve got there, but I know how stressful it must be. Oh, and congratz on pulling it off. We’ve been stuck with the same digs for weeks though, don’t forget. You’re still not off the hook for helping me re-purpose this tattered top to look like it’s had some kind of posh event on. You’ve already made me rich with ideas this week!      Aye, and I’m stuck slinging bricks all week in the swelter. ‘Course, breakfast, no doubt about that. Mate’s house alright for a crash though. I pity the poor sod that’s got to move out. Still, the food smells like something that could actually hold it together, luv, what’s for dinner? I’m bloody famished.      Recipe from my gran’s best friend—it’s basically lemon and herb chicken, but humblebragging-style. Mate’s been helping me out, and I’ve just about got the skills. More importantly though, tell us more about this whole new place you’re working at, Smitts, huh? Our Smitts. That’s a suspiciously posh title for someone whose brother’s a doorman—job’s got to have a sinister secret.      Look, it’s not that posh, I just do what they want. Turns out the boss likes Mexican takeout for midweek lunch. Basic stuff. Going to be easier to get a week off if I up my game to do something proper ‘cos I’m playing for Manchester United in the company tournament. Banging at me to sort it out quick.      Proper impressive you’ve taken it on. We could really do with some of that player attitude at our conferences. Do lunches ever count as work? ‘cos I took the kettle back from the kitchen, and now I’m like a man with a mission goin’ on. If I could just meet up properly with the lad I like in the team, I might be in with a shout.      So romantic.

Rather a dreary day outside, isn't it? Seems like the perfect one for a nice cup of tea and a natter, don't you think?      Oh, I’d agree with you there, dear. A nice cuppa and a biscuit is just the thing to make the day a bit brighter. I’ve got some scones in the tin if anyone's feeling peckish.      Splendid idea! I always say, there's no such thing as bad weather—just the wrong cup of tea. I like mine with a splash of milk and a bit of sugar... like three spoonfuls, mind.      Three? That seems rather excessive to me. I'm a one-sugar-and-no-milk kind of person. Ten to one the English would say I’m too picky!      Hah, now that’s a notion! We’re all somewhat old-fashioned up this way. Milk after the tea, and a bit of sugar is a must, mind you. I say two lumps, no more.      My, we are all rather consistent, aren't we? Back in the old days, you couldn’t live without having a cup of tea at three. My parents used to say, “If you’re not at the table with a cup of tea, you’re not really living!”      Now there's a line worth remembering! You know what I find interesting? Folks in the North tend to take their tea with one teaspoon of milk—unless it's a rush, then it's preferably black with a bit of fury.      Oh, I’ve never thought about regional differences, but it makes sense about the North. I remember the kids I taught talking about different cups depending on the time of day. Lunchtime cup, half-time cup... I tell you, the English are quite attached to their tea!      To say the least! There's a bit more ceremony to it than meets the eye. Do you know, I always strain mine through a saucer first? Not to be fussy, just to get out the leaves.      A bit of tradition, if you ask me. Still, I think it’s lovely how it brings us together. There's really no better way to start or end a conversation than with a bracing cup of tea, don’t you think?      Pass me a cup when you're ready, and perhaps a biscuit while we're at it! I think we could go on for hours on the subject, and over tea, why not?

Rather annoying to be honest, having to do a CRB check for the college. Felt like it was ages before I got the result. You’d think more people would know how these things work by now!      I know the feeling. When I started at the call-centre in Newport, they dragged out mine for weeks. Kept asking for more evidence. My mum had to send a photocopy of my birth certificate. Fair dos, I suppose, to be safe.      Oh, and you had to do one for what?      Just a regular customer service job. Didn’t make it sound so intense, did it? I found it rather tedious, but like Anita said, fair enough. Still, enough to put someone off.      You're lucky, I used to think it was just for teaching or working with kids, but now it’s incorporated into all sorts of jobs. Like when I did some contract work at a hotel in London, they required one, even though I was just a lecturer.      I know, you get sent links and told to upload documents left, right, and centre. I had to tell them twice that my passport had been stolen—it wasn't exactly helpful.      How much red tape they must cut through! Though I suppose it's par for the course these days. Now don't get me started on phone calls to the DVLA about a driving test. That’s its own world of chaos.      Oh, I had to rebook because I got caught in a massive protest near my uni. It was being held in central London, but it backup traffic all the way to about Barnet.      That sounds typical. I had to drive out past one last month—you know the one with the art installation on the pavement near Trafalgar Square, they tried to rebrand it as “public expression” or something.      Provincial folks probably don’t get the art bit.      Honestly, while you're at it, just propose doing away with pubs trying to charge for a pint of beer and free chips if you're not wearing a shirt. I once had to wear a man’s t-shirt go to a pub in Norwich if I wanted a drink. Not much else I could do, really.      Well, I’ve had some issues with hotels too. Booked one online via this travel site, and when I got there, someone else was supposedly already checked in.

I can't believe you've been away for a whole week and I've only just seen you! How was Yorkshire? Oh, it was so good. My nan's house is right by a little village, and it honestly couldn’t have been more peaceful. I spent half the time walking in the hills and the other half pretending I’m a farmer with my little cousin. Oh my god, I love that. I wish I had a nan who gave me space to go wild in the countryside. My sister’s kids were driving me crazy when I called in, but still, at least you had good vibes. Definitely. Now, I need to know—what have I missed? Did the turkey still fall off the pan? And have you remembered to water the plants this time? Eww, no the turkey’s fine, actually, but the plants are definitely waiting for you to murder them. I mean, I did water them once… sort of. I looked at them, said hi, and that was it. You’re hopeless. Come on—personally, I’d be happy to let the plants die as long as you remember to actually  cook  something tonight. I’m starving, and I’m not about to eat left-over sandwiches for the third night in a row. Hay, I’ve had a rough week. Three staff members resigned within a week, and I’m left with a room full of confused teenagers in a group project. It’s madness. Oh, sounds like a nightmare. Some people just don’t have a clue what real work is until they see someone actually  managing  people. Not that I’m bitter about finally fulfilling all my duties from 8:30 to 6 every day. I know! I mean, it does sound glam in theory. My sister’s always like, "Oh, you're just putting spreadsheets together and making minor decisions." As if holding any event as civilised as it is accurate is easy. It is not. I swear to god, if one more person lunches on a Grindr date I’ve had enough. Speaking of, you remember Jack? The one who got go-karted for his birthday and tried to propose at the end of the line in front of 30 people he barely knew? Exactly that one. Well, I finally broke it off with him after two months of him pretending I had friends.

Rather annoying that the new planning application for the old manor house was rejected, really. They'd been talking about selling it for years, and it would've sorted out that awkward path by the primary school.      Not to mention finally giving the village some decent facilities—like a proper community hall or a café. Still, I suppose the committee was worried about overdevelopment.      Yes, but surely building a place like that wouldn’t erase the character of the village? I mean, it’s not as if they were going to put up a skyscraper. Although, come to think of it, I heard someone suggesting a luxury hotel. That is a bit much.      Honestly, I’m not sure whether the hotel idea was even serious. Maybe someone on the application committee was just trying to stir things up, push for a bit more resistance? But then again, it’s a nice old house. I don’t want to see it divided into apartments or taken apart piece by piece, you know?      Absolutely. It was in the papers over the summer that the Waterhouses were considering selling—personally, I hope they keep it in the family.      It’s funny how such things go. The Waterhouses have been in this village for generations. You’d think selling the manor would be the end of an era.      Let’s not forget, life has other things going on for them too. Last we heard, Mr. Waterhouse’s cancer was starting to respond to treatment—after such a tough year, it’s a relief to hear he’s made some progress.      Oh yes, I was so relieved when he rang me last week and told about the scans showing improvement. He’s such a good bloke, always had a soft spot for the village kids. Sarah brought round some of the treats he used to give out in school. My kids went for the story about the guest speaker who passed out lollipops at open day. I remember that event too well—had to catch someone before they tried to eat a spoon while the lollipop was stuck in their mouth.      Classic Julian Waterhouse. At least the cancer news is going in the right direction, after so much bad luck.      For what it’s worth, I spoke to Dr. Patterson at the surgery today. He said that between the chemo, the new diet plan, and some supportive therapies like hydrotherapy, there’s a really good chance he’s out of the woods.

Rather annoying this newfit here eh? D’ya notice how everything sticks to her like glue?      Aye, it is. D’ya think she's annoyed the uni canteen staff as well with all her comments about the fanny of the sandwiches. Honestly, I’ve seen een better in my nan’s place.      Naw, not as bad as the guy in sector A2. Constantly complaining that this ain't top-notch accommodation. I’ve seen some dumpier places. Know me cousin was stuck in Salford for a while and said it was right grimy.      Oh, I heard about him. I had to help him with some of that paperwork since his room key was lost. Funniest thing is, he keeps demanding to be relocated as if them rooms pick and choose who they take in.      Tired o’ breakfasts too. Constantly this same Anglo Indian curry for eggs. Me da’s right blether when we used to go to those fella in the chippy, real hot fish and chips with a bit of vinegar, that’s what I call food!      Aye, real greasy spoon stuff there. Me folks always fancied a little West Indian from time to time. Back home we had a bisto pot, and now it's all this mundane fare. I reckon the kitchen staff are just mortal and have limits.      And the toilets! Honestly, what someone at Spilsby thought when they designed them, I have no idea. I swear one’s hotter than the other. It's like some strange test of heat tolerance.      You try getting about with that kettle. It's so bleeping heavy. I keep dropping it and it makes this clunking sound that echoes like some big explosion. The lad up the corridor dropped it and panicked like he’d just caused a nuclear incident.      Signals too. No one can get any bloody signal in the showers. Me da’s always waiting on me to come out to tell him what time the game is. Next time I've 'ad a couple of whiskeys I’m gonna play it out for him via the shower. Piss on the system!      If I could just change one thing at this place, it’d be the study hours. I know it might baffle some what your actual study hours mean at 10 pm to midnight, but I think I'm meant to be bouncing with intellectual energy at that hour?

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You think when you get a few people in the same place, like a café, you'd at least be able to get your cake! Mind, I think the queue's probably doing the rounds with the carvery over there.      Aye, it's all the holidays bringing people in. It was peaceful enough here before the spring break – now they've a grand piano on the seafront and touts hawking seaside rock under a bunting arch. Antwerp it ain't!      Didn’t it get worse with all those caravanners from Dorset last summer? Not that I complain much, mind. I had only two appointments on the south coast last week, and I managed to get my niece’s birthday present from a little vintage shop right by the lagoon. Made me think of the little place in Herne Bay by the old railway station.      Oh God, Herne Bay in January – the sales, the oversized teddies, the puffin chocolates! I still remember buying my mum that sweater with the herring print and being convinced it was the height of fashion!      You and your fashion, love. At my age, I reckon the height of it is when the queue stops moving. Ha – but it's nice to see people still enjoying it all. Got some good laughs with old Tom last night, he was talking about trying to pick up a language with the help of a retired nurse in Bristol.      Language learning? Now, that's one I can do without. Though I’d be lying if I said I didn’t miss having a bit more education when I spoke to my students in about five different accents every day.      Oh come on, Nana, you could make a cabby learn to rhoyme if it helped! Maybe I’ll do something like that for the uni group. We’re all going to celebrate after our last thesis submission. You know, a proper ‘get together’ with puppys, cake and everything!      Puppies again? Is there anything you lot do that ain't outrageously expensive these days?      It’s something for them, dear! The kids need companionship. But I suppose it's more of a romantic element than practical.      Romantically complicated with的好处, blokes who don’t know what a washing machine is, and dogs that bark all night? Yeah, I'm onto it!      I'll stick to my dolls and overcooked sprouts any day of the week.

I just learned about the equality vote in Cork. That’s in Ireland, right? Our teacher said it passed like... last year or something. But why is that so important? I mean, sure, equality is good and all, but how does one vote change things that much? Oh, sweetheart, Ireland’s a place where people used to think very differently about marriage and relationships. The vote was about allowing same-sex couples to marry under the law. Imagine this — back when I was your age, it would’ve been impossible. Two men or two women wanted to get married? Not legal at all. But after years of campaigning, jokes, even TV shows made fun of it, people started to change their minds. That equality vote changed the law, helped change hearts too. So, you're saying Ireland used to be super behind the rest of the world? I didn’t know that. Wait, why would people even vote on it? Aren’t laws just decided by politicians? It’s the thing with countries, you see. Ireland is a very religious place, full of Catholic traditions. So for a long time, marriage meant man and woman. But people — especially the youth — started to say, “No, love is love,” and others thought, “Well, maybe they’re right.” The national vote showed that people were ready to move forward. And it was a shock to a lot of older folks. Like, “Oh my! You mean we’re just supposed to accept that now?” Whoa. That’s actually kind of cool. Like a big change for the better. But what about other places? Like... in the UK? Are we allowed to do all that? We have civil partnerships, yes. But not full marriage equality in the eyes of the church. Though I suppose things are changing there too. Not as dramatic as Ireland, but slowly. Maybe in your lifetime, you’ll see the UK catch up! So, did people have big arguments about it before the vote? Like, did they shout at each other? Oh, you bet they did. Some of the most eloquent speeches were from mothers of gay teens, embarrased but proud. Some said things like, “If this is how my child is, can I still love them?” And others said, “I raised my son to love girls, but now I suppose I need to loosen up.” Joking aside, yes, it was all very emotional.

Rather annoying this new lathe tool business. I used me dad’s old one for years, ‘til he passed, and it were fine by me. Now they call it all digital an’ fancy, but I can’t see the point. Still, the telly’s on about them things all the time. Got eeny weeny parts, don’t they?      My George used to have a lathe. A real proper one, made in this country back in the ‘60s. He used it to do nice cup-handled things. But when he retired, he gave it all away. Still, I’ve got a microwave! Not made for tools, mind you. I found ol’ Syd in there yesterday—y’know, our hamster. He’s a right escape artist, ain’t he?      I think he turned your microwave into an adventure, Syd’s very resourceful. As for the lathe tools, I’m a bit in the know. I review some of these educational tools, even though I work in curriculum. One of the new models—there’s a Thames and Coss one that’s got apps linked in! You point your phone at it and it tell you what to do.      Apps, eh? Well then, who needs no’ one else?      Right cheery it is, but I’ve had enough of gadgets. All that electricity and beepin’. Still, I ‘ate to cook with the old microwave. Our food just don’t taste the same. I made a lovely beef pie last week, and I put it in for ten minutes—only to find Syd nibblin’ at the pastry when I looked in! He nearly about blocked the fan.      Oh come now, he’s just a harmless little tyke! Though I agree, you don’t get the same depth of taste in that. My grandma had a proper Aga, roasting things all day. Nothing flash, but honest food. Lathe tools? I think it’s very confusing for people who just want to make spoon handles. There’s a learning curve, as they say.      I think it’s all too posh these days. Me dad used a hammer and chisel like a man. No app goin’ on then! Though I s’pose they got to keep up with the times. I suppose Syd’s box might need a bit more zip to stop him escapin’. I might get me grandson to help, he knows a bit about all that electronics.      Oh, that ‘d be good.

Rather unusual this mirror-writing lark, isn't it? I read about it in the paper today. Seems someone got so confused they had to write everything backwards so their cat could read it.      A cat with reading skills? That's a bit of a stretch. But it was a good laugh all the same. I don't think I'd have the patience to write backwards all day. Though I suppose it's not too different from trying to fill in a cryptic crossword after a few glasses of wine.      I remember once when I was teaching, a child came in one day with everything written in reverse. I thought he'd been practicing with a mirror pen, only to find out he had a Myōshin-kyō school eccentric left-handedness. Tenacity, I give him that, but handwriting is one of the few things I fear becoming obsolete in the digital age.      True enough. I mean, with all this talk about technology nowadays, you'd think we'd have moved to telepathic communication by now. But no, we're still glued to our smartphones and reading cat news. Though I have to say, the one about the cat buying a house offeiling ...      ... because the bank thought it was a human? Yes, that was something else. I laughed so hard, I had to cover my face. Though honestly, don't get me started on banks. If I could blame one thing for our debt, it would be their ability to turn simple financial transactions into a game of interpretive dance.      You're not wrong about that. I mean, it's obvious to anyone that house prices in this country make no sense about half the time. Paying half a million for a shoebox is madness. And if you're not paying for it with your own money, you're paying for it with your children's future, so to speak.      And what's that got to do with the state of American politics, one might wonder. I hear they've reached a new level of madness. As if you had to have a constant sideshow to detract from the fact that their healthcare system is barely holding together.      Then again, if you're into the American goings-on, you'd know that plastic bags are still a contentious issue. They started tripling cost to charge for plastic, and suddenly everyone’s in a tizzy.

I just do not know how they can play with those electronic toys for hours and not even look at a book. It's making me lose my patience. I’m more than happy for them to enjoy their time, but where is the balance with reading? But it's so much fun, mummy! I'm building my Ninjago castle with the controller. I got this cool new character last week who can fight super bad guys! Yeah, I’m playing Minecraft with Rob. We built a giant fort and a whole village inside the computer. It's way more exciting than reading a story. I understand it's exciting, but reading is important too. It helps you learn new things and use your imagination. Just imagine if you read a book and then built what you read about in Minecraft, what would that be like? But mummy, in the books there are no cool character moves, no cool toys and no explosions. They are for babies! Yeah, plus we can rewatch the videos and get tips. That's like real learning—about building and strategy, not reading! I can see that your points both have their weight and I do not want to discourage your curiosity and passion for building and strategy. What about we create a reading nook – just for you both—to explore, and maybe pick some books that match your interests, like books about Minecraft and Ninjago? Oh! Reading about our toys? That may be okay. As long as we also get to keep building. Yeah, I'd read a Ninjago adventure if it had real characters and moves in it – like the ones in Lego or the games. That's the spirit! How about we set aside one hour after dinner as reading time and the rest of the evening you can continue building and playing. Deal? Deal! But mummy, if it gets boring, are we allowed to just play with our toys then? If it gets boring, we can always mix it up. We could read one story and then create a Lego or Minecraft space around the story we read. That sounds cool. Like, if we read something amazing, we could make the world we read go in Minecraft on the computer. Exactly. Let's give it a go this week. Alright team? Alright, mummy. But only if you read with us! Yeah, otherwise it will feel like doing homework again.

Rather lovely to have you both over. You know, ever since that little hurly-burly in Llandudno, it's been a while since we all properly caught up. How was your holiday, Clara?      Oh, it was brilliant! The fresh air and those little seaside shops reminded me of holidays as a kid. It was like time just stood still for a bit. We should go somewhere like that more often.      I loved hearing about it, Clara. I couldn’t go this time; final exams hit me like a brick wall when I least expected it. But I did manage to sneak in a mini-break to the Peaks last month. What a way to unwind!      Now, Elise, you must tell us all about that. I know the hustle of university, but it's good you took a bit of time for yourself.      It really was, Mum. The walks along the trails, the pubs in the evenings with a tray of oversized loaded nachos, and the stars at night—just magical. I reckon that’s the kind of holiday you don’t need a plane for.      You know, I’ve been meaning to suggest that as a trip for us three. Maybe later in the summer when the weather behaves itself. We can cycle down from Manchester and stay in a cabin somewhere.      That sounds rather tempting. I'll be honest, I’ve missed the peace and quiet outside our town, and the coffee here just reminds me how cozy it is to have my family close by.      Oh, yes! Mom, your scones and jam tea ritual is something I’d forgotten in the chaos of uni life. It's like hitting a pause button on the world.      And I’ve already got my cap on that manager training course I’m taking. So, while I won’t be able to take off for long breaks, I can at least manage a few days at the end of the summer for something like that.      I rather like the sound of all this talk about plans and time together. With work and studies always whirling, I think it's important we don’t forget our little traditions and set a time for ourselves.      Definitely go for it, Clara. I promise I’ll get my final project out of the way in no time so I can go with you both.      Then it’s settled!

: Alright lads and Lucy, what do you reckon about that new sandwich place in the food court? I had the "Spicy Fusion" one and it was actually legit! It was okay, but I reckon it's overpriced for a sandwich with half a lettuce leaf. Miss Drew, like, doesn't have it in her to actually teach anything. Like, she just stands in the corner and stares at the wall."     : "I know, I'm telling you—she's like Mr. Gregg’s evil twin. She doesn't even know the difference between a metaphor and a simile half the time. I swear, if she wasn't our form tutor, we'd probably get no English at all."     : "Exactly! You'd think she gets a discount on tuition because of how useless she is. Oh! And remember that time at our 8th form coffee morning someone smuggled in a fizzy drink and it went everywhere? Rather annoying I know, innit? You know what, I've been trying to get us booked up for a proper weekend away, and I’ve got this brilliant idea about going to Transylvania. It might seem mad, but I reckon we’d knock the socks off those backpackers with our mad drinking skills. Got eeny plans for the summer yet?      Ay, that's actually not a bad idea. I've always fancied a bit of a spooky castle vibe. Oh, and you’d better not be expecting me to wear nothing but a sunnies and flip-flops like the last time you tried to drag me abroad! Still, if we're talkin' Transylvania, I’d suggest we make it like a My turkey, my sunset kinda vibe. Fun innit?      Oh my gosh, Transylvania? I love a good little adventure! But I was about to say something similar. I've heard that laser eye surgery happened for someone last week in London and they went from five by five to, you know, normal. Should I start saving up, or is it just one of those, like, is it worth it things?      Crikey! Transylvania? Hells yeah, sounds bloody awesome! You reckon we'd have time in between all the castle exploring to stop for a good flat white? I, like, take my coffee pretty seriously. And, yeah, don't know much about the whole eye surgery deal. Last I heard, it's a case of 'sort of depends, aren’t you?'      Oh yeah, we can definitely manage some good coffee spots. I've heard the café scene in Transylvania is like,  chef's kiss . And look, about the surgery... maybe once the trip's planned, we can take a quick pit stop in Birmingham for your check-up, shall we?      Cheers, luv! Jokes, jokes! I was just curious. But seriously, are we all on board? Transylvania as a summer trip? I think it sounds wicked.      I'm in! Just make sure you don't book any of us into some dodgy 'romantic' B&B again. Remember last year with the haunted dolls and everything?      Haha, classic gothic vibes on your own if you don’t mind! But personally, I just want quality gelato and a castle with a moat. And what's all this you two were talking about before? Something about other friends?      Oh right! Lucy was saying she’s doing some studies or something over in Greece.

Right, so the photoshoot is on Saturday at 10. I've just double-checked with the photographer—she's happy with the location. I’m thinking of doing it in the garden, where we had Alice in Wonderland day with the kids last year. Remember how frightened Thomas got with the mossy log and the aerial hoop rigged up as the caterpillar?      I’m  still  afraid of that log. It looked like something out of a horror film.      Oh, come on, you were fine once you hit the muddy obstacle course chase with Alice and the Cheshire Cat. You even managed to avoid falling in the mud that one time, which was a miracle.      It was  horrible ! I slipped and got so muddy. Thomas said I looked like I had been dragged through a swamp backwards in a wheelbarrow. But I  loved  it! Wait, does the photoshoot include me in some mud this time?      Only if you want, love. It’s mostly about capturing the memories over the last year—your dance class, the party we had in the living room blasting that chaotic mix of your dad’s old rock and the Spice Girls. I might even pull out the mini aerial hoop we’ve been keeping from the “big day” for some fun shots with the kids, like old times.      Can we dance in the photos again like we did for the party? I still don’t understand why you put the aerial hoop someone at the party jumped on. I thought it was a prop, not a literal hoop to jump through!      It worked out being an actual hoop—I mean, your ballet instructor nearly fell off in about five seconds. That was the gold moment of the night. We were laughing so much we couldn’t even take photos because we were too busy gasping for air.      My dance teacher said she was still recovering from her pride. I think she meant her pride, not the fall—well, mainly the fall.      Anyway, back on track. We need to figure out what everyone’s doing beforehand. Thomas, do you want a little snack while we’re waiting? We’ve got that bag of chocolate-coated biscuits from the muddy obstacle course day— go on, I’ll share if you promise not to fight over them.      I will  not  fight, but I reserve the right to steal them. I have a  history  of fighting and stealing in the name of justice, thank you very much.

Rather annoying the new testing system they've got at the school. My lass, she's real bright—what with the exams, she's been working her fingers to the bone. I've told ‘er a thousand times, “Mum’s proud, but take things steady.”      Aye, dear, I’ve seen the stress it puts on the children. My Liza, she’s a year younger, but I swear she's got every exam marked on a wall calendar. It's quite a circus, if you ask me.      Indeed, but the education system isn’t getting any kinder. Still, it’s not all bad, is it? When I first started teaching in Birmingham, the kids had to be dragged to school! Now they take GCSEs, A-levels, Dfe, Qualifications—on it goes! But then, I was lucky, got to study for a postgrad while teachin’.      Ugh, I  hate  exams, Grandad. I got a shout from Mumsy for not taking them seriously, but you lot always say I’m clever anyway. I’m not even a student council member or anything.      Yeah, plus we’ve got extra stuff like driving lessons coming up. I’ve already started preparing for theory test, but I think it's easier if you’ve seen a real car before!      Driving! Bless ‘em, at our age, we never drove out of necessity. I barely remember the steering wheel from when I tried once at the Royal Automobile Club—piece of toast is a better driver than I am. Still, at least y’all don’t have to make your own roulade like we did.      Oh Charlie, let’s not go into that! I still remember the school feast when I nearly set the hall on fire trying to do a ‘proper’ baked Alaska. To this day, I think the headmistress feared I might try again.      I tried once too, bless. Ended up with a runny middle and a sprite of steam out the oven. Kids were laughing for the whole of next term. Some lesson, no doubt!      Honestly, the best bit is goin’ on parents’ evening and trying not to cry. I made my mum leave after I got into a sulk with Geography—said I might ‘ruin my future at 13!’.      Yeah, but I think we all agree PE is more thrilling. Last term, we had this epic play fight with the Year 7s, and all I got for it was detention.

I can't believe the weather’s better today. That’s a relief. I was just in the garden picking the last of the berries, and it’s actually quite a good harvest! Mind you, I’d have a proper rest after all that, wouldn’t you? Yeah, it was pretty awful yesterd—wait, I’m still sore from Chinese chess last night. I’ve never been good at that. A lot worse than I.imshow in this morning, honestly. To be fair, you haven’t been beaten like I was. Didn’t even see the mate coming. You know what my dad is like. Winston Churchill once said something about learning from the past, and clearly, I wasn’t doing that. Ha! Don’t take it to heart, love. I play Darcy too, and I think he turned out a piece with one hand while the other was mid-sip of tea. Honestly, I only knew the basics, thanks to my Nan. She used to tell me the story of the emperors and that—something about sacrificing a piece to win the war. Well, your Nan was on to something. Chinese chess is more about strategy. You can’t just rush in like in Western chess. You’ve got to plan three moves ahead at least. You know, while you two were deep in thought, I was thinking about breakfast. I made a lovely batch of mexi—no, sorry, someone said beans. But also, I had to check the dentists for the kids. That’s a proper chore, isn’t it? Beans at breakfast? That’s a culture clash right there. I remember university—beans on toast, the English lit major watching Jane Austen and cooking what looked like fails. I’m not cruel. No one mentioned that. My sister’s over from Scotland, by the way. She’s been giving me the lowdown on the whole independence shizzle. Do you know how intense that is? We had to talk about it at work as well. One of the customers was shouting about the whole English vs. Scottish hierarchy nonsense. Honestly, you think after the 20th century, with Churchill and go—well, never mind. Churchill was alright, yeah. I’m trying to teach English in Korea now, actually. South Korea, I mean. It’s a big difference to Northamptonshire’s garden culture. You poor soul. Do they talk about contraception there over tea?

Rather annoying the new testing regime they've introduced for the students. I've had to adjust my course plan once again, and I'm not even officially employed at a school anymore! How do you think your students are holding up with all this new bureaucracy?      Honestly, they’re managing, but it’s beginning to grind on me too. It feels like we’re more concerned with paperwork than actually making a difference in the students’ lives. I wish more focus was put on teaching methods instead of records and assessments.      Tell me about it. Speaking of which, how's the new school you started teaching at? I heard it's just outside Manchester. That’s quite the commute, don’t you think?      It is, especially on the days when the trains are delayed, which is far too often. But the place is lovely, the students are enthusiastic, and it’s a nice alternative to teaching breakfast clubs in universities. I've been thinking of moving for a while now. I even considered getting a place abroad, maybe in Spain or Portugal.      It's a big move, but maybe it's what you need. I remember moving from Cambridge a while back and living in Turkey for a couple of years. It taught me a lot, and it was a great time to reset. How does your experience with teaching abroad sound, and what made you decide on Spain or Portugal?      Mainly the weather and the cultural immersion opportunity. I heard that the pay is better in some countries too, which is also a big draw. Working in Spain, for instance, I could also save up a bit more than in the UK and still enjoy a high quality of life.      I did enjoy the save-ups a bit! Although the English here [in Poland] is progressing a lot thanks to the EU requirements. Not that I've got any issues with student loans in my day, but I've seen the way things are for young teachers now. Parents are expected to contribute to the education budget alongside any grants, it's very intense.      I agree, the pressures are immense. I have to say, I've been lucky but not many friends of mine are in such a spot. My parents set us up with a nice head start in the pension fund as well, which I think is going to help a lot.

So, I heard you got into Oxford for Human Sciences, that’s massive mate. How’s that feeling like?      Yea, honestly still pinching myself, like, is this real? I applied mostly because I love the idea of mixing subjects—like biology, psychology, even anthropology. I'm kind of fed up with the idea of just doing one pure science.      That’s wild, I get that. I’m still trying to decide whether to go into Maths or maybe something more stats and business based. I don’t want to chase money, but I also don’t want to end up stuck in some lab forever.      Yea, I’ve been in that limbo too. But with Human Sciences, I think I can do more research, maybe even policy or sustainability later on. Have you given any thought to where you want to apply?      I’ve been short-listing Cambridge and UCL for Maths, but my brother keeps saying I should try Imperial, even though I’m not a huge fan of the culture there—too corporate for me, maybe.      I get that. Cambridge is beautiful and academic-wise, it's top-tier, but if you don’t vibe with the rhythm of it all, you’ll be miserable. Mate, have you two considered coming up to Oxford for a weekend? We could grab some flat whites and actually discuss your essays.      That’s not a bad idea. Our barista at Spuybroek in Slough is already a walking dictionary for oddly sour shots. Some hotter beans’d do me good. What about you? Any plans for drinks this week?      I’m actually seeing Anna later. We’re having those buttery croissants from Schulke’s and some lagers. Don’t know why I’m even trying to sound sophisticated—I just want something that  stays  buttery after the alcohol.      Yea, it's a balancing act, man. I still haven’t nailed my cocktail game. My nan taught me how to cook but only to burn out陉      No worries, I’ve got your back. My grandad taught me how to shoot and how to make a proper stew. Doesn't map well to Thai food or social engineering, but it's a start.      Speaking of, any plans for rugby this term? The older lads are organising a 10s league after Christmas.      Oh man, I need it. Uni is overrated if you can't at least half-broach the conversations and then chase them at the pub.

Rather annoying this new tax isn't it love? I remember back in the 60s when tax rates were far higher and yet we managed. Times change, and I suppose governments do too, but this feels like it's all falling on the middle man like us.      Dad, I know it’s tough on everyone, especially with the cost of living where we are in Birmingham. But have you thought about how these taxes are actually used? Some of it does go toward healthcare services and education funding, which as a language teacher, I rely on occasionally for professional development.      Aye, I suppose you're right. Though I still can't fathom why the government deems another percentage from our hard-earned cash a necessity. I did my duty for thirty years, and now I’m watching the value of my savings dissipate.      It's tricky, isn't it? The government doesn't just wake up and decide to take more; it's part of a broader strategy to redistribute wealth and invest in the future. Have you looked into any of the new investment allowances for over-65s? There might be some things I can help with.      To tell the truth love, I’ve read a bit about it, but it’s all a bit too complex. Back in my day, you just filled in a form and paid what was owed. Now it's an absolute maze of codes and numbers. You know what I blame? These bloody computers. It’s all changed too much since my time.      I get that, but it's also an opportunity for transparency, at least in theory. If you're comfortable, maybe I can show you how it works? Not only about the tax policy but also the benefits you might be missing out on as an accountant and a senior citizen.      That sounds a bit ambitious, but I'm up for the challenge, so long as you promise not to speak in riddles about GDP growth and budget deficits. You know how I get when you start quoting economic journals.      I won't. We'll take it one step at a time. Perhaps start with your current tax rate and what we can do to reduce it. Even a small change might give you a bit more room to breathe.      That would be splendid, thank you. I always knew education was the key, and it seems it's never too late to learn your way around the system.

So, I just got an email this morning from the client. They’re saying our timeline is unrealistic and they’d like to renegotiate the deadlines. Honestly, I find it so frustrating when they think they can just rewrite the contract based on a spreadsheet they read somewhere.     Deer, that happens all the time, I understand the frustration. Having done this for thirty years now, I’ve learned a thing or two about how to handle unreasonable requests from people. Have you spoken to your project lead about pulling someone in as a mediator or was that the plan when you called the meeting today?     I was going to talk to him, but I wanted to ask your opinion first. You know, like that one time when you had that problem with the senior students not taking exams seriously, and you sat them down individually and showed them the consequences? I’m just trying to find a way to approach this better than I would have a year ago.     That’s a good point. With people, especially professionals who think they have leverage, it’s important to show that you’re not only here, but that you’re consistent and fair. I remember when your mother did that job at the food bank, and someone tried to demand something unreasonable. She just smiled and said, “If you want to speak to me about changing procedures, I’d be happy to hear you out, but the process is set in place to protect everyone here.” You know what? That man walked out and never came back.     That’s brilliant! That calm, authoritative tone just dissolves so much of what you’re up against. It makes you wonder why more people don’t respond like that. I’ve seen so many people flinch at confrontation or back down entirely.     Yes, and it’s easy to forget that you don’t have to be loud to be unshakable. I think, personally, the bravest things are often said quietly. So, maybe just have that meeting as planned, and if they give you the runaround, smile, take your notes, and stick to the facts as presented.     Thanks, that gives me more courage than I’ve had all week. I’ll set the meeting for 3 P.M., and I’ll make sure to bring my notes and be as patient as I can. I swear, some of these people think they're in the box office or something when what they're really dealing with is just planning.

Rather than chuck the old bottles out wi’ the bin, I’ve taken to recyclin’ ‘em. You know, a chance to climb higher.      Oh, that sounds exciting! If you got that, I’ll come up for a grand break with lunches and a couple o’ bottles. Well, if you’re goin’ in t’ interviews armed with what your mam used to call “a bit o’ charm,” and a couple o’ nibbles, I’d say you stand a better chance than most. I ‘d never applied fer anythin’ wi’ that much flair since my days in biomedical work, but I was never really much for suitin’ up and casting runes on CVs.

It’d be great for me to see how someone else structures a presentation—there’s always that new person to learn from.     : I’ll see if I can get you on my invite list.

Rather annoying this, having to pull over every so often for directions. I thought internet would solve that by now... What was the name of the road again?      It was Jasionka Road, I think. Fair enough. Honestly, I’m just delighted we’re here. It’s been years since I’ve had the chance to travel like this. Being out of the house has done wonders for my head.
