That must be tough, not having anything much to fix on. I always feared that sort of emptiness. Travel helps, of course, but there are days when I question myself too. How do you stay positive?      Well, I’m a Grinch with a mismatched wardrobe compared to someone like you, but I find joy in the small things. Like cruising in this campervan, talking nonsense about books, or just trying not to dent the van on every rocky corner we go through.      Haha, fair point. I can't help but think though, we’d make a heck of a team for a life survival show on TV.

Rather than the new moonlight kayaking weekend I was thinking of, maybe we should opt for a road trip up to Connemara? I've also been reading about immortality theories, and it's quite a mind-bender. If we land a week to ourselves, we could actually start by visiting some geratology research centers. If we're already stepping out of our comfort zone, then by all means visit the Gerontology Research Centre in Limerick. It's one of the top facilities out there. That's right, and it's mind-blowing what you stumble upon when you look at icons and their age progression. There's so much to learn from them. I know of academicians who are big on Viking legacies and the related history of Ireland's west. While you're delivering the amazing minds and theories of the past, I go for details on the future improvements in our own aging process. Let's also line up accommodations for the weekend. I can send you an itinerary draft by your preferred virtual channel.

Rather annoying the new baby’s chair’s not fit yet, innit? Me an’ nan ‘ad to cram in the seats at Costa with mugs o’ tea an’ a £7 scone between us. A lot o’ folk in this place seem to forget where they keep vouchers. I’ve boxes of them under the sink. And I were thinking, mebbe when we get the new chair up, we could pop down to the Lakelands and grab a few plants to brighten the summerhouse? It’s well dark in there, bless.      Aye, well, the summerhouse needs a bit o’ oomph. I’m up to me ears in customers at work — better days when I could sit an’ watch the daffodils in season. Blooming planting’s not really me, mind — chickens are the only patch o’ green I can handle.      You know, I’ve been thinking about that referendum — what if we end up buying grief? And ‘money’ at that — we’ve all got different ways of using it. I’m glad you’re thinking ahead, sweetheart.      Aye, and thinking ahead, I’d say it’s time we considered a new coffee machine. Ours leaks more about our finances than actual coffee. I’m the only one blinking watching it fizzle and sputter like some corroded water feature.      I could run out to the market, see if they’ve got some nice sunglasses — and maybe a sundress while I’m there. I do love something fresh when it’s warm.      Argh, I just lost 10p on the coins out the window trying to catch the wind — it whistles in here! Was going to drop it in a charity bucket.      Don’t go wasting binoculars on coins, lass. Just give it a rest an’ let it go. We’ve got more bloomin’ expenses what your 10p could have been.      We should get a cheap fruit tree from the garden centre this weekend. Just talk about it ‘neath a cherry when we’re all older and sipping homemade marmalade!

Rather annoying this new sat nav eh gran?      Aye, it’s mair confusing than the cow paths back home. I’m more used to askin’ folk where t’go.      No, I mean, it's supposed to help, but if it een tell yer when t'exit is, it’s   useless  .      Maybe that’s because yer rushin’ past every exit, Stella. You're driving like yer in a race to the farm!      Didn’t ask fer yer opinion, Daniel. It’s not like I’ve even seen a proper tractor since I left school. Y’all guid with machines and cows and whatnot, ye’d know!      Tenr, Daniel – I’ve seen them new push-button cows in the sheds now. Back in Timperley, we’d have been breakfast, no doubt if they’d been switchin’ off in the early hours.      Grandad’s always had a soft spot for overactive livestock. I mean, do tell, have cows started taking shifts now or are they still chewing the leaves as usual?      Tell me yer not serious. Cows, workin’ shifts like us? I’m takin' it back – I’m not goin’ to Hayle Farm. Let’s sommat arson proof and   not   animal based.      Laugh, y’know what I mean though. It’s a bit grim trying to explain a GPS to a herd of preferably docile bovines. Just   imagine   the headlines: “AI Attempted but Bovine Prime Minister Refused Appointment”.      Haha! Y’know I had a cow named Ada once. Sat in her doorway every morning and gave me a   look  , like she knew the bin day ‘fore I did.      So you were technologically outdone by a cow – any ‘at all.      You cheeky lass. She didn’t   outdo me  , she just always knew the lunches to keep and whin I was goin’ t’get lost in a field again.      That goin’ on for life if you ask me. Just don’t expect her to tickle you when you dream anymore – she might have retired from the tickling gig.      Daniel, ya givin’ my gran cow retirement benefits   again  ? She’s had it in for ya over this steer’s cow-boys!      Oh Arry, leave her be. She may be y’unusual one but, 'appen, she’s got taste in cattle and technology alike.      Yeah, well, long as we reach the farm   before   the cows arrive for tea, I’ll be a happy consultant engineer.      Woulda been e'en betther if this damn sat nav dinnae cut off.

Rather lovely to have you all under one roof again, especially with everything the world's been through. The first thing I say is, let’s not be like ducks and go our separate ways once we've eaten! There is far too much to catch up on and far too few opportunities.      I agree, Mary. I’ve been keeping busy with some transcribing and editing work on the side. Though I must admit, it’s not nearly as fulfilling as I'd hoped. Oh, and I was reading about someone local who started a choir in the village school. Didn’t you, Jerry, say you used to sing in choirs back in your day?      That’s right, Jo. I was in a choir before I moved to Walsall. The singing, the camaraderie, the discipline—it was a special sort of bubble in the world of oil and technical jargon. Though I suppose it’s a strange contrast from where I am now. Not a single thing to do anymore, thanks to this “retirement” nonsense.      Good for you for starting something new, Jo. Might I suggest we start a midweek singing group if we land a few more singers from around the hamlet? Nothing warms the bowels like a decent trot rhythm in Beethoven.      I’ll vouch for that, and I know the village school misses a good community project. It might be good for the kids too. Speaking of which, Liam at the school mentioned they’re in dire need of music resources. If we start a choir, a small fund for instruments wouldn’t go amiss.      Now you two be careful. That’s where I drew the line in my past life about planning—always anticipate a need you can’t control. Start with one or two songs a week, and maybe cap it at ten people. I don’t fancy a chorus of thirty to start with.      Good thinking, Jerry. And while we're at it, Jo, I do recall something you mentioned about trying to grow vegetables in your garden. I happen to have an old compost heap and a few tomato cuttings if you fancied a hobby a little more nutritious than the chocolate I’ve been eating far too much of.      Oh, I’d go for it! But let’s make arrangements for a midweek workout as well. I’ve been trying to keep up with box jumps and squats, but Mary, you could at least bring in the chair!

Rather annoying this new tax on rented houses, isn’t it? I’d have thought it would be easier on families with small kids, but no luck there.      It does seem a bit unfair, doesn’t it? I know the rent’s gone up for our house again, and we’re barely scraping by as it is with the one child to look after.      Maaaaaaam, can I have some custard cream bites again, please?      Not right now, Oisin, you’ve had them just after lunch, but we’ll see what else we can find for dessert tonight!      Now Oisin, don’t go on like that. My, look at the way you’re talkin’, like you’re well into your teens already! D’you pick that up in school?      Yeah, Mummy! She doesn’t no nothin’ about me!      Oi, no need for that, you wee puffin. Just a bit of over-enthusiasm for sweets, that’s all.      I’m with your mother on that. Sweets only once a day, no more. Speaking of, how are we on birthday plans for the big day next week – have we got any ideas yet?      Well, the curtain shop staff don’t seem to be interested in helping with the budget, and Liam’s working in the garages, so someone has to be treasurer again.      That’s oddly literal. You mean Liam’s the kid working in the garages and being their unofficial treasurer – I’m not sure it’s a great idea about mixing birthday funds with garage money!      Aww, they’re just wee kids! Let them be creative with it. I remember when I was runnin’ the school, they always made the most exciting guest speaker outta spare parts.      I was thinking something simple, like the park, cake, maybe a little performance from Oisin.      Naaaah! No! Do a rugby match and biggg cake!      That’s a wee idea with a bit o’structure to it. We could get the kids from Liam’s garage to help set it up, and maybe even do a mini match with the other blokes on the team.      A big cake and a rugby match, now that sounds like fun, though I’m not sure I’ve got the legs for a match this time of year, ha!      Oh I love that, Colm. Just make sure Oisin promises not to copy your style of talking from the field, alright?      Mummy! Yeah, Grandma copies me, not me her!

Rather than chuck afit of the vapours, I were doin’ this internet game ‘ere where they showed us the word ‘quarantine’ spelled backwards and I were like, blimey, that's near genius. Not quite up there with bemusing as a word, mind you.      That’s a bit more droll than 'quarantine' spelled backwards, isn’t it? I’ve been playing too — just got side-tracked by a word search involving ‘pandemic’. Found it nestled in 'pan-de-mic' like a rogue word, but the bloke next to me went full Quincey, tried to spell it with a 'k'. Still, can't fault the creativity.      I did an experiment last week, tried to throw together some real bonkers words. Knew ‘floccinaucinihilipilification’ by heart and ‘antidisestablishmentarianism’ — proper mastering of alphabetical soup for me. Me old mam would’ve looked at me like, are ye mad or so?      It’s wicked fun, innit? We used t’do it at the pub — quite a laugh to see what grief the other blokes could come up with. One time, we got into a right row over whether ‘supercalifragilisticexpialidocious’ was real or not. Some said it were just a daft line from a Silly Stones film or summat.      Honestly, I've been in discussions where people argue over the legitimacy of a word just to justify it's not what you were looking for. It's like real life being played out with vocab — right tussle there, eh?      I reckon you could do it for a living, mind games and stuff. Maybe not as fun as bein’ a proper bloke, but near enough. I do be daydreamin’ about being some guest speaker at a grammar conference. Can just imagine me on the stage, holding forth on all things lexical.      You’d need a stick to knock sense into some of these blokes out there. They've 'split infinitives' whippin' their arses over there for ages, and they'd sooner shout than spell 'incorrectly go'. But I digress, you lot fancy another go at it? I just started a new game based on obscure Latin roots.      Aye, what could be more riveting than obscure Latin? Must be tighter than those Oxford tutorials I had to sit through to get me postgrad, ‘precius quam’ or whatever them academics like to mutter about.      Only if we're gonna do it, I suggest we take it outside. Sat in the flat for too long, want a bit of fresh air and a scribbled word on my wrist.

Blimey, I've just had the best nap ever, do you believe it? Felt like I was lying in the sun on one of them park benches down by the canal. Aw, I wish I had the time to have a decent nap! I've been stuck in the library writing eeny weeny essays for uni. It's ridiculous. I reckon I'd finish all them quicker if I just took a little break. That's what you keep telling yourself! But who's gonna do it if you don't? You always say that when it's the night before the deadline... Right, let's talk about something more cheerful. I've been listening to this new album by Lewis Capaldi that Myra told me about. It's wild. The man can belt! D'you know what I think? I reckon he's gonna be the next big thing. He's got that James Arthur vibe 'bout him. Reminds me of when we used to go to concerts in Manchester, remember them days? Yeah, those were the days! Remember when we dressed up like mad and snuck into that one indie gig dressed as elves and fairies? Hilarious. Blooming hell, I remember that! Looked so bonkers – Mateo nearly got us kicked out trying to take photos. Oh God don't get me started on Mateo. Still sends me these photos every now and again and dares me to not laugh. But anyway, you trying to sort a gig of your own yet or are you still just busking near the uni quad? Aye, still busking there, most nights about five. I've a mate who's the lead guitarist of this band called The Warrington Whigs. Going to be playing at some open mic up near the town hall in a couple of weeks. Oh well if that doesn't cut it, at least you know it's a hobby you can fall back on. Guess I'll just have to keep doing what I'm good at and that's being academically fantastic! Haha! That's if the university work's not trying to kill us with deadlines. I swear, the more go's on my pond life, the more boring it gets. Right back atcha. But in all seriousness, we're near your mum’s bar. I reckon if I behaved nicely and had a couple of poxy hours off, maybe even she might appreciate it more than the studies or the music!

Rather annoying that the council planning meeting is tomorrow. I haven't had the chance to go through the application thoroughly yet. You've checked it, haven't you, love?      Yes, I've gone through it quite a bit, but we should definitely go over it together. I don’t want to mess this up, especially since it’s the first big sale we're facilitating as self-employed consultants. The last thing we need is a small mistake derailing the whole thing.      You're right. It's important that the structure of the application meets all the council's criteria. Did you look at the proposed layout plans? I’m still not entirely sure the footprint of the new extension is in line with the local bylaws.      Oh, I did, and I think it's within the permitted range. The architect has specified a 3m setback from the boundary, which is more than enough for residential developments here in London. I’ve seen similar cases pass, so I’m fairly confident, but maybe we should double-check the maximum floor area ratio too.      That’s a good point. I’ll take a look at the zoning guidelines again. I also need to confirm the design impact on local residents. They asked for mitigation strategies, like noise dampening during construction – have we addressed that fairly?      We’ve included the noise barriers around the perimeter and have scheduled the work for weekdays between 9 and 5. That should keep disturbance to a minimum. Oh, and remember the buffer planting they wanted? We’ve specified hedges on the eastern and southern sides specifically.      Perfect. That demonstrates good consideration for the community. I think we’re covered on most key points. What about the financial section? We were allowed to present a contingency plan for any delays.      Yes, the £10k contingency is listed under planning risks. If construction is delayed due to weather or council hold-ups, we'll still be within budget. I think it shows due diligence.      Honestly, I think we’re in a strong position. It’s always a bit of a nerve-racking process, but I do love working on these things together. You bring such a calm and precise approach to it.      And you're great at picking up the small details I sometimes overlook. That's why it's a team effort, innit? Now, let’s have a final look-through before heading to bed.

Rather annoying the new Spotify Wrapped app, isn't it? I've been trying for hours and it just keeps crashing. Honestly, what's with the mobile apps these days? They need an update every time you blink.      No, I mean—get in, they added a feature where it gives you a timeline of the songs you've been listening to over the year. I actually found it pretty insightful. I hadn’t realized how much I've been going back to 90s records lately.      Oh, I got mine sorted last night when I was prepping a piece on music nostalgia. It's funny, isn't it? I've been speaking to a few artists for BBC and they're all commenting on how listeners are rediscovering tracks from their debut years. Probably due to the influencer culture on TikTok and the like.      That’s a really interesting point. I've noticed that when I do interviews now, a lot of people mention being reintroduced to old songs through younger audiences sharing them. It's a kind of time machine for everyone—especially for Gen-Z, who are sampling music from decades they weren't even born into.      Haha, as someone from Leeds, I reckon the Pendulum rhythm mix was all the rage in my school – but it's wild to see people still referencing it on TikTok today. Though, honestly, don’t get me started on phone apps. I was trying to write a radio piece on climate change in the North last week and my phone dropped me from my interview because the app crashed oddly. It was so floring!      It’s not surprising, really. I speak to a lot of students in about mobile tech developments and a frustrating number of them struggle just to keep up with the changes in apps. Not even mentioning how that data then affects their studies if it’s part of online learning. My kids had issues accessing their lesson links constantly.      I have no problem admitting it—this is bloody stressful. Recently, I tried to update my waiting list app for a car to buy as we’re planning to upgrade out of the Mini next spring. The new version of the app asked if I wanted to monetise my parking space around my house via a new service called ParkShare. I didn’t even know that was a thing! But it made me rethink how much I really need a bigger car, blooming honest.

Rather do share a drink and bring us all up to speed. I confess I’d forgotten how long it has been since the big move down from the North.      It was over fifty years ago now, wasn’t it? I remember arriving in town after my interview. It was a bit of a fiasco—got the time change wrong for the bus and ended up missing it all because of a blithering transcription from my watch!      Missed it, you say? I think it must have been luck was with us for finding the house when we did. Still under the previous owner’s ownership, of course, but he was a civilised gentleman and allowed us to paint the walls and lay that carpet you still see under your floorboards!      I had the same situation, Vivian [assuming the name is implied by ANON's rules for storytelling]. Cats would have been breakfast, no doubt if I had happened upon someone a bit less accommodating.      That’s putting it gently. I was a bit overwhelmed, yes. The solicitor was a jolly fellow, though, and managed to assist me in getting land a week before term began. It took two days of trips from shop to shop for basic furnishings.      And then marrying – that’s a tale fairly long, isn’t it? You met yours while delivering a speech on methodology for new teachers, didn’t you?      Absolutely. She was the principal at that time. Very sharp and suspicious of my French accent, but once she came around, life was made.      I’d be lying if I said mine wasn’t in a lecture hall at a dental conference. I was fulfilling the requirements for the postgraduate course at Athens University. Rather a wild time—that very day was the first day of the dictatorship! The univalley in Athens was just a hub for lectures and treacherous anecdotes after that tragedy.      You would have told any bloody tale at the time, wouldn’t you, Tom? I could see the security forces as tight as a safety pin at every space!      At least the educational path forged our way into housing and marriage. Then again, Tom! The notion of time goings really affected your life if you were there.      Oh, I remember it well. The course started the very minute the government changed. The time at the university was charged with suspicion and champagne, in equal measure.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun gracing the windows just right—the sort that makes you want to drag out dusty old paintings and let them bask for a bit. I've been humming about a little painting of mine that's tucked in the attic. It's picked up quite the patina over the years, like most things do if you give ‘em time and peace.      Oh aye, I love a bit of sunlight in this old house, especially with that wooden furniture casting patterns on the floor. You mentioned before you were an artist. Didn’t you also dabble with some antiques?      Indeed I did. I sold paintings and the odd antique now and again, though now that the turkey shop's closed, I mostly just left it all be. Retired to Taunton, and it's been quite the slow patch for me—painting for relaxation, really. The gallery doesn’t run itself these days!      I imagine it was quite different from your childhood, though, wasn’t it? I mean, growing up in Somerset, I’d say it was very rural for you?      You're quite right. We moved to Taunton as I grew older, but I was born right in the heart of Somerset. That countryside is something else – open fields, sheep fairly dancing, and not a whisper of a noise. My mother used to say I did all my painting at home because I could never find enough colour in the fields!      Oh, my—what a shame! I grew up in Sydney oddly enough. That’s in Australia, you know. So quite the opposite of Somerset. Can you imagine birdsong in the streets and the distant chatter of the city? I adored living there, the sun, the sea vibes. I suppose you could say I was charmed by it all.      I bet. My, I've never been to Australia, though I passed through a friend once and he told me the sky is a different blue there! But talking of Australia, you mentioned your job was a language therapist—how did you end up being one out there?      Oh it was a fairly straightforward path really. I studied linguistics, something I’ve always had a nose for. Then go out to work with kids, mostly. If I was at home now, just chuckling away, I might be the tiniest bit proud about that.      I can see it.

I can't believe it's already December! You know what that means—  Christmas   is just around the corner! What are our plans this year? I know, right? Time flies! I was just thinking about how we need to start baking the   candy   canes and cookies. Got a new recipe I  really  want to try this year. Something with cinnamon and white chocolate. Aww, that sounds  delicious ! I’m going to have to pick some up for the   café  . I also need to start thinking about how I’m going to decorate the place. It's a bit daunting, but I love a good festive vibe. Yeah, like that one turkey leg tattoo I saw you got last winter. It looks ridiculous on you, but I still love it! Always thought you'd be the   tattoo   type. Ha! Thanks—still doesn't hurt though. Honestly, I only did it because I was dared by a customer, and I’m kind of stuck with it now. But it  is  one of my favorite body art pieces, in all honesty! You know, I've been considering one too. Nothing too big, something subtle. Maybe a snowflake or something. I mean, I’ve already got three   small employers   under me, so I  need  something that calms me before the madness starts. Speaking of business—how’s your   business   going lately? I heard people are raving about your new vegan pastries. Pretty amazing for a   café   in the middle of a cold and harsh winter. It  has  been good! Kind of about time I invested in a bigger   oven   though. Might take on an apprentice during the holidays. Another person would make life easier. And if we ever want to do something, like   buying   stuff for the   dinner   party, just say the word. I'm a professional at all things edible, I swear! I could use an apprentice too—don't know what I'd do without you with lunches and all the writing I have to do. Anyway, back to   Christmas  —should we head to the   market   this Saturday for decorations? I’d love that. Let's meet at the café at 10. Who knows, maybe we’ll pick up some   food   stuff for the big night too! I'm in! And maybe grab some new   candy   for the kids. Sounds like a plan. I’ll bring the list—this is going to be our best   Christmas   yet!

Rather annoying driving back from Cambridge, isn't it? But I suppose it's just the reality when you live in London and go to university in the sticks.      It does take a bit of time, but it's nice to have a chat as well. How are you finding it in Cambridge?      It's brilliant, really. The history, the architecture… it's a bit old-school but I'm getting used to it. I’m halfway through my thesis, though, and let me tell you, writing it has been like dragging teeth.      You always did like to take your time with things—especially when it involved heavy reading. Still, you’ve got a good mind for it, and I know you’ll get it done.      I hope so. But I was thinking about the future after this—maybe looking for a job eventually? Not sure if I want to teach or just freelance.      Well, you’ve always been quite the creative type, so anything in that direction might suit you. I know you’ve been keeping in touch with some of your tutors up at Cambridge—they might land you a decent position. And of course, Oxford still remembers you went there for your undergrad.      Yeah, I remember the days of dragging my books along between lectures, barely getting any sleep. I miss it sometimes—but don’t get me started on their tea times!      [laughs] Honestly, I always said you were too young to start trying to live like an old professor.      Also, about my future—have you and Dad talked about the house in London again? I've been thinking about moving back there after I finish my studies.      We have a little. We're not sure yet what we want to do with it long-term, but if you wanted to move back in, we’d be happy to let you rent it. It’s not a huge property, but it's quite peaceful.      You mean I could come back to actual proper London life after being academically-traumatized by Cambridge? That sounds perfect!      You always were a city person. Just don’t forget your folks still go there to visit occasionally, if you start filling it with other people and posters and books, I might not even recognize the place!      Fair enough. I won’t get too wild. Just enough to live out my intellectual eccentricity.

Rather exciting to be here at Cambridge Law Faculty for Alumni Day 2, isn’t it? I’ve been doing some work on multilingual legal frameworks recently—always interesting to observe how legal systems adapt where languages meet.      Yes indeed, I've spoken at several alumni events in my time. As a university lecturer, I often find the greatest value in these gatherings is the cross-generational exchange—they remind you that knowledge is never static.      Absolutely. And it gives you a chance to share field experiences! I'm just coming off an archaeological dig in southern Lincolnshire.      Oh, truly? I spent years excavating a Roman village in the Shropshire hills. It was like peeling back time, layer by layer. You left any Roman treasures back there, I hope?      Ha! If only. But we uncovered an Anglo-Saxon village beneath the Roman structures. Felt a bit like detective work. Reminded me of reading about the social stratification in settlements we discussed in your lectures many years ago, Professor.      Ah yes, tell me—what fascinations are capturing the next generation of young archaeologists? The ancient world is only as vibrant as those who study it.      I’d say it’s more than archaeology – it’s language, too. I was actually researching the linguistic shifts in regions that once were crossroads of civilisations. Take Silchester, for example, the Roman town that later became a bilingual hub.      That’s very much my focus too. Trying to map how dialects evolve alongside architectural and social changes. It’s as much a historical puzzle as it is cultural.      I did some survey work in a small Shropshire village last summer, just adjacent to an old crossroads. The local dialect there is still peppered with Norman-French influences, but there’s something quite charming about the way the words hang on.      A remarkable continuity. You know, I was giving a lecture once in Cairo about the linguistic diffusion in Araby al-Adhriyat and how rural dialects outlived their urban counterparts. The students were astonished to learn how such isolated regions preserve archaic expressions.      That's fascinating! I go every few years to see if anything's changed in the village I excavated. It’s interesting that rural communities often act as linguistic Time Capsules, especially when they’re insulated from broader influences.      Absolutely. I'm also curious about how global travel influences this. I had a stint in China over the summer, working at a language institute.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what they do. Just one of them viral videos that comes up in the news feed and you're like, "Oh my God, I've seen this a thousand times."      No, I mean—some people take things the wrong way. Got eeny weeny passive-aggressive messages today from some mate saying he watched it and wanted "a bit more context," like I owe him or summat! I mean, what are you even referencin' if it’s just some daft TikTok dance?      Oh, I know what you mean. My gran even mentioned it when I picked her up from the hairdresser. She said something like " My loony granddaughter dances like that now!" left me blushing like a beetroot.      Honestly, I think it's just a symptom of how fragmented storytelling is becoming. The internet doesn't want a narrative; it just wants a moment. Which is kind of bizarre, considering it's one of the most powerful tools for communication in the history of the world.      Haha, fair enough. Though I guess it’s also quite a contrast to how things were when we were at uni. Remember, Marcus—what with your audiovisual presentation about dyslexia in film directors? Mate, you got a standing ovation, it was bonkers.      It was moving as heck. Silly if you think about it, but that whole idea—this is just someone who found an alternative way to see the world, and it counts for something. I dunno, something about that resonates in the way young people look at jobs and success today.      I do wonder if there is a type of “indie” professional class emerging now. I mean, you've got folks starting their own small businesses or trying to do untraditional things in their fields. Like Lucy over here—own café at her age? That takes guts.      Yeah, I was thinking about it the other day. It’s not unlike the sort of freelance filmmaking I do. I mean, academically, we've all got a couple of degrees—myself, Marcus, maybe even you, Lucy—so it seems like we started with the same go-to plan, right? Job-for-life, regular hours, respect.      And now we’ve all kind of flipped the script. Maybe it’s the system—it just doesn't fit all of us the same way it used to.      True to that. For me, every day is different.

Rather annoying, the new tax policy. You think they ever do anything to help lecturers, do you? I got the email from the uni about the new VAT rules on course materials today.      Honestly? Not a chance. Look at us—working our socks off and getting nibbled at on all sides. I mean, even the National Insurance changes feel like a slap in the face.      I know! I had this student crying in my office last week because she couldn't afford to do a PhD. She's got debts from her undergrad already, but the bursaries are getting frozen. It's absurd!      That's harsh, love. You know I like to think of university as changing people's lives, not dragging them deeper into debt. And now the government's focused on privatizing everything in sight.      They’ve got to prioritise breakfast, haven’t they? I mean, with the NHS in bits and the social care crisis getting worse every year, who’s looking after the people who actually need help? It's all tax cuts for the rich and handouts to vested interests.      It is. And tell me, what do we get in return? Climate policy that treats it like a joke and “stability” – Mate, stability with austerity doesn’t mean much if you're destitute. I reckon the public are fed up enough for something to change soon.      True, the people out there are definitely beyond angry. But maybe not angry enough? It just feels like nothing changes no matter who's in charge. It's like painting the politicians into a box – same old, same old.      I hear you. At least the telly’s watching this mess. I caught  The Crown  yesterday—it’s wild to see how things have moved on, yet still entirely the same nonsense.      Honestly, I'd switch it off and have me a glass of wine if it was all it was. I tried to read about the new funding models again while you were out. I swear, if I read the word 'sustainability' one more time in the wrong context, I’ll scream.      Try not, love. That goon of a man over there is trying not to eavesdrop as it is.      Who, bloke in the tweed jacket? Shaw. I have known him for 30 years, we had a barrow boy incident in Wymondham once. He still refers to me as Professor when we meet.

Rather lovely to have you all here for lunch, I must say. I've made my old-school shepherd's pie, and I daresay it's better than any I've had in years. A bit of nostalgia is always good with a nice meal, don't you agree?      Thank you, Maud! That smells absolutely divine. I didn't know you were still in the kitchen like this. You should be writing recipes — or at least this one should top every search engine. It deserves it.      Oh, she practically taught generations of children how to analyse poetry, and now you're suggesting she publish a cookbook!  laughs  Still, as someone who’s had only two meals since moving into that new flat, I’m not objecting to the feast one bit. And I do mean feast.      I’ll be the first to say you lot were far harder to please than any breakfast, no matter if I cooked eggs or oatflakes in my early days as a teacher. You lot, you didn’t spare a word of mercy. But now, you practically treat me like a queen.      Because you are! You’re a gem to this family and only deserved better appreciation. Besides, this shepherd’s pie tastes like a time machine. I got instantly transported to Gran’s kitchen back in Derby. I almost expected her to slap my wrist for hovering the dessert spoon around before finishing my meat.      And speaking of time machines, we should be watching that new period drama. I heard it’s got everything — scandal, sumptuous costumes, and an out-of-this-world plot about a science experiment gone wrong. Sounds as wild as the research your colleague wrote about last week.      Yes! I picked the thing up from the publisher this morning. Honestly, some of the projects are so niche you barely need to read the title to know what it’s about, but that one was interestingly vague. All I know is it involved something to do with the digestive systems of wasps. Wild.      Wasps? I hope they weren’t trying to replicate that incident in 1973 with the cricket club and the garden pond. Remember? We almost had to call the fire department.      That was classic. Maud, your life was like a documentary about eccentric British retirees.      Hopefully, they'll remember us for the food first and the chaos second. But at least the wasps' guts aren’t quite as messy as those pies, I’ll say that much!

Rather than playing video games all the time, what d'you get up to for fun these days? We’d be curious to hear what you're up to more than just football and superstardusts, aye?      Hmm, I kind of like strategy games now—Deer Hunter and eeny kind of  Legend of the Lightbringer  on the console. They let me think a bit more. A lot of mates just press buttons and call it a day, but I like figuring out the puzzle parts. What 'bout you, Dad?      Well, I don't know what the difference is, really!  Legend of the Lightbringer  sounds lovely, but do you have to worry about turkey on the map or something? I left all that behind when I was your age, truth be told, but Eimear—our little star—plays with her stuffed bear and giggle-sing, and that seems just as magical. Maybe she's in for a bit of gold dust as she grows, ha!      Huggah Bear save the day! I put Bahador the Big in the tower and say  “shhh”  so he sleepies. GIRL!      You’re creating whole worlds with soft toys, eh? That’s actually kinda smart—strategy begins in the mind, not in the box. Maybe you should record her lines or something, Liam! She's got better ideas for adventures than most people.      Aye, and it's oddly therapeutic. You ever think about walking with him, Cathleen? It’s not as bad as it might sound. You take the stroller about the park, walk a loop, and the little one’s watching everything—birds, other kids, and even leaves fallin’ off trees. It gives you a kind of peace that the office, for example, just can't provide.      Aye, me and the wee one take the afternoon walk most days. I meet some other mums too, which is nice to talk about  actual  things. Websites and game trailers with lunches delivered keep the big one occupied. Not that I mind—it's easier than delivering something around this house.      I bet walking with your own kid is like a mobile game. You’re the active player, making sure the avatar—Liam—doesn’t collapse or run off with a pigeon. I sometimes imagine it's a side-scrolling level against the hours of the day and belly rumbles!      It's a bit of a grind, that's for sure. I go for walks to clear my head, but I kind of miss the old days when it was just me and Cathleen.

Rather a lot of excitement in the air, isn’t there? Blimey, it’s only been a few weeks and I’m already starting to feel like a Christmas pudding! Any plans for the big day then?      Oh, I do hope you’re coming over again this year, Harold. That mince pie of yours is one of the few joys of this time of year. We’re going with the children to my brother’s in Guildford. His wife is making a massive turkey and some sort of fancy au gratin.      Blimey, sounds gloriously over the top! I’ve enough trouble just getting the sprouts to stop going to seed, let alone do some sort of posh turkey like you young folks!      Tenr, I was just speaking to Viv, and she said she’s turned her garden into an art exhibit again this year — lights, strings, installations… Rather theatrical this time. She’s taken in a couple of students for the month to help, you know, for extra credit and the like.      Can we go and see it? Lucy and I have been talking about doing a little installation for the school play.      Me too! I asked our teacher about it, and she said we can use the drama room for a week, and maybe even the hall if we get the budget sorted. It’s about winter and dreams, you know?      What a lovely idea, girls. Now, Harold, weren’t you trying to sort a car servicing before the big trip?      Yes, and let me tell you, it’s no easy task in this part of the country about this time of year! Half the shops are already lit up like Father Christmas lives there — what with the lights and the tinsel!      Maybe I can do something, Harold. I’ve still got a couple of contacts at the garage. And Viv told me the other day she was giving one of the lads a lift to visit his girlfriend in Leicester. Quite smitten, he was.      Do people still say "smitten"? That sounds so old-timey. Still, I suppose it’s better than saying “crushed.”      Horses and car servicing and love! You’re all in separate worlds, Harold. But it’s all part of the same big picture, isn’t it?      You’re not wrong, Elsie. Life does like to throw a few elements together — and somehow, they make the whole thing more interesting.

Rather annoying I had to take the day off work, but Sarah’s birthday was her big one — fifty. I got her a lovely candlestick set, you know the one we saw by the river? Thought it would make a change from the usual kitchen gadgets I buy her!      Aha, well if there’s one thing Sarah doesn’t want handed to her on a silver plate, it’s a clean kitchen. That candlestick would serve more as a decoration, unless we're having tea by the fire every night. Speaking of which, I hope you're not planning a roast today? The smell of meat means I’ll have to cancel my walk to the park.      Ooh, I like that set you got her, Auntie Emma! When’s the last time you bought something from the charity shop on Kemsing Road? A bit of recycling with style is always a hit. Though if we’re talking food, maybe I can bring some homemade soup for lunch — just a bit different from the usual chicken, you know?      That would be smashing, Liv! Sarah can have a nice cup of soup and maybe I can sneak some freshly baked banana bread in as a little welcome back gift. Listen, on another note, how are things at Westgate Gardens lately? I heard they're doing something new with the horticultural section.      More new staff and fewer plants, if you want the truth. I blame the universities! All the students they’re hiring just want experience — which is great for them, a nightmare for us professional gardeners. I tried talking to them the other day, but I think the word ‘pruning’ meant nothing to them.      I’m disappointed to hear that, Uncle Mark. It’s always struck me as a peaceful walk there. I know that university students barely know the difference between a tomato plant and a fern, but they’re enthusiastic. If anything, maybe they can help us with that new social media exhibit the botanical garden is planning.      Ah, right, I’d forgotten about the exhibit. Those young things are full of ideas but always trying to 'brandify' everything with hashtags. I do miss the good old days when a rose was just a rose! Still, I suppose go with the times — unless you want to be left behind.      Well, I don’t know about all that, but what I do know is we could have a few too many conservationists and not enough gardeners.

Rather annoying this, having the power off all day, isn't it? Me radio's been playing up like mad, and I've had no luck getting through to the council! These modern days, you'd think they'd have some backup plan for emergencies, like the good old days.      Oh, don’t you worry, George. It was lovely not having to worry about the heat roaring all night. A bit of fresh air does one the world of good, even if we had to huddle by the blanket to keep warm! Remember the time the children held that party when the pipes froze? Tore the house apart but had a grand jolly.      What I found fascinating was how some folks made that heating turkey on a bit of fire-place! Makes you wonder what people did back in the day without all these gadgets. Now I think modern life is convenient—Don’t get me started on how incompetent some breakfast shows are these days; I mean, Big Brother was in another league!      That's right, Heather. And the other day, I heard on the wireless that one woman managed to get through to a shop just using her mobile! Funnily enough, her dogs were the real heroes—they stood guard like bodyguards watching for the postman. Well, from what she said, at least?      Mobiles, laptops, gadgets—it’s all the same nonsense to me! Back when I was at secondary school, we never had a single one of these distractions. Our biggest worry was getting in for church on time or knowing which ones had mistresses.      Oh, don’t mind him, Harold. He’s just set in his ways. Though, there is something touching about how close people get during a power cut. You know, like this—just chatting over what you normally do at home. Not that I mind staying in, but we did miss that celebration last week terribly for the children.      I did manage to get some shopping done the day before the blackout, as it were. I always keep a few tins ready just in case, good habits and all. Let’s not forget, we've lived through a couple of lean years. Now, the recent work reform for quality and curriculum—it’s made me think the system is improving, at least on paper.      Just don’t expect me to give up reviewing curriculum without a fight—no bloke tells me what to think without a proper argument.

Rather than chuck a DVD in eh, innit? Thought we'd cook summat first, ‘ow? I got us sorted with some chilli, like, proper red chilli, not the watery supermarket variety we had at Kim’s house last year. Remember what a slap it was? Sat there in that eeny weeny passive-aggressive sauce with the beans just floating about.      Oh aye yeah, that stuff was absolute telly! I mean, edible, but don’t get me started. Right, so you said sommat about spaghetti on the side? Or are we doing vegan burrito bowls like we did last time?      Nah, the spag still, but I managed to get the turkey mince in, you know, left it in the back of the fridge from the co-op. But I thought I'd be the little bit merrier with kale instead of rice this time. Cos, um… eco? I mean, not that I’m replying to social media trends, but we talked about it at uni. Also got the hot sauce, directly from— flicking the packet —Guatemala, innit?      Guat-e-ma-la? Blimey, fancy watching where you are. I thought we were just cooking. Not pretending to be National Geographic with a chapati and naan slap in the oven. Anyway, what film did you bring? ‘Interstellar’? ‘Lone Survivor’? Or are we doing the old classic ‘big chickenpox nightmares with my sister’ flick?      Nah, nah, it is a family type thing. It being weekend and all—I thought  About Time . Prime romantic comedy, about how you save your dad's goldfish from the lit window, then f    off cooking lasagne and crying at it. Not that I've ever done that.  laughs  Just thought, you know, warm and treacley. All that tragedy about growing up and stuff.      Oh,  About Time , yeah, I’ve seen it. My nan adores it—watched it every Christmas with a grandkid next to her. Grumbles about the "drownded sentiment," but you know, she’s secretly crying into the turkey stuffing. go on then, chuck it in. I’ll get the chilli ladled up in, like, two shakes. Then, bloke, if it's all too soppy, I’ve made a special list—got roles in it where you_ratings are ranked by belly-laugh to tear slots.      Righty-oh! Sorted. Now—got my cousin coming over at 9, bringing her toddler. They want to watch  Moana , but I drew the line—went and got popcorn and swore it would be family-own.

Rather than share a fabricated conversation, I'd be happy to help you craft one based on characters and topics you’d like to explore! For instance, we can create a natural exchange between an experienced Maths Examiner and a student in a Yorkshire dining room, discussing the Scottish referendum as it relates to their personal perspectives — or whatever else you’d like them to talk about. Would you like to explore specific elements like their stances on independence, family history, or how the referendum might impact education, jobs, or travel? Let me know the direction you'd like to take, and I can build a detailed, authentic conversation with dialogue, conflict, nuance, and even Yorkshire dialect quirks. Just give me a prompt, such as:  “Write a 400-word conversation between a Yorkshire schoolteacher and a student discussing the impact of the Scottish referendum on national identity in the UK.”  And I’ll deliver a tailored response! What would you like to focus on? 😊         What I find most fascinating is how to bring characters and their voices to life. Imagine a room in Malton, with sunlight through a stained-glass window. A mother – no, a close family member, and her son, a sixth-former. They’re sitting by the window, cups of tea steaming between them, and the current political topic on the air is this big Scottish vote. Maybe the young lad is arguing a pro-independence point, or maybe he’s still figuring out what he thinks and wants to be told. Either way, the dynamics in a family when it comes to politics are always interesting. Would you like the mother to take a pro or anti-independence position, or maybe her views are shaped by her education and background as a Maths Examiner? Let me know where to begin, and I will write something that feels human, that reflects real dialect, real concern, and something fresh. What would you like to read? You’re in charge here.      Let’s go ahead with this:   Speaker_1 :   Well love, I’ve just been marking these year ten mock papers and the lot of ‘em still bin gettin’ quadratic equations wrong. Any road, I were readin‘ the paper again this mornin‘, an’ it were one o’ them days I just thought, “Does it really matter if we're still in one country or not?”   Speaker_2 :   Honestly, I dunno, Ma. It feels a bit like we all just got left out of the conversation, y’now?

Rather annoying this Jeremy Kyle luv. You can tell 'e’s tryin’ to ‘ang 'is accent, but it’s still all posh like. Blows me mind what folk think is proper on telly.      Oh I ken what you mean, like ‘Deer lew een?’. Proper passive aggro if you ask me. I reckon his bloomin’ accent irritates a lot o’ folk, but he knaws how to liven up a chatshow. It’s interesting tho’, watchin’ how the different people from all corners 'a the country speak up under pressure.      Still, it’s dead fun t'watch the glares and stuff. On that note, what’s wi’ all the elision though? I mean, most o’ us northerners or midlanders drop owt in a sentence if we can an’ it’s still understood. But when breakfast is referred to as 'brekkie', or 'abbrevi-abbrevi-abbrevi-ate' - it’s near gibberish!      Aye, it’s the way we talk naturally, innit? I never puts t’s in words like 'past' or 'host', sounds bloody odd if I do. But we all ken what we mean. It's like – why do folk often try to make their way o' talkin' seem more posh on TV? It’s like they think we're not all already clever enough as it is, innit?      I remember once me Gran read me a story and thought I had a cold cos’ I’d dropped a few T’s in the middle ‘o words – said I was soundin’ like a bairn! But innit the same story the other way too? I had a teacher once who couldn’t understand a word I was saying until I stopped trying to speak up for 'er. My accent ‘asn’t gone though, not even after A levels.      An’ it shouldn't have to, love. We don't owe them a performance. I don't know why folk think we need to alter how we talk to be taken 'seriously.      Some people, like that guy on Jeremy Kyle earlier with t’Yorkshire accent an’ goin’ on aboot his partners or wotever. Gave me a chuckle when he said ‘gettin' th’vessel out ‘ere’ and the host looked like he lost 3 vowels and a spelling lesson. Proper comedy innit?      Blimey, ‘vessel’! I think he meant ‘weather’ or ‘conditions’ but nooooo, Channel Four decided he’d be the supreme chef hero.      Likewise, I ‘ate when he goes on about people 'scoring points' in a debate - it's just two people chat'in' on telly for goodness sake.

Rather annoying this half-time’s longest than the whole match, innit? Our lot look knackered. I swear the lads at Sunderland train harder than these lot. Not saying I've trained with them or nothin'… but I've seen the film clips!      Haha, y'know, I’ve been watching this one bloke on the pitch—his legs are like noodles. I’ve only just remembered he’s the one from that social media story we saw last week.      Which one was that?      The one with the knitting. He’s part of a football knitting collective—apparently, fans from the north, south, Midlands, and like everyone else, they knit jerseys for each other to cheer themselves up. Ten hours of knitting and five hours of football, he said.      Oh, now that’s bonkers! Wait, does he actually know how to knit?      Blooming hell, yes! He’s got this massive group. They even knit scarves for pyjamas for players who can’t get their own in. Y’know, if they’re stuck in quarantine and all that. Kinda sweet, really.      That is a little something. So is he good at football though?      Far from it! But he gets a lot of support from his team. Seems like his wife’s the one who handles the matches. She’s the manager, someone said.      Aye, that counts for something. I remember talking about something like this at a conference I worked on. The sociology of sports hobbies!      I did something similar for my PhD. Though I focused more on Olympic watching habits—mainly how people consume and make meaning of that data.      No way? That’s clever, ‘cos I was talking to someone at work about baby names based on Olympic themes. Like Lani or Geli. ‘Course, the lassie there said, “No, just stick to Daisy or Millie.”      Aye, we keep it simple whishtle if we can. Though you remember my cousin saying she wants to name the baby Euron. After the Game of Thrones bloke.      I just said, “No, don’t go further bloke, I already can’t bear you joking about him.” The seriously, why anyone'd name a child Euron is beyond me.      Same with that ‘Stormy Daniels’ lot, innit? I tell ya, my missus got so bored of that saga, she started podcasting instead.      Oh, no—went and made it worse she did.      You have no idea. I've started knitting my own jock for the pain.

Rather annoyingly, The Bee Movie is on request again, do you two know it's about real bees and...imaginary ones? And no, I’m not rewatching it by choice      But Mummy, do bees have kings like in King Arthur?      I saw a butterfly once, does it have a crown too?      Well, a butterfly isn't a King but some insects have queens and kings, like bees but not butterflies.      So, was King Arthur like a dragon or a bear or a man with a squirrel hat like the bees in The Bee Movie?      I think he was a bear in my dinosaur My Little Pony book.      Well, King Arthur was a real person who supposedly existed, he was said to be the King of England many, many years ago. He had something called the Round Table where he had lots of knights...but in real life he’s more legend than fact, especially with the magic sword and the grail.      Then do we have a king now? Like老爷国王？      We still have a monarchy, yes. Like we’ve got a king or queen, and it’s called the Royal Family. And they live in palaces with all sorts of ridiculous stuff, like the Royal fruit. They grow fruit on apple trees and they paint it gold for the Queen to eat - don’t say I never gave you any food that looked silly.      So, can we pay to go into the palace and paint the apples?      Er, no – but you can pay to go into most palaces and gardens. They open them up for the public, which is quite an aristocratic concession. Some people think we should be a Republic and have no monarchy.      Can we be kings then?      Well, you can certainly be politicians. You would have to pass entrance exams, study very hard, and then campaign your way into becoming a parliament member first.      But if we take lunches to a restaurant like Granny used to do, can we be royalties too?      Restaurants aren’t the same as royal dinners, but it's still a social event – just much less regal. Imagine being so quiet at a restaurant, like silent films from the Olympics diving matches you see at the stadium.      Like pooping those fruit flies from The Bee Movie?      No, very different. We silence them so the commentators can describe how they soar through the water and how often the people in the water pop up again.

Rather a lot of dust in the back of the car, I do say. Still, it’s been a good clear-out. Never realized how much one keeps, eh? Not a hint of a thing we need, I expect. Not since I’ve seen those boxes of old books.      Aye, and there’s more where that came from, I reckon. Bill and I had the same with his dad’s place in Darlington last Christmas. Proper dust bunnies under the floorboards. But worth it once you can actually  see  the floor again.      Can we not chuck those comics, Gran? They make  Firestar  look square. What’s the point in keeping them?      They were your granddad’s, Jamie. And back in the Sixties, you didn’t go pickin’ and choosin’—we made do with what we had! Still, if you really fancy them, you can have a flick through once in a while. Just not in the kitchen, mind, or the flour will settle on the panels.      Funny, I had a similar experience tidying up my in-laws’ in Kendal. I found a box with my gran’s best china—unmarked, practically new. Turns out she never used most of it. Makes you wonder about all the things people hold on to, doesn’t it?      It’s bonkers. I mean, who leaves a box of saucers in the garage for forty years and never uses them?      That’s the magic of the North, son—there’s a mystery behind every attic and boot. Not all of it’s exciting, mind you. I did find a horsehair sofa once. Fit to burst the holes, it was.      Aye, that was ours! I remember it. Black as soot and combed like a horse. Your great granddad had high standards.      Well, the modern world’s not got time for that. I tried using them horsehair ones in the classroom. The kids thought it was a joke. Even mentioned it in the staff meeting. Grumbles from the caretaker, mind. Says it set his cat off for weeks.      That’s the world I write about, you know—those old stories, the quiet lives. It’s fascinating how a cup of tea and an old picture frame can say more than hours at the planning office.      So, where’s all the stuff going then, Gran?      Some to the auction, some to the charity shop. There’s a few trinkets that might get a second life.

Rather than chuck afit in the bin, I was just doin’ a bit o’ thinkin’... What d’yeh reckon about makin’ a visit to the Maritime Museum up the road this weekend? I heard they’ve got some fresh exhibits in.      Aye, that een? I went there last year with one o’ me uni groups. It's all them old warships an’ paintings o’ the Mersey. Proper interesting, actually. But yeh gotta pick a time when it’s not packed.      Right, right. Let's go first thing... like, ten o'clock! Not only will it be quieter, but I heard the café do a decent scones turkey sandwich. You know I’m partial to a bit o’rarebit if I’m in them parts.      Aye, I’d fancy a scone better than breakfast, to be honest. Now while we’re out an’ aboot, I need to pick up that shopping list I scribbled down—restock the loo rolls, some veg, and, yeah, some of them fancy vegan sweets I like. Thought ye’d like to help me carry the bags?      Course I will. I’m a proper humble man. Though I swear that estate agent got the meter wrong again, because the other day I was ticketed somethin’ awful just for parkin’ on the corner. Near cost me ten quid!      That’s Adjacent! That place is a nightmare. I been told the council’s thinkin’ about weighin’ in real hard on their backs. Still, I heard they are doin’ a few free parking zones in the city centre round the festivals season. We could plan our trip around that.      Speaking o’ festivals, me gran up in Bootle said she found this real tres bon treacle toffee in Liverpool ONE last Christmas. Said it was a bit pricy but was ‘definitely worth it’ for a weddin’ gift. Ever thought about sprucing up the flat a bit for a real grand proposal?      Ah, I took the liberty o’ settin’ up a nice telly feed the proposal idea away goin’ on. If I do say so meself, it were very picturesque in the garden that day. But I’ve got an interview for a Masters in clinical psychology in January. I might be movin’ out o’ Birkenhead after that.      Blimey, ‘at’s serious. I’m proud o’ ye. You’ll go all the way, luv. And where d’yeh want to shift to, then? Manchester? Or maybe somethin’ fancy like London?

So did you watch The Crown last night? That episode was mental. I was just gobsmacked when they showed the Queen's face-off with Harold Wilson.      Yeah, I caught it this morning on my lunch break! Honestly, I had to lie down after. It’s so drama-ey, like a  proper  Netflix soap. But I haven't watched the whole thing yet — too many Instagram stories to scroll through. Do you ever  not  check your phone?      Oh, I check it  all the time ! I literally can’t walk past a coffee shop without like, taking a photo of my latte. I swear someone once told me I was "spying for Starbucks."      Ha! Yeah, I tried to do the London cappuccino vs. the E-Midlands espresso myth-busting thing last weekend — let’s just say, breakfast at my nan’s suddenly has a new status after that.      I love that! You should do a TikTok about it. I reckon your bloke of the moment, Oliver, would follow you after that.      Left to read my grief. We  barely  spoke on New Year’s Eve. He was too busy being best man at his mate’s wedding. All I saw was, like, 999 photos of the speeches and no him.      Oh no! That’s cringe. He’d better reply to this group chat soon before I personally go over there with a bag of mozzarella sticks. I  live  for pizza by the way, and I want it now.      You’re always saying that about pizza. I’m eating it every week from that place near campus, The Spicy Barn. Have you tried their “Blue Cheese and Ham” one?      Not yet, but I’m saving it for my next Friday night tragedy session. Binge-watching  Ginny & Georgia  with microwave chips and intense cheese — you know the drill.       Nods in agreement.  Honestly, I’d do that too if it wasn’t for my dog-phase. My sister just got a golden retriever and I’m the number one away go-to dog sitter. I’ve gone full Roald Dahl parent by slipping him popcorn in the living room.      Aww your life is  so  cute right now! Eventually, he’s going to outgrow those chew toys and start chewing your life to pieces.      That’s not a bad metaphor for 2024 if I ever heard one. Speaking of — have you done your uni readings? I'm definitely not doing them tonight.

Rather annoying this, really. Sorting through all these old things. I’d quite like to keep some mementos, but I’m not sure where to start yet. I found a box today that smells slightly musty, but inside it seemed to contain the strangest things.      Do tell! I find the same, you know. It was like time has stood still in cupboards like these. I came across our old "Bako" building set just yesterday, much to my delight. It brought back such memories. We used to build the most intricate houses and castles, don't you remember?      Oh yes! The Bako set! We'd spend hours at it, wouldn’t we? It was our little world back in Margate. The bursts of creativity back then, the way the pieces clicked into place, and the joy of the little plastic roof tiles assembling for our tiny homes.      And then there was the gardening set... I remember you winning the prize for the most awards we gave out to our imaginary vegetables. Such a showoff, you were—vain and proud, but we loved it. Do you still have that green trowel with the flicked-edge?      Oh, I do! Buried deep in another drawer, I expect. Looking for it would be like a treasure hunt these days. Still, memories of playing in that tiny set of plots, making soil and pretending to weed rows. And oh, the sun—do you recall how many afternoons we played in the garden under that glorious Kentish sun?      How could I not? It was always delicious and warm, even when the sky had a bit of gray in it. I daresay the weather does affect our moods still. We were always most cheerful in sunny spells and more contemplative when it rained. Still is, if we’re being honest.      Poetic, that. All those years, shaping our tiny experiences into grand landscapes. It's funny how those small sets could weave worlds within them. You know, I wonder what my grandkids would make of these things now—mobiles and computers, I expect.      Probably roll their eyes and laugh, but I’d love to see the curiosity come back in them when I show them. It's not about keeping these things, is it? It's about remembering. And the box might stay on the shelf, gently collecting dust. It's part of our past.      Yes, and I think we should do this more often—tidying, but remembering too.

I swear those bloody mosquitoes are out to get us today. Every time we go out for a walk they’re like...  shoo , shoo,  come back ! Honestly, it’s like walking through a feeding frenzy. No, I know what you mean. They’re relentless. I tried eeny-meeny-miny-moe the moment I tried to swat one— missed ! It was like watching a comedy sketch. Why do they always target me? Is it the coffee or the cologne? It's probably the cologne, don't you think? That expensive stuff you wore last week does smell like a mosquito buffet. Honestly, I'm still thinking about that gig you took me to on Friday. Marco Cogliatti’s set was electric! I didn't know you liked his style so much. Yeah, he was brilliant, wasn't he? His encore, though— shocking . I still can't believe he rolled his own synth wires mid-set. Spectacular to say the least. I hope he does another tour soon—vibe like that, maybe we can take Lucy next time. I think she’d appreciate it. Haha, only if there's a baby-friendly version. But seriously, yeah, maybe. She loves Ladybird Mate. Bring her a sneaky drum, and watch her go bananas. Though, her dance moves are questionable at best. Silly little thing. She's a star in the making. Now, speaking of madness, have you read about the rush hour congestion last night? That was chaos. I swear it took me three hours to get through Central London because someone had a ballet competition in the middle of Tower Bridge. Someone clearly cares more about ponies than the commute. Honestly, you could write a manifesto on that madness. I mean, it’s not like we’re not used to it. But I miss the days when you passed through Cambridge with that caffeine-fueled mentality. Those were the days, eh? Oh, bless. I could still do it if I had to. Let’s not forget, I've lived in a city where you can't walk without bumping into someone who's delivering something. London tames you, baby. Or goads you on to be a masochist. True. But let’s enjoy our stroll. Who knows, maybe the mosquitoes will leave us alone—for now. And maybe traffic will clear up soon. We can pretend we're somewhere else—maybe Cornwall, hearing seagulls caw, and not this madhouse we call home.

: Right luv, long day today innit? Got that practice session at Ashford and it was pissing with rain the whole time. Alright luv, I’m going over this job application with you tomorrow, so I’ll go have my dinner and be right back.     : Sounds good to me.

Rather annoying that the kid’s sleeping in his pants again. I swear it was her idea, ‘normal pjs are too restrictive, she said. Like he’s got a thesis to defend or something.      Well, he seems happy enough. You know kids—whatever gets them to sleep is usually good enough.  I’ll say.  Not like   I   sleep in pants— or  a clean shirt, for that matter. Got one too many parents’ evenings under my belt.   Doesn’t mean you can blame me for his pyjama rebellion.        Alright, alright. You’ve had your sarcastic comment. I’ll forget about the time you still called him "he’s got the turkey!" during dinner last Christmas. Fun for everyone, really. Probably.      A classic, and I’ll be the first to say you looking for the cat behind the sofa while breakfast was burning was prime material. Fair’s fair.       Mumbles from bed  Kart, kart, kart.      He’s dreaming of karts, if I had to guess. Might be about that short track he wants to go to.  Or  he’s still trying to launch something on a remote control.      Hmm. Looking at this estate, maybe he should be dreaming about extensions instead. Got some great ideas sketching on the back of takeaway menus the other night. Imagine—extra room for the kids, a conservatory for the garden view. Heaven.      Extensions, yeah? I can do the measurements if you’d like. Don’t think I’d be able to match the creative side of it, but I can at least make sure we’re not trying to bung in a hall where the loo used to be.      That would be a help. The problem is not the planning, just making it financially feasible. If he was dreaming about building costs, he might want to open a venture capital fund alongside.       Smiles from bed, still asleep  Shhh... kart.      Ah, ignore the dream machine. She’ll whine about being tired the next morning, anyway. But serious talk—how long do you think we can go before he starts charging his dream kart by solar panel or something?      Hopefully not too long— or until  he wants one of those model rocket shelters for the extension. 3D-printed, I’m guessing.      Okay, let’s not tempt fate. For now, let’s just focus on the house. I’ll get the tape measure and forget this was about his weird sleepwear habits.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? That sun is just beginning to warm up the office. Mind if I join you for a brew? Been a bit more than I can take today, I must say.      No bother at all, George—get on with you. Over here. Got a bit of a meeting storm this morning with the committee about our funding proposal. Almost wanted to send a formal letter of complaint about the coffee provisions before that! I don’t suppose you had any tea?      A cup or three, yes. Funny you should mention funding—I was just reading up on a new grant announcement. Seems they've made funding for collaborative projects involving the Hadron collider easier to access. Being older hands, perhaps we should consider applying. Fun stuff. It reminds me of the days I used to argue with funding panels and say, "Theoretical physics isn’t just for dress-makers!" Though perhaps we’re still somewhat in that space!      Ha! A bit dramatic, but not wrong, I'd say. I've always been more of a details person, like Water company regulations—always fascinated me, oddly. Though I might take a break from research funding to go to Tredegar, redecorate the house a bit. My wife refuses to put up curtains again—I’ve no idea why?      Decor and water policies, really? Strange companion subjects. I’m quite taken with Italy at the moment for a sabbatical trip. I might propose a field study in Rome. The architecture and ancient engineering—it's not just about the ruins, you know. I’m thinking about something very interdisciplinary—urban planning and ancient civil engineering through the ages.      Ooh, I do like that. Maybe I’ll join you from Tredegar to Rome—mid-sabbatical architecture and coffee capers. Not to mention I might have to unplug from all that water funding nonsense for a little while. Speaking of which, passed by a water company rep at the copier. They told me they were reconsidering how they meet rural demands. You’d think they'd crack it by now.      Ah, yes, but we keep on whining about the same things, don’t we? Funding, infrastructure, coffee quality. Still, it's good go have a break now and then. Reminds me of my pre-lecturing days, when I had time to go to Italy and actually relax. Though I’m sure the Hadron accelerator made it to the conference then, too.

Alright, nurseries, it’s time to sort out all this Lego. I know it's half past four on a Saturday and you'd rather be bickering over whether Snape was in love with Lily, but this is for your own good. Is Snape a good guy though? Hasn’t anyone  not  watched the movies?   Anyway  , this is about your Lego. Your sheets of yellow bricks should not have red bricks in too. I’m not interested in attacking Voldemort right now; someone once told me you tidy the mess. But can we build Death Star first? No. First, everything is sorted. All the green bricks go into that box; blue into that one. Just keep going until you get to the purple one. Why do we have purple ones anyway? Maybe for mermaids in the sea! Or, alternatively, if you want a continuous supply of micro figures, we sort the lego carefully! No, you didn’t have a purple costume for a mermaid last summer—so I do not see why we need mermaid lego now. Want to watch  Simpsons  after? Can we watch  Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles  too? No doubles! But maybe, if the room looks like a proper brick museum rather than a disaster zone, and you use up the purple bricks in sensible ways, we can discuss. Oh! Like my purple castle! That sounds lovely, yes—  if   you can find the purple bricks. Can I remind you that we are going to the cinema about half eight to see a film about a man talking to a green wizard? Maybe Harry fails his O.W.L.s and turns green. He’s not green, Amy! Harry’s like Professor Dumbledore. Well, let’s not sort the green bricks into any ‘Dumbledore traps’. I am not about to tidy up a war again. As long as we stay on task, we can always talk about lunches and Easter eggs after. Was there chocolate there too? Enough to feed the four of us goody bags on Easter morning if you tidy  properly . While I’m on the topic of Easter, don’t go raiding the stash before the proper time. The rabbit doesn’t bring chocolate for people who live in a courtroom full of exploding bricks, right? Do we talk about dolls and stuff? No! It’s a  Lego  day. But if we finish the sort, I won’t say no to a bit of quiet doll time after.
