Rather chilly this mornin', innit? Thought me ‘n the missus’d pop ‘round first thing wi’ a spot o’ tea an’ a few scones for you two. Best get yer feet up before it all gets too cold again.      Cheers, Gran. I'm just finishin' me homework on the laptop. Mr Aykroyd said we’ve got a test Friday on quadratics. Not exactly laughin’ stock, but easier than last week’s cosine rule mess.      Bit of numb3rs again, eh? Still, not as bad as me time at school! In me day, we didn't half run, only walked up ‘ill like that an’ still managed to learn everything. Fun times.      Oh, you shut yer gob, Ewan. A body might think you were in the army the way you talk. I still remember the time I walked four miles to school in the snow and back, barefoot!      Aye, and still came back with your knickers round your knees, if I remember rightly.      Oh, not that story again. I tell ya, it still gives me shivers—Elizabeth disappearing for ten minutes in the middle of winter. Though at the time it looked like a real case of ‘disappeared’!      It was not! Just hid under a bush after slipping ‘n’ grabbin’ a bramble in the leg. Spent half the morning with a face like a plum and a hanky full of blood.      You mean you  still  got inspected? No one told me that!      That’s the thing wi the old days: we were used to th’ worst. Nowdays you lot complain if you get a six-pointer.      My, ‘eard that lot from education inspectors now. Said they can't get teachers no more. I’d say give ‘em a sjambak an’ you’ll get em sortin’.      You mean  a stick , Grandad.      That’s what I said.  Sjambak . You're just too young to know proper go.      Aye, but at least wi the sjambak they learned to obey. These days blokes jump through hoops ‘fore they get to sum 1+1.      Well, speakin’ o’ hoops, I’ve got the kettle boilin’ again if anyone fancies a proper brew. Or—got my fingers crossed—will someone get that new electric kettle next week once it's delivered?      Mum said she ordered it last week. Hope it comes soon before me gran breaks a few more cups.       I  don't. That kettle’s on its last legs anyway!

Rather than going to see the latest blockbuster, I thought we could talk about one of our old favorites —  Peter Pan . I remember when I used to read the book to you both by the fire. What do you think?      That film with those sparkly fairies — it was so pretty! Do we get to go to Neverland again?      Of course we do, love. But I was thinking — would you like to see a new version of Peter Pan, or would you like to watch one we remember?      The one with the pixie dust and the crocodile — is that one on TV?      That’s the 2003 version — the one with Johnny Depp! The new ones are a bit different. I think the best one, though, is the Disney animation. But there’s also an amazing film about the Tinkerbell character. I remember seeing it at the cinema. It was beautifully made — all the fairy photography was so magical-looking.      I like the book best, though. I mean, the cinema is fun, but in the book you have to imagine the land.      And that’s what makes Peter Pan so special. The books are by J.M. Barrie, and he wrote the story for a children’s hospital, you know — the Great Ormond Street Hospital.      Is he still there?      No, that was a long time ago — someone donated the copyright to the hospital to raise money for the children who need care. It helped out a lot of kids.      So Peter Pan is like —  for  kids?      Exactly. That’s the lovely story behind it. And it’s fitting, isn’t it, that the idea of flying to Neverland and staying a child forever was inspired by children.      If I was Peter Pan, I’d never grow up at all.      Oh, I think there’s something about growing up that makes getting older a bit exciting too, but I know what you mean! Perhaps we’ll find a way to relive some adventures today — grab a book, set some imagination free, and head to the park with the wind in our sails?      Can we go first thing after lunch? I’ll bring the teddy bear.      And your fairy lights! We could have a Tinker Bell!      Well now, that sounds like the perfect adventure to me. Let’s start planning, fellow Neverlanders! On second thought — I’m the Captain of this ship, so I get to choose where the next port of call is.

Rather annoying this, having to get up so early on a Saturday. I was just starting to get some decent sleep after the kids were out of the house last night. I’ve had trouble sleeping since we moved into this flat in Exeter. It seems the acoustics in these new places are terrible — every time eeny tiny sound wakens me. It was much better where we were before in Taunton, a bit noisier, but at least one knew what to expect. Oh, and how was your time in Barnstaple, Jan? I remember when you lived in that house with the big garden — I like to think of it mostly because I can still recall the lovely Sunday roasts you always served.      Thanks, Pete, you always make me feel awful when you mention the roasts I served in Barnstaple. The house turned out to be an absolute nightmare by the way — the damp was awful and the roof needed constant repairs. Honestly, I’m just glad to be out of there! I suppose you didn’t have the same problems in Exeter, Sam?      Not really, we had a survey done before we moved — quite a different approach to buying a house than back when I lived in Wellington, where we just sort of winged it. That said, the commute to work is a bit of a trial. I take the bus most of the time, but it gets quite crowded, especially when I’m trying to catch the one to Exeter for work meetings. Our new flat is near the train station, which is a bonus, but nothing beats the old house in Truro — the gardens there were a dream.      Aye, commuting can be a trial at times, I remember doing the same type of grind from Bournemouth to London once during my managing days. It was not fun. But I see your point Jan, it does take time to adjust.      I agree, commuting can be such a drag. I have no idea how you did it for so long, Pete. I tried working from home when I started teaching again, but it was impossible. Though being in Devon is always a nice bonus — I think it's one of the few places where the beauty of the landscape can somehow make travel a little less grueling.      Well, you've always got a better eye for these things than I do, Kath.

Rather a lot of folk taking a rest in these seats, do you not think? Felt like a panto last weekend, with all them local volunteers skint and slap! Mind, I think they might be holding a working party over the track refurbishment. Be as it may, can't deny it’s good een to sit out here and catch one’s breath 'fore the next bit of toil. You with a working party group?      Aye, I'm with one of them, pulling weeds and clippin’ the hedges for this new trail through the park. Not a bad day for the toils of it, mind—Managed a nice square of the fence, only another row left by the water’s edge. Oi, you lot talkin’ 'bout the benefits of a good back rub, I see? Anyone I know gone for that Swedish massage at the hospice last week?      Oh 'eck, no! I only mentioned it because I read the ME event will have some indulgent workshops next year—plenty for the ladies, I’d say. My Florence—passed on a few years back—loved her a good shoulder rub. Did I tell you, she once tried to launch a nursery for the village? All in the name of “female education,” as she called it, fairly radical, mind, but quite the noble pursuit.      Aye, and I've a wife who could shake a stick at the principles they follow in modern nurseries now. She keeps insisting they treat the lads and lasses the same.  Same ! As if a lad shouldn’t be helped with their sums more than a lassie, or a girl not about to fall off the back of a boulder! She’s had quite the debate with a few of the ladies at her book club. One mentioned the term “gender parity.” I asked her what that meant, and she just looked at me like I'd grown two heads.      Ah yes, all that terminology these days! It’s rather exhausting, I must say. As if you had to parse every sentence out before speaking! Do 'ee keep up with the news about the ME event next year? Still trying to get more women involved. I told 'em if goin' on that masseuse is the bait, then I personally guarantee I shall bring a deck of cards and a flask of brandy to make the recruitment alluring!      Haha, sounds like my kind of tea!

Rather than going somewhere extravagant this year, do you think we could do something more low-key, like a staycation in the countryside? Maybe somewhere local, like Exeter or even a few days in Totnes?      Hmm, a staycation sounds very appealing — especially with the timing of the school holidays and the holidays themselves often being so full-on with family and commitments. But are you sure you don’t want something more exciting? Like maybe the south of France or even Spain?      Honestly, it’s just me and the kids this year. Didn’t plan to be with you otherwise. I’d like to keep it gentle, just to give us a break from the usual routine and not have to worry about planes and airports. Although I do miss jetting off somewhere warm — just not this time.      I understand that. A good little countryside retreat with a proper cottage, nice walks, fresh breakfasts and evenings of just sitting outside. Sounds lovely — in fact, I’d be happy to come along, if you’d like. We could make memories over tea and shared stories instead of the usual big getaways.      I’d love your company! We might even get you off your tablet and onto a camera again. But what would work best for you? Are you free most of the first week of July?      That’s perfect, I’ve got no set plans for that week. I might even bring along some knitting and read a bit — it’s been ages since someone made me read for more than ten minutes. Children are very impatient nowadays.      Oh, don’t mind the kids. It’s their energy that keeps me going. If you’re up for it, I’ll start searching for a lovely cottage to rent nearby — something with a garden and a view of the hills. Let me know if you’d prefer it near a lake for boating, or a quiet area for strolling.      A quiet area would be ideal. No sirens piercing the silence, no neon lights confusing the wildlife. Just green fields, fresh air, and good conversation over a cup of tea. Sounds like a perfect holiday to me.      That’s the spirit, Mummy. I’ll shoot off an email to the local renting go-to-place on Monday and keep you posted. Any preference on colour scheme inside? I’ll let that influence my choice of cottage.

Rather annoying I had to pay for my books online and now they've charged me extra for shipping.      Awe no luck, mate. D'ya need me to lend ye a fiver for emergencies? Not all things are worth the hassle sometimes.      Nah, I'm good. I've got the cash, 's just the prices creep up all the time, aye? A lot for a student tho.      Aye, I get that. Prices do seem to be somethin' else nowadays. Y'know, even at work I can't keep up with some of the costs. Still, it's the real world now, innit?      You must be gettin' good money in yer job, ain't ye? D'ya pick and choose what ye spend?      Yeah, I better. I'm no longer chasin' bargains like a student in rep. When I'm out o' hides, I indulginate. Still, I got to balance it out—especially with the twins, aye? One of 'em got into that drama school a while back and she's takin' it serious.      Mate, that’s wicked. D'ya take her to open-mic nights or prom stuff like that?      Yeah somethin' like that. Last week’s was killer—she was on as Juliet. It’s all in the eyes and the gestures. Honestly, I don’t know how they pull it off so young. Some o' the kid's got a star quality.      No way, are ye sayin' about da twin y’all took to the drama school thing?      Aye, and not long after that she got cast in some series. Quick up-and-coming. My sister ‘eard someone mention her name in the news once.      No siree, any ‘at famous type mentions? Names like them from telly or cricket?      Well, she did meet some English cricket player—can't remember the name. Some Broad or Johnny no, Brad or Jack something. Said it was a man 'o got goin' on for his hat and his wickets or whatever they call it.      Haha, bloke sounds like what your daughter would like. Real charm o' sport and all.      Aye, and she came back to tell me it was the ‘driest meet-up o them all.’ I tell ye, my lot's got sense of humour, aye?      Mate, that kid is on her way. If she’s meetin’ real pros, you won’t be braggin’ in the park no more—just in the papers, aye?      Hah, aye.

Rather annoying this newfit Skype eh? You've got to do everything with your finger, it's not like when we used to send proper letters through the post, eh? I remember when I was a lad, we’d write to pen pals in Yorkshire, and wait weeks! But well, at least I can see y’all now.      Oh, I reckon it's wonderful! Though I don’t use it much now, but I do enjoy a show or two on the telly. Last night’s Doctor Who was a treat. Did you catch it, Rod?      No, I didn’t. Too much school work to mark. I've got the Y6s doing a project on globes and maps, you know, all about where places are in the world. I tell you, their geography is far better than I ever was.      Aye, they’re far too clever for old folks like me! When I was at Costessey Secondary, we learned by heart that the Prime Meridian’s in Greenwich, and not much more. But I still remember the time I went on a school trip to the Yorkshire Dales — quite a walk to the youth hostel. Hilly as blazes, but good country air!      That does sound nice. My Richard used to love the countryside, and he had quite the long leg — the walking sort of leg! Not like mine, which’s a bit dodgy these days!      Aye, but it’s a shame you can’t just hop on the underground like you do in London and go anywhere at a moment's notice. Mind you, I still like to take a colleague up there for a day about once a month. Just the gardens round the area, you know, the Kew stuff.      Not that I’d get up to Kew, but I do enjoy a good garden. I’ve got a few herbs at home, sage and thyme, mostly. I used to have a nice rose bed, but that went with my hip!      Oh dear. You mustn't overdo it with that leg of yours. But I do like the tea you brew, Rod — a bit stronger than usual, but the good leaves!      I do like a strong brew myself, though I do prefer the Italian style — they always go with a bicciole or some biscuit. I have a few students from down there who’ve been helping me with pronunciation, though I’m not sure I’ve got it right!

Rather annoying this, innit? I’ve been tryin’ to book these flights for the conference in Barcelona... got the email from work ages ago, but the prices keep going up by the minute. An’ it ain’t even summertime yet!      Oh, that’s a pain. Got eeny plans to go with me? I was actually just saying to me mam this morning that me next job might’ve taken me to Spain or Portugal in a coupla months. Not sure yet, though.      Naaa, me job here doesn’t run when it should. Still plannin’ the autumn conference, even! Not like I’ve got much of a life, only work and Netflix and chips on the side, innit? C’mon, telly this or telly that – I’m not even watchin’ the same thing me and you had on last week.      Yeah, no doubt about that. I remember you told me in Donny about needing to coordinate so many speakers, you didn’t have time to breathe. Good for you, though—sounds proper stressful.      Oh, it is! But don’t get me started on trying to tell people "no, we’ve got a three-hundred-person limit"—you’d laugh. “Ooh, sorry Mate, but we can’t fit you in because the room’s booked.” People start getting all snobby and professional like they should be on the list automatically.      Harf, imagine someone acting full in your face over a bloody conference spot? It just goes to show, innit? Though, hey—what about the flight? Any chance I could come along if your colleague can’t make it? I mean, I’m not bad at round the houses, you know?      Maybe—that depends if Sarah decides to ditch me at the last minute. She’s mentioned to do something in Marseille for her mate’s wedding. But if she doesn’t, I’ll have me a spare seat. You any bloody good at coding or presentation stuff?      Ehhh, not exactly, but I’m professional enough to know how to take lunches and keep the coffee pot running. Not bad, is it? Still, if you’re nice and invite me, I’ll even go out of my way to be helpful.      You’re on! Just let me know. And in the mean time, let’s eat these chips and see if something good comes on tv. Oh—did we order the chicken or the pasta?      Chicken it was, ‘cause you asked why we were ordering pasta like we were posh enough to afford it.

Rather annoying this, isn't it, the whole cost of living business. I've had to cut down on mince and onions, same as half the street, and I can't see it getting better any time soon.      No, I know what you mean, Dad. It's been awful for all of us, honestly. I've been struggling to explain to my students how inflation actually works, but even I'm not too sure now with everything hitting all at once. And don't even get me started on supermarket prices!      Oh, don't get me talking about supermarkets – I saw frozen fish sticks that cost more than I used to pay for fresh ones back in the 80s. It's shocking, really. I’ve had to plan my week around the weekly specials to make the shopping manageable.      Aye, I had an argument with the shop manager at the Waitrose down the road last week. Told him I’d be hard-pressed to keep supporting places when we can't even afford milk. He looked like he was expecting me to slap him over the shop, I swear!      I think we all need to speak up more and tell the supermarkets what we think. Otherwise they’ll just keep hiking prices without a care. I left a scathing review about their customer service the other week – sometimes it just helps to vent.      All that ranting and venting was what got me thinking about the bank accounts, mind. Our joint funds at the moment are looking suspiciously low. Should we maybe set up some sort of shared budgeting app, like some of the younger customers talk about?      Apps, are they? Sounds a bit daft to me, all that fiddling on blinking phones. I've always balanced my books the good old-fashioned way – pen and paper and a ledger. No need to trust some app, in my opinion!      I know what you mean, Dad, but the modern way has its perks. I can set weekly targets, track where we're spending, and get alerts if we overstep. It’s a bit like trying to catch the spending before it gets out of hand, you know?      Then again, if you can’t even trust the app developers, what can you trust anymore? Mind you, I suppose if you're in the teaching biz, you know a thing or two about what your phone is actually doing behind the scenes.

Rather annoying I had nae gotaways this year, me an’ the flat internet cranked through m’ coursework. Just sat ‘ome with m’ tabby kitten, Bella. I've grown bleedin’ attached to that wee furball! Did you lot take yer holidays anywhere nice yet?      Right, holidays? I meant to go an’ visit m’ mam in Bishop Auckland, but with a floater shift in the hospice, I couldna sort it. Oh but I watched me nan’s horse videos. She’s got these videos where she walks the whole of the North York Moors with her setter, Barney. It were brilliant. I canna go, but at least I still got a wee window into that life.      Oh, not fair! I flew over to Bray from the States, my brother is workin' there this summer. Living with ma again, but at least it were breakfasts with the fam an' early morning coffees on the coast. And, you ever looked at hides, you’d not believe the qwickies they had in the market—vastly better than anything we get here. Yer might want to keep your flat as it is, but food-wise, it were a different world.      I went up to Holyhead in Wales at the end of June with a chap, and we swam in the Menai Strait despite the chill. Cold enough to mortalise you, but beautiful. And we ate at this little café—this 'cwtch chicken' they had. Just divine. Y'know, cwtch means 'a warm hug' in Welsh. So the meal and name—fee-fi-foo! We were away for a week and about five meals richer.      Oh, I had this job in a farm in Cumbria, herding sheep with barely a mobile signal. I was so close to the sheep, I thought I was one of them. All I had was a soddenŜweedie and a few shillings, but the scenery? Mentally, I came back a new woman. Feels as if I lived in the hills themselves.      Gracious, I do like the sound o’ that! Next holiday, I’m tippin' the chance away goin’ on a lake trip up there. Any chance one of you bruvvers would fancy that?      Time y’sort your holiday, you could all have a big get together. We could take it in turns—Wales one year, Ireland the next, farm stays in the mix. Imagine, we’d be tourists in our own country—close enough to appreciate it, yet far enough to love it.

Rather annoying this new essay, eh? You've done it already then?      Not yet... got to start it this weekend. Otherwise I'll be properly stuck in by Monday. How are you getting on with yours?      I’ve basically started it. Just haven’t finished writing it all up yet, I’ve done most of the research and got the main ideas all planned out on a paper. A lot of this just ends up being about social trends in art since the 60’s or something. Know what I mean? It's like looking back when people were younger and trying to predict what the future is like.      Yeah, I reckon I get it. Honestly, I like that the lectures are about art history more than just telling us how to paint or sketch. It's kind of given me a whole new appreciation for the little stuff—like how someone’s childhood can shape their style when they grow old. I've been thinking about this for ages, though. I keep wondering what we will be like in 50 years? You know, like, walking around with bones like this, and being old and everything. Got me thinking if we even stay as artsy as we are now, with everything we’ve got on our phones and gaming and stuff?      Oh totally – I swear I could be sat in my living room just  hunting  the cheapest paint set in the shops just like this! You know what I mean? Like, even if we carry the passion, someone at our age has so much more opportunity to just  produce  more art because we're out in the real world now. Or at least… being older matures you in a different way, so there might be a whole new kind of art evolving all the time from those who grew up on pixel vibes and stuff like that.      Speaking of which, have you managed to beat that new game I told you about yet?      No way, not even halfway. I tried the first few levels and got all confused trying to figure out the puzzles. You must be doing so well to have gotten so far. Let me know if you fancy a proper gaming night on the weekend—my brain needs the distraction from this essay otherwise I'll go mad.      Yeah go on then, that'd be ace. If I can crack it by then, I’ll let you know.

: Right, I've just got through scrubbing the grime off the sink. Do you think it's worth investing in a showerhead attachment for the kitchen tap? I feel like I've been elbow-deep in suds half my life washing this thing.     : Honestly, if it cleans your mind as much as it cleans the sink, I say go for it. But have you tried a clean cloth and some proper dish soap? I swear I got it much easier when I started using a microfibre.     : Oh, I’ve tried the lot. You know what I like to cook, even mostly phased out the processed meat, but the oil residue still turns this place into a black hole of dirt. I’ve met enough people cooking themselves a vegan pot roast, only to clean their kitchen for hours afterward. I think it's just a rite of passage at this point.     : I know! My housemate once accidentally cleaned a pan with the nonStick side down, thinking it showed off the pattern nicer. Good ones, gone in like two minutes. My point is, we can survive this. I mean, we’re not as bad as my ex. He once tried to hide a burnt pizza in the microwave for a week because he didn’t want to wash it – it’s been a fairly long week in our relationship.     : Oh don’t get me started on messy relationships. Speaking of, did you hear that Sarah from our flat in Bristol is back in town for a month? She said she wants to catch up over sourdough baking and something about moonlit yoga in the park.     : Yes, she’s been trying to get us back together every time the moon’s the right shade of green. But I'm in. Maybe this weekend? Let’s do it. I’m up for a reminder that I still have kneading techniques that put bread shops to shame.     : Perfect, I will totally steal your bagels recipe during the session. For once, I want to make something stick. As long as we end up eating the results and not trying to lunchesort a new emotional wholeness from it.     : Deal. Now, can we get the actual go-to recipe on the table? Something hearty, maybe a one-pot wonder? I don’t fancy being elbow-deep in pots until the weekend.     : I was just about to say the same.

Rather annoying this new speaker’s consent form innit? Seems like we need to list our qualifications  twice  in the bloody thing. Just went through it yet agin, and I've a right proper headache.      No, I ken what you mean, Martha. It’s unnecessarily repetitive een my opinion. But I suppose the committee just want to make sure people know what they're getting into. I’ve only had to delete one paragraph so far though, to be fair. The rest was quite straightforward.      Well, for what it’s worth, I agree with you Jane. I just wish they’d trust us to do our jobs without re\-hashin’ our CVs thrice over. My postgrad qualifications seem to have been written left, right, and centre, innit! And what with the seminar comin' up this Thursday, I’m run off me feet tryin’ to get it all ready.      I agree with ya both, but maybe it's worth takin’ the spare time to make the form sound more  inclusive , y’know? Might get more students interested in the topic. I’m thinkin’ about addin' a bit more on non\-verbal cues and cross-cultural communication. We’ve been focusin’ so much on verbal – especiallly with the examples from European business – but other regions like Asia or Africa have some quite differen’ approaches.      That’s a good point, Laura. Our seminar is supposed to be about  international  business communication after all. Maybe suggest we include a case study from each region? Just a short section to highlight key differences. That’d make the seminar feel more rounded, and I think our students would appreciate a bit of variety.      Aye, I like that. We could split the seminar into three parts: verbal, written, and non-verbal, ‘cos quite a lot of people overlook the importance of written communication in international contexts. Letter writin’ still matters, despite all the digital communication these days.      Definitely, and as lectures we should also remind them that tone matters  massively . In some cultures, directness is seen as rude, whereas in others it's considered respect. I think it's worth goin' on for a bit more about  assumptions  made in business communication, too. You know – the ‘we’re all the same’ mindset. It’s all too prevalent in students' essays, and it’s quite concerning.      True to life, yes. I’ll make sure to include a section on that in my part.

Rather annoying day today, isn't it? That meeting dragged on far longer than it needed to.      I know what you mean. I thought I'd be done by two, but then Professor Lin kept rambling about some administrative folly. Honestly, it's enough to make me lose my patience on a good day.      At least we're both not alone in that, I suppose. A lot of the faculty were side-eyeing him during lunch.      Haha, wasn't that the best? You should’ve seen Dr. Yang with that chopstick in her mouth, staring daggers at him like he was some sort of foreign invader. Still, I managed to get the lectures prepared. You?      Yeah, more or less. I had to adjust the slides for the translation unit. Some of the students are really struggling, and I think we’re going to need more practical examples next week.      Absolutely. I’ve been thinking about that too. I had a student come to me after class, almost in tears, because the theoretical reading just wasn’t clicking for them. Honestly, it leaves a sour taste in my mouth that we can only assign what we can find.      Tell me about it. Looking for resources is like searching for a rare book in a store that only sells copies. I’ve been trying to find more bilingual texts, but even the university library is hit or miss.      Well, one good thing is that we’re finally settling into the house we found. That’s been something, at least.      Oh yes, I  love  the garden. It might be a little far from the campus, but the area is so green and quiet. It’s like an oasis!      I know it is a bit of a trek, but at least the rent’s not astronomical compared to what we'd be paying in London. Still, the damp is a bit too much for me. I swear, I’ve had socks that could hold water after just a week.      Ugh, I keep meaning to do something about it, but with work and everything... I did find this lovely Chinese shop the other day that makes these really cute soapstone dishes. I’m seriously thinking of getting some for the kitchen, just to ease the tension of box meals every night.      That sounds like a brilliant idea. We could even turn it into a theme, maybe even make it a proper homecoming celebration sometime soon.

I can't believe half the meat was left on your plate, Sarah. We had just thawed it in the morning, and I thought you'd be hungry today. I know you're busy with your engineering jobs, but we can't keep wasting food like this. Oh, I'm so sorry, Mum. I didn't even think about it. I got distracted by this new TV series on my phone. A lot is happening at the office too — I’ve barely had time to cook a proper meal in the last three weeks. Didn’t your friends come over last week? I saw the spread I had baked mostly go to waste. That’s why the government introduced the 10p plastic bag charge, after all. To make us think twice before throwing things away. Yeah, they did. I think it turned out a bit chaotic in the end. Catsy spilled something when she was trying to film me while everyone was eating — in the end, I ended up cleaning more than cooking, to be honest. I remember that—your father and I often had similar experiences in our day. I mean, we grew up in a different time when food wasn’t as easily available as it is now. My parents used to grow most of what we ate in the back garden. I wish I had room to do something like that. Now everything is so fast-paced and high-tech. I was reading about urban farming initiatives the other day. Our city is actually experimenting with vertical gardens in high-rise blocks. That's an interesting development. Also, have you considered arranging some practical career advice sessions at the school I work in? Some of the kids are really excited about engineering and the technology sector but don’t know where to start. That would be great! I barely considered the tech side until we went on that work experience day at the local factory. It was only after that I chose to branch into engineering. You know, I once thought I'd become an architect when I was your age. But life takes over. Though I’ve never looked back from the path I took. I can believe it, Mum. I’m just trying to get my footing in the field. It’s tough being young in a pretty competitive market. But I’m getting there. And that's all any of us can really do.

Rather annoying when the oven’s on and the timer goes mad. I swear it just decided it’s not like to be used beyond 5pm.      Well, you can’t blame it. Five o’clock is often when the chaos begins—dinner, kids, emails, coordinates sent half-dead at midnight. I’m just grateful the vegetables haven’t caught fire yet.      A lot worse could have happened. Honestly, I’m just delighted that this stew isn’t pulling out of the pot and into the air. It smells good, though, don’t you think?      Oh, it does. I love that you’ve managed to make something warm without burning it. My turkey casserole last week? Carbon left. It tried to defy gravity and stick itself to the ceiling, bless it.      It must be about the upbringing. You Northerners—relentless in mastering comfort food... but in your case, occasionally charred.      Haha—and you Southerners, all politely pretending you enjoy it when you bring out your ‘x-factor’ side in the kitchen. What did you say to me last week, by the way? “I’ve always considered myself a rhythm cook, but lately, it's been a bit of a beat mismatch.”      True, but the jury is out on whether that counts as culinary skill or a desperate attempt to avoid using the microwave. Either way, it feels someone at least one of us is making an effort to not rush to the nearest sourdough with a takeaway receipt.      Exactly. I mean, where’s your colleague when you need them? I remember you told me about the lecture you watched where the professor had this whole debate on cooking as emotional involvement.      Yes, it was a classic one. The title was, ‘How do baked goods form deeper bonds between partners.’      Sounds like it was a psych professor with pottery wheels. I tried to read about that study on your desk. It had a bit of a thing about shared culinary space contributing to 'romantic synergy,' didn’t it?      Yes, something around shared messes and the notion of companionship in common tasks. The idea is that working together on something practical—like cooking—builds connection between people.      Then your research is backing up all the things I’ve been saying this whole time about putting the tea down, helping with veggies, and making sure we talk about our day over chopping.      I’m not entirely surprised.

Rather lovely day today, isn't it? I was just down by the sea for a bit o' fresh air. You'd think with all the rain we've had, it'd be muddy, but nary a puddle in sight.      Aye, that’s a lie in’t een! I went out last week to visit one o' me nieces by the coast, and it was gloomy as all, but today's quite a treat. Still, I’d rather be by the seaside 'n’ staring at nothing than staring at the telly again. It's full of squabble these days.      I can relate, love.Been out there myself, though I managed to get more turkey than seascape, I’m afraid. The birds are back! I saw little blue tits building a nest in one o' the trees by the shore. It was sweet, really — quite heartening, if I’m honest.      Oh aye, the baby blue tits — they always bring back memories. Used to feed em when I were a lad. My gran had a way with birds, she did. I miss that, quite a bit.      Honestly, I’ve been feeling a bit low lately. I blame age. Mind you, most days I just feel like hiding under a duvet, but the other day I reckoned I’d better make an effort, so I started volunteering at the local library. It’s not much, but it's something. Takes the edge off the loneliness.      That’s a good move, Joan. Volunteering helped me too. It’s not just about filling time — it's about giving something back and about people needing you. I sometimes wonder if the problem is that we’re too alone. I’ve seen it with my pupils — not school kids, but older folk too. They’re struggling. Depression, loneliness — it's hiding in places no one's looking.      You say that like it's easy to spot. I tried to talk to my son a while back. He's drifting and I can’t say a word without him shutting 'imself off. It’s the money, the stress, the housing crisis, the whole shootin’ match. They can't go out and get a life if they've not got a roof over their 'eads, can they?      You're right, Bert. It's all so tangled. Me grandkid, she’s in her twenties and just can’t even rent a decent place without a side job or two.

Rather annoying isn't it? I've tried so many brands. My sister swears by [Brand C], but I don’t think she’s had much luck yet. I prefer something that actually lasts.      Oh, honestly, I've tried half of them and nothing really works for more than two days! I went to the nail bar with one of my Post Office colleagues last week—Lara? She said I should go for this brand that uses this gel-based top coat. She promised she’d get me a little pot!      Oh, that does sound promising. Do you think it’s expensive like the salon ones? I'd rather do it myself, unless the cost’s not that bad.      Naaah, she said it’s actually quite affordable. Probably about the same as what I spend on [Brand B]. Lara turned me on to an online beauty forum a while back. She says it’s a goldmine for hacks. Maybe I should show you at some point.      That'd be brilliant. I could do with some help on that—especially with the hair, maybe? I’ve been meaning to get that short cut done, as suggested by my hairdresser, but I’m a bit… well, you know. I’m a bit sensitive about it.      True, changing your hair is kind of a big thing. But I reckon you'd love that short cut. Silly question, but is that what you wore for your class the other day? The blue one with the blazer?      That’s the one! Some students were saying how much they liked the way I looked—though I'm not sure whether it was sincere or just being polite. I'm lucky I have you round to talk sense into me.      Hey, that's what friends are for! I mean, if you're going to step out with a ‘new look,’ you need someone to back you up. Speaking of which, remember when we did that shopping trip to the city last year? That nail polish we picked up there was a crack!      Oh yeah, that coral one with the glitter! It was perfect for the wedding we went to. You looked absolutely smashing in that red dress.      Thanks, really meant to say you looked smashing too. Just don't go getting all heady with compliments, okay?      Aww, thanks. Now what about going to get that special brand and then maybe we could go for another cuppa and finish this off with a spot of shopping for something new this time next week?

I can't believe the new History Museum’s opened up near us. I've been meaning to take a browse. It got heaps o' good reviews. Yeh gone? Yeah, I went a week back. Real £20 entry, though. That's a bit daft, innit? I saw the Pompeii section—it were brilliant, all them mummified bits an all. You should go. Yeah, I'll probs save up me cash for it. It were easier parkin’ up there last week, though. Not like the chase it can be. Aye, I had me bro drop me off. That’s the only way, really. You know I’m still working five shifts a week, so enough hassle left for findin’ a parking spot. Roight, I hear ye. Work’s been chaotic for me too. Started teachin’ breakfast clubs—kids gone antsier since the weather turned for the season. Bloomin’ non-stop. Still, at least you're not stuck dealin’ with Waterstones or shopkeepers—personally, I’d be nuttier than a pike as their stockroom manager. Hah! Easy there, I tried workin’ in a shop once. Not ideal for me. But, yeh, still, it's all relative. I imagine a wedding set up would be far more organized than me classroom. Smashing the toilets and chasing misbehavin' lads is a lifestyle choice. Haha. Oh, did I tell ye? My cousins had the most adorable Christmas decorations installed in the communal area at their new flat. Blimey, did they source any local stalls for their stuff? I’m mean, mind ye, I’ve been scoping out some vintage markets to get a gift for me gran up North. Yeah, they found a local guest speaker who passed on a few shops. He told them the minimal budget Christmas was ‘get it cheap, get it accurate, an’ get it quick’. Right ho. That’s a philosophy. I've 'ad a couple of whiskeys with the same man over there for a couple of months. That's yer go-to then. But tell me more about yer interview for that Masters—still line in? It’s brutal these days. Aye, all booked. I've been planning to fill me gap in between roles after next year. Hope to get some bellyful of analysis and pedagogy, ‘cause this job’s startin’ to feel a bit—close my door. I know where ye’re coming from, mate. Think I need to boost me earnings.

Rather annoying isn't it, how grown-ups think they have to glue sticks and glitter in order to know anything about children? I mean, look at Sarah—always trying to play the perfect stepmum with a Pinterest board thrown into every new situation. Honestly, it's exhausting pretending to care about those crafts.      Ugh, I know! I feel like I'm constantly having to prove I'm not just "the babysitter" or that woman who follows every rule in a book. It's not like it's a competition to be the most Instagram-worthy parent. But, come on, at least she means well, even if it does feel like she's trying to live through the kids now.      True, I suppose she's just trying to make a connection. Probably felt left out back in the day, given how things went with her parents. Still, she could at least try to talk to  kids , not just at them through some idealised version in her head. I remember the day she thought Liam, who’s six and about as keen to paint as a cat is to dance, needed organic lino for a collage—what on earth possessed her to think that was a good idea?      Oh good lord, I saw the little lad was already eyeing the loo roll with more hope than he eyed her supplies. At least  I  know the secret is to keep things moving and not expect them to sit still for long. Liam’s more interested in inventing a new kind of chicken song than in making a 3-D papel mache volcano.      Also, it's a wonder to me how she doesn't see that  they  are the ones dictating about half the time. I mean, just the other week she had this elaborate plan for a "nature walk" and ended up being chased by two tiny children down the garden while she was screaming something about leaf textures.      I know, it was hilarious. Honestly, the most independence I achieved was when I just handed them a leaf, a little beetle, or a worm and said, "Go on then, what is it trying to tell you?" and left them to it. Some days, I think you  gotta  be a bit of the village idiot to go the step parent route.      Oh, absolutely! But in the end, it's just about doing your best—and trying to remember to laugh at the mess.

Rather annoying when the telly breaks down on a Friday night, innit? I was hopin' to catch up on episodes of that new boxset me mam and I agreed on.      Aye, we’ve had the same problem—router and telly gone mental together. Got eeny idea when they’ll fix it? Me and mate were reckonin’ on dossin’ a film but no signal, nothin’.      Oh, I’ve had it a fortnight. Tried me own fancy techy skills—unplug it, mess with the sockets—all to no good. Tink it's just one o' them things. What’s the plan if we can’t get that sorted?      Oi heard tell o’r lass from Birmingham—Laura, innit—settin’ up a Pinterest board for everyone for her 30th. I fancy havin’ a proper themed dinner with a twist in Cambridge. Maybe cook somethin’ we never ate before?      That sounds right bloomin’ fun. My gran’s always on about Pinterest—says I should be using it for recipes innit. I tell her, “Gran, there’s a thing called the telly.”      Aye, but Laura’s got a real knack for organisin’, so if she’s dossin’ up the board, it’ll be somethin’ special. Me mam might even join in. She’s always been full of ideas—never got around to doin’ any o’ 'em.      Oi, let’s be honest, most o’ 'em sound mad anyway. Though I did like the one about a weekend trip round the area, you know, with vibes and stuff. Maybe next month?      Aye, long as it's not the weekend, ‘cos I’ve got stuff at the uni. Said to me mam I’m dossin’ up a paper on all things polymer chemistry, but I’m fairly sure I’m just stickin’ words together and hoikin’ out anything that comes with 'ore'.      Sounds spot o’ you! Gobsmacked you're still in the system, really goin' on for a PhD and all that.      I’ll let that slide. Sue me, I'm nearly through. Passin' the time at the moment, y'know, and I’ve got my hours counted, so I’m not exactly suff'rin'.      Right, and them reports you dossin’ up—how's that going for yer?      Grand, really. Right amount o' stress. Got to keep the brain busy while me TV's gone wonky.      Oi, you're on a winning streak then, mate. Just don’t start on me with yer fancy lectures.

Rather annoying that the chandelier we liked on eBay is now sold. I was hoping it would work in the dining room and give it a bit of elegance.      Yeah, I remember that one. It was £200, wasn’t it? Cheaper than the ones I’ve seen on other sites. But I suppose it got snapped up pretty quick if it was sold in two days. Maybe we should look through a few more before settling.      I was going to, but it crossed my mind that the dining room ceiling might need a bit more work anyway. You know, wiring needs to be checked. I’m still not sure it’s safe to hang anything heavy up there without an electrician looking at it.      That’s true. Probably safer to play it cautious, even if it costs a bit more. I just don’t want it to look like something we chucked together. The chandelier was a nice option because it wasn’t too garish.      Exactly. I’ve been looking at a few more on Rightmove as well, just to get an idea of what’s available. I think we should measure the dining room and sketch out a few possibilities.      Good idea. I can’t imagine we’re the only ones who’ve had lighting problems in older houses. Let’s just confirm if the wiring is safe first. It might be better than trying to use a large fixture and having it buzz every time we turn the light on.      I agree. I’ll call the electrician later. Oh—while I’m at it, have you seen the new listings on Rightmove? I saw one close to the train station about five minutes from here.      What size is it? And how much?      Three-bedroom semi-detached, asking £320,000. Not bad for the area. Historic building too, with tiled floors and open fireplaces. It might give us quite a bit of character without being too restricting.      Hmm, and how far to the shops and everything?      Around half a mile, but there’s a bus route that goes around once an hour—which the previous owner mentioned in the details. It wasn’t rated highly though.      I’ll take a look. If the price is right, it might be worth a visit. I’m not sure if we’re looking to move anytime soon, mind you, but it’s always better to keep options open.

Rather annoying the new cleaner at the nursing home, Fran. She’s promising one thing then forgets it. I got to check everything she does. Otherwise poor Mrs. Bell will end up with a blistered bottom again.      That’s not good, Lorraine. Should you report it or give her another chance? I’ve been in her shoes, you know. First week on the job and it’s a minefield.      Honestly, I’d be easier off training a goldfish! At least they can remember to float up occasionally for food. Fran, are you still fostering Tiddles? I like to keep up with who’s looking after our fella.      Yes, and now that Myra’s kids are back at school, they’re taking him back over the weekend. I’m thankful. He likes to open every single cupboard and knock things over in the morning. Cats are better than breakfast, no doubt about that!      My Joanne works there too, as a support worker, and she’s told me that the staff turnover is immense. You sign one and then you get sent some tall, skinny lad from Manchester two weeks later.      It’s deadly how much we’ve got in common, the three of us. Be it work or home. My partner works nights at Royal Victoria Hospital, and I barely see him these days. You two have better shifts, I suppose?      I’m doing a course to become a support worker in a couple of months. Tutor also said I’d read like a million pages before I start. Lorraine, did you ever have a shift like that? Any tea left?      Oh, you know I did. Once I worked a 12-hour shift and found myself elbow deep in a cooking pot of boiled eggs gone bad. Not that I’d tell it to a student, but that’s how we learn! And no, no tea. Would you like a coffee?      I’d love something fresh, love. We haven’t spoken about your little ones, Lorraine. How are they settling into school again?      Oh, ages and ages from my time at school, let me tell you. But they’re trying their best! The youngest is into go-karts on the weekends if you can believe it.      I’d let that boy go-kart with me any day if it meant getting out of the house. I can hardly cope with my two hours after work.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know what they do—say you just need to ‘set a routine’ and ‘avoid screens’ before bed. But what about when you’re actually out in the wild and it’s not that simple?      It's true. We were camping in the Lake District the other week, and even with the 'ideal sleep hygiene,' I was up half the night. Maybe that coffee before heading up the hill had too much caffeine.      It's interesting, though. We've been doing some research for the new retreats, and the findings suggest that even a little bit of exposure to natural light during the day improves sleep quality at night, no matter where you are.      Oh, I'd believe that. Camping really does reset your body clock, you know. But getting used to sleeping under the stars is quite an adjustment for some people. How do you get guests to adapt?      Haha, honestly, the first few nights are a disaster, but after a couple of days, the body adjusts. One bloke even said it reminded him of being in a war zone—changing tent zipper, no toilet paper, and trying to tell time without any light.      I can see it. When we got lost in Birmingham once—roads are a nightmare there—my phone died, and I was counting on the map. We had no idea where we were! You know what struck me? When you're in a city, you just can't intuitively find your way like you can in a forest.      That’s something the study touched on too—natural landscapes being navigated more easily because of environmental cues, while cities can overwhelm people with choices. It makes you wonder why the pilot can fly around the globe without a map yet manages to get lost in his hometown.      True! I spoke to a friend of mine whose husband got lost in London once, even though he’s been there a thousand times. Streets got rebranded, I think, or maybe he just got distracted by the market stalls.      It’s always funny with people who can navigate by the stars or by their instincts, but when you give them a city with one-way streets and no clear landmarks, they're map zombies.      Just don't expect me to follow anyone into the wilderness without a compass box and an app.      Fair enough.

Rather annoying when a hamster takes off wi’ the bedding an’ sticks it in the middle o’ the floor, innit? I jist tried skypin’ it back an’ now it’s a mad hooman with whiskers. Look at it—gettin’ all depressed cos I ledder it down!  sigh       Blimey! Sounds like a job fer a Aardvark or sumfink. I’ve heard tell o’ hams, but ain’t clued up on the Yorkshire hamperative. Do they want carrots? Mithose meaty chips, or jist . . . dead leaves?      Oi, calm yer posh turkey, mistress o’ Caaam-beidge! I’ve had a ginger hamster called Darcy, he used to think he was a lion—puffed up his sides an’ stalked breakfast, no doubt about it.      Oh aye, you ever looked at a ginger, even a furball one? They’re like red pyrotechnic lanterns wi’ a soul, innit? My Nan reckons we’re all ginger innit, human an hamster combined.      Na, we’re not, Nan got hers mixed up at the Baptism: True reds, like me, they burn furiously. Me mate over there’s black as coal, and Sil’s a . . . oh don’t be blushing, Sil!      Honestly, you all read like a ginger dictionary. I mean, there’s floring, roan, red and then…  me , pale as a ghost. My nan used to say I was daft as a hatter, not ginger!      Tha’s where your fails start, love. Cos if you’re not ginger, you caaant have ginger, ‘cos you ain’t got that spicy soul passed down by da generashuns.      Oh, I once had a ginger friend, from Middlesbro’, who told me we were  earth spritez , or somethin' 'ort of magic-like whispy things, an' he’d be  able  t'dig like a man with a pick goin' on a lofine!      You’re all in separate houses, I’m in the boxset house. I’ve watched all of  Doctor Who  and I still don’t kow what we’d do wi’ a regenerated hamster, let alone a regenerated person.      C'mon! It's a  close  lot of gingers and ginger-ness, innit? Our hamsters always copy us, so mine used to pace in its ball, looking all . . . like it was running in a mill, but of course, much less satisfying.      Blimey! Ours used to look like it was moonlightin’ it on a beach—wriggle and ripple, like the sun off the Seaton.      That does sound very exotic.

I can't believe Aaron didn't bring snacks for the game. Again. I know it's his house, but when we play Risk, maps and luck are one thing—but chocolate, music, and alcohol make it a proper experience. Aye, fella, I agree. But it was his mum’s idea to play, and we’re just along for the ride. Honestly, I don't know why I agreed. A game of Risk tends to last from dusk till dawn. And with his records blasting, who needs to sleep anyway? Oh, Steven, it's childish fun. You know you get competitive. Besides, it's not like we're tackling ethics or the child policy debate again. On second thoughts… Oh, you mean the last time we tried to play, the discussion about Chinese medicine and pregnancy tests turned into a conspiracy theory? That was chaotic. Blimey, I nearly fell off the sofa laughing. Reminded me of Genghis Khan, the way we argued, thinking we were experts. Still, the way Sarah mispronounces "Bedford" is hilarious—personally, I say it "Bed福德" in my head to mock her. Rob, there's something to be said for mock battles in games. At least it's not the real thing. Though I do wonder, sometimes, if having children is like choosing a new set of positions to fight for. Silly, I know. Sarah, you're in a funny mood. That reminds me, I need to check the latest version of the game. Mary updated it recently—there's a new section on sterilization and child policy in board games now. Who knew? Kinda about time we stopped playing by the same rules from 1977. Maybe they should add “Faith in doctors” as a challenge card. Maybe something to do with luck and confidence. Like "If you survive your next pregnancy test with accuracy, you gain extra armies." Do you mean with accuracy or accurate results? You know I could stick up for medical ethics over that. Let’s not go there again with lunches and shots and whatnot—my breakfast took an hour to return after that debate. Look, all I'm saying is, map your life if you must, but don’t forget the snacks. I’ll go see if they’ve got crisps or something. And if they do, I might just take over the whole North and start moving in on Aaron's position, moral repercussions or not.

Rather annoying to be honest. I mean, I thought I’d love it, right? Painting and stuff. But honestly, I’m just sitting there, like,  bloody well stared at a canvas for an hour and thrown half a moon and a rabbit on it !      Yeah, I'm like,  this is the one . But   no  , now I’m all self-doubty.      That’s a bit normal, innit? I started as some sort of wanna-be accountant and now I’m like,  nup, want to be a vegan animal rights influencer full time !      Oh no! You’re not going to make me like that too, are you? I already have to feed my one cat and he’s a menace! You know, I once thought I wanted babies. But now I’m like,  nope, better off breakfast, no responsibilities .      I used to want lots, you know, like, little mini me’s running around the park. But now, I just want to lie in bed, get my nails done, and maybe occasional cuddles with a rescue.      That sounds fancy. Bet they’d be mini you, trotting around in little dresses and sarcastic comments –  ha!       Anyhoo, back to the real problem. What are you going to do with your life?      Dunno! Honestly, feels all too big. What about you? All vegan influencer and stuff?      Yeah, but it's a stretch. I still got exams to pass,  literally, how do you paint about money management .      Oh come on, I had to document a  landscape and my emotions  last week. I gave the tree existential dread!       Exists ! That’s brilliant. Should go viral, you know. Just me on the side hustle – any advice on how to get it done?      We could run our own  influencer academies . Me:  teach people how to whinge about art . You:  teach veganship basics .      Yeah, go viral or get arrested, I dunno. Any real advice?      I think just be you, bloke. And what your cat tells you. It’s right, seriously. Mine told me last night I'm meant to be a garden designer. True to say, it was licking a cushion, so maybe not trust them.      Fair enough. Maybe we get our heads in sixth form mode once more, revise, get degrees, then plunge into madness.      Yeah, maybe it won’t all be a waste, just some major drama, bad hair days, and a bit of me-time, as you call it.

So do you think we should base our project on the impact of consumerism on poverty in the UK? I mean, it's kind of relevant after the recent press about the cost of living.      Yeah, I think it's a solid topic. But how are we going to back it up scientifically? Do we have enough stats on the issue?      My cousin actually helped me with a paper last week about income inequality and shopping habits. I got a few references from that. Plus, there's lots of research from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.      Oh right, they do a lot of work around poverty. I can probably get access through the school library's database. But have you thought about how we address the counterarguments? Like rich people also spend on consumer goods.      True, and I think it's important to make a distinction between luxurious spending and essential expenses. Poorer people are more affected by marketing and have less disposable income, which makes them vulnerable to financial strain from shopping.      That makes sense. I mean, I grew up with both parents working, so I’ve seen the impacts of short-term spending solutions. We might want to include real-life stories as case studies in our project.      Yeah, maybe we can interview someone – like a teacher or a social worker – who's seen the effects up close. I reckon Miss Patel would be cool with that. She was helpful with my last Science Fair.      Definitely. While we're at it, maybe we can also consider the political aspect. How do you think the government's policies have influenced consumer habits in the last decade?      That’s a good point. I remember reading about the marketing laws brought in to protect the vulnerable, but they’re not always strictly enforced. Maybe part of the solution is better regulation and education.      Yeah, education is underrated. Like, if people understand how much they actually need versus what they want, the whole cycle could break down. Speaking of, I tried cutting down on shopping last week. It was tough, but I feel better financially.      Me too! It’s easier said than done, but it makes you think about your priorities. You know, it's kinda funny how go-to hobbies like reading comics are more cost-effective than so many other things these days.      Definitely – box sets can be free on your phone with a Wi-Fi connection, and comics are often cheaper than takeout pizza.

I've been meaning to call you, love. That recording session for the audio book was a bit of a marathon, but the producer said she was thrilled with how it turned out! How have you been? I feel like it's been ages since we last caught up. Honestly, I haven’t been brilliant. Things have been a bit quiet round here. I tried getting into physio last week for my knee—it's been giving me serious trouble since that fall back in November. The physio was quite strict, to be honest! She was like "No excuses!" whenever I winced. Oh, poor thing! I've been doing some gentle stretches as well. My joints are getting on a bit now that I'm in my fifties. I left my kettlebell back in Stratford and I dare say I’m glad of it. A bit heavy for my old bones now! Ha! I can only imagine. I mean, you always looked in tip-top shape, even back when we used to go to the gym together when I was younger. Speaking of which—did I tell you, I've started thinking about cutting down on takeaways? Like a real effort this time. Oh? Good on you, love! I remember when you first moved into that little flat in Guildford. All that takeout, and now look at you trying to get into a healthier routine. What did you say you were trying? I’m not sure what exactly, just someone at the physio centre mentioned a Mediterranean way of eating. I thought I’d look into it. Though, honestly, my wardrobe is starting to feel like a problem—I need to do a bit of a spring clean about now. I’m not trying to be the shape of my old jeans back from secondary school, but this lard is getting to me! No pressure, pet. My idea of a 'diet' is less puddings and more salad. Though I have been making a mean chicken and leek pie lately. Nothing fancy, but it hits the spot. My joints are grateful too—less sugar, more of a sustained energy. That actually sounds good. I do miss proper home cooking sometimes. But honestly, with how I've been feeling recently, go out of my way for anything more than a frozen meal and I’m ready to chuck in the towel. Well, if you ever want recipes you know I’m only a call away.

Rather than chuck a DVD in eh, innit? Thought we'd cook summat decent for a change. I got us sorted with some chilli, see? Dug it out this morning after a proper longo for a tin. Chilli seems like a fanny-warmin' kinda night, eh?      Couldna agree more, 'specially if it's not all meat-free hippy stuff. A real proper beefy one? Proper stuff, innit? If na, me nan’s got that recipe book we used to use when I was a kid. She always said it made the meat tender like you wouldn’t believe.      Allrighty then, only if we can add some of the turkey mince I’ve got. Terry left it in the back o’ the freezer for weeks, bin too picky to touch it. But I'm thinking if it’s chuckin’in it when naone's lookin’, who’s to bleedin’ know?      Nah, you can’t have a proper chilli without bleedn’ ground beef. I do tell you—personally I think turkey takes one look at a spice rack an’ faints like a real div. Tell me there's summate decent in that packet of beans then. Dint want it all to be limp ones, cos I ain’t plannin’ on makin’ a sommat outta that.      Dinnae worry, I’ve been forensically sorts out. Letting one of the suspicious ones: read the bag, weighed them up, then put ‘em in the colander. So, as long as they weren't all gross, which na, they’re still in about half decent shape. Just not gold standard, touch wood.      All right, that’ll do. Need to plug the hob in while it does its bob, eh. My sister ‘ad the same treacle o’ happenings once, took 'er three weeks to sort it out. Proper ‘get it sorted’ moment for 'er. You know, while we crack on with that, I’ll pop out to fetch some coleslaw to add on the side—cos if we’re going all Mexican road trip, might as well travel like a man with luggage.      Bless you, Jackie. Any chance of a cold drink to chuck in while I’m pourin’ ‘ere? Sommate carbonated to make you feel all healthy-like. Me and Terry had a one-night stand with those fruit infused ones last week, and to say it made me feel ‘appy is an understatement o’ epic proportions.      You know what they say: “A soft chilli, a short life.”

Rather skip the new horror flick everyone’s on about, honestly. I’d much rather watch something old-fashioned like  The Wizard of Oz . Just binge it with some crisps and ignore the world for a bit. You in?      Be as it may, I reckon it relies on individual taste. I went to the cinema last weekend and saw that horror film people rave about — it was a bit of a snooze, but I still had a decent time. Found myself watching  Sweeney Todd  afterward to keep in the mood.      Yer don’t say. I watched that horror film as well. I mean, sure, it’s got the glitz and glam of being in the cinema, but honestly, I’ve seen enough gory stuff on the telly to last me years. D’you know what I fancy? A little bit of  Aliens  — old school sci-fi vibes, no doubt about it.      Oh aye,  Aliens  is fookin brilliant. Rich was showing it to us the other night, and I swear, the suspense had me on the edge of my seat! Felt a bit like being back in the library, reading those bookies on Marcus Fenix during exams.      Hmm, I haven’t seen  Aliens  yet. My cousin showed me  Titanic  a while back. All that love and tragedy! Honestly, I prefer watching musicals at the weekend, they’re just so much fun. I saw  Mamma Mia!  once and it had me singing for hours!      Aye, musicals be right up me street too! We had a bit of a theme about daft ones in da weekend — binged  The Prom  and had a right laugh. There was even a cabaret at school last term and it was a proper laugh. I do daft ‘numbers’ just like Julie Andrews in  Mary Poppins .      Oh, I was at that cabaret last term! It was a laugh, I must admit. There was a  Singin’ in the Rain  number with proper umbrellas and everything! Would’ve killed if the ceiling hadn’t started flooding in the middle. Picked up the vibe straight away goin’ on — it was like our own version of Showbiz.      You know what’s a bloomin’ classic, though?  Singin’ in the Rain  itself. Such a heartwarming story — heck, I even cried at the end like a toddler. Know where you can get the full version with the extra bits? Searing my fingers over here trying to get it.

: Right, I am just unpacking all these trinkets I bought from Paris—the Eiffel Tower cookie cutter and a €5 scarf that is definitely more of a fashion crime than an accessory. But otherwise, it was amazing. We had this little flat in Montmartre, like totally charming, but it was beginning to get  beyond  me when the boiler broke and we had to heat water on the hob with a pan from a 1992 film set.     : Oh, dear! Sounds like you had the full "charming European chase of hot water and questionable plumbing" experience. I remember when we had our boiler replaced back in ’03—it cost us nearly a week's pension and resulted in me developing a lifelong hatred of plumbers.     : Honestly, I’m just envious of Paris altogether. I turned down a chance to go for a short trip to Lisbon last weekend, and now I’m regretting it like a burn in my arm hairs from using the wrong desktop cleaner.     : I know, I know, but I will say it was definitely a nice break from the endless crop of emails and frustrations around here. Did you hear about the catering kitchen issue today? One of the walk-in fridges refuses to cool, and the head chef is pretending it's a new recipe phase—“fermentation chic!”     : Oh don’t start again, Sarah! You know what it’s like with outdated appliances in these places.
