It’s just the vibes. I’ve been trying to cook something that isn’t barely edible and it is killing me. I made some kind of ‘stuffed baked potato’ that came out more like a deflated balloon at a kid’s party.     : At least no one is restricting your macaron recipe again. Last time you overused salt as a joke and it ended with lunches being a new dystopian novel.     : Still, I did come across a nice recipe the other day— go and check my iPad, if you like. Roast beetroot and goat cheese in filo, it's a bit of a charmer.     : I’m in. I’ve been obsessed with Greek food since my hours of watching cooking shows while nursing this dodgy ankle I got from ‘dancing’ too hard at a friend's 30th.

Hey Victoria! Just a minute, I saw you walking by before class. I was just heading for a coffee—care to join? Hi Tom! Actually, I need something hot after walking from the student centre in this chilly Chichester wind. Be right with you. Chichester? I went there last weekend to visit an old mate. They’ve got this amazing arts centre—they put on some great amateur theatre. Got tickets one rainy Saturday, and it was surprisingly good. It reminded me of that musical we used to do at the university when I was an undergrad. Oh, like  Les Mis  or  Chicago ? No, actually, it was  The Effect of Gamma Rays on Man-in-the-Moon Marigolds , of all things. It was emotional, but the student directing said she was training for a bigger production in London. Honestly, it made me reconsider my own theatre ambitions. Haha, you and theatre dreams. Last year I thought I'd go back for a master's in creative writing, but that would mean juggling this supervisor job and tuition fees. My sister recently started a novel, and as much as she griefs about it, I think she's holding back. Doesn’t have time for all the referencing and structure. You remember? I do. She swears passive voice is her enemy. But seriously, after working as an English instructor for a year, I’m considering a postgraduate degree in linguistics. Who knows, maybe even a master's in TEFL? It just feels oddly satisfying to teach others while still learning myself. Hey, look at you—an academic! Look, as for my goals, I just want to finally take a real holiday. I still haven’t been back to Bedford in months. My parents keep giving me that look when I don’t mention Greece on holidays. Should come up with a plan soon. My flatmate is proposing his girlfriend at the end of the month. If you all come, there’ll be drinks, food, laughs, maybe some fireworks from the estate. Count me in! And by the way, speaking of your flatmate, do you know any of his friends? I had a row with the bloke I go out with—he says he doesn’t like my brother. Is it serious? Hopefully not. He’s a bloke alright, but your brother’s a funny bloke. I seriously think your exes just live together.

Passport photos do cost a bit, don't they? I remember going to the shop in our town when I first needed mine and my Gran had to be there because I was underage. Aye, and it's probably £20 or so these days as well. Just like the stamps for the passport and all that. But I don't think they take your photo if you're not actually applying for a passport. Yeah, I've heard that. They send your photo off with the form, or something. We had to send the form and photo through the post, but now I think you can do everything online. Oh, I wouldn’t know the first thing about doing that on the computer. My son helps me with that sort of thing. I can barely send a text half the time. Easier in the world now. Back in the day, we used to have to get it all done in person. Like when my grandma got hers, she remembers needing to go to an office, get the documents done and so on. Everything was paper-based. My mum told me something like that as well. I never thought about it as much. Did you know that back then, people used to get their passport books stamped by customs officers when they got off the plane or boat? I didn’t, but that’s interesting. These days, you just don’t get as much contact with people at the passport control. It’s more about scanning and biometrics. Sounds a bit complicated. I’d much rather just have someone check a picture and stamp something. I think the system is supposed to be more secure now, though. You can't just make up a passport photo the same way you used to. Maybe so. But I think part of that is because technology has made it easier to forge things. I do wonder, though, whether the processing time is any quicker than it used to be. I'm told it was quite slow once, but now there are expedited services if you pay. It's a bit of a safety blanket, especially if you've got to go somewhere in a hurry. That's for sure. You don’t want to miss the ferry or something go bad because the postal service was late or there was a waiting list. Yep, I don’t think anyone likes the idea of being stranded because of a processing delay.

Rather annoying this new tax they’ve brought in, ay? Cheques I was expecting, not more moneys off the top. I can’t even get a job properly, let alone afford a pint with this lot.      No, I heard about it on the news the other night. Got eeny weeny passive income tax or something. Like, if you’ve got a tiny bit of cash in a savings account now, they’re taking that too. Proper daft, innit?      My sister’s uni was talking about it. Didn’t even want to start coursework ’cos of the stress. She said even part-time work is barely worth it now the tax eats into it. It’s like everyone’s poorer, even if they’re not spendin’ more.      I’ve seen it too, and I’m earnin', barely. It’s like every week you’re better off when you start the week than you are at the end. The council’s been advisin' us to keep sums tucked away, but that’s a tough ask when you’re tightenin’ your belt just to get by.      I’m strugglein’ as it is. I only started sixth form as a second chance… plus, I’m workin’ part-time just to afford food and bills. Sometimes I wonder if I’m even smarter because I study, or if the system is set up to make me feel smarter?      Ha! Smarter? I’ve degrees in this ‘ere chicken and egg scenario. Just because you’ve a paper taped to the wall don’t mean you’ve got more of a clue than I do. Still no job, no house, naught but a past I can’t seem to walk away from.      We were talkin’ about what you could do with your qualifications. Cos I mean, it’s a shame for both you. My sister’s got a mate who moved abroad for work. Said they took his degree at face value and it was a doddle to get a job.      I could see that, but you’ve got to consider the cost of living elsewhere. Family’s a big one too—my nan’s older, and I’m here for her. You travel too far, you might as go out of orbit for all you see of home again.      I’ve been studyin’ about support roles, infact. Proper trainin' you could do post-sixthform. Thought maybe roles in care, those jobs are solid even now, and there’s slots for them.

Rather than chuck a barbie out the back, I fancied a bit o’ lasagne ‘n’ chips, what d’ya reckon?      Lasagne an’ chips? Now there's a proper meal. Chuffed to bits I am—get a bit o’ peace an’ quiet een th’ place, yeah?      Yeah, it's not easy havin’ a chat without th’ TV on or the kids runnin’ about. Oh, how’ve yeh been, by the way? It’s been a good while.      Still pluggin’ along, I guess. Lakelands is still me square mile. Y’know, do some bits an’ bobs, keep mebleed body off the sofa. Tryin’ to get back into the habit o’ push-ups I reckon—fiver a piece an’ all.      Haha, yeah, I've been tryin’ to get fit too. I started doin’ Pilates, even though I keep thinkin’ why I'm not just taking me mat into the village and doing some lunges in the supermarket queue instead!      You and me both, love. Listen, on another note, how's work been?      It's a proper ball of chaos, I can assure ya. One minute I'm wranglin' dance-offs for staff conferences, the next minute I'm panicin’ cos the room isn't big enough for a PowerPoint presentation. But hey, it's a job, aye?      Some o’ us is just stuck in the real life here—me, I'm stuck with the telly an' a about five square inch conversation with the goldfish the wife gave me fer Christmas.      Oh! You know that goldfish! I remember it, unbelivable. I do take it personally that they called it Sid, though.      Aye, well, it's a nickname ‘n’ all. I tried givin’ it a proper one, Daisy, but he just ignores me. No matter, Sid it 'as been.      Some people, no respect for proper names.      Speakers, I reckon go out one night? Maybe if you've had a real proper pre-planned line in conversation, see if we can go further than the "did it rain yesterday" talk-over?      Love to, yeah. We 'ave to arrange something soon—go to that new pub in Cambridge or ‘nother, why not? I'll give yer a bell later an' we can sort out the finer points, yeah?      That 'as been the very idea. ‘N’ try not to cancel, I swear you ‘ave me datebook full already!      Ha! I would never do that. Side note: on that goldfish, if yeh need to give 'im a real holiday—end it.

Rather do the washing up now than leave it to tomorrow, lads. You’d think it'd been done by aliens and then reinfected after dining.      Fair enough, Liv. Let me grab the plates. I'll have you know, I picked up some world-class culinary skills in Seoul—well, passive observations more than practice—and trust me, if you leave dishes in the sink for a week, you might find your provisions grown legs and started socialising.      Can someone just do the bread bin again? It exploded when I opened it, and the bread was like bidding for its own miniature Olympics.      Honestly, the bread bin only explodes if you block the door with turkey legs. You’ve gotta leave it alone for a bit. Probably need to play psychiatrist with the bin, see what trauma it’s carrying.      Honestly, forget the bread bin, lads. Look at the mess with your Gameboy spaghetti across the table. Put it in the dishwasher, not the spare sock drawer.      By the way, Oliver, your Instagram is full of close-ups of your face with your facial hair stylised to grief. You sure that's not a meme page watching for unsuspecting teens to follow?      My Mate Joel showed me a chap with a goatee and a quote about brushing the wrong way. It was somehow profound and wrong at the same time. Now I’ve got ten thousand principles and two brows.      Let me guess, this chap is just one oddly-tattooed guy who’d rather have a documentary than real friends. Anyway, speaking of bizarre things to get fascinated with, your history about how you stumbled upon a tennis camp story the other week was bizarre but entertaining.      Yeah, that was grim! I mean, it snowed, and you had binoculars for 'strategic movement' and then passed out after sundown. I feared for your mental state for weeks. Do they even have glaciers in Germany?      Not to be morbid, but have you seen young men trying to 'improve' their lives by reading various edgy translations of  Mein Kampf ? It's like the 20 goths of my day, but more risk of losing a limb in ideological wars on the internet.      I dunno, what if some kid’s like, “I’m seriously into conservation and facial hair” and then ends up earnestly quoting belly photos from a third-rate militia blog? It's a crime.

Rather annoying I had to take the furniture to the tip meeself. That’d be such a mither if I was younger, mind you. I’m more used to just passing on the old stuff to a relative, but none of them wanted the armchair.      Aww, that’s a shame. I mean, it’s an older model but if it was in good nick they might’ve said yeah. Me nan still uses one that’s nearly got a pulse, but she refuses to get a new one. She says it was her mum’s when she was a kid or some bloomin’ thing.      Lakelands is always a good bet for new furniture, if you can afford it that is. Just wish I had somewhere big enough to put anything. Tenants, see – the flat I’m in is poky as a cupboard and I can barely move the washing machine without bumpin’ a wall.      Ah, I know precisely what you mean, love. I remember once, my cousin’s partner tried to give me a Christmas present directly from her Mum – it was some ugly Christmas bauble with a picture of Baby Jesus with quite a rude message. Did I tell you that one?      No, I didn’t hear about that. Sounds like a real knife?      Right cheery, really. But what are you supposed to do? Gift wrapping’s already done, and I didn’t fancy insultin’ the whole family by binning it. I put it up on the tree and my sister noticed it and thought it was a joke—piece of work, it was. I swear the beaver scouts had a better sense of decor at their Christmas party.      I went to a scout thing once too, but it was the older scouts, like the network scouts. Not that I’d really handle it now, not with finals comin’ up. Though I miss the tradition. My gran used to make me and my cousins go every year before she was taken ill.      Aye, I remember your gran. She had a bit of sprite to her, didn’t she? Always ready with a comment and a swearword if the kettle didn’t boil quick enough.      Still, I reckon goin’ on that journey from here to Macclesfield is made better just by having a chat between us. Who knows, maybe we’ll stop and get a cake somewhere nice. I’m sick to death of toast for breakfast every day.

: Right, Ma, long time no chat. Thought we could drive out to Ashford tomorrow for that DIY store, and pick up some tiles for the kitchen extension?     : That sounds a good idea, love. When do they start the fitters? I wouldn't want it to get held up again like when your daddy was laying the floor and handed over the paint roller to your cousin.     : Oh, don't remind me. His top was bleedin' pink by the time he sat down! Anyway, the fitters start on the 16th.     : Right, right. So, everything is going okay with your new job, then?      My new job? Oh, you mean the redundancy. It was a bit of a shock, yes, but I landed a new project co-ordinator role with an added bonus — a gym membership! So I've been trying to go religiously. Honestly, I used to live on crisps and milkshakes, you'd not believe the mess I was in.      I do, you know. But I’m not surprised they gave you a good package. You were always a sensible worker, careful with time and money.     : Well, thank you. I’m hoping to find something new before the end of the year, just to keep the momentum going.     : That's the spirit. And while you're looking after your health, maybe look after your grandad a little too. Let him have a real meal once in a while. Just make sure to stretch your legs before you climb into something with an engine!     : As long as I don’t belly-flop into the lake, I reckon I’ll be fine. We can meet up there if you'd like; I could do with a laugh, and you always looked like you'd enjoy a bit of flambéed chicken.

Right, so what's the plan for tomorrow? I don't wanna just stay in the house all day like I did last week. Maybe we could go for a swim? I need to actually start using that pool pass Grandpa got me.      That's a great idea, sweetheart. The pool’s only a few minutes from here, and the weather has been lovely. Maybe after the pool we can get an ice cream from Mary’s van? She always has those weird flavours, like that one with bits of blackberry and mint. You liked that one, didn’t you? I’ll hold the iron, maybe try to steam a t-shirt I don’t like anymore. But can I play  Stick with Mick  while we do it? I reckon the circle dance rhythm will make it more fun.      Mikey! Mikey! But let’s make our plans again so I don’t get lost in the day. So… we go to the pool, get ice cream, do some chores at home, then guitar practice?      And after that maybe we can go to the park? I saw that there's this new swing set at the green near the school.

Rather than chuck a DVD in eh, innit? Thought we'd catch up for a mo ‘fore plopping on a film? Just binn’t run down to Aldi for some chips ‘n a tin o’ sweetcorn. Aye, wasn’t no photographer, were ‘im! Looks like he’d bin told to not show ‘is teeth for a week!  laughs  I reckon ‘is crown shifted, only lik’e ‘avva bit of turkey on ‘is dinner!      Tenr, innit? You D’you pick up the dentistry patch? Or was it one of them free ones ‘in Norf, innit? I ‘ad one like that once in Leece.      Nah, didn’t have the qvall to bleed it off, so I bin doin’ a book, ‘xorcising some riddles, innit? ‘ave you read the one by that fancy bookshop in Liverpool One?      No, but I’m takin’ it in at the uni, chekin it for the students. Some of them reckon it don’t make sense ‘cos their accents are too Scouse!      Bloomin’ ‘ell, language is a bluddy trip! Could be a laugh! ‘ave we got enough to do with gig ‘planning, tre’ guest speaker in Liverpool next week. Binn’ told to sort it out quick. ‘ve you bin to the Cavern lately?      Couple o’ weeks back. They ‘ad a bit of a weird band, think it was ‘folk-rap’ o’ sommat. But the food ‘vver there, innit? go for a curry ‘after if you like a bit o’ spice.      You know I go ‘n’ on for the ‘curry and chips at Fatbobs? Binn’ there last week, nigh on cried over the belly, innit?      Yeah, why not? Aint like we’re goin’ up for a hike or anything, are we? Binn’t watchin’  The Right Stuff , yeh alright for that? Or want sommat lighter?      You decide, innit? I ‘ave nae clue, ever binn’ one for Netflix on my own. Go on then, blast it in.      Y’know what, I reckon we’ll ‘ave The Office US, innit? Analogue overload and a bit o’ cringe. Women ‘vver their we’re, and no lad’s ‘aving a laugh!

Rather skip the new job for a sec love, what about that Easter cake you made last time? The p... p... what was it called again? It was very fancy!      You mean petit fours? Not quite Easter appropriate, but I bet you loved them.      That's it, yeah! Made my mouth water just saying it. My Nan used to make a traditional Victoria sponge with raspberry, but I think that's a bit passe now.      Honestly, you can never go wrong with a Victoria sponge. But when are we talking? You know how many frozen cupcakes I had baked in the freezer? I used to live the life of a sugar-coated vagrant that March.      Fun for you, not for us, I had to scrape the icing off the microwave I think! But seriously, how did you find being a teacher? You were always the type for structure and organisation.      It was challenging, the first month was like, ordering lollipops and printing colouring sheets for twelve different classes over the weekend, but it's brilliant. The children are so full of beans, though their attention span is only ten seconds.      Makes you wish we'd been taught from the start that most kids – especiall ones with hyper motio – actually learn best by being up and about, yeah? It's a wonder you didn't use a trampoline in the classroom!      I wanted to, but my line manager wouldn’t even let me have a rubber duck. I think they’re still waiting to find me in the staff room being ‘fee-fi-fo-fum’.      Well, I’m proud all the same. And the christening this Sunday – did I tell you about the sister of that manager you told me about? The un-named one?      Your new friend guest speaker?      Not me, the one you told me was nice to drink with? Her little sister is waiting on a bridesmaid. She’s looking for something sprite-like. Websites mentioned space bunnies and a couple of whistles.      Still, I’m happy with anything except a man in a white goatee waving my hand over a suffocating child – give me air horns and popcorn, I’m brutal.      A bit your style, yeah. Alright, planning-wise, perhaps we can manage roles after the christening with the Easter garden clean up? I’ve had it in for two overgrown hedges on the front!      Fair enough Mother, if they come with flowers and soft mud, I'm always game for a bit of frost-free fun.

I can't believe it's been ages since we last met, Sarah. I was just telling my students about how I got to visit Birmingham often when I was at university. I miss this place. I might one day try applying for similar postgraduate courses for specialisation, though I'm quite content where I am right now.

Rather annoying to be honest, eh? You know, having to talk about freedom for eight whole nights when we're stuck in our own flat with the same lot. But I suppose it gives you a chance to actually  learn  what it's about, right?      Andrew, it’s not just "standing there passive". There's a reason we do each of these things — all the symbols on the table have meaning. I once hosted a Seder and got letters from friends who were  dying  to understand. We can't just gloss over it. Didn’t your mum teach you anything?      Honestly, Mary, I can handle a matzah, but don’t ask me about maror. I still can’t remember what order to do it in. Ten plagues, the Exodus, the bitter herbs, and I’m already headachy. It's like storytelling 101 for breakfast, but with more singing.      Oh come on, you lot. You think Passover’s complicated? Try eating in Italy and not knowing what  ortolan  is. One of my cousins nearly swallowed a whole one in one bite. You know, the tiny bird? It's traditionally eaten in a bag… watching it fight for its life in your mouth. So… dramatic.      I wouldn’t mind that for once — something a bit  more  exciting than four glasses of wine and a plate of brisket that’s basically wallpaper. Although, fair play, someone at our last Seder dropped a glass and panicked like it was a sacred relic.      I thought the wine bit was being overdramatic. I  mean , it’s because it’s about redemption, right? But redeeming our ability to drink responsibly? I had to stop my little cousin from knocking them all back at once.      Maybe we’re all just rebelling against the baked-in formality. I passed on going to London last weekend for a formal dinner at a kosher place called  Mykale . It’s on the South Bank. We could’ve had proper  p’tach im ramen  or some weird fusion thing. They do incredible  shakshuka .      You're missing the point. It's not about the food — well, not just food. But yes, I agree the rituals are important, but they need explaining, not mockery. And what your cousin did was… unkind. The Seder is meant to remind us of where we’ve come from and what we still fight for.      Look, I’m not dismissing it.

Rather annoying this, innit? These bloomin’ phones. I've had it in my case all week and barely turned it on. Just binn’t sorted out the networks yet. Rather annoying when the bar’s out of lager, innit? I was in this club ‘n’ all, and they only had cider. I’m more of a🍺 kind of gal, y’know? My cousin was showing me once, full tables, like terrines and puddings and Christmas hams. Everything roasted, it were like a feast!      That’s only because they properly celebrate it. Over here we’re stuck with mince pies and tinsel that’s been reused since 1982.      But there’s beauty in simplicity, darling. You know what I miss? When the hills were covered in snow, and someone would come knocking to sell bulbs for next spring.      I remember those door-to-door salesmen. Always had these strange beards and green outfits. I used to pretend there was a conspiracy about hidden transistors in the bulbs.      Both of you are reminiscing about the good old days, but I’m worrying about the future! What happens to the traditions, ‘cos I mean, if places like Bognor Regis were converted into hotels, who would remember them?      That’s what worries me too. My nan used to tell me how they used to light a fire in their barrio to keep the whole village warm. Now it’s all air conditioning and fake snow.      That’s because goon culture has seeped into our festivals. Just last week, I heard about a man trying to sell mulled wine in the park with what he claimed was ‘Eastern Arabic’ pronunciation. Ridiculous.      And I’ve had bellyful of racism myself. Once in the ‘80s, I was called a ‘weather voodoo’ because I refused to muck in with the corporate chemical Christmas lights.      Honestly, we should make a trip and try to combine our vibes.

Rather annoying the new series of  The Fall , don't you think? It's alright, but it pales in comparison to some of the older ones like  Foyle's War . I think I might take a break from detective dramas for a bit, to be honest.      I can see that— The Fall  has its moments, but it just doesn’t have the same… bite as a proper British noir from the 70s. I've taken to watching a few old episodes of  Inspector Morse  now and again. It helps me unwind after a long day of slogging through emails as an administrator.      Oh, I much prefer the BBC’s newer offerings, like  Death in Paradise . It’s light, but still clever—it’s good for when I need a laugh while I’m writing. Speaking of which, I’ve turned to a Kindle for most of my reading these days. It's just easier for me when I’m working late or on the move.      I quite like the portability of a Kindle too. Although I still enjoy the smell of a real book, especially when I’m proofreading transcripts. I find the physical sensation helps to sharpen my focus. It's strange, isn’t it, how we’ve all got such different little habits?      Definitely. I often wish I could read physical books more, but as much as I try, my work somehow always claws back at me. I’m already foreseeing a chaotic week, and I might just have to put in for some overtime.      That's oddly enviable. Some weeks I’d rather have a bit more admin and a lot less writer’s block! At least when there's a clear structure to fall back on, it’s less maddening. Have you had any particularly busy projects lately, Jackie?      Actually, it's unseasonably quiet at the moment, so for once I’ve got time for things like proper meals. I tried making that new recipe I saw on the BBC Food website last night—carrot and coriander soup. We should try it as a group one of these weeks—perhaps over the weekend?      That sounds lovely. I've been surviving mostly on sandwiches these days, like a man with no social life. But I'm up if you're making it.      Count me in too. It'll be a welcome break from my usual writing schedule. Shawna, have you made it to any new restaurants lately?

Rather a gray day, isn't it? That sun's been hiding all week. Don't you think it's got the lot of us in a bit o' a mood?      Yes, dear, it's been quite dreary, I must agree. I wouldn't mind a few proper bright days to clear my mind. I do miss the sunlight. Still, it's not all bad — a bit of peace and quiet never hurt anyone, did it?      No, not at all. Truth be told, I was just sitting here this morning thinking about how the days seem to zip by these days. You two are older-than-me, no doubt, but the years do slip by like water off a well-parked umbrella, if you ask me.      That's the truth, Harry. It really is. I think the world moves so fast most of us aren't even sure what we’re doing half the time. I mean, with all the clocks running and the news blaring, you'd think you'd have spare time to breathe. Goodness, I still remember when I owned that shop—ah, there was pace for you!      Did you ever close the doors, David, or just leave something on the shelf for a few days when the weather was too foul?      Oh, absolutely. I had to. There's something about a rainy morning in London that makes even the most determined of shoppers hide under bridges. Still, business carried on. People just wanted a bit of routine, I reckon. Makes them feel steady.      That rings a bell with me. I always worked from home when I was younger — nothing fancy, mind you, just a few odd jobs about the house. But it kept the money coming, and the independence meant a lot.      Independence is key, isn't it? At our age, the last thing we want is someone else telling us what to do.      Well said, Margaret. And it's not just about money, though that’s never far from the mind. It’s about dignity and control over your own life. Even small things count — a little freedom over your day, your schedule, your choices.      Pah! I say we enjoy the rain then, shall we? Fetch the cups of tea and forget about the gloom, eh? I don’t know about you two, but I’d rather be indoors with warmth than out in the rain.

Rather annoying that the recording of  Horace  only ends with five minutes to spare, don’t you think? It’s rather cutting it close for the party music to kick in properly.      I were thinking that myself! Should’ve sorted the playlist a bit earlier. But it’s not like eeny of us liked admit we’d be early, eh?      Honestly, I didn’t think about it. I just assumed the DJ or whoever was in charge would make sure it’s seamless. But now we’ve got twenty minutes and no clear timeline of what happens next.      I reckon we make the most of it. Grab a drink, wind down a bit, and contemplate that one turkey who managed to fly seven feet before the net caught him. Probably gon’ hear about it again at tomorrow’s debrief.      Actually, about the turkey — have we incorporated it into the press agreement? Because if not, I’m not at all happy about the chance someone hides it in the printing house and expects us to reloc it like we’d reloc a printer with a jam.      I mean, we did a similar thing with the cockroach infestation in the bindery in New York. We tried to keep it light, but eventually had to relocate – very carefully – with a series of jars, swatters, and huge quantities of mint tea. It was somehow professional and deeply disturbing.      That sounds like a right mess. I’d not want one of them blundering over my coffee table here. I’d definitely not want it landing in the cheese board. What’s next? The next animal – a  ferret  or a  pigeon ?      Oh come on, this isn’t a cooking show where they make you roast that turkey you barely relocate. This is a  press launch , not a wildlife reserve.      All right, all right. Let’s not get worked up over a few bloody turkeys. We’ve got bigger stuff to worry about – like who’s responsible for the  actual DJ player  not working.      I think we’ve got enough time to reach out to the tech crew again. This is a Cambridge publication, so go on then, make it about tradition or something.      I’ll do that. But before I send the message, has anyone else seen Mike’s latest email chain about fluency tests? Thought we decided we’d nix the surveys for tonight.      I have not seen it, but honestly, I’m half expecting a pop-up form to appear over the cheese board at any moment.

Rather annoying the new system at work. You know, the one we had to switch to for processing client requests... It crashed twice today, and I was already behind on my workload. I've been over this with management, but they don't seem to have a fix yet.      Honestly, it's beginning to grind my nerves too. I was organizing a client onboarding meeting when all the data disappeared. I’ve been having to delete documents and start from scratch. They gave us a week of training, and you’d think they’d have ensured the platform was stable before we even went live.      Right, I’ve heard you two talking about it before, but the real question is, do you have a workaround? I know I’m not in an administrative role or anything like that, but I’ve had enough of software issues in my day. A good sales system had an update once that nearly wiped our customer records. Funnily enough, I happened to have a spare in my car boot, thanks to my desktop being fiddly back then. Still got the CD, actually.      To be fair, we can still use the old version if we land a week’s notice. But only for two more weeks, they said… I reckon the IT team is in chaos. I mean, most of the bugs they knew about beforehand, didn’t they?      Yeah, and the worst part? We’re all supposed to be working remotely this week. Everything that isn't online has to be emailed back and forth. Honestly, I miss my office. It had its clutter, but at least you had the Wi-Fi working 99% of the time.      Work’s never quite as serene as you think it is when you’re the one stuck in it. Both of you take what you've got for granted. I used to take the lorry out every Thursday to deliver the goods, and for the first few years, I’d passed out by sundown. Still, I finished it every time. That’s discipline.      I appreciate the reminder, Mum. It’s easy to get caught up in what we don’t have versus what we do. At least the company took the grace period into account and hasn’t pushed too hard.      Actually, I need to reach out to our clients about next week’s timeline. If the system goes down again, we’ll need to let them know what to expect.

I can't believe today is here already. You've done more for me than you know, thanks for helping me with all the housework this week. I’m feeling ready for the operation, sure I’ll be fine. I've got £20 left in my bank account after the surgery. Hopefully, I can get on top of my bills after I’m out. Of course, anything for you, love. I only wish I could do more than this. I’ve heard about a few of the kids pulling pranks at school again. My daughter got into trouble last week when she was caught with a phone in class. It was her first detention. Teenagers, you know? That sounds like something my son Mya would do. He's always getting into mischief, much to my husband’s frustration. You'd think they’d be more mature by the age of 15, but no. He went out with some friends the other night to a cafe without a supervision in sight. When I asked him where he was, he didn’t have the decency to tell me. I still can't get over it. I know, I worry about mine too. She’s at that age where she'd rather sneak out to parties than sleep in. I tried to keep a light touch, but it's so hard when they start becoming more independent, and sometimes it feels like I'm losing the grip. It’s something you just have to ride out, I think. For what it’s worth, someone at the vet told me the other day that she's had treatment for cancer. It gave me a bit of motivation—life's too short to be stressing over every little thing. That does put things into perspective, doesn't it? I'll definitely keep that in mind. I'm cooking lasagne this weekend—you know that's your comfort meal. I’ll drop it off after my shift on Saturday. Burgers and chips for me, if that's all right? You’re a saint. Lasagne it is. I’ll owe you for that. I hope you get Saturday off as well. You've been working so hard lately with lunches and deep cleans. If I do have some extra cash after the operation, maybe I can persuade the bank to increase my credit limit. It’s on my to-do list.

Thought he’d ordered “a goon box” or something.      So summat! I seriously think we live in a world now where you can’t even order a pint without gettin’ it wrong, ‘cos people pronounce everything like they're in a dictionary... so what I'm sayin' is: where’s the fun in that?      Mate, I feel for you and the dirty work you're doin’. But no wonder you're good at it.

Rather annoying I had to cancel my trip to Scotland last month. My sister had her baby, and I couldn’t get the time off work. You’d think as a library assistant, I’d get a bit of flexibility, wouldn’t you?      Ah, bless you. Congratulations to your sister! Ireland’s nice at that time of the year, but family is always top priority. I actually went on a quiet holiday to Killarney last summer. The mountains were breathtaking. Oh, and the pubs—glorious!      I heard Killarney’s lovely, but the queue at the pub fetches ages for a pint! Not that I complain much, mind. I’ve only been up there once. But what’s a holiday without a pint?      Ten out of ten for the pubs, Viv, but I’ve been more into history lately. So I spent my last vacation at the Tower of London—relaxing place, very historic, and in summer, the gardens are ever so nice. Bit of a contrast to the hustle of the City, I’d say.      Libraries are usually full of history too, Sean, don’t forget. But still, I love a good old-school bookshop on holidays—it always beats a selfie at a landmark. Mind you, most of my books are borrowed, not bought, and none of them are on travel.      Haha, you and me both, Derek. Last year, I read the entire Br’nst’w books in one trip—Dublin. Perfectly content with just a good read and an occasional flan from the cafes. So much better than being crowded out at the Cliffs of Moher.      I respect the calm type of travel, Marie, but I’m more of a "sparkle and hustle" kind of person. Last summer I went to Blackpool for my cousin’s wedding, and for the record, yes, I did go on a funfair ride at 60. Older folks have got all the fun, I tell you.      That’s my good side, Viv. Let’s not forget, we've got to keep the youth in us. I took the kids to Six Flags once, and I nearly fainted on the rollercoaster. But really, holidays are about having a change of pace. Funfairs do tick that box, I’ll give you that.      Yeah, but what about the beach? I’ve been obsessed with the coast lately. Did you know Sullom Voe in Shetland has the clearest water in the UK?

I can't believe the new James Bond film isn't coming out until next year. I was hopin' to see it on the telly by now, like the good old days. Oh dear, we used to go to the cinema every week back in our day. We'd pop in after eeny and catch a matinée with the 'gram and auntie. Those were the days, aye. A real treat. I remember taking your grandma to the cinema, John. She'd always wear her best coat and carry a thermos of tea. She still has the ticket stub from the day they showed Mary Poppins. Found it in the attic last year, rolled up in parchment like a treasure map. Oooh, that was a beaut, was it not, Vivian? Made me laugh more than any film had done in years. And those dancing cherries! I happened to like the kitchen in this flat more, thanks ever so. No, you didn’t have a kitchen in the old days, we had a coal range and a scullery, and a separate tin bath that never worked quite right. Haha, still sounds better than my office canteen. I been eating from the vending machine most lunches – Mate, have you tasted that stuff? It's slap-up if you like the taste of cardboard and regret. Oh, I could cook you a proper Sunday roasting if you just gave me the time. Let me whip you a real beef joint, greens, Yorkshire pudden—piece of cake. Just mind the marshmallows on the pudding, I still make a bit of a mess of those about half the time. Oh come now, Jane, let the man be. He's got enough to do with managing the building site. Besides, he's got the bike, don't he? Aye, my '08 Trek. Good one, a few dents and the chain’s a bit worn, but it gets me everywhere. Tryin' to stay off the cars as much as possible with the cost of fuel these days. That's a proper bit of kit. My first bike was a ten-speed go-kart I cobbled together from a lawnmower engine and bits I scavenged from the scrapyard. I crashed into the garden wall the first time I tried to race it. The sparks were a sight though, mind you. You gave me a right heart attack with that ‘kart’ of yours, Vivian!

Rather annoying that half the class threw their pancakes away at lunch. I've had to discuss it with the head... What was the point of them making them if they don't even take a mouthful? Beans on toast is fine, but honestly, they have to learn what a proper meal is.      I didn't like mine because it was all thick and gooey. I wanted them like the ones you make, Mummy. With lemon and sugar and not funny squiggle bits.      Well, that was the standard school batch. If it was too runny, you could have frozen part of it for later. I've been saying for ages the school supply only has cornflour now and barely any eggs. You must insist on taking left-overs home.      D'you think Paris is in France? I asked Miss Betty in the library, and she said it is, but I thought it was in Anglo-France or in Protected-Valleyland where they have lots of scientists and puffins.      Paris  is  in France, yes—personally I visited it twice last year while we were teaching in the Festival Hall and the Science Museum. Rather brilliant there. The kids were fascinated by the rhythm of light from the lasers. Though I'm not sure Little Jimmy will remember, least of all the other children who are growing up without basic kitchen skills and end up not eating their food!      What's a puffin?      Let's not get into a long story now. We do need to think about the weekend—what do you say to a weekend trip to the museum  again ? This time we could do the Green Knowe tour. You remember the talking wall and the ghost larder?      I do! I think the larder was run by children who were poor and couldn't buy food, so they had to make food with rocks and candlelight.      Do scientists use larders too?      Not really, as such. Though they do live in poverty in some parts of the world. But we must brush our teeth now, and you must wash your hands. We're eating the rest of the goopy pancakes on toast tomorrow if you don't mind. Then beach day—if the tide is out, we might be able to see the rocks where the puffins live. So all in all, it's been a good Pancake Day. Even if the pancakes had gone to waste.

Rather do I! The other day, I sat with old Mr. Pembroke in the garden — you remember him, don’t you? The one who used to tend the rose beds by the church. He told me that in the 1940s, children would come with their mothers to pick vegetables from his plot and that he’d give them extra if they handed over a drawing for his cat, Nell. Rather sweet, wasn’t it?      Oh, aye, Nell! That damn mischievous cat was always causing mischief. Didn’t even blink when the new council car came to clear the rubble after the floods. I can still recall her sitting on the windscreen, licking her paw like that Myra, mistress of the house, had left her a tonic water! I’m glad I’m not on the council anymore — not enough discipline now.      Cats do have character, don’t they? I’ve been thinking of getting one in my new house, you know, in that little conservatory looking out onto the patch of lawn I managed to keep after the builders left. Though I hear some of the newer houses near the motorway have a rather temperamental water supply. Something to do with the council’s drainage work.      That’s putting it lightly! My father’s new bungalow near the school has had three plumbers in a week. He nearly had a heart attack when the phone line was disconnected because one of the builders thought the cable looked redundant. They had to call in a specialist from Exeter.      Nothing surprises me with these newfangled houses. Back in my day, you built with brick and mortar, not this flimsy balsa-wood stuff. I remember when I first retired, my wife Jane had me teach a weekend class for young accountants. Not that I’d say it helped them any — handled numbers the same, but for the life of them couldn’t balance a simple ledger. A bit like me grandkids nowadays with their telephone things.      I know what you mean. We had to have a family discussion over dinner the other night because two of the children couldn’t spell the word "neighbour." Not because they’re careless, mind — it’s just that the context of actual goings-on on the street are getting swallowed up by the screen world.      You might be on to something there. I’ve been told that the latest experiment at the university has to do with how attention is distracted when you speak to people in the new type of driverless car.
