I’d like to know just  exactly  what’s goin’ on with all them tax breaks for the rich.      It’s all in the papers — full of jargon. I don’t pretend to understand half of it. I do what I can, but it’s a stretch sometimes. Any tea left, love?  Sips a cup of tea.  I did catch a news review the other night, talking about all this “cost-of-living crisis” nonsense. Going stir-crazy trying to find out if it’s real or just another spin.      I do watch Question Time once in a while. They do a good job of holding politicians’ feet to the fire, but it’s always the ones with the best PR, not the best ideas. Honestly, I’d rather read the gossip mags and watch a good drama like Broadchurch. At least you don’t get informed with hot air!      Aye, well if you ask me, real talk is always better than spin, no matter how comfortable. I’ve got Time Team on tonight — better than half the political puffery I see.

Rather skip the telly tonight, love. That drama on earlier was a bit of a letdown, if you ask me. Never mind them bickering yet another time! How was your day, by the way?      No, I saw it! I wouldn’t say it was the worst I’ve ever seen, but I’m with you, it did drag on toward the end. My day? Usual chaos, I’m afraid. Got a call from a new charity contact this morning. They’re supposed to be wanting to support the cause, and what do they ask first? Whether I’ve got tea for the meeting. Honestly!      That’s odd! I supply tea for people on the daily and they don’t even bat an eye. Wait, so is this a new path to funding then or what?      A bit of both. It seems like they’ve got something better than breakfast, but not quite enough to commit. Fund raising is like fishing at the best of times, love — bait, wait, hope. Also, the old ones, bless, keep asking for the same thing every other week. It gets a bit samey, honestly.      And then, my co-worker’s in a flap because she missed work last week, and now she's negotiating her – what do you call it – her leave, because her other job is piling up. Now don’t get me started on that.      That’s not the first time I’ve heard someone juggle two jobs and two lives. You’d think they had more time to do one properly, but no — it's a wonder these people still look as sprightly as they do come Monday.      I agree. I sometimes wonder if the problem is that people are too quick to take on more and not quick enough to learn to say no. But anyway, enough of my tales. How was  your  day?      Honestly, it was just the usual sort of day. Catching up with Mum again. You know, I miss when she used to come round to our place and stay over. She’s getting grandkid crazy again, I think.      Was it Annabelle who set her off again with that tale about the baby's first go-kart on the lake? She's not going to give it up, is she? It becomes a dream every time, I swear.      Indeed. It's like I live with Santa and Father’s Day every other week!

Rather annoying this wet weather, eh? You know, in Cambridge we’d have just wrapped up with a nice cup of tea and some quiet reading. I’m feeling under the weather a bit today, nothing serious, probably just this damp Polish air getting to me.      Honestly, it’s not half miserable outside. I’ve been runner’s sore all day just walking about the flat! Though I don’t suppose that counts as proper exercise. I had this terrible chesty cough last week, started after I came back from the UK for my uncle’s funeral. Funny how being home, or what I think of as home, seems to get to you.      Oh, I’m so sorry to hear about that. Funerals are such tough trips. I left London a few years back, didn’t look back, but I still feel sad every time someone I know goes back for one. I can never quite decide if I miss it or just resent the memory of it. The funny thing is, you ever looked at photos on social media of London and think, oh why did I ever leave?      Oh, I know what you mean. I did quite a bit of therapy back home when I first moved out, just to deal with the loneliness. But it’s curious how you can still feel at home here. I love the vibe in Tarnow, even if the rains never let up. It’s somehow homier than I expected. I teach English online, so I can live anywhere. But what about you? You said you teach privately sometimes?      Yes, occasionally—more like dabbling now. I’ve worked in a lot of jobs over the years, from office work to administration, about five decades ago. I prefer the teaching, though. It makes me feel useful. I suppose you could say I know what I like and I’m trying not to regret not working full-time. But I’m not bitter.      That's so true. I think the most important thing is being happy with the life choices you make. I remember once I did a TV show about jobs and I came to the view that the ideal job was one where you were appreciated and felt like you contributed. That's where I am now.      Oh, go on then, spill it about your future plans.      Well, I’m actually thinking about a small trip somewhere warm soon.

Rather annoying the queue was at the pub earlier, wasn't it? I was just trying to get a nice cup of tea and some nibbles after work.      Yeah, I mean, it is a cash-and-carry kind of place, so you can't really expect it to be rush-hour-free every single time. But honestly, they should open an extra till if it gets that busy on a Thursday. A shame, because I love that place.      It was quite worth it once we got to the table, though. Those scones are always the perfect size—not too big like you get in some cafes. I can't get enough of the jam, either.      Honestly, I’d marry that jam. It’s like someone just spooned London’s best memories into a jar. Made me think of the little sandwich shop near uni, by the way. Do you know, I haven’t been back since last term ended?      Oh, you miss being a student, don’t you? I remember when you were still taking classes and getting free coffee and being loved by all your lecturers. You’ve been a bit busier since you started working on that survey design project.      Honestly, it’s got its charms. I'm doing part-time at the same university I studied at, ironically enough. Some of my old tutors don’t even know what I look like now. I blame the mask situation. But, yeah, it feels weird not having an exam season every few months.      I definitely understand what you mean—there's a weird comfort in the routine, even if it does make your brain feel like it's been flammable at times. I envy you a bit, really. I’m back to being a copywriter and not having any chance of ever having a week off.      My, my! When did you turn sour on your dream job?      Hey, don't assume I don’t love it. I do, for the most part. We just run into clients who can’t tell the difference between good copy and a random dog sitting behind a computer. It’s the creative equivalent of telling your cat where to shoot its laser!      That sounds brutal. I get it though.      Finally, someone who knows what I go through daily. You'd be surprised what a comfort it is to talk to someone who also had to endure the full buffet of Oxfordshire mornings and then came to London to find it even more overwhelming over here.

Rather annoying to be woken up by two over-excited children at the crack of dawn, if you don’t mind.      It isn’t  that  early, Mummy! Look, it’s half-past seven! That is  very  early, though.      I can  do  a tricycle wheelie on the tricycle! Proper one! Like a proper circus person! I bet they do that too, don’t they, Mummy?      Well done, sweetheart, but for now, let’s get changed and then we can talk about the plans for the day, yes?      I want to go to the Neon Moon event at the festival park! I saw jelly and glitter bursts and ultra slow-motion dancing on the poster!      Oh, the Neon Moon—sounds like it could be nice. I hadn’t even heard of it earlier this week. What did you think, Thomas?      I saw the flashlights and the disco lights. I like the bloke in the bunny suit, though. He can do cartwheels in two different sizes!      Hmmm. Well, there’s something to consider—and it may be a little crowded. So let’s see – we’ll have to have some food and snacks because the journey there is a fair one. Now, who wants pancakes for breakfast, or would someone prefer ‘crumpets’ with jam and butter?      Crumpets sounds like what a kangaroo might eat. I remember Mummy saying the Australians have a word for delicious and it’s  arvo , but that’s when they say it in about five o’clock.      Actually, “arvo” is short for “afternoon,” but I like the way you think, love! Maybe we’ll have something a bit more like baked beans for that “Australian-style” lunch later on. Just kidding—though it is a popular cuisine there!      I am going to learn a balancing act! Like tightrope walking or holding a tray full of lunches and not dropping them!      That sounds hard, but I bet you are like a man with a magic go-kart on wheels!      Show respect, both of you, but yes, Thomas could go further than the Go-Kart Road if he’s lucky!      Can we wear costumes to the Neon Moon, like neon dresses or glow tattoos?      We’ll see—maybe glow sticks will do for now, so we don’t have to get changed a dozen times. Right, come on—let’s get our clothes on and make a plan of the day. It’s going to be a shiny, sparkly, busy one!

Rather annoying this new road tax policy, isn't it? I've yet to hear a single convincing reason why it's necessary beyond some vague environmental promises. It's not as if small publishers like the ones I work with suddenly have cash lying around to afford the hike.     Debates about environmental priorities and fiscal responsibility often seem to clash, but I do think it depends on how the funds are used. If the money is actually going towards improving public transport or incentivising clean energy, then arguably it’s reasonable. Still, I'm not blind to the burden it places on lower income households. Particularly families living in rural areas without robust transport options.      Honestly, I don’t think the politicians are doing anything to help. I’ve met enough interns and students who spend most of their time watching the government argue with itself instead of doing what’s needed for people. It feels like they’ve forgotten what it’s like to be in ordinary working life.      Oh, don’t get me started! I remember my father’s stories of the 1980s coal strike. He worked near Castleford, loved it, but the impacts of short-sighted policies were brutal. It’s only now, with the book projects I get to handle, that I see a little of the way things might change – through culture and education. Sometimes, I think that's the best we can do.      Education has always been a powerful lever. When I was at Aberystwyth for my undergrad, I found discussions rooted in history and tradition made me consider the political present oddly clearer. You can’t ignore the past if you want to understand the here and now. I’ve had many debates with colleagues about whether we’re influencing the next generation enough.      We were talking about that in my politics class! Our professor said that understanding your own national and family narrative is crucial in developing critical thinking. I realized reading about the National Eisteddfod and Welsh Revival wasn’t just academic—it was personal. My great-grandfather was a disappointed nonconformist waiting for a new leader. It makes you question how much of our heritage is always trying to catch up with the times.      That’s very Welsh, in a way. Pondering the past while gripping the present. I remember your father telling me once about walking from Nantyglo in the snow, between jobs.

Rather than share a new story today, I've decided to do something a bit different—the Linton Book Festival is coming up in a couple of weeks, and I thought I'd take the kids along. It's a lovely little event with storytelling sessions and book stalls. You two might find some new books to read at home!      Do they have   Helen Moss   stories there? I liked the one where the little girl talks to the clouds! I want to read that again.      Can we go to the story corner and get ice cream when it's over Mummy? I saw frozen waffles last time!      That's the plan, yes. There's a well-known local storyteller called Marco who does a fantastic performance on the last day, and I've booked us tickets for that. I think he even has a story about a giant storytelling bear.      Oooh, a bear! Does it talk like a real bear, or is it more like, you know, a story bear?      Ah, clever question, luv. I think Marco takes inspiration from stories we all know as kids and remixes them in his own way. He probably writes his own books, too. Maybe we can spot one of his at the book stall and buy it for you both. Any preferences?      I want a bear story! With pictures and glaciers and—do they have hot cocoa in the glacier?      Well, if they don’t, I can always suggest it to the author—Marco’s very responsive.      Mummy, I’ve had an idea. Maybe we can write about our own story while we’re there. Like, the one where we had our tea party in the woods! You know that one with the squirrel and the muddy car boot?      Oh, that’s perfect! We can make it a fun book and maybe even leave a copy at the event entrance as a little present for someone else.      Can Daisy be in it too? She’s a very good listener and she likes mushrooms.      Of course, Daisy will be a star character. We’ll make the story special because it's really about your own adventures. How does that sound?      It sounds brilliant. I can’t wait until the weekend already!      I’m going to build a bear out of doughnuts for practice, just in case!      Very creative lad—Marco’s going to be very impressed when we meet him!

Rather annoyingly, I haven't been able to get hold of decent cruelty-free vitamins in the chemist. I got the vegan kind once, but now they're completely sold out. I've been over this with Clara, we both think we're pretty strict vegans—no fish, no dairy, no processed meat—but then we can't even find the proper vitamins!      I know, that's a bit of a shame, but I think that's just a result of the market not being as regulated there as it could be. Maybe you could look for online suppliers? I get a lot of vegan stuff from these little UK health stores online, and they've always been pretty transparent.      On the other hand, you know, I’ve actually been thinking a bit more about cultured meat lately. I watched this documentary on it last week, and it turned out that lab-grown meat could actually be part of the plant-based movement in a weird way. It still uses animals in production, sort of, but not in the way you'd think.      That is fascinating, I mean I do like the idea of shmeat—there I go saying that again!—but still, I'm not sure how I feel about eating something that's basically a by-product of cells from a live animal. It does sound kind of sci-fi, but still, it's way more ethical than the current system of factory farming and all the cruelty involved.      And I suppose the environmental argument for it is pretty strong. I read a report recently saying that producing a kilo of beef can require up to tenfold the water it would take to make a kilo of meat using cell culture techniques.      Yeah, I agree. I mean, I know it still has a way to go before it's accessible and not prohibitively expensive, but I think the future is headed in that direction. I just wish farmers could be retrained rather than being forced into obsolescence.      Oh, I was thinking about that the other day. It’s a little bit like transitioning out of fossil fuels—there has to be a system in place to take people who depend on the old industry and help them move into the new one. But honestly, with the way things are going, even govt support on that front is pretty patchy.      Yeah, and I think it's also the same with the food industry.

Rather annoying the new washing machine still hasn't arrived, isn't it? I was hoping it'd be sorted before we crashed out for the night. Otherwise poor Jonny's going to be left with socks that are see-through at the heels.      It's been like that since before Christmas, and all the holidays, I swear. It was ridiculous enough with the old machine's dithering on a high spin cycle before it flatly died one too many times. Still, it gives you a chance to introduce that new one you've got coming.      The kids love the one you bought, but honestly, even they've made comments. I swear Jonny’s taken to hiding his socks in my sock drawer since the laundry room disaster last week. Speaking of, you haven't told me the full story of Aunty Elinor’s New Year’s Eve party last year — the one where she almost breakfasted with the prime minister thanks to some dodgy inflight snacks and a bottle of non-alcoholic prosecco, have you?      Oh, that was a monumental do, truly. We were meant to be up at Aunty’s by 8, and we only made it by 10:30. Over half the guests were asleep from the “energy drink” – Matey Mix, I think it was, swilled with Prosecco. The prime minister’s car did turn up for some reason. Turns out one of the volunteers thought the toilets overflowed in the kitchen — full-blown emergency.      That's oddly British, isn't it? Also, have either of you seen the new series on BBC iPlayer — the one about the village where people about to die randomly walk out the front door to touch the sun? Very strange vibes. I’ve only watched the first two episodes, but I've already started questioning the universe.      Oh, I watched the first episode last night — it's bonkers, but I finished it before going to bed. I had to Google if there was a theme or a hidden message. It's as mysterious as our Aunt doing a jazzercise routine with a cactus on her head during the wedding last year.      That wasn't a cactus, that was gooseneck pond weed from the garden — and don’t forget, she was in a licorice dress.      Either way, it’s unforgettable. I take it seriously, really, though, we need to start thinking about our garden clean-up this Easter.

Rather unusual to see butterfly forks on the table, aren't they? I was just wondering if they’re part of some design choice or just randomly picked up at a market. Not something I've seen in years!      They look like something from fairy tales. Are they special for a reason? I saw them at a fancy event last year, but I haven't had the chance to use one since.      Dad, what's a 2-minute silence? Miss Thompson mentioned it in class today. We had to be quiet for two minutes and chase it, but nobody told us why. Was it to remember something?      Ah, the 2-minute silence. It's like a moment of reflection, especially on Remembrance Day. People take two minutes to think about the fallen soldiers, those who died and those who served. It’s quite an important tradition in the UK.      That’s deep. I didn’t know. I thought it was for the Queen!      Haha, not quite. Though we do remember monarchs and national events—personally, I associate the 2-minute silence quite a lot with the Queen and the warmth of old-school traditions.      But it’s only people who left the country or died?      Not just that. It’s also for peace, and sombre moments in history—like the Sillet Stones or the Russian invasions. Though we’d better keep politics out of dinner, yes?      Why? It just sounds oddly sour. Anyway, hotter topic— Mom, when's your real birthday? The card at the Mantle says one thing, and your Apple Calendar says another. Which is the real story?      Both are. The one you normally celebrate is because that was the actual day I was born. The one in my secret diary, well, let’s just say it’s my “spiritual sundown” at 6 a.m. on the 7th.      You’re 47. How do you  still  have 7th birthdays?      More importantly, how do you still not know how candle blowing works around cake tarts?      But I thought life improvements stopped after 11.      It only stops if you stop eating cake or learning.      Exactly. So maybe I’ll throw a conference with roles in Cambridge where those 2-minute silences, birthday circles, and yes—butterfly forks—can co-exist!      The fork first, then the cake?      And 2 minutes silence after each slice?      That’s the plan. Let’s just remember to keep the conversation light… even if we’re mixing Russian history, birthdays and cutlery.

Rather than going up north this year, do you think we could do something closer to home, like Cornwall? I remember the kids were really taken with the Adventure Island series we watched a few years ago, and there are some beaches there that would be perfect for building sandcastles and spending the day by the sea. Has anyone ever been there?      Cornwall is brilliant! My grandma used to take me there with my Aunty. I love the coastline and the seaside towns; it makes me feel like I'm on a real adventure. We could go for walks along the cliffs, or maybe even try some of those little seaside cafes with fish and chips—though I don’t suppose the vegetarian supply there is very vast.      I’d love to go to the beach! But I can't eat fish because of my food intolerance, and I’m allergic to shellfish. So if we’re going to do something like breakfast, can we make sure to bring some supplies or find a place that has vegetarian options?      Of course, love—and I’ll pack sandwiches, too, so you don’t have to worry about what’s on the menu. I know a couple of great places with gluten-free and vegetarian options. Have either of you heard anything about the V&A exhibition in Bury St Edmunds? I remember it’s been showing some interactive installations and art pieces for families, and I thought maybe we could make a day out of it before heading to the coast.      That’s a great idea. I think one of the exhibits is inspired by nature and the sea, which would definitely tie in with our Cornwall trip. It could be a good way to inspire imaginative play and make the adventure feel more real before we even get there.      Exactly! And speaking of real-life adventures… I’ve been marking some GCSE English exams this week, and it’s killing me—I can barely do basic math without overcoding someone’s essay. But if I can survive this marking season, maybe by the time we get to Cornwall, I’ll have forgotten all about them!      Ha, good luck with that! Let’s just hope the break with lunches on the beach and watching the tide go in and out helps you forget all those essay rubric codes.      I bet it does! Nothing like sand in your shoes and salt in your hair to reset the brain after a weekend of comma splices and archaic vocabulary.

I can't believe today's History class. Mr. Thompson gave us another essay on Winston Churchill, and it's like we don’t have anything else to talk about from the 20th century! Honestly, I feel you. Churchill is cool and all, but like, two essays in a row? I almost spilled my drink while he was going on about the “Few” speech again. Yeah, but he's one of those teachers who believes in repetition. It's kind of annoying, but maybe we’ll end up understanding him better. Still, I'd rather write about something more recent, like maybe the Troubles or something. At least then we'd get to talk about what’s still affecting people today. True. And I’m not the only one who feels this way. Lisa was complaining about it to me in the library. She says it’s like, no teacher actually wants to understand our perspectives or make the topic interesting. That's what teachers do sometimes. They get stuck in their ways. Last week I overheard Mr. Patel being inappropriate in class—somebody actually reported him. You know he still got grief from the Head for being too lenient on us. Oh no, what happened? He just said, like, it was “exhausting” to have to deal with us all the time. Honestly? I understand he's tired, but we’re doing the best we can with the workload. That's harsh. He’s not the worst—Mr. Johnson is a nightmare. I can’t be around him for more than 20 minutes or my allergies go through the roof. Same! I’m waiting for the vibes from today’s Prefect meeting. Sarah told me we’re organizing the upcoming House party, so I hope the food isn’t going to be like, all nut-based. I actually can't have that. If Sarah's in charge, I think we’ll be fine. She’s good at delegating stuff and keeping things professional. Even if it’s just lunches and a couple of games, the party last year was actually fun. Yeah, and the movie we watched in the common room after wasn't bad either. Any chance of action movies this year? I’m really into those. Only if your eyesight’s good at 10 paces. I still can't get over those jump scares though. Tell me about it.

Blimey, I've just seen this load o' roadworks on the A19 again — it's a proper nightmare trying t’get into Sunderland these days. I’ve had t'veer into Gateshead and it’s chock-a-block. Y’wanna take the motorway again? Yeah, I'd rather take the motor than get stuck on that A19 snarl-up. I’ve been working from Durham this week and that lot’s a proper hassle. If I’d known it was gonna be this bad, I’d’ve cycled instead. Oh, you won’t get far on a bike around these parts, Mark. That lot o’ roads are still potholed and they’ve barely done no proper resurfacing. I left mine in the shed last winter and I reckon it’ll still be there when I get back from uni. Fair enough. Though if we’re on the subject of wheels, have you caught the cricket in the park this week? The lads from my office were saying it's the best they've seen since the summer tour against Australia. Yeah, Lucy and I went down two Saturday’s ago. It was proper hot, but the game was brilliant — Durham bowlers were on it. I reckon they've got a good crack at the county championship this year. I wouldn’t mind a bet on them, if the weather holds. You and betting’s a bad combination, Rach. Still, if they carry form from this summer into September, they might surprise a few. Speaking of form, have you had a chance to go over the corpus tool updates? I need to double-check some data flow stuff for your colleague, Neil. Yeah, I sent the revised schema to Neil last Tuesday. I had to tweak a few things after the system crashed that data plug-in. It was a proper faff, to be honest, but at least the processing time's down now. I’ll let him know if he needs a hand testing it any further. Cheers, I’ll pop him a note this afternoon to clear up some of the filters. And if you fancy a proper break from the whole lot, the cricket’s on again Saturday. Still got a couple of passes left if you fancy watching the away game. I’ll take that up, love! Just let me not crash into that lot of lorries on the motor on the way.

I can't believe we've never done this before. Tonight is going to be the night—the night we finally order Chinese food and discover what we've been missing out on! Yeah, I mean, it's not like it's rocket science, is it? We just pick something off a menu and phone it in. But honestly, I’m excited. I’ve been craving something other than leftovers for days. Spare us the dramatics, Evan. But honestly, I'm with you. I’ve never been a fan of Chinese takeout before, but now I’m thinking maybe the problem has just been my frozen takeaway chicken with lettuce balls. Tonight is our culinary renaissance. Fabulous word choice, Myra. Let’s start with some basics. Jamie, what do you usually get from the Chinese places? Oh, the usual. Curry prawns, sweet and sour chicken. Wait, does Thai chicken count? I mean, it's on the menu at the place I use? No, no, no—Chinese food, Jamie. It's important we do this properly. Okay, I think we need to make a plan. Let’s start by agreeing on the type of food we want. Are we going traditional or are we open to fusion? Fusion, I’m in. Let's just go with something spicy. I’ve been craving hot wings or something with that kick. I’m done with boring stir-fry chicken and broccoli. That’s a dangerous crowd. You just might wish you’d stuck to the boring stuff when you're halfway through a red-hot delicious melting pot of heat and regret. Ooh, I love hot food. Let’s all be a bit daring tonight. We can mix things up a bit. How about ordering one spicy dish each and a couple of classic dishes as well in case the spiciness overpowers us? Perfect compromise. Now, let’s open the app. Any suggestions? I see Dragon Garden, which has some decent reviews. Dragon Garden sounds good. I’ll propose we split the order: one Peking duck wrap each, one Szechuan hotpot , and one deep-fried spring rolls for everyone. Sounds delicious, Catherine. I’ll go along with that. If anything, your suggestion alone will make this the best Chinese night yet. Well, that was easy. Just like that, we’ve planned our gourmet Chinese meal over text at the last minute, like the true professionals we are.

Rather annoying the new folk in the flat next to mine, they’ve got this German-looking bloke in a... got to be some sort of German organisation, more or less, comes by once a week with a clipboard doing some sort of checks or whatever, and the children! They wouldn't be out of their house een if the place wos on fire. Not like   we’re   bothered about all that noise most a' the time, but still—      Is that a new blocks of flats near you? My sister moved to sommat like that when she came from Finland. She told me the housing... like, it's brand new, everything is spotless, but the people, they’re quiet, and they do what they're told. It seems... eccentric to me, you know? I’m from Liverpool, I can’t imagine not having a bit of loud music coming through the walls at 10 o'clock breakfast, no doubt about it.      Oh aye, you ever looked at that, you'd think it's a drug den. I dunno, I mean I do like the way it's built, but the people in there, well, as I said, they’re real quiet. Like maybe they’re on watching for the police.      Hmm. My partner works in the Royal Liverpool Hospital, and sometimes it feels like the whole NHS is like sommat of a German model too—so much paperwork, so much procedure, so little soul, you know? They've got to be trying their best with everything they've got, but it’s so... impersonal.      You worked in it yourself?      Oh aye, nearly about ten year’s now. And you? With English lit and all, you must be a bit of a reader?      Aye, aye, I like the older stuff. Dickens, Poole, that sort of thing. Bit different from health checks and clipboard men.      Oh, I tried Dickens once, waiting for a friend who was visiting from Germany. I gave up after a chapter.      Aye, the old language can be a bit much sometimes, I grant you that. But the points the man makes—about the system, about people being left behind—that's still relevant, even in the NHS, I'd say.      True enough. It's all very well having the best system in the world, but if you can’t get people to trust it, to engage with it, then you're wasting good effort and money.

Rather a lot goin' on, innit? Seems like everything's on edge 'round here these days... What d'ya make of the welfare system, eh? I mean, sure, it's there to help, but with all the scrunity and the lot of 'em now gone automated, it feels eeny weeny passive-aggresive, like they want to trip you up as much as help.      Ay, that's just the way of the world now, innit? When I were a youngster, the dole was a given if you was out of work. No tests, no three-line essays. Just showed up and got a pound. Now, it's lik' "If you want the turkey, you gotta prove you ain't got no belly." Ten years I ain't worked and I can tell ya, I ain't turned into a violent criminal in that time. Cats would better off plantin’ a garden 'n worryin’ about some form.      There we go, right? I say to me students, over and over, "Education is the key, lads, it's the ticket outta short streets." But as much as I say that, I wonder ... Times are odder now. My neighbour got turfed out of the utility provider's office – cheeky bloke mistook her accent for foreign and thought she was “illegally accessing benefits.”      Oh, that's a cracker! What d'ya 'spect someone with a Liverpool accent should be doin' in a room full o' sour-faced officials with clipboards, hey? Probably shouldn' be talkin' at all – speak  too  loud and you invite a question. I'm walkin' down the street and the coppers keep an eye on me like I've got a grudge against Parliament. I'm just out for a constitutional, for Pete's sake!      You're not wrong about the police. They could be a bit less... selective, innit? I don't mind them restricting when it's fair, but there's a  tone  to how they speak to certain folks 'cause of the way they talk or where they come from. Even you and I, as old tarts with the same dialect, go out and get treated differently if you've had a fight at the pub than me in a jumper and a blazer. That bloke yon what your son-in-law?      Ay, Christopher? Poor lad. He comes 'round every Sunday, brings a cheap bottle of lager and overcooked chicken. Cares more 'bout        Arry, luv, the chicken is irrelevant.

Rather annoying the queue at the canteen today, innit? I was starvin’ ‘n all... got to wait ‘age for a chicken pie. Blows me mind what they charge for a tin lid nowadays.      Oh I know what you mean, but honestly, I skipped it and grabbed a sandwich from the café instead. Not as good as the chicken pie mind—more of a plain white bread affair—but at least I got in and out quick.      I had a salad bar. Know how to make me swoon when you chase it with a pot of tea? It’s like, decent enough if you ignore the slight chilli oil dripping the dressing had.      [laughing] You all crack me up. I’m from the States, so I still think of a pastry and omelette as the height of sophistication at lunch. They’ve got something better here? Egg and bacon sarnie happened. Not a bad thing if you ask me.      Honestly, I’d say the sarnies over here are blooming terrif, but you get what you pay for—some are dodgy, others are as good as you get. For instance, today’s mushroom on sourdough? Mate, it was out of this world. I might just be holding out for that same one every day.      Yeah, somethin’ to be said for the charmin’ bits ‘n bobs that make sense in the heat of someone’s kitchen. Though I’m still trying to track down the staff canteen at the Press that had the better scones and real butter. Anybody know if that place still exists?      I heard they moved the setup to a different area last month. I haven't checked it yet, but maybe you should be heading that way instead of the regular lunch hall?      Should we be discussing treacherous food deserts or actually working on the language corpus by the time we clock out?      C’mon, RELAX. If we crack this good lunch and end on a high, we've probably just lunches our way into speaking English better. Not bad for 50 quid a plate.      That's the go, really. It's about savourin’ the little things.      Hopefully, they'll update the bean soup recipe soon. ‘Cause aside from the summat-somethin', it's one heckin’ of a lukewarm bellyache.      Agreed. I mean, food and dialect—they both can be tricky, so let's be thankful for those that do it right.

I've been meaning to ask you, mate — what d'you think about that new BBC series they’re piling out on iPlayer? It’s got me more hooked than football on a Sunday afternooon. Oh yeah, I saw what you were on about — it was on iPlayer? I thought I’d seen it somewhere before, but I reckon it's not as gripping as most. I’ve only watched half an episode before I lost interest. Still, easier said than done when it’s just sat there waiting to be watched, innit? Didn’t even get round to it at the weekend... like, I had better plans. Well, I'm still loving it — and you know what’s great? You don’t even need to watch it live. Probably, the real strength of the internet these days is that you can relax and catch up at your own pace. Cats at home, breakfast, no interruptions. I've been doing that a bit in my gap between thesis chapters. Ah, spare time! I know why you need it, man — I do envy you a bit, working on that PhD. I never thought I’d see the day someone like me actually  enjoyed  reading research papers for fun. But it does make me humble. I’m at the stage where I often just feel like I'm swiping through academic copies while the kettle boils. It’s not as romantic as you’d think, eh? Fair enough. I mean, at the end of the day, it's just a job, like any other. You just try to make it a bit more intellectually delicious. But you know what I’ve been thinking about, though? How people about the world learn languages these days. I watched this documentary — something on Africa — and it made me ponder how diverse their pickups are. One child grew up speaking three languages by the time they were six. That’s nuts. I did basic French and Spanish at school, and even that was a chore. Whereas these kids just pick them up organically. Makes me wonder if we should be teaching languages to kids a lot earlier here. I mean, the whole English-dominated world doesn’t really let it happen for us, does it? We’re too proud of the one go-to tongue. But it would do our kids a real service in the long run.

Rather chilly this mornin', innit? Thought me ‘n the missus’d pop ‘round first thing wi’ a spot o’ tea an’ a few scones, sure we’d best get this flat sorted before the rest o’ the mob drift in wi’ their muddy boots an’ muddy ideas een!      Thanks, Nan. I reckon me mam's gone afta clean a clean one ‘gain, but I'll best go see. She was bletherin’ earlier about dumpin’ the old fridge or sommat. Slightly odd for a woman wi’ a PhD in domestic order, but hey, even examiners made mistakes.      That fridge was me and Arthur’s best friend when we were first settled ‘ere. ‘E used to put his dinner in the veg drawer. Still, o’ course, the little ‘un should do as ‘e’s told. Your mam, dear—she’s cleverer than most professors I’ve ever met.      Oh, don’t spare the old fridge, Emily. I still see me Mum standin’ by it wi’ a pint o’ tea in ‘er ‘and as if it were a concord, holdin’ the whole universe on its shelf. But it’s gone all humble now. Let’s just chuck it in with the rest, and mind yer ‘ands on the broken mirror, eh? It’s got more claws than Silas’ old cat ‘e once had.      Silas’ cat? Nan, you mean the one wi’ the one good eye and the ambition hotter than the summer sun? That beast bit the radio ‘gain! I swear I heard it mutterin’ in about quantum physics ‘fore it went off.      [Laughs] Aye, and not long after that ‘e told me me handle on the kettle went clickin’ and ‘e said 'You’ve got to steady yer grip, Mavis. It’s me life’s blood you’re holdin’ there!'      You musta dropped it.      Nup, but it’s the first time I heard someone whinge about kettles.      Then again, dear, the kettle was yer go-to best mate for life if you ask me.      Oh, let’s not go nostalgic on ‘un now, Tom. ‘E’s barely older than the child in the corner. Oh, and we’d best start unloadin’ the boxes, else we’ll be talkin’ ‘till bed’s time and them young ones’ll be the ones ‘aving to move ‘em.      That's the spirit, Nan! I'll get the kettle for when we need it. It’s resurrected after 10 years and ready for action.

I can't believe we've been in China for almost six months already. I was just looking through some old photos from back home and it really makes you miss familiar faces and places, doesn't it? Yeah, it's quite surreal sometimes, like we're living in one world but our hearts are in another. I was just speaking to Tom the other day. He's moving out of London, of all places. Oh, really? Why’s he moving out of London? It was quite a vibrant city for him wasn't it? With his photography gigs and the friends he had there. It's more of a phased move. He's relocating to Norwich, actually, to be closer to his parents since his father isn't too well. He’s going to start working remotely to make the transition easier. He says he's been thinking of doing something like that for a while now. That sounds sensible of him. Moving closer to family for support while adjusting his work. I remember when we talked about doing something similar. We could always pack up and travel more—settle somewhere new, maybe for a year or two. That would be beautiful. Travel and experience other cultures while still having a stable job—it would give us a rhythm of our own. You know, maybe we could start planning something fairly soon, like, take the spring or summer next year. I would love that. You know what I miss the most? The weekend visits from friends, just someone knocking at the door with coffee and a cake, a rush of laughter and chatter filling the house. It's the little things being abroad. That social energy, which is so much more interactive in person. I'm lucky to have you here to share the journey with. It really does make being away from home bearable. I couldn't agree more. We're quite the team. And every time we look at those photos or remember a friend, it shows me how much I value where we’ve all come from—and it makes me even more eager to see where we’re going next as we travel together. Absolutely. Whether it's London, Norwich, or some other destination, there's always a sense of shared travel adventures with the ones we love. Looking forward to the next chapter together. And maybe, just maybe, adding some more smiling faces into our photo collections along the way.

I can't believe we actually made it through the whole night without falling into the bin again! I think that penguin got the better of me last time, honestly. Oh, come on, that was totally your own fault for dancing on the bar like a madwoman. No wonder the bouncer sent eeny-meeny-miny-mo for the bin-liner. Yeah, but you should've stopped me. I was doing a  perfect  penguin imitation, bless me. You were doing the penguin and also the chicken when the lights went out. Honestly, I didn’t know what species you'd turn into next. Besides, the real question is, how on earth are you still alive after four rounds of melon-balls and a mystery bottle you brought from the back room? I think it turned out to be jasmine tea, by the way. Not sure if it was even alcohol at this point. Honestly, though, it still ended up being a brilliant night. I bumped into this guy from my Politics class. We actually talked for ages before he sneaked off with that girl from his seminar. Harsh. Ugh, don't even get me started on Liam. He's so attached to his group work partner, it's practically suspicious. Like, do they have to flirt  through  their essays? It's tragic. I feel bad for Margot. I saw her waiting outside the nightclub in about five pairs of heels, trying to look the part, and he just texted her "cncld" at 2am. cruel monde, luv. Cruel monde. But hey, at least you didn’t have to sleep on his floor again. Last weekend I had a pillow fight with his three dogs and ended up waking up in Armani pants with a sprained ankle. No way! What were they even doing on the floor? They're not supposed to be there for  that , they're supposed to fetch the kebabs go out of my room. Yeah, well, next time just bring your cat, Mr. Whiskers, he's got the vibe of a barista at 10 am and a kung fu ninja at 2 am. True, Mr. Whiskers is more reliable than some boys at the bar.

Rather lovely to sit down and have a chat with the lot of you lads and lasses. The peas and chips don’t half hit the spot on a dusky evening like this, sure enough. Now then, I was wondering when we might finally have our dear grandmother over for one of our little get-togethers. She deserves more than the occasional twitch on the telly.      Oh aye, Aunty Mo would love that! I’ve had a few scraps of conversation with her about it. She mentioned she might be coming up for a short visit in the next few weeks. Would you like me to sort it out, organise everything? I can manage the bookings easily, only if you’re in agreement.      That’d be grand of you, love. I know you’ve the ears for these things, and I’m a bit heavy-handed with phone calls now. Just try to make it breakfast, no doubt she’d appreciate a morning visit after her usual morning constitutional. I hear the path by the felling’s looking nice this time of year.      As long as she doesn’t try to give us all the occasional riddles with your mother as usual. Did I tell you, by the way, how much I reckon FIFA football resembles strategy in the oil industry? It's all about long-term planning, evolving plays, and understanding the natural ebb and flow of a game or a pipeline.      Oh, I can foresee you two getting into a right old debate again. Let’s just hope she doesn’t audition my laptop for her own FIFA skills. I’m still recovering from the last game night, and I thought being an editor would help me make some sense of it all!      That game night brought a laugh! She’s got this peculiar ability to take what you say and turn it into something you barely meant. But it’s all in good spirit. My, I do miss the old-time guest speaker days at the school. Though I have to admit, it was a different kind of airspace.      Aye, I could see the two of you in that type of environment, eloquent yet with a bit of fire behind your words. Now, the next topic, you remember delivering the peas with chips like that the other day? I still think it’s a bit reckless of you to go at it without a line of inquiry into the individual's culpability, if you see what I mean.

I can't believe the laptop crashed again. You think they'd make these things more reliable, don't you? I got to backup everything before it went dark. Honestly, technology can be so unreliable. I keep wondering how we managed before the internet. By the way, did you manage to get that voice recognition software to work yet? Voice recognition? Blimey, that sounds a bit high-tech for me. I just press buttons! I don't even know how to work a sat nav. Still, I've walked around Brighton quite a lot. It's quite the place. Yes, Brighton is lovely! I used to go there with my family a lot when I was younger. But that laptop of yours, I remember my nephew had the same one. He said it works if you do a software reset, and I think he turned out right. A reset sounds better than a trip to the technician. I just wish I didn't accidentally throw my glasses out last week. I thought they were broken, but they turned out to be under the sofa. My goodness, I can't imagine not finding my contact lenses. I’ve gone to the opticians so many times for more. I think what you really miss is the water taste you used to get. The local water companies in Sussex have better bottled water for drinking than Kent, at least in my opinion. Speaking of the local area – any updates on the bin strike? I thought you said your block was getting a refund from the council. No word here yet. I think I heard it was related to the water company protests over charges for water, something around monopolies or price gouging. I remember your partner telling me about setting up a BlackBerry phone once. I don’t see anyone with those anymore, but they were handy for your texts and emails.

Rather annoying that the results haven't been on the telly yet. I was hoping to see if Manchester United won or crashed out again. Have you checked online yet?      Oh, I saw it on my phone before we came in the coffee shop—some mundane day. Ten out of ten games and United drew again, of course. It was ridiculous. I reckon Solskjaer needs a rest.      Fair enough. Honestly, I’m so delighted we’re here in Tarnow. The light’s different, the people seem warm, and the coffee tastes like it has some proper beans in it. It even smells nicer than that awful store near my flat back in Cambridge.      My feelings exactly. I’ve already got my second cup, and I’m not even half through the week. But I do miss the rain sometimes. Or rather, I miss knowing when it’s coming. I still haven’t got the hang of when to put on an umbrella here!      That’s typical SAD for you—and me, to be honest. It’s not just the rain, it’s the dark too. I sometimes feel like a landlocked fish. But this place gives off something... comforting. Good for the soul, if you ask me.      True enough. I had a message from my sister last night, and she said she’s growing chillies on the farm and making them into habanero jam. She’s got a dog the size of a horse, someone called Spud. Honestly, I miss my family a bit, but oddly not the farming bits.      Farms and dogs and being outside in the rain all day—that’s not for me. I did some odd jobs while I was younger, but I prefer my cups of coffee and my books. Have you been reading much lately?      A bit, mostly about educating abroad. One of my students—I’ll tell you about him another time—is exceptional. He works hard, and it makes me feel responsible for them, you know? I want them passing their exams so they can have proper careers. You being a TEFL teacher too, do you keep up with your students?      Occasionally. Most are serious, trying to get jobs or visas. I go at it on the weekends if I’m not shopping or drinking in town. Boots in the shops are nice, but the prices... Well, I’ve learned to wait for the sales.

Rather than chuck a DVD in eh, innit? Work’s been bonkers this week, ‘ow. I got to sort out this conference in Leeds next month and I’ve had me head in a whirl! Got to follow up with the hotel and the contractors and—      Sounds proper stressful eenough. I’ve been more stressed with the bloke I reckon fancied me—went out for a pint last week and I swear he fancied me off, but then didn’t call me back.      Oh, I heard that! Didn’t you get a WhatsApp bloke last week? Or was that me?      Oh, the one who only likked me profile pic and MySpace pic? I bin too busy to reply. Honestly, dating’s gonner gone off the rail for me this year.      It is, innit? All proper tactical. I’ve been more interested in mastering me cricket game on the phone than talkin’ to anyone!      Well, I’ve got zero time for that—work’s been bonkers too. I’ve got this new production line in, and it’s like herding grief. One bloke still calls me “ma’am,” even though we’ve been in the same building for six weeks. Mate, I ain’t forty, and I ain’t Texas!      It’s proper bizarre how people talk about professionalism these days. Me mam tells me if I carry on in this work I’m doing, I’m gonner die of a heart attack before I’m thirty.      Don’t I know it. Still, at least I get to dress up nicely for most meetings about now. I finally pulled the plug on the cargo pants and high-vis laces. I’ve switched to proper trousers and that burgundy blazer me dad bought me as a joke that I bin using for over five years.      Oh, that’s mes too. No more leggings and stripy jumpers. I dyed me hair for work too—swapped the grey back for some ash blonde. Doesn’t look like me, but it’s professional.      Yeah, well you lot get to run around in nice shoes and proper hats while I’m bin on me back laying tiles or gutting sinks. Gave me back in pieces today, I did.      Proper due some R and R, then. Make me feels guilty, being sat in here watching Broad City, while you’re bin on your back doing the physical labor.      Aint no guilt.

Rather annoying the chuggers, really. I mean, they’re out here in full force even in Gordon Square. Just as well I had a coconut cake and coffee in me before I left the flat, otherwise I’d be low on sugar and even more grumpy.      I’ve seen a few too since I arrived from the station. Having said that, it is quite easy to spot most of them. A lot of them just walk in a straight line, like they're patrolling rather than pulling someone over. Speaking of which, I got mobile coverage just outside the station but still couldn’t get hold of my colleague.      Ah, that’s the thing, right? You can have coverage and still not get through. I remember when I left London last time to go to the Isle of Wight for a family getaway: every single traffic sign said to phone in for help, and you still had breakfast with no internet. I hated it.      Blooming annoying. I remember that, you didn’t spare a word about the chuggers or the lack of phone signal, you just moaned about missing your coffee. I still don’t understand why you still carry around that thing, by the way. It’s so 3G.      It's not just about the phone, I’m not a fan of the way lime trees are placed in certain parks. All these trees line the path here, and it splits the park in two. It’s kind of like someone just cast an invisible dividing wall. That said, the pigeons are oddly abundant.      I noticed a couple of pigeons too. In fact, I saw a boy trying to catch one about five minutes ago. I don’t quite know what he was aiming to do with it — maybe sell it as a trinket to some unsuspecting tourist.      My, that does sound shady. Speaking of which, I had a friend once who taught in China. They had a nickname for those kinds of scammers — something about dragons or ghosts.      Oh that’s right, they mentioned it in the lunches we had back in Devon. They had such an interesting perspective on things like delivering English around China and how people sometimes get tricky with go-betweens. I think they had a real issue with how much salt is in food, by the way. That might have something to do with all those trinket sellers.

Rather annoying this, innit? Traffic’s mental again, stuck outside the roundabout. They say it’s a lorry’s broken down further up the road. Blows me away, how often this happens.      Aw, don’t worry, we’ve got time. Ten minutes won’t make eeny difference. You’ve got that meeting for the corpus upload at 12, yeah? Should be grand. Aye, but I wish they’d just sort out the main roads around here. It’s like it’s always stuck-in sommat.      Oh, I know right? I’ve been thinking of getting a bike—might ease me onto the busier roads less. You know I like my Myfi, but I’ve lost count of the amount of times I’ve been late because of this bloody traffic.      Nah, don’t chuck the car just yet. The winter doesn’t exactly scream 'cycle to work'. Aye, in fact, what’s the deal with you lot, you Northern lasses and the cold? You bleed through your jackets like Waterstones do puddings—always inappropriate dressin’ up!      Shut it! You’re only saying that ‘cause you’ve got a higher metabolism, or something. And yeah, I might’ve worn a jumper over a blouse, but I didn’t want to slap a coat on in the city centre. It’s not as cold as you make out!      Right, carry on in your North-East lass fashion—proper cold, no coat, and yet you’re still bragging about hotter blood than the rest of us Southerners. Anyway, speaking of fashion, your colleague, Laura, said she’s stopping by your office later. You fancied her last office party, didn’t you?      Don’t you start! It was just a  slight  fancy. She’s got her own projects, and her work ethic’s not cut out for small chitchat. She told me she’s bringing some new data sets, you know, ones I could stick on my hard drive and maybe use as a side project.      Aye, so it’s the brains over the looks, then? Proper nice, like! Maybe you can set goin’ on that thing about mutual academic interests.      Oh, shut up. It’s not a bloomin’ date, your ego’s way too large as it is!      Well, well, someone’s got a little crush to sort out. But for real, if you need help analysing data, I’m always here. Unless I’m at a meeting, which I kind of always am, but you know me, I make time for the lasses and the data alike!

Rather annoying I caught flu last week. You know, me being a conference co-ordinator, it kills me when I’m off work for ages. I’m more used to stress than lying abed all day!      Oh no, I heard—how are you now? I was in Lewisham and my sister had the same thing, and she nearly lost her groove for a week. Though I reckon that coffee from the 24-hour shop helped a bit.      You should’ve had one of me mates’ remedies. He’s got a recipe that includes garlic and lemon—sounded dodgy, but I tried it once. Bit strong, but I felt better in a few days.      I did try some herbal stuff, but I think I’m just still tired. It’s the rest I’m missing the most. Living with work, you’ve got to prioritise breakfasts and whatever. But this happened at the worst time—before a big conference.      Have you arranged anything about that? I’m in production, so I get it when you get knocked out of the loop. I mean, did your boss step in?      Aye, my colleague—name’s Claire—she stepped up. She’s good. Made the arrangements for the speaker panel, even shifted some dates for the catering. I owe her somethin’.      If I was in that role, I’d be carryin’ out someone at full pace for that. I work my own hours, so I can’t relate exactly—job’s all hands on deck type, you know? Still, mates help mates!      I did offer her a tip for the catering change, but she said no. Both our threesomes of work and life are complicated enough. I mean, it helped unblock the workflow, so I’m grateful for that.      I feel for that. Relationships with colleagues become something else when you’re all tied up with deadlines. I once had a breakup happen at a team event. Not ideal.      Aye, relationships add more spice to your plate. Some people let work drop for love, others run with it like it's their main gig. Either way, communication is key.      You’re not wrong, mate. I’m currently in a bloke who’s always due to be home. It’s like I live with a conference seminar—juggling my hours with his shifts and all. True to say, it’s a full-time job in itself!

So did I tell you yet about my project meeting last week? It was one of those days when everyone seemed to be on a completely different page. I’m just exhausted trying to coordinate these timelines now.      Not quite detail by detail, no—get on with it. Was it the design team? I remember you mentioned they were a bit all over the place.      Oh yeah, that was them. Like, one side was all, “We can launch this feature by Friday,” and the other was like, “We don’t even know where the code is.” And then the marketing team chips in with, “Do we even have a plan for the branding?” I’m thinking, "If you had shown up on time, you might have found the damn code!"      Sounds like the same dance I used to do before the client came to their senses and split the team into better-defined roles. Maybe that’s what you need. Less jazz hands in the air and more accountability.      Honestly, I’ve been thinking the same. I’m starting to think I should just handwrite each person a map of their responsibilities and pin it to the wall with feathers and glitter. For dramatic effect.      Overdramatic, yes. But only just. How’s Jen holding up with all this, by the way? You said she was the one trying to keep the design team in check?      Oh, Jen’s been a saint. Like, someone just cast an angel on her. She’s been the only one who’s not treated the project like a game of Jenga. I honestly don’t know what we’d do without her.      Well, respect to her. I can only imagine the kind of chaotic energy vibes they must be handing around the office daily. Not that I’d want it. I’ve had enough chaos in my day job for a lifetime. Speaking of which, did I tell you that Darren broke up with Lissa?      No! Wait, Darren from the waiting room station or the receptionist Darren?      The ortho Darren with the tribal tattoos and the whistles. He took Lissa out for a coffee, said something nice, and left the coffee untouched. He's really on his own mission these days.      I just can't wrap my head around why he did that. They seemed genuinely into each other. So romantic, right?      Romantic, yes. Sweet, maybe not.

Rather than share a specific sentence, I'll describe what happens next. The teacher, Speaker_1, decides to leverage the moment as a teachable one. She smiles warmly at the children, balancing a steaming mug of tea in her hand and a plate of scones on the kitchen counter. She coordinates her tone to be engaging yet comforting, laying out an idea that would spark deeper thought about the moral of most folktales. Her voice gains just the right hint of narrative to draw the kids closer into the discussion.           That's a very insightful question. It's like how the turkey in 'The Golden Goose' is not cruel, but neither is it the hero who finds the goose, is it? The story shows how acts can be either, depending on why they’re done. When someone helps another out of kindness, that’s good. But if they help for selfish reasons, that's more on the side of the lesser. Good and evil are more like feelings and choices, you see?      I don’t think the witch in ‘The Magic Porridge Pot’ is evil... she was just watching for the pot. She didn’t know the pot was magic at first?      Right you are, darling. Not all characters are purely good or bad. Some just make wrong choices for the wrong reasons, and some make right choices for the simplest of reasons. The stories are for us to reflect on why people do the things they do. It helps us think about the choices we make in our real lives.      But what about when there is a monster about to eat someone? That's bad, isn’t it?      Absolutely. There are some clear lines that are drawn when someone treats another cruelly or wants to harm. That, my darlings, is definitely not okay. But even then, sometimes the reasons behind a monster's actions are something we can try to understand.      Like the wolf who huffed and puffed?      Except in the 'Three Little Pigs' tale the wolf is the one who's set on delivering something bad. He doesn't have a reason that makes it okay. But life is more like the lesser or more complicated folktales in the end, full of grey areas, not just black and white. Rather annoying this school trip lark. You know, grannies would be proud watching it all back on the telly, but it's bloody freezing now at night. I can't cover for you endlessly, darling. Rather annoying the new changes at the GP surgery, aren't they? I had to wait over an hour last week, and they told me they're now requiring more paperwork. I asked what all the fuss was about and they just muttered something about the health budget and the Green Party wanting to shift more towards preventative care. I'm just thinking, I don't want to be handed a leaflet on how to grow cress—it's a broken hip I've got, not a garden problem.      It's interesting you mention the Greens. I was at the boot sale last Saturday in Hove and had a long chat with one of the stall owners who'd recently voted for them for the first time. Said he was fed up of the same old, you know? I get it to an extent—what with the climate stuff and their push for local jobs and small businesses. But I tell you, if it’s harder to get into the doctor, no policy is going to cheer me up.      I hear you. I'm not against the Green ideas, mind you. My son, who's working in one of those solar farm jobs, is a big fan. But there's quite a gap between their policies and the real, everyday problems we’ve got. Take relationships, for example. My Julie and I have been married 38 years, but I still can't work out the remote control. Some things, no policy in the world can fix.      Ha! That’s true. I mean, even at my age, I still remember when you had to change a light bulb yourself, not a seven-step process just to charge a phone. You know, being a business owner, I’m always seeing trends coming and going. I run a little newsagents in Hove, and the other day this lass from a local startup came in to ask if I'd heard about the new jobs policy from the council to support small employers like us. I just looked at her and said, "Tell me something I don’t know. Last time any ‘policy’ did something, it took them ten years to sort out the VAT form."      That’s right. It’s like we keep dancing to the tune of someone else's kettle. Even boot sales are getting run with spreadsheets and Facebook ads now.

Rather annoying when the barista at my local café misses the pronunciation of the pasty, innit? Like I said, I asked for a steak and kidney pasty, not a steak and negativity pasty! Got me chucklin' to myself when the lass nearly spilled the tea.      That sounds like a proper laugh. I mean, I haven't had a pasty in ages, but I’ve only ever gotten them in the West Midlands. I’m assuming they're the same as in the North? Or do you lot in Sunderland have some secret sauce or something?      Secret sauce, love! No, honestly, it’s much the same. The difference comes in how you dip it. My nan still uses HP sauce with a splash of vinegar, like back in the day. I’m not a fan of ketchup in a pasty. Blasphemy, innit?      Fair enough. Moving on, though — in all seriousness, I’ve been getting into plants, you know, due to the lockdown. My flat is now bloomin’ over with ferns and snake plants. Any pointers for a PhD student with no idea about horticulture and only ten pence to spend on soil?      Well then, start with variegated pothos — they’re basically indestructible. Just don’t water them too often. And don’t go out and buy that cactus, or you might end up with a crispy critter in a couple of weeks.      Thank you, Ms. Plant Pro. Now, shifting from plants to politics — have you been watching the news recently? I mean, with Trump gone, it feels like about five billion yanks are trying to win the role of ‘funniest man in America’. Ron DeSantis rolling into that office like he's appearing on The Apprentice again? Come on.      Oh, that’s right. I did catch that. He looked like a man who’d probably removed all his wallpaper with a cheese grater. You know, honestly? Politics these days is like fashion — fast, outlandish, and people think a new slogan makes them the boss of the world.      You're spot on. That reminds me, have you ever tried designing a presentation or a poster for one of those posters you see in Tory election campaigns? I tried doing one once — it looked like it was made in 1998 with a kinaesthetic spelling mistake.      It's alright, we've all been there. At least you've got the passion. I’m the one who added clip art of a cat falling over in my latest podcast infographic.

Rather annoying that the TV’s trailing through the hall again, isn’t it? I swear it’s been like that since the kids were born. You’d think my mother would’ve gotten an aerial fixed by now.      Charming as the chaos is, at least it keeps the place from being too posh. Still, I don’t think the splitter cable has ever been replaced in all the years I’ve known her. What’s this one showing?  Blue Peter  again?      For someone with a PhD you’d think she’d be more interested in documentaries, but no. She’s got a soft spot for old  Blue Peter  repeats. Honestly, sometimes the only way to get her to stop talking is to hand her a badge and a jelly bean.      I’m not laughing. Last time, I was given a badge for making a paper boat in 2008. And breakfast, no less. I swear half of my education was in repackaging old craft projects as awards ceremonies.      Well, it’s not all nonsense, is it? She taught you how to make sturdy cat food out of cardboard and glue. Brilliant survival skills for a human of your tender age.      Wise woman. But I’m curious—how’s it going at the uni? Still bemoaning the lack of killer whale footage in the lectures?      You know what? I  am  slipping in some killer whale footage. It’s the perfect way to make people pay attention—nothing distracts from bad prose like the sound of a orca’s echo location.      I’d be scared out of my wits. Though, honestly, most people I teach are far more interested in what Channel 4 is showing at 6 than they are in 19th-century literature.      And the  violence  on the news. I swear someone showed their pupils a bit of  Peaky Blinders  and they all thought they were in a murder mystery.      Not unlike our parents’ house. There’s a mysterious yellow sprite of a woman mentioned in passing with a machine gun and a whippet. I’m fairly certain no one knew what a whippet was.      Exactly. Though I have to say, your parents’ place was at least less… squat-like? I remember your flat in Brixton—vastly more intriguing. The smell of hot toast made me question why anyone would want central heating.      You mean besides to survive? I still have a jar of jam bought from a guy who said it was homemade, so I refused to believe it was actually Clarissa’s.

Rather annoying this new hostel they’ve set up down the street. I blame the council, always investing in flashy ideas without considering the noise or the local folk like us. I can hear their music through the walls! Used to be quiet here, and now it's like being at a motor show every night.      Oh, I understand the noise issue, but I reckon it's not all bad. The hostel gives work to some of the younger lot in this town, and I've seen a few nice photographs of the rooms. Bright and tidy, like a school dormitory run by angels! Do you know many of the people who run it?      I've met the chap who owns it. Fairly likeable bloke, if a bit too keen to chat about engineering. Ten minutes, and I was nearly convinced I should pick up a spanner again! But then he goes on about the cars they use for breakfast deliveries—some fancy Mercedes van, he says.      I hear the Mercedes van hides a few surprises. I had a student who once did a project on hospitality management and mentioned that the van serves as a mobile kitchen too. Pretty clever, quite a step from the hostels of my student days. At least they're managing it with proper methods, not like the old way.      Speaking of old ways, I remember your parents, Jim, running the shop. Now that was hard work! Always at the crack of dawn, and you at your books, huh? Our parents all had businesses one way or another—your father's a butcher, my folks had a school—everyone had to pull their weight in the world back then.      We did, but it wasn't about work alone. There was a sense of duty. Learning to take care of things from a young age—that's part of what got us through the education system. These days, I wonder if the kids get that same push. My pupils often talk about future jobs with that dreamy look in their eyes, but not many seem to know how it works!      My favourite part of hearing you talk about school and academies is always the mention of the abattoirs and the food supply chains. Makes me think of my visits to the shops growing up! The butcher would personally go out of his way to help you pick meat, or give you advice on cooking it, not just serve you like a box in the supermarket.

Rather unusual to find an academic type with a recruitment background, isn't it? I mean, they handled university lecturers and the like before starting their teaching role here. I can't say I would have put a recruitment person in front of a class evaluating academic literacy.      Yeah, it is a bit different. But I guess the skills they bring from recruitment—understanding what makes people tick, how they communicate, and how to identify competence in candidates—could actually be quite useful. It's surprising how transferable those skills can be, especially when it comes to working with students or colleagues.      That's true, but when it comes to academic literacy specifically, I still wonder how effective someone like that could be. I mean, you can talk to someone all you like, but academic writing is a whole different ball game. I think evaluators need a firm grasp of academic conventions, and sometimes it's a struggle to even teach that to students.      I get that. I remember one of my students showed up with a dissertation that read like a marketing brochure—vibrant, full of buzzwords, but lacking in academic rigor. It honestly leaves you wondering how someone like the lecturer, with such a different background, is supposed to assess work like that.      Oh no, I've had my fair share of that too. It's almost like a new kind of literacy has crept into their work—corporate speak, colorful expressions that look flashy but don't mean much at all. It makes the real evaluation tough, because it's not just about the knowledge they've absorbed, but about how well they can present it through an academic lens.      Exactly. I mean, I know marketing jargon can be tempting for students to slip in. It's what they hear all the time. But then you've got to draw a line somewhere. I do think, though, the lecturer has been managing well so far. There's a real clarity in their evaluation criteria, and it's nice to see someone who brings a practical, no-nonsense perspective to the table.      I suppose it comes with experience, whether in recruitment or in teaching. Some people just have that eye for delivering something effectively. Plus, it's good to see different paths bringing people into education. It keeps things fresh, don't you think?      Definitely. I might have to lend them one of my student essays at some point.

Rather annoying to be honest. I’d rather be hanging out with you lads than crammed in here like a sardine. Maybe I could be skint and I wouldn’t be studying      Aye, we do spread the wealth out as well      Yeah it een’t nice at all, we’re just inching closer and closer together      I reckon that is because it is just before Christmas too      Yeah, yeah, there ain’t a spare bench to be seen. I came from Punjab      Oh I like that      Oh, so you’re always in the library doing all of your work, yeah?      Yeah, before I came, I used to just hang out with them anywhere, but since becoming a student, I have to get on it a lot more.

I can’t believe the new war film’s coming out next month. Have y’seen the trailer? It’s all proper gritty an’ realistic. Y’know, not one o’ them glam’rous Hollywood jobs where everyone looks sun-kissed an’ healthy in the middle o’ a battlefield. Yeah, I liked the preview. It was actually pretty respectful to the soldiers’ experiences. I don’t reckon I’ll go by meself tho — too much crying, an’ I don’t need to dump someone’s crisps with me snot. Haha, true. But I heard it’s based on a real-life Major from Yorkshire. That’s got to make it feel closer to home for us, what with being from the North an’ all. I’ve got a cousin who works in the Royal Engineers. He says these sorts of films help people understand the mental grind it’s got on you. He doesn’t mind people thinking he’s some rugged hard case, I hope. I remember one fella who showed up at a family wedding once, full pyjamas under his coat, because he had PDAs after coming back from Afghanistan. Aw, that’s rough. Poor lad. Reminds me… I reckon I should call him this week. Tell him I’m takin’ over one o’ them charity event coordinators for the Forces. Magazines like Warrior an’ Soldier are always sponsorin’ events. Bit dodgy sometims, though, they’re all about sharpenin’ image for the military. Yeah, but I can see why they’re still popular. I read a couple of them at college — mostly because I had to in order to make sense o’ some lectures about military logistics. Turns out the layout an’ presentation is actually really good — like, they make you feel part o’ somethin’ big even if y’re just sat on a sofa with toast. Aye, an’ that’s somethin’ I’d never have got into before. Since I started workin’ in events, I’ve had to learn a bit about everything. Computers, especially. There were lunches where I walked out with my head full o’ encryption protocols an’ coding standards. Crikey, an’ go me — I run a production line. If I go wrong, I simply line up the team and ask for a Wi-Fi reboot or something equally sensible. Still, you learn summat every day, eh? I reckon one day I’ll start writing articles for them mags. Or maybe a film — that sound over-ambitious?

Rather annoying when a lad turns up to London to visit, do they? You’d think they'd know by now not to dress like they’re about to go to Notting Hill Carnival on a rainy Tuesday!      Aw, calm down, Becca! You wouldn't be so wound up if eeny of 'em had asked you out properly, eh?      Oh, shut up, Aiden. Like I’d ever go anywhere with someone who can’t tell the difference between Camden and Kings Cross!      Honestly, sometimes when people come from London, they think they’re the life and soul of wherever they end up. Like we haven’t got anything going on outside of that posh turkey shop doorstep!      Well, fair play, London is the main event. But I’d say in our patch? We got charm in spades. Cats working better than breakfast, and the sky at this time of year... Game on!      Yeah, fair, but not many people get that. And I reckon it’s worse for us girls, you know? Try dating in this country these days and you land a gem with their head full of turkeys and racists in charge…      Oh Becca, you’re so right – Mate, have you heard what some of the lads say when they meet the wrong sort of accent?
